NDT Level III Consulting Services in Alaska

Short answer: Atlantis NDT provides ASNT NDT Level III services to Alaska employers remotely and onsite at the client's own facility: outsourced or interim Level III coverage, SNT-TC-1A written practices and audits, procedures and technique sheets, personnel qualification exams under the employer's written practice, and audit preparation. Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, and every scope is quoted on request after a short call.

Alaska is an unusual NDT market. The work is concentrated in a handful of very large assets that sit thousands of road miles apart, and many of them are reachable only by air, by the Dalton Highway or by barge. The North Slope oil fields, the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System, the Valdez Marine Terminal, the Kenai Peninsula refinery and Cook Inlet platforms, interior refineries and power plants, hard-rock mines, military bases and one of the world's busiest air-cargo airports all need inspection programmes that hold up to owner audits and federal oversight. What most Alaska inspection companies and in-house quality departments struggle with is not finding technicians; it is keeping a qualified Level III available for a programme that runs on rotations, seasonal construction windows and short summer turnarounds. This page explains how outsourced Level III support works for Alaska, which regulators and codes shape an Alaska NDT programme, and how to start. If you already know what you need, ask for an Alaska Level III quote.

Why Alaska NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: Every SNT-TC-1A programme needs a Level III to own the written practice, approve procedures and examine Level I and II staff. In Alaska that role is harder to fill because work is remote, rotational and seasonal, while owners on the North Slope, along TAPS and at the refineries audit contractors closely. An outsourced Level III keeps the programme compliant without a full-time hire.

Start with the industrial map. On the North Slope, the Prudhoe Bay and Kuparuk River units and the satellite fields west toward the Colville River and the National Petroleum Reserve run thousands of miles of flowlines, gathering lines, process piping and pressure vessels in drill-site modules and central processing facilities. New development, including the Willow project west of the Alpine field, adds module fabrication, pipeline construction and welding inspection. Inspection on the Slope is dominated by ultrasonic thickness surveys and profile radiography on insulated lines where corrosion under insulation is the main worry, weld inspection on tie-ins and repairs, and visual inspection of supports and modules that see extreme thermal cycling.

The Trans-Alaska Pipeline System carries crude roughly 800 miles from Prudhoe Bay through pump stations and over the Brooks and Alaska ranges to the Valdez Marine Terminal, where storage tanks, loading berths and ballast-water facilities add API 653-style tank work and terminal piping. Southcentral Alaska adds the Kenai Peninsula: the Nikiski refinery, the former LNG export plant, Cook Inlet offshore platforms and gas fields, and the gas pipelines that feed Anchorage. In the Interior, refineries at North Pole, coal and gas-fired power stations, the military bases around Fairbanks and gold mines such as Fort Knox and Pogo all run mechanical-integrity or maintenance inspection. Southeast Alaska adds Juneau-area mines, shipyard repair work in Ketchikan and marine infrastructure. Northwest Alaska has the Red Dog zinc mine and its port.

The regulatory picture matters too. Alaska is not an NRC Agreement State, so industrial radiography using sealed sources such as iridium-192 is licensed by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, while X-ray equipment falls under the state's radiological health programme; confirm current requirements with both before mobilising a crew. Boilers and unfired pressure vessels in commercial and public buildings fall under the Mechanical Inspection Section of the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Division of Labor Standards and Safety. Pipeline safety is unusual: Alaska does not run a PHMSA-certified state pipeline safety programme, so PHMSA's Office of Pipeline Safety inspects both interstate and intrastate gas and hazardous-liquid operators directly, and TAPS is overseen through the Joint Pipeline Office, where state and federal agencies coordinate. The Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation's oil discharge prevention rules add requirements for oil storage tanks and facility piping, and the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission regulates wells. Each of those regimes eventually asks the same question of a contractor: show us the written practice, the procedures and the certification records. A Level III is the person who makes sure the answers exist.

Direct answer: The core Level III services Alaska employers buy are an outsourced or interim Level III, written-practice development and audits, procedure and technique-sheet writing, administration of qualification exams, and audit readiness. Most Alaska clients combine remote document work with short onsite visits timed to a rotation change or a summer work window.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: A written practice is the employer's own document that sets how NDT personnel are trained, examined, certified and recertified under ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis writes new written practices for Alaska employers and audits existing ones, so the document matches how your crews actually work and what your clients audit against.

Many written practices in Alaska were copied from a parent company in the Lower 48 or from a template, and they drift out of step with reality. A common example is the rotation problem: the written practice says the Level III will witness practical exams, but the Level III works a different rotation from the technicians, so exams are delayed and certifications lapse. Another is method creep: the company added phased array or digital radiography for a North Slope contract, but the written practice still lists only conventional UT and film RT, so the people doing the work are not covered by the document that certifies them. A third is experience records: technicians move between employers in a small labour market, and the transferred experience is accepted without the documentation the written practice requires.

A written-practice engagement covers scope (methods, techniques and levels the company performs), training and experience requirements referencing the current SNT-TC-1A edition, examination structure and grading, vision examination, certification and recertification, interrupted service, transfer of certification, and the duties and authority of the Level III. Where a client requires ANSI/ASNT CP-189, NAVSEA or another standard, we show where that requirement changes your practice. For training hours we point to the training requirements matrix rather than restating figures. For the standalone service, see written practice development and the SNT-TC-1A guide. To start, request a written-practice review for your Alaska programme.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in Alaska

Direct answer: Alaska NDT procedures are written to the code that governs the asset: ASME B31.4, B31.8 and API 1104 with 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 for pipelines; ASME B31.3 and Section VIII with API 510 and 570 for plants and refineries; API 650 and 653 for tanks; AWS D1.1 for structures and modules. Cold-climate service adds specific technique concerns.

Procedure work in Alaska has a few local twists that a Level III has to think through rather than paste in from a template:

  • Low temperature. Ultrasonic couplants, transducer wedges and calibration blocks behave differently in sub-zero conditions, and velocity changes with temperature. A UT procedure for Slope work needs to address calibration at the examination temperature, couplant selection and temperature limits for the technique. Magnetic particle and penetrant procedures need temperature ranges that match the products used, and penetrant work in the cold usually needs a qualified low-temperature technique or heated enclosures.
  • Insulated piping and CUI. Much of the North Slope inventory is insulated. Procedures for profile radiography, pulsed eddy current screening, guided-wave screening and follow-up UT need clear acceptance and reporting rules so screening results are not treated as wall-thickness measurements.
  • Pipeline construction and repair. API 1104 and the operator's specifications govern girth-weld inspection; automated UT and radiography procedures need technique sheets matched to wall thickness and joint design.
  • Tanks and terminals. Tank floor scanning, shell UT and weld inspection at terminals and refinery tank farms follow API 653 inspection plans prepared by the owner's authorised inspector; the NDT procedures have to deliver data in the form that inspector needs.
  • Mining and heavy equipment. Mines run magnetic particle and UT inspection on haul-truck frames, shovel booms, mill shells, trunnions and crusher components, usually to OEM requirements and AWS D1.1 for weld repairs.
  • Aviation. Anchorage and Fairbanks MRO work follows aircraft OEM NDT manuals and FAA requirements; personnel are often certified to NAS 410, and the Level III must be clear which standard each technician is certified under.

We write procedures, technique sheets and qualification records, review procedures supplied by others, and resolve the cross-reference problems that appear when an owner's specification, a code and your written practice say different things. Sector background is on our audit-support pages for pipeline, refining, LNG, offshore, mining and tank terminals.

Outsourced and interim Level III for Alaska crews

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III is a named, ASNT-certified Level III who acts as your programme's Level III of record under a standing agreement, while an interim Level III covers a gap. For Alaska crews this works mostly remotely, with onsite visits arranged around rotations, the summer construction season and planned shutdowns.

Three engagement models cover nearly every Alaska request:

  1. Ongoing outsourced (retained) Level III. Atlantis is named in your written practice as the Level III. We approve procedures, administer exams, answer technical questions from the field, review the programme annually and stand behind it in client audits. Suited to inspection contractors and fabricators that need Level III authority but not a full-time Level III salary.
  2. Project-based work. A defined deliverable: a new written practice, a set of procedures for a new contract, technique sheets for a phased array scope, or an exam campaign before a construction season.
  3. Audit-preparation sprint. A focused review of records, procedures and certifications ahead of a known audit date, with a corrective-action list and support while you close it.

The logistics matter in Alaska. Document review, procedure writing and most technical questions are handled remotely, which suits companies whose people are on the Slope or in a camp for two weeks at a time. Practical examinations need the candidate, real specimens and the examiner together, so those are scheduled onsite at the employer's facility, typically in Anchorage, Fairbanks or the Kenai, or at a location the employer arranges. Atlantis has no office or training centre in Alaska; all onsite work is at the client's premises. For the details of interim cover see interim NDT Level III, and to discuss your rotation pattern, talk to us about outsourced Level III coverage in Alaska.

The Level III who leads engagements is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Buyers in this market usually want to know exactly who will sign their procedures and examine their people; with Atlantis that is a named person, not an anonymous pool.

Audit readiness: customer, owner and accreditation audits

Direct answer: Alaska inspection contractors face operator prequalification and contractor audits, prime-contractor flow-down audits on construction projects, federal pipeline inspections of operator qualification records, and quality-system audits such as ISO 9001 or ISO/IEC 17025. A Level III audit-readiness review checks the written practice, procedures, certifications and records before the auditor does.

The findings that recur in NDT audits are predictable: certifications issued against a superseded written practice; missing or expired vision examinations; practical exams without documented specimens or grading; procedures not approved by a Level III or not matched to the code edition in the contract; equipment calibration records that do not tie to the instrument serial numbers in reports; and technicians performing a technique, such as PAUT or digital radiography, that their certification does not cover. Each one is fixable, but not in the week of the audit.

An audit-readiness engagement samples personnel files, procedures and reports, maps them against the written practice and the client or owner specification, and produces a prioritised corrective-action list. We can then support the fixes: revised procedures, re-examinations under your written practice, and a short summary your quality manager can present. For aerospace and MRO shops, we can help with Nadcap-style audit preparation as context, though the audit itself is conducted by the accreditation body. For laboratories considering ISO/IEC 17025, we help with the NDT technical content of the quality system. Sector notes: aerospace audit support, power generation and maritime. Facing an audit date already? Book an Alaska audit-readiness call.

Inspection programme support around API 510, 570 and 653 work

Direct answer: At Alaska refineries, terminals and production facilities, API 510, 570 and 653 inspections are performed and signed by the owner's authorised inspectors. Atlantis supports that work from the NDT side: method and technique selection, procedures, data quality and personnel qualification. We do not provide authorised inspector certification training.

The refinery at Nikiski, the interior refineries, the Valdez terminal tank farm and the North Slope process facilities all generate large volumes of thickness data, weld inspection results and tank floor scans. The value of that data depends on whether the NDT was planned around the damage mechanism, whether the technique could actually detect it, and whether readings are repeatable from one inspection to the next. A Level III can help an owner or contractor tighten thickness-monitoring location practices, choose between conventional UT, PAUT corrosion mapping and profile radiography for a given circuit, and set reporting formats that the authorised inspector can use directly. For background on the services we describe, see the API 510, API 570 and API 653 support pages.

Cities we support across Alaska

Direct answer: Atlantis supports employers anywhere in Alaska, remotely and onsite at the client's facility. Most requests come from Anchorage, the Kenai Peninsula, Fairbanks and North Pole, Valdez, the North Slope and Southeast Alaska, and the support model is the same in each place.

The headquarters city for most Slope operators' contractors, inspection companies and engineering firms, plus air-cargo and military MRO at the international airport and Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson.   • Fairbanks and North Pole. Interior refining, power generation, Eielson Air Force Base and Fort Wainwright, and service companies for TAPS and the gold mines.
  • Valdez. The pipeline terminal, tank farm and marine facilities, with related tank and terminal inspection.
  • Juneau, Ketchikan and Southeast. Underground mines, shipyard repair and marine structures, with inspection often done by small local contractors that need an outside Level III.

Training alongside the Level III service

Direct answer: Many Alaska clients pair Level III consulting with SNT-TC-1A training for their own people, delivered live online or onsite at their facility. The Level III who writes the written practice and procedures can then align classroom content and exams with them, which removes the most common gap between training and certification.

Training covers Level I, II and III in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET, structured to SNT-TC-1A and the employer's written practice. Live online classes suit technicians on rotation who can attend during their off weeks; onsite classes suit a crew assembled before the summer season. The Practical NDT simulator lets trainees practise twelve methods in five virtual environments, including an oil and gas site and a storage tank, before their practical exams; it is a practice tool and does not replace a practical exam on real specimens. See training, online NDT training, corporate NDT training and ASNT Level III training for candidates preparing for their own Level III exams.

How an engagement works

Direct answer: An Alaska engagement starts with a call to understand your methods, clients, codes and rotation pattern, followed by a written scope and quote. Document work proceeds remotely; exams and site visits are scheduled onsite at your facility. Timing is agreed in the scope rather than assumed.

  1. Discovery call. Which methods and techniques you perform, which owners and codes you work to, how your crews rotate, and what is driving the request: a new contract, an audit, a lost Level III or growth.
  2. Document review. You share your written practice, procedures and a sample of personnel files and reports. We identify gaps against SNT-TC-1A, the governing codes and your client specifications.
  3. Scope and quote. A written scope that lists deliverables, what is remote and what is onsite, and who does what. Pricing is quote on request; we do not publish rates.
  4. Delivery. Written practice and procedure drafting, approval and issue; exam administration under your written practice; corrective actions from audits; ongoing Level III duties if retained.
  5. Onsite visits. Practical examinations, procedure demonstrations and audit support at your Alaska facility, planned around crew rotations and seasonal windows.
  6. Review. For retained clients, an annual programme review and updates when codes, clients or methods change.

Frequently asked questions

How do I find an NDT Level III consultant in Alaska?

Few Level IIIs are based in Alaska, and most are employed by operators or large inspection companies. Many Alaska contractors therefore engage an outside Level III who works remotely and visits onsite when needed. Atlantis offers that service, led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III.

What does an outsourced Level III do for an Alaska inspection company?

They act as the Level III named in your written practice: approving procedures and technique sheets, administering general, specific and practical exams, reviewing certifications, answering technical questions from the field and supporting you in client audits.

Can a Level III work remotely for North Slope crews?

Most of the work can be remote: written practices, procedures, exam preparation, record reviews and technical questions. Practical examinations need the candidate, real specimens and the examiner together, so those are scheduled onsite at the employer's facility or a location the employer arranges.

Is Alaska an NRC Agreement State for industrial radiography?

No. Alaska is not an NRC Agreement State, so radioactive-material licences for gamma radiography are issued by the NRC, while X-ray equipment falls under the state's radiological health programme. Confirm current requirements with both agencies before mobilising a radiography crew.

Who regulates pipeline safety in Alaska?

PHMSA's Office of Pipeline Safety inspects pipeline operators in Alaska directly, because Alaska does not run a PHMSA-certified state programme. TAPS oversight is coordinated through the Joint Pipeline Office, and ADEC regulates oil discharge prevention.

Who inspects boilers and pressure vessels in Alaska?

The Mechanical Inspection Section of the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Division of Labor Standards and Safety, oversees boilers and unfired pressure vessels in commercial and public structures.

Do you write SNT-TC-1A written practices for Alaska companies?

Yes. We write new written practices and audit existing ones against the current SNT-TC-1A edition and your clients' requirements, including the rotation, transfer and interrupted-service rules that matter in Alaska's labour market.

Can you write cold-weather UT and PT procedures?

Yes. Procedures for sub-zero work need to address calibration at examination temperature, couplant and penetrant product limits, and any qualified low-temperature techniques. We write those to the governing code and your client specification.

Do you provide API 510, 570 or 653 inspectors in Alaska?

No. We support API 510, 570 and 653 inspection work from the NDT side, with method selection, procedures and data quality, alongside the owner's authorised inspectors. We do not supply authorised inspectors or provide API certification training.

How much does Level III consulting cost in Alaska?

Pricing is quote on request. It depends on the number of methods, whether you need a retained Level III or a single project, the volume of exams and how many onsite visits are needed. Atlantis positions its services as affordable, accessible and fully customisable.

Do you have an office in Alaska?

No. Atlantis has no physical office or training centre in Alaska. Work is delivered remotely and onsite at the client's facility.

Can you help us prepare for an operator or prime-contractor audit?

Yes. An audit-readiness review samples your written practice, procedures, certifications and reports, then gives you a prioritised corrective-action list and support while you close it.

Whether you need a Level III of record, a written practice, a set of cold-weather procedures or help before an audit, the first step is a short call. Contact Atlantis about Level III consulting in Alaska.

NDT Level III Consulting Services in Alberta

Short answer: Atlantis NDT provides ASNT NDT Level III consulting to Alberta employers: outsourced and interim Level III cover, SNT-TC-1A written practices and audits, NDT procedures and technique sheets, personnel examinations under your written practice, and preparation for owner, ABSA-related and accreditation audits. Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, and are delivered remotely or onsite at your facility or site. Atlantis has no office in Alberta; the Level III works with you online and travels to you when the work needs it.

Alberta is the most inspection-intensive province in Canada. Oil sands mining and in-situ plants around Fort McMurray, Cold Lake and Peace River, the refineries and petrochemical complexes of Edmonton and Alberta's Industrial Heartland, the Joffre petrochemical site near Red Deer, thousands of kilometres of gathering and transmission pipelines, gas plants across the foothills and the north-west, and a large module-fabrication industry all run on qualified NDT. Most of that work is done by inspection companies certified under Canada's national scheme, CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (ISO 9712). A growing share, though, is done for US owners, US-code projects or US customers who expect an employer-based SNT-TC-1A programme with a named Level III behind it. That is the gap this page addresses. It explains which scheme applies when, what ABSA and the other Alberta regulators expect, and how to request an Alberta Level III consultation.

Why Alberta NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: Any Alberta employer that certifies its own NDT personnel to ASNT SNT-TC-1A needs a written practice, method procedures and a responsible Level III who examines and certifies Level I and II staff. Alberta inspection companies and owner-users also answer to ABSA quality-system requirements, owner prequalification and audits, so a named, qualified Level III is a practical necessity, not a formality.

The province's industrial map shows why. In the Athabasca oil sands, mining operators and upgraders north of Fort McMurray run extraction, bitumen upgrading, hydrotreating and utilities plants with enormous inventories of pressure vessels, heat exchangers, piping and tanks, many of them in erosive and corrosive service. Steam-assisted gravity drainage projects around Cold Lake, Conklin, Christina Lake and Peace River add steam generators, high-temperature piping and produced-water systems. Every turnaround in these plants is an NDT event: thickness surveys, weld inspection on repairs, phased array on critical welds, radiography crews working nights, and magnetic particle and penetrant on rotating and structural components.

Alberta's Industrial Heartland, centred on Fort Saskatchewan, Strathcona County, Sturgeon County and Lamont County, is Canada's largest hydrocarbon processing region. It holds refining, upgrading, chemical, fertiliser and petrochemical plants, along with storage terminals, pipelines and hydrogen projects. Edmonton itself has two large refineries in the Strathcona area and a deep bench of fabrication shops, pipe spool and module yards, and inspection contractors. South of Red Deer, the Joffre site is one of the larger petrochemical complexes in North America. Calgary is the head-office city for pipeline operators, producers and engineering firms, so procedures, written practices and audits are often specified there even when the inspection happens hundreds of kilometres away.

Pipelines tie it all together. Alberta's gathering lines, provincially regulated transmission lines and federally regulated interprovincial systems make pipeline construction and integrity work a steady source of NDT demand, from automated ultrasonic testing on mainline girth welds to radiography on tie-ins and station piping. Gas plants and compressor stations in the foothills and the Montney and Deep Basin areas around Grande Prairie add another layer. Southern Alberta, around Medicine Hat and Lethbridge, has gas processing, fertiliser, agricultural processing and fabrication shops that serve the whole province.

All of these buyers eventually ask the same question: who is your Level III, and can we see the written practice? For a company whose people hold only CGSB certificates, the answer is the certification body and the employer's own quality manual. For a company working to an SNT-TC-1A programme, the answer has to be a person. Many Alberta NDT employers are small: a shop with two magnetic particle inspectors, a contractor with a handful of UT and PAUT technicians, a fabricator with a radiography subcontractor. They cannot justify a full-time Level III, but they still need the functions a Level III performs. ASNT Level III consulting services fill that role without a full-time salary.

Which certification scheme applies in Alberta: SNT-TC-1A, CP-189 or CAN/CGSB-48.9712?

Direct answer: Canada's national NDT personnel certification scheme is CAN/CGSB-48.9712, the Canadian adoption of ISO 9712, and it is what most Alberta owners and codes expect. ASNT SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based scheme used by US owners, US-code projects and many cross-border contractors. Some Alberta employers need both. Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A Level III expertise; it does not certify or train to CGSB.

The difference matters because the two schemes put responsibility in different places. Under CAN/CGSB-48.9712, an independent certification body examines and certifies the individual, and the certificate travels with the person. Under SNT-TC-1A, the employer certifies its own people according to its own written practice, and a Level III designated by the employer administers the examinations. ANSI/ASNT CP-189 is a stricter, consensus-standard version of the employer-based approach that some owners and nuclear or defence customers prefer. Note on the national scheme: the Canadian General Standards Board, which published CAN/CGSB-48.9712, ceased operations on 1 April 2026. Published guidance from Natural Resources Canada and CWB Group says the standard remains valid and certifications continue, but you should confirm the current certification body and transition arrangements before relying on any one source.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: A written practice is the employer's own document describing how NDT personnel are trained, examined, certified and recertified. Under SNT-TC-1A it is the document an auditor actually checks. For Alberta employers it usually also has to explain how CGSB certifications, ABSA-related quality requirements and owner specifications fit together, without contradicting the company quality manual.

Most written practice problems in Alberta are not about technique. They are mismatches between documents. A contractor's ABSA-related quality manual says one thing about personnel qualification, the SNT-TC-1A written practice copied from a US company says another, and the certification files follow neither exactly. A written practice may list methods the company no longer performs, name a Level III who left, or require training hours that were never tracked. Files may be missing vision-test records, practical exam checklists or evidence of on-the-job experience. In oil sands and heartland work, owners often add their own requirements for PAUT, TOFD or corrosion mapping that the written practice never mentions.

When we develop a written practice, we start from the work: which methods, which techniques, which codes, which owners. We then set out levels, training and experience requirements (linked to the training requirements matrix rather than invented numbers), examination content and grading, vision testing, records, recertification and how the Level III function is provided. For dual programmes, we write a clear clause on how a CGSB certificate is treated: as evidence of training and experience, with the employer's specific and practical examinations still required for SNT-TC-1A certification. The result is a document your quality manager can maintain. Our written practice development page covers the structure, and our note on written practices for oil sands work looks at the sector-specific points.

An audit runs the other way. We take your written practice and a sample of certification files and test one against the other. Typical findings include expired vision tests, practical examinations graded without a checklist, experience claimed without records, procedures citing superseded code editions, and Level II technicians signing reports in a method or technique they are not certified for. You get a finding list ranked by audit risk, with suggested corrections, and where you want it we help close the findings before your owner or client arrives.

If you also train staff, the written practice and the training programme should line up. Atlantis delivers SNT-TC-1A-based training online and onsite; see NDT training in Canada for how that suits Canadian employers, and corporate NDT training for programmes built around a company's own written practice.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in Alberta

Direct answer: Alberta NDT procedures are written against the code that governs the equipment: ASME and CSA B51 for boilers, pressure vessels and piping registered under ABSA, CSA Z662 for oil and gas pipelines, CSA W59 and AWS D1.1 for structural steel, and API 510, 570 and 653 practices for in-service inspection. The procedure must match the code edition the contract or owner names.

The codes and regulators depend on the asset:

  • Boilers, pressure vessels and pressure piping: ABSA is Alberta's pressure equipment safety authority under the Pressure Equipment Safety Regulation. Design registration follows CSA B51, which calls up ASME Section VIII, Section I and B31.1 and B31.3, and equipment carries a Canadian Registration Number. ASME Section V governs examination methods. See our ABSA Alberta compliance, CSA B51 and CRN registration pages.
  • In-service inspection by owner-users: ABSA document AB-506 sets inspection and servicing requirements for in-service pressure equipment, AB-512 sets the quality-system requirements for owner-users holding an integrity management certificate of authorization, and AB-515 sets quality-system requirements for inspection companies. NDT procedures used in those programmes have to fit the owner's or inspection company's approved system.
  • Pipelines: the Alberta Energy Regulator regulates provincially jurisdictional pipelines under the Pipeline Act and Pipeline Rules, which rely on CSA Z662. Interprovincial and international lines fall under the Canada Energy Regulator. Girth-weld NDT is usually radiography or automated ultrasonic testing to CSA Z662 and the operator's specification; API 1104 appears on US-specification work. See CSA Z662 compliance.
  • Structural steel and modules: CSA W59 for welded steel construction, with fabricators certified to CSA W47.1 through CWB Group; AWS D1.1 on US-specification modules. CSA W178.1 governs certification of welding inspection organisations and W178.2 the certification of welding inspectors; see CSA W178.1.
  • Radiography: gamma radiography with sealed sources is licensed federally by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, and exposure devices must be operated by CNSC-certified exposure device operators or under their direct supervision. Industrial X-ray equipment is a provincial matter in Alberta under the Radiation Protection Act and Regulation, which require registration of designated equipment. See our CNSC compliance page.

A good procedure does three things: it states the code requirement, it states how your equipment and people will meet it, and it is specific enough that two technicians would perform the examination the same way. Technique sheets then translate the procedure into settings for a particular weld, nozzle, component or thickness range. For phased array and TOFD on heavy-wall vessels and piping, that means scan plans, coverage evidence and calibration blocks that match the material. For corrosion mapping in oil sands service, it means grid definition, data-file naming and repeatability. For radiography, it means exposure arrangements, image quality indicator placement and density or digital-image requirements, sitting alongside the licensee's radiation safety programme. We write procedures and technique sheets, check them against the edition the contract calls for and, where the code or owner requires it, demonstrate the technique on representative specimens. We also review procedures written by others when an owner has rejected one; the cause is often a missing calibration requirement, an acceptance criterion from the wrong code, or a thickness range the procedure never covered.

Outsourced and interim Level III for Alberta crews

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III is a named, qualified Level III who carries your programme's Level III responsibilities under a standing agreement. An interim Level III covers a gap. Atlantis provides both for Alberta employers: remotely for documents and technical questions, and onsite for examinations, demonstrations and audits, scheduled around the spring and fall turnaround seasons.

Three engagement models cover most needs:

  • Ongoing outsourced Level III (retainer): we act as your SNT-TC-1A programme's Level III, approving procedures and technique sheets, maintaining the written practice, administering examinations, answering technicians' technical questions and attending client audits. This suits Edmonton, Nisku, Calgary and Fort McMurray contractors that need cover year-round without a full-time Level III.
  • Project-based work: a defined deliverable such as a new written practice, a procedure set for a new method, technique sheets for a turnaround scope, or examinations for a group of new hires. Scope and deliverables are agreed up front.
  • Audit-preparation sprint: a focused review before a scheduled owner or client audit, with findings and corrections, so the programme is ready on the day.

Timing matters in Alberta in a way it does not elsewhere. Turnarounds in the oil sands and the heartland concentrate a year's inspection into a few weeks, and contractors staff up quickly. If your Level III leaves in the middle of that, you can be left unable to certify a new hire, approve a technique sheet or answer an owner's corrective-action request. Interim Level III cover keeps the programme compliant while you recruit. Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, so you always know who your Level III is. For companies working across several provinces or with US sites as well, see multi-site NDT programme harmonisation.

Audit readiness: owner, ABSA-related and accreditation audits

Direct answer: Alberta NDT programmes are audited by owners and EPCs during prequalification, by ABSA as part of quality-system certificates held by owner-users and inspection companies, by accreditation bodies for ISO 9001 and ISO/IEC 17025 laboratories, by CWB Group for CSA W178.1 certification, and by radiation-safety regulators. Atlantis prepares the NDT personnel and procedure side of each.

Owner audits are the most common. An oil sands operator or heartland refinery will often review a contractor's personnel qualification records, procedures and calibration records before mobilisation, and prequalification platforms such as ISNetworld, Avetta and ComplyWorks gather some of that evidence in advance. Inspection companies working under ABSA-accepted quality systems face periodic review of how they control procedures and personnel. Contractors certified to CSA W178.1 are audited on welding inspection personnel and procedures. Laboratories accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 are assessed on method validation, traceability and personnel competence. Radiography licensees are inspected by the CNSC for radiation safety, which is separate from NDT certification but often handled by the same quality manager.

We help by reviewing your written practice, procedures, technique sheets, certification files, vision tests and equipment calibration records against what the auditor will look at, running a mock audit and helping close gaps before the real visit. We do not grant ABSA certificates, CWB certification, accreditation or owner approval; we help you get ready for the organisations that do. The refining audit support, petrochemical audit support, pipeline audit support and fabrication audit support pages explain what each type of audit focuses on. If an audit is on your calendar, ask about an audit-preparation review for your Alberta programme.

Sector notes: what Alberta industries ask of a Level III

Direct answer: Oil sands and upgrader owners ask for corrosion-mapping and PAUT capability with tight data control; heartland refiners and chemical plants ask for code-matched procedures and turnaround-ready personnel records; pipeline operators ask for CSA Z662 girth-weld procedures and AUT or RT qualification; module and vessel fabricators ask for procedures that satisfy both Canadian registration and US client specifications.

Oil sands mining, upgrading and in-situ

Erosion, corrosion and high-temperature service make thickness surveys, corrosion mapping and weld examination on piping, slurry lines, vessels and exchangers the backbone of oil sands NDT. Steam generators and high-temperature lines in SAGD plants add weld and creep-related inspection. A Level III supports these programmes with technique sheets that make data repeatable year to year and with personnel qualification records an owner can audit. The Fort McMurray refining NDT training page describes the training side.

Industrial Heartland refining and petrochemicals

Refineries, upgraders and chemical plants around Fort Saskatchewan and Strathcona County run large turnarounds with heavy PAUT, TOFD, RT and surface-method scopes. Contractors need procedures matched to the owner's specification and ABSA-registered equipment, and personnel files that survive a pre-mobilisation audit. See NDT consulting in Fort Saskatchewan.

Pipelines and gas plants

Construction NDT on girth welds, tie-ins and facility piping, plus in-service integrity digs, keep pipeline contractors busy from Grande Prairie to the southern border. Procedures must match CSA Z662 and the operator's specification; US-bound projects may add API 1104.

Fabrication, modules and vessel shops

Nisku, Leduc, Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary host vessel shops, spool fabricators and module yards that build for Alberta, the rest of Canada and the US. Shops exporting to US customers frequently need an SNT-TC-1A written practice alongside their Canadian quality system, and that is a common reason they contact an outside Level III.

Cities we support across Alberta

Direct answer: Atlantis supports NDT employers anywhere in Alberta, remotely and onsite at your facility or site, including Calgary, Edmonton and the Industrial Heartland, Fort McMurray and the oil sands, Red Deer and Joffre, Grande Prairie, Lethbridge and Medicine Hat. We have no physical office in the province.

Calgary. Head offices of producers, pipeline operators and engineering firms, plus fabrication and inspection contractors in the south-east industrial areas. Written practices and procedures for province-wide work are often specified here. See NDT consulting in Calgary, NDT training in Calgary, Practical NDT in Calgary, third-party inspection in Calgary, and method pages for ultrasonic testing and radiographic testing in Calgary.

Edmonton, Nisku and Leduc. Refineries, fabrication, pipe spool and module yards, inspection contractors and the supply base for the oil sands. See NDT consulting in Edmonton, NDT training in Edmonton, Practical NDT in Edmonton and third-party inspection in Edmonton.

Fort Saskatchewan and the Industrial Heartland. Refining, upgrading, chemicals and fertiliser. See NDT consulting in Fort Saskatchewan.

Fort McMurray and the oil sands. Mining, upgrading and in-situ operations with heavy turnaround demand. See NDT consulting in Fort McMurray, NDT training in Fort McMurray and Practical NDT in Fort McMurray.

Red Deer and Joffre. Petrochemicals, gas processing and fabrication in central Alberta. See Practical NDT in Red Deer.

Lethbridge, Medicine Hat and southern Alberta. Gas processing, fertiliser, agricultural processing and fabrication shops. See Practical NDT in Lethbridge.

Grande Prairie, Cold Lake and the north. Gas plants, in-situ projects and pipeline work, supported remotely with site visits for examinations and audits.

Province-wide resources: the Alberta Practical NDT hub for simulator practice before practical exams, the Alberta NDT ERP page for certification and calibration tracking that records CGSB and ASNT certificates side by side, and the Alberta digital twin page.

How an engagement works

Direct answer: You describe your methods, codes, owners and deadlines on a call; we agree scope, deliverables and the remote and onsite split; the work is done and reviewed with your team; and for ongoing cover we stay on as your named Level III. Quotes are given on request after scoping.

  1. Scoping call. We discuss your operation, the methods and techniques you perform, which certification schemes your people hold, the codes and owner specifications you work to, turnaround dates and any audit findings.
  2. Document request. You send your existing written practice, quality-manual sections, procedures and a sample of certification files. If you are starting from nothing, we gather what is needed to build the programme.
  3. Proposal. You receive a written scope: deliverables, what is done remotely, what needs a site visit, and who does it. Quotes are provided on request.
  4. Delivery. Documents are drafted and reviewed with your quality team. Examinations are scheduled and administered under your written practice. Site visits are arranged around production and turnaround windows.
  5. Handover or ongoing cover. Project work ends with final documents and records you control. Outsourced Level III arrangements continue with approvals, technical support and audit attendance.

To start, book a Level III scoping call for Alberta.

Your Level III

Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. In this field, buyers want to know who the Level III is, because that person's name sits on the written practice and the procedures. With Atlantis that is stated up front. Anoop also leads Atlantis NDT's SNT-TC-1A-based training, which keeps programme documents and training content consistent.

Frequently asked questions about NDT Level III consulting in Alberta

Do I need an ASNT Level III if my technicians already hold CGSB certificates?

Not for work that only requires CAN/CGSB-48.9712 certification. You need an SNT-TC-1A written practice and a responsible Level III when an owner, client or code specifies employer-based ASNT certification, which is common on US-owned plants and US-code projects.

Can one written practice cover both CGSB and SNT-TC-1A?

An SNT-TC-1A written practice can state how CGSB certificates are treated, for example as evidence of training and experience, and what additional employer examinations are required. CGSB certification itself remains with the certification body.

Who certifies NDT personnel in Canada now that the CGSB has closed?

The Canadian General Standards Board ceased operations on 1 April 2026, but published guidance says CAN/CGSB-48.9712 remains valid and certifications continue. NRCan's NDT Certification Body and CWB Group have both issued notices on the transition; confirm the current certification body before relying on it.

Who regulates pressure equipment in Alberta?

ABSA, the pressure equipment safety authority, administers the Pressure Equipment Safety Regulation, including design registration, owner-user integrity management (AB-512) and in-service inspection requirements (AB-506).

Who licenses industrial radiography in Alberta?

Gamma radiography is licensed by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, and exposure devices must be operated by CNSC-certified exposure device operators or under their direct supervision. Industrial X-ray equipment is registered under Alberta's Radiation Protection Regulation.

Which codes apply to pipeline NDT in Alberta?

CSA Z662 for oil and gas pipeline systems, applied by the Alberta Energy Regulator for provincial pipelines and by the Canada Energy Regulator for interprovincial ones. Operators add their own specifications, and US-bound work may call up API 1104.

Can an outsourced Level III approve our procedures and technique sheets?

Yes, when your written practice designates that Level III and they are certified in the relevant methods. The review must be real and traceable, not a signature on a template.

Can you administer examinations at our shop or site in Alberta?

Yes. General and specific examinations can be administered under controlled conditions, and practical examinations are performed onsite on suitable specimens under your written practice.

How much does Level III consulting cost in Alberta?

It depends on scope: the number of methods, whether you need a new written practice or a review, how many people need examining and how much onsite time is required. Quotes are given on request after a scoping call.

Do you provide ABSA inspections or API inspector services?

No. We are not an ABSA-authorised inspection agency. We provide Level III support to inspection programmes, such as NDT technique selection and procedure review for API 510, 570 and 653 style work. See API 510 programme support.

Can you train our technicians as well?

Yes, to SNT-TC-1A only. Atlantis delivers Level I, II and III training online and onsite; it does not train toward CGSB certification. See NDT training and the Practical NDT simulator for practice before practical exams.

Talk to a Level III about your Alberta programme

Whether you run a PAUT crew heading into an oil sands turnaround, a vessel shop in Nisku shipping to a US client, or a pipeline inspection contractor working to CSA Z662 and API 1104 on the same season, the Level III questions are the same: is the written practice right, are the procedures right, and can you prove your people are qualified under the scheme your client specifies? Ask about outsourced Level III cover in Alberta, or request a written practice review. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Quotes on request.

NDT Level III Consulting Services in Arizona

Short answer: Arizona NDT employers can engage Atlantis NDT for ASNT NDT Level III services without hiring a full-time Level III: outsourced or interim Level III cover, SNT-TC-1A written practices and audits, method procedures and technique sheets, Level I and II examinations under your written practice, and preparation for prime-contractor, owner and accreditation audits. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, leads each engagement. Work is delivered remotely and onsite at your Phoenix, Tucson or rural Arizona facility; Atlantis has no office in the state.

Arizona's NDT market does not look like Texas or Louisiana. There is no refining corridor. Instead the state combines the largest nuclear generating station in the United States, an aerospace and defence manufacturing base concentrated in the Phoenix and Tucson metros, several of the country's biggest open-pit copper mines and smelters, a fast-growing semiconductor manufacturing cluster, refined-products and natural-gas pipelines that bring fuel in from neighbouring states, and a desert climate that complicates field inspection for much of the year. A Level III serving Arizona has to be comfortable with aerospace customer specifications one week and heavy mining equipment the next. This page sets out what Arizona programmes need, the agencies that regulate them and how to request an Arizona Level III consultation.

Why Arizona NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: Any Arizona employer certifying NDT personnel under SNT-TC-1A needs a Level III-approved written practice, method procedures and Level III-administered examinations. On top of that, Arizona's aerospace primes, nuclear utility, mining companies and semiconductor fabs audit their NDT suppliers and expect to see a named, qualified Level III behind the programme.

Start with power. Palo Verde Generating Station, west of Phoenix near Tonopah and Wintersburg, runs three pressurised-water reactors and is the largest nuclear plant in the country by generation. Refuelling outages bring in-service inspection crews working to ASME Section XI, and the plant's suppliers work under nuclear quality programmes with strict qualification and documentation rules. Gas-fired plants run by the state's utilities, hydroelectric plant on the Colorado River at Hoover and Glen Canyon dams, and the pumping plants of the Central Arizona Project canal add boiler, piping, penstock and rotating-equipment inspection.

Aerospace and defence is the second pillar. Honeywell Aerospace has major engine, auxiliary power unit and avionics operations in Phoenix and Tempe. Boeing builds the AH-64 Apache in Mesa. Raytheon's missile business is one of Tucson's largest employers. Northrop Grumman builds launch vehicles and satellites in Chandler, and General Dynamics Mission Systems has a major presence in Scottsdale. Luke Air Force Base, Davis-Monthan Air Force Base with its aircraft storage and regeneration group, Marine Corps Air Station Yuma, Yuma Proving Ground and Fort Huachuca add military maintenance and test work, while Pinal Airpark and other desert sites store and maintain commercial aircraft. Each of these organisations flows NDT requirements down to machine shops, special-process houses, MRO providers and inspection contractors across the Valley and southern Arizona.

Mining is the third. Freeport-McMoRan operates the Morenci, Bagdad, Sierrita and Safford copper mines, and Asarco runs the Mission and Ray mines and the Hayden smelter. Mine haul trucks, shovels, crushers, mills, conveyor structures, leach and solvent-extraction plant, and smelter vessels all need weld and structural inspection, much of it ultrasonic and magnetic particle work on heavy sections. Semiconductor manufacturing is the fourth and newest: TSMC's fabs in north Phoenix and Intel's Ocotillo campus in Chandler, along with their suppliers, drive high-purity process piping, gas and chemical delivery systems and structural steel that need visual, radiographic and other examinations during construction.

Few Arizona NDT companies can afford a full-time Level III for every method they offer, yet every one of those customers expects Level III oversight. ASNT Level III consulting services let a smaller Arizona programme put a qualified Level III's name on its written practice and procedures, and keep it there when the customer audits.

Level III services for Arizona employers

Direct answer: Atlantis provides every core Level III function for Arizona companies: written practice development and audit, procedure and technique-sheet writing and approval, examinations for Level I and II personnel, outsourced and interim Level III cover, audit readiness, NDT programme set-up and technical support for in-service inspection programmes. Scope is agreed on a call.

ServiceWhat it coversTypical Arizona client type

The consulting overview lists every service. If your interest is a single method or an unusual application, such as ultrasonic inspection of mining-equipment welds or eddy current on aircraft structures, say so on the first call and the scope will be built around it.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: The written practice is the employer's rulebook for NDT qualification and certification. SNT-TC-1A recommends what it should contain, but auditors check your document and your records against each other. We write written practices that match how your Arizona operation actually works, and audit existing ones before your customer does.

Arizona's mix of customers creates specific written practice problems. A Tempe machine shop may supply both an aerospace engine maker and an industrial customer; its written practice has to cover SNT-TC-1A certification while recognising that some aerospace contracts call for NAS 410 or other customer-specific rules. A Tucson inspection contractor may work at a copper mine in the morning and a defence facility in the afternoon, using the same technicians under different specifications. A company that has grown quickly with the semiconductor build-out may have certified technicians under a template written practice that never matched its methods. In each case the written practice must say clearly which methods and levels are covered, how training and experience are documented, how examinations are built and graded, how vision is tested and who acts as Level III.

Our process is straightforward. We collect your current documents and talk to the people who use them. We write or revise the written practice, keeping training and experience requirements tied to the training requirements matrix rather than invented figures. We then check a sample of certification files against it. The outcome is a written practice you can defend and a finding list for any certification files that need correcting. See written practice development for detail, and SNT-TC-1A training and certification for how employer-based certification works.

A written practice audit is often the simplest protection an NDT company can put in place before a customer visit. Typical findings in programmes we review include examinations administered by someone not designated in the written practice, missing practical exam documentation, near-vision tests that lapsed between projects, procedures referencing an old code edition, and technicians signing reports in a level or method they do not hold. Each is easy to fix before an audit and hard to explain during one.

Where the written practice calls for formal training, Atlantis delivers SNT-TC-1A-based courses online and onsite; see NDT training in Arizona and corporate NDT training.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in Arizona

Direct answer: Arizona procedures follow the governing code for each sector: ASME Section XI and plant programmes for nuclear in-service work, ASME Sections V and VIII and B31 piping codes for pressure equipment, AWS D1.1 for structural and mining-equipment fabrication, API 1104 and federal rules for pipelines, and customer specifications for aerospace and semiconductor work.

  • Nuclear: in-service inspection at Palo Verde is performed to ASME Section XI under the utility's programme, with performance demonstration requirements for certain ultrasonic examinations. Suppliers work under nuclear quality assurance programmes. Our role is supporting suppliers' NDT documentation and personnel records, not acting for the plant owner's programme.
  • Aerospace and defence: prime-contractor specifications commonly invoke ASTM E1417 for penetrant, E1444 for magnetic particle, E2375 for ultrasonic testing of wrought products and customer-specific eddy current and radiography requirements. Technique sheets are usually tied to part numbers.
  • Pressure equipment and boilers: ASME Sections I, V and VIII and B31.1 and B31.3. Boilers and fired pressure vessels in Arizona fall under the Boiler Safety Section of the Arizona Division of Occupational Safety and Health (ADOSH), part of the Industrial Commission of Arizona, which handles certificate inspections and authorises inspection companies.
  • Mining equipment and structures: AWS D1.1 and equipment manufacturers' repair specifications for haul-truck frames, shovel booms, crusher structures and conveyors. Ultrasonic and magnetic particle testing dominate.
  • Pipelines: API 1104 under 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195. Arizona receives refined products through Kinder Morgan's SFPP lines from the west and east, and natural gas through interstate systems. Intrastate pipeline safety is overseen by the Arizona Corporation Commission's Office of Pipeline Safety in partnership with PHMSA.
  • Semiconductor and high-purity piping: project specifications that often call for borescope visual examination of orbital welds and other examinations defined by the owner. Procedures must match the owner's acceptance criteria exactly.
  • Radiography: Arizona is an NRC Agreement State. Industrial radiography is licensed and inspected by the Arizona Department of Health Services Bureau of Radiation Control under Arizona Administrative Code Title 9, Chapter 7.

Arizona adds a practical twist: heat. Summer surface temperatures on pipe, tanks and structures in the desert can exceed what couplants, penetrant materials and magnetic particle media are rated for, and ultrasonic calibration has to account for the temperature difference between calibration block and component that ASME Section V limits. A good procedure addresses these limits explicitly: when examinations must be rescheduled, which high-temperature consumables are allowed, and how calibration is verified. We write procedures with those field realities in mind, and we review procedures written by others when a customer has rejected them or an auditor has raised a finding.

Outsourced and interim Level III for Arizona crews

Direct answer: Outsourced Level III means Atlantis serves as your programme's named Level III under a standing agreement. Interim Level III covers a temporary gap. Both are available to Arizona employers, with document work done remotely and examinations, demonstrations and audits done onsite when needed.

Engagements usually take one of three shapes:

  • Ongoing outsourced Level III: we approve procedures and technique sheets, maintain the written practice, administer examinations, answer technicians' technical questions and attend audits. This suits Valley and Tucson inspection companies and suppliers that need continuous Level III accountability but not a full-time hire.
  • Project work: a defined deliverable such as a written practice, a procedure set for a new method, PAUT scan plans for a new weld configuration, or examination of a new group of technicians.
  • Audit-preparation sprint: a concentrated review before a customer, owner or accreditation audit, ending with corrected documents and a clean set of certification files.

Interim Level III work is common in Arizona because the state's large employers recruit experienced Level IIIs away from smaller companies. When that happens, a supplier may be unable to certify a new technician or approve a revised procedure, and customers notice quickly. An interim arrangement keeps the programme running while you recruit or develop your own Level III. All engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, so your customers know whose name is on the documents. If you run sites in Arizona and neighbouring states, see multi-site programme harmonisation.

Audit readiness: customer, owner and accreditation audits

Direct answer: Arizona NDT programmes face aerospace prime and Nadcap-style audits, nuclear supplier audits, mining and semiconductor owner audits, ISO 9001 and ISO/IEC 17025 assessments and state radiation-safety inspections. Atlantis prepares the NDT evidence each auditor will ask for and runs a mock audit so there are no surprises.

Aerospace audits examine traceability: whether every technician's certification is current and matches the work signed, whether each procedure revision was approved, and whether penetrant and magnetic particle systems are checked and recorded as required. Our Nadcap AC7114 audit readiness page describes how those audits approach NDT. Nuclear supplier audits look closely at qualification records and document control. Mining and semiconductor owners usually audit contractors before mobilisation, focusing on certifications, procedures and safety. Accreditation bodies check ISO 9001 competence records or ISO/IEC 17025 method validation and traceability. Radiography licensees are inspected separately by the Bureau of Radiation Control.

We prepare the NDT part of each audit. We do not grant approvals or accreditation and do not claim vendor approvals on your behalf. Related pages: aerospace audit support, nuclear audit support, mining audit support, power generation audit support and pipeline audit support. With an audit on the calendar, ask for an Arizona audit-readiness review.

Sector notes: Arizona industries and their Level III needs

Direct answer: Nuclear suppliers need disciplined records; aerospace suppliers need part-specific technique sheets and traceable certifications; mining contractors need robust UT and MT procedures for heavy, cracked and repaired sections; semiconductor contractors need procedures that match owner acceptance criteria; and pipeline contractors need API 1104-ready documents.

Aerospace and defence in the Valley and Tucson

Engine components, airframe parts, missiles and space hardware all need surface and volumetric NDT to customer specifications. Eddy current, penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic and radiographic testing are all in play. See aerospace NDT consulting in Tucson and aerospace audit support.

Copper mining and smelting

Mine maintenance shops repair heavy equipment continuously. Crack detection on frames, booms and buckets, weld inspection after repair, and thickness surveys on tanks and pipe in leach and solvent-extraction plants are routine. Procedures must account for rough surfaces, thick sections and field conditions.

Nuclear and power generation

Palo Verde's outages and the state's gas, hydro and solar-thermal plants need boiler, piping and turbine inspection. See power generation audit support.

Semiconductor fabs and construction

The north Phoenix and Chandler build-outs need high-purity piping examination, structural steel inspection and large numbers of qualified technicians quickly, which puts pressure on written practices and examination capacity.

Steel fabrication and infrastructure

Fabricators supplying data centres, fabs, bridges and the state's growing logistics sector work to AWS D1.1 and D1.5. See steel NDT consulting in Phoenix and fabrication audit support.

Cities we support across Arizona

Direct answer: Atlantis supports Arizona NDT employers statewide, remotely and onsite at your facility, from metro Phoenix and Tucson to Yuma, Flagstaff and the mining towns of the east and south. We do not operate an office in Arizona.

Phoenix metro (Phoenix, Mesa, Tempe, Chandler, Scottsdale, Glendale, Peoria and the West Valley). Aerospace, defence, semiconductors, fabrication, power and the main pipeline terminals. Related pages: NDT consulting in Phoenix, steel NDT consulting in Phoenix, Practical NDT in Phoenix, and method pages for ultrasonic testing in Phoenix, radiographic testing in Phoenix, magnetic particle testing in Phoenix, penetrant testing in Phoenix, eddy current testing in Phoenix and visual testing in Phoenix.

Tucson and southern Arizona. Missile and defence manufacturing, Davis-Monthan, aircraft storage and MRO at Marana, Fort Huachuca near Sierra Vista and the copper mines south of the city. See NDT consulting in Tucson, aerospace NDT consulting in Tucson and Practical NDT in Tucson.

Technician training is covered on the Arizona NDT training hub, and trainees can rehearse methods on the Practical NDT simulator, which is practice only and does not replace practical exams on real specimens.

How an engagement works

Direct answer: A scoping call establishes your methods, codes, customers and deadlines; we send a written scope and quote on request; documents are drafted remotely and reviewed with your team; examinations and audits happen onsite where required; and outsourced cover continues as long as you need it.

  1. Scoping call. Tell us what you inspect, which methods you use, which codes and customer specifications govern the work, and what deadline you face, whether an audit, a contract start or a mine shutdown.
  2. Document review. Send your current written practice, procedures and a sample of certification files. If you have none, we start from your scope of work.
  3. Scope and quote. We set out deliverables, the split between remote and onsite work, and the Level III responsible. Quotes are provided on request.
  4. Delivery. Drafts go to your quality team for review. Examinations, procedure demonstrations and mock audits are scheduled at your facility, planned around production, outages or summer heat where field work is involved.
  5. Close-out or continuing cover. You receive final documents and records under your control, or the outsourced Level III arrangement continues.

Ready to start? Schedule an Arizona Level III scoping call.

Your Level III

Every engagement is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Arizona buyers, especially aerospace and nuclear suppliers, want to know exactly whose name sits on their written practice and procedures; with Atlantis it is stated from the first call. Anoop also leads Atlantis NDT's SNT-TC-1A-based training, which keeps programme documents and training content consistent.

Frequently asked questions about NDT Level III consulting in Arizona

How do I find an NDT Level III consultant in Arizona?

Look for a Level III certified in the methods you perform, with experience of your sector's codes and customers, who will be named in your written practice. Atlantis provides this remotely and onsite across Arizona, led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III.

Can a small Arizona NDT company use an outside Level III instead of hiring one?

Yes. SNT-TC-1A allows the Level III function to be provided by an outside agency, provided the written practice defines the arrangement and the Level III holds the relevant method certifications.

Who regulates industrial radiography in Arizona?

Arizona is an NRC Agreement State. The Arizona Department of Health Services Bureau of Radiation Control licenses and inspects industrial radiography under Arizona Administrative Code Title 9, Chapter 7.

Who handles boiler inspections in Arizona?

The Boiler Safety Section of the Arizona Division of Occupational Safety and Health, part of the Industrial Commission of Arizona. NDT on boiler and pressure-vessel repairs follows the ASME and National Board requirements that apply.

Who oversees pipeline safety in Arizona?

The Arizona Corporation Commission's Office of Pipeline Safety oversees intrastate pipelines in partnership with PHMSA, which regulates interstate lines.

Can you help us become a supplier to an Arizona aerospace prime?

We can build or upgrade your NDT programme so it meets the prime's flow-down requirements and prepare you for their audit. Approval itself is the customer's decision.

Do you work with Palo Verde suppliers?

We support suppliers' NDT written practices, procedures and personnel records. The plant's own in-service inspection programme is run by the plant owner and its contractors.

What does an outsourced Level III cost in Arizona?

Cost depends on the number of methods, the volume of procedures and examinations, and how much onsite time is needed. Quotes are provided on request after a scoping call.

Can you write procedures for mining-equipment inspection?

Yes. UT and MT procedures and technique sheets for haul-truck frames, shovel and dragline components, crushers and conveyor structures can be written to AWS D1.1 and the equipment maker's repair specifications.

Does SNT-TC-1A certification satisfy every Arizona customer?

Not always. Many industrial and pipeline customers accept it; some aerospace customers require NAS 410 or their own schemes. Check the specification, and we can help you map your programme to it.

How do you handle summer heat in field procedures?

Procedures should state temperature limits for consumables, require high-temperature materials where allowed, and control calibration temperature differences as ASME Section V requires. We build those controls into the documents.

Can Atlantis train our Arizona technicians as well?

Yes. SNT-TC-1A-based Level I, II and III training is available online and onsite; see NDT training in Arizona.

Put a named Level III behind your Arizona programme

From a Chandler machine shop supplying engine parts to a mine maintenance contractor in Morenci or a pipeline crew in the West Valley, the questions are the same: is the written practice right, are the procedures right, and can you prove your people are qualified? Ask about outsourced Level III cover in Arizona or request an Arizona written practice review. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Quotes on request.

NDT Level III Consulting Services in British Columbia

Short answer: Atlantis NDT provides ASNT NDT Level III consulting to British Columbia employers: outsourced and interim Level III cover, SNT-TC-1A written practices and audits, NDT procedures and technique sheets, personnel examinations under your written practice, and preparation for owner, shipyard and accreditation audits. Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, and are delivered remotely or onsite at your facility, yard or site. Atlantis has no office in British Columbia; the Level III works with you online and travels for the work that has to be done in person.

British Columbia's NDT market has changed fast. LNG Canada's export terminal at Kitimat has started shipping, the Coastal GasLink pipeline feeds it from the north-east, the Trans Mountain expansion is in service to Burnaby, and more LNG projects at Squamish and on the north coast are being built. Add naval and commercial shipbuilding in North Vancouver and Esquimalt, the Montney gas fields around Fort St. John and Dawson Creek, pulp and paper mills, copper and metallurgical operations, aluminium smelting at Kitimat, large hydroelectric assets and a busy port system, and you have a province where the same inspection company may work to Canadian, US and international codes in a single year. Many of those projects were engineered or are owned by companies that expect an employer-based ASNT programme with a named Level III. This page explains what BC NDT employers need from a Level III, which regulators and codes apply, and how to request a British Columbia Level III consultation.

Why British Columbia NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: A BC employer that certifies its own NDT personnel to ASNT SNT-TC-1A needs a written practice, method procedures and a responsible Level III to examine and certify Level I and II staff. LNG owners, pipeline operators, shipyards and US-based EPCs working in the province ask to see that programme, so the Level III has to be named, qualified in the methods used and available for audits.

Energy megaprojects drive much of the demand. Liquefaction trains, cryogenic storage tanks, marine loading facilities, compressor stations and thousands of pipe welds all need examination during construction and then a lifetime of in-service inspection. Construction NDT on these projects is heavy in radiography and phased array on process piping, automated ultrasonic testing on pipeline girth welds and specialised techniques for nickel-steel and stainless cryogenic welds. Many of the engineering contracts for LNG and pipeline work are held by international or US EPCs whose project specifications call up ASME B31.3, API 620 or API 625 for tanks, and SNT-TC-1A or equivalent personnel qualification, alongside Canadian requirements.

Shipbuilding is the second anchor. Seaspan's Vancouver Shipyards in North Vancouver builds non-combat vessels for the federal government under the National Shipbuilding Strategy, and repair and refit work for the Royal Canadian Navy's Pacific fleet centres on Esquimalt, home of CFB Esquimalt and the Esquimalt Graving Dock. Ship and marine fabrication involves structural welding, heavy ultrasonic and magnetic particle inspection, and classification-society or naval specifications.

The resource economy supplies the rest. Natural gas production and processing in the Montney around Fort St. John, Dawson Creek and Chetwynd; pulp and paper mills in Prince George, Kamloops, the Fraser Valley and on the coast, with recovery boilers and digesters that need regular thickness surveys and weld inspection; Highland Valley copper near Logan Lake and other mines with crushers, mills and heavy mobile equipment; the metallurgical complex at Trail and the aluminium smelter at Kitimat; and a large hydroelectric system with penstocks, turbines and gates. Each of these sectors employs NDT technicians directly or through contractors, and each eventually asks who the Level III is. ASNT Level III consulting services let a small BC employer answer that without a full-time hire.

Which certification scheme applies in British Columbia?

Direct answer: Canada's national scheme, CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (ISO 9712), is what BC owners and Canadian codes generally expect. SNT-TC-1A applies when a US owner, US-based EPC, US-code project or US customer specifies employer-based ASNT certification, which is common on LNG and pipeline construction contracts. Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A Level III expertise; it does not certify or train to CGSB.

In BC the two schemes meet most often on construction projects. An inspection contractor's technicians hold CGSB certificates, but the EPC's project specification asks for an SNT-TC-1A written practice, procedures approved by an ASNT Level III and examination records for the specific techniques used, such as PAUT on cryogenic welds. The contractor then needs a written practice that recognises CGSB certification as evidence of training and experience, defines any additional employer examinations, and keeps one set of records. On the national scheme itself: the Canadian General Standards Board, which published CAN/CGSB-48.9712, ceased operations on 1 April 2026. Guidance from Natural Resources Canada and CWB Group says the standard remains valid and certifications continue; confirm the current certification body and transition arrangements before you rely on one source.

Situation in BCScheme usually asked forWhat the employer needs

LNG or pipeline project with a US or international EPCSNT-TC-1A or equivalent, often alongside CGSBSNT-TC-1A written practice, approved procedures, technique qualification records, Level III sign-off

Shipbuilding and naval workCustomer, classification-society or naval specificationProcedures and personnel records matched to the specification
Aerospace maintenance and componentsCustomer specification, sometimes NAS 410Technique sheets and records per customer flow-down

See the CAN/CGSB-48.9712 compliance and NRCan NDT certification pages for the Canadian scheme, and SNT-TC-1A guidance for the employer-based route.

Level III services for British Columbia employers

Direct answer: Atlantis covers every Level III function for BC companies working to SNT-TC-1A or US codes: written practice authoring and review, procedure and technique-sheet development, examination and certification of Level I and II personnel, programme audits, audit-readiness support and outsourced or interim Level III cover. Scope is agreed on a call around your methods, projects and owners.

Written practice developmentA new or rewritten SNT-TC-1A written practice that also states how CGSB certificates are treatedInspection contractors bidding LNG, pipeline and terminal construction work

Procedures and technique sheetsUT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET procedures to ASME, API, CSA, AWS or classification-society requirements; weld- and component-specific technique sheetsShipyards, module and vessel fabricators in the Lower Mainland and on Vancouver Island
