Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: A written practice is the employer's own document describing how NDT personnel are trained, examined, certified and recertified. SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, so the written practice is what an auditor actually checks. We write it to fit how your Massachusetts operation really works, then audit your records against it.

Most written practice problems we see are not technical; they are mismatches between the document and reality. A written practice copied from another company may list methods the shop no longer performs, require training hours nobody tracked, or name a Level III who left years ago. Certification files may be missing vision-test records, practical exam checklists or evidence of on-the-job experience. In aerospace supply chains, the customer's quality clause may also call for a different standard, such as NAS 410, which is a separate scheme with its own rules. A Massachusetts machine shop serving both commercial aerospace and general industrial customers can end up needing to show how its programme satisfies more than one requirement, and the written practice has to say so clearly.

When we develop a written practice we start with the work: which methods, which techniques, which codes and which customers. We then set out levels, training and experience requirements (linked to the training requirements matrix rather than invented numbers), examination content and grading, vision testing, records, recertification intervals and how the Level III function is provided. The finished document is something your quality manager can maintain. Our written practice development page covers the structure in more detail, and the SNT-TC-1A guidance page explains how employer-based certification works.

An audit runs the other way. We take your current written practice and a sample of certification files and test one against the other. Typical findings include expired vision tests, practical exams graded without a checklist, experience claimed without supporting records, procedures that reference superseded code editions, and Level II personnel signing work in methods they are not certified for. You get a plain-language finding list ranked by audit risk, with suggested corrections. Where you want it, we then help close the findings so the programme is ready before your customer arrives.

For employers that also train staff, the written practice and the training programme should line up. Atlantis delivers SNT-TC-1A-based training online and onsite; the NDT training in Massachusetts hub explains the options, and corporate NDT training covers programmes built around a company's own written practice.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in Massachusetts

Direct answer: Massachusetts NDT procedures are written against whatever code governs the part: ASME Sections V, VIII and the B31 piping codes for pressure equipment, AWS D1.1 and D1.5 for structural and bridge steel, API 1104 and federal pipeline rules for transmission welding, and customer specifications for aerospace and defence parts. The procedure must match the code edition the contract names.

The codes depend on the sector:

  • Aerospace and defence manufacturing: customer and prime-contractor specifications, often invoking ASTM practices such as E1417 for penetrant, E1444 for magnetic particle and E2375 for ultrasonic testing of wrought products, plus special-process approval requirements. Technique sheets are typically part-specific.
  • Pressure equipment and boilers: ASME Section V for examination methods, Section VIII for pressure vessels, Section I for power boilers and B31.1 and B31.3 for power and process piping. Massachusetts registers and inspects non-residential boilers and pressure vessels through the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Program in the Office of Public Safety and Inspections, part of the Division of Occupational Licensure.
  • Bridges and structural steel: AWS D1.5 for bridge welding and D1.1 for general structural work, with MassDOT and project specifications on top.
  • Gas pipelines: API 1104 for welding and inspection of pipelines, under 49 CFR Part 192 for gas. Intrastate gas pipeline safety in Massachusetts is overseen by the Department of Public Utilities' Pipeline Safety Division working with PHMSA.
  • Offshore wind and marine structures: project specifications that frequently reference AWS D1.1 and European or classification-society standards; ultrasonic testing of thick plate welds is central.
  • Radiography: Massachusetts is an NRC Agreement State. Industrial radiography with radioactive sources or X-ray equipment is licensed and inspected by the Massachusetts Department of Public Health Radiation Control Program, and radiography procedures must sit alongside the licensee's radiation safety programme.

A good procedure does three things: it states the code requirement, it states how your equipment and people will meet it, and it is specific enough that two technicians would perform the examination the same way. Technique sheets then translate the procedure into settings for a particular part or joint. We write both, check them against the current edition the contract calls for, and where the code requires it, demonstrate the technique on representative specimens. For phased array and TOFD, that includes scan plans and coverage evidence. For radiography, it includes exposure arrangements and image quality indicator placement.

We also review procedures written by others. If a customer has rejected a procedure or an auditor has questioned one, a Level III review often finds the issue quickly: a missing calibration requirement, an acceptance criterion from the wrong code, or a procedure that never covered the thickness range being inspected. If your concern is limited to certain methods, our note on Level III method scope limitations explains how certification scope works.

Outsourced and interim Level III for Massachusetts crews

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III is a named, qualified Level III who carries your programme's Level III responsibilities under a standing agreement. An interim Level III covers a gap, for example when your own Level III retires or leaves. Atlantis provides both for Massachusetts employers, remotely for document work and onsite when exams or audits need a physical presence.

Three engagement models cover most needs:

  • Ongoing outsourced Level III (retainer): we act as your programme's Level III. That includes approving procedures and technique sheets, maintaining the written practice, administering examinations, answering technical questions from your technicians and attending customer audits. This suits Massachusetts inspection contractors, fabricators and aerospace suppliers who need Level III cover year-round but not a full-time employee.
  • Project-based work: a defined piece of work such as a new written practice, a set of procedures for a new method, technique sheets for a new part family, or examinations for a new group of technicians. Scope and deliverables are agreed up front.
  • Audit-preparation sprint: a focused review before a scheduled audit, with gap findings and corrections, so the programme is ready on the day.

Interim Level III cover is often urgent. A Level III leaving can leave a company unable to certify anyone, approve a procedure or answer a customer's corrective action request. We can step into that role while you recruit or develop your own Level III. In Massachusetts, where the labour market for experienced Level IIIs is tight and many inspectors work for large aerospace or defence primes, an outside Level III is often the fastest way to keep a smaller programme compliant.

Remote delivery covers most document work: procedures, written practices, record reviews and technical questions. Onsite visits are scheduled for practical examinations, procedure demonstrations, audits and programme set-up. Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, so you know exactly who your Level III is. If your company also operates in neighbouring states or runs several sites, see our page on multi-site NDT programme harmonisation.

Audit readiness: customer, owner and accreditation audits

Direct answer: Massachusetts NDT programmes are audited by aerospace and defence primes, by plant owners and EPCs, by accreditation bodies for ISO 9001 or ISO/IEC 17025 laboratories, and by state inspectors for radiation safety. Atlantis prepares the NDT side of each: written practice, procedures, certification files, calibration and equipment records.

Aerospace audits are the most demanding. Suppliers to engine and defence primes may face customer source audits and Nadcap-style special-process audits that test whether every technician's certification, every procedure revision and every penetrant or magnetic particle system check can be traced. Our Nadcap AC7114 audit readiness page explains how that kind of audit looks at an NDT programme. We help suppliers prepare the evidence, run a mock audit against the checklist the customer will use and close gaps before the real visit. We do not grant Nadcap accreditation or customer approval; we help you get ready for the people who do.

Owner and EPC audits come with energy, utility and construction work. A gas utility, LNG terminal operator or offshore wind developer may audit an inspection contractor's qualification records before work starts. ISO 9001 audits look at document control and competence records, and ISO/IEC 17025 laboratory audits look at method validation, measurement traceability and personnel competence. Radiography licensees are also inspected by the Department of Public Health Radiation Control Program for radiation safety compliance, which is separate from NDT certification but often reviewed by the same quality manager.

The aerospace audit support, offshore audit support, LNG audit support, infrastructure audit support and nuclear audit support pages describe what each type of audit focuses on. If you have an audit on the calendar, ask about an audit-preparation review for your Massachusetts programme.

A Level III's priorities change by sector.

Aerospace and defence supply chain

The North Shore and Route 128 corridors hold the most technically demanding NDT in the state. Penetrant and magnetic particle lines need system performance checks, process control records and technique sheets per part number. Ultrasonic inspection of forgings and bar stock needs reference standards and procedures written to customer specifications. Eddy current is used for surface cracks and conductivity checks. Forging, casting and precision machining in Worcester County

Worcester and the Blackstone Valley have a long metalworking tradition. Forgings and castings need volumetric and surface inspection, sometimes radiography for castings, ultrasonic testing for forgings, and penetrant or magnetic particle testing for finished parts. Our Worcester NDT consulting and Worcester steel NDT consulting pages cover this region.

LNG storage and handling involves cryogenic materials and welds; gas transmission and distribution involve API 1104 and Part 192 work. Contractors serving these owners need procedures that match the owner's specifications and records that survive an owner audit. Our pipeline audit support page describes what owners usually check.

Offshore wind and marine work

New Bedford and Fall River have become staging points for offshore wind, and South Coast fabricators and marine contractors work on structures, vessels and port facilities. Thick-plate welds call for UT and often PAUT, with clear scan plans. The New Bedford NDT consulting, Fall River NDT consulting and maritime audit support pages cover this work.

Bridges, transit and fabrication

Steel bridge rehabilitation and transit structures need AWS D1.5 procedures and qualified UT, MT and VT personnel. Fabricators supplying structural steel for laboratories, hospitals and commercial buildings work to AWS D1.1. See fabrication audit support for how fabrication audits look at NDT records.

How an engagement works

Direct answer: You describe your methods, codes, customers and deadlines on a call; we agree scope, deliverables and the remote and onsite split; the work is done and reviewed with you; and for ongoing cover we stay on as your named Level III. Pricing is quoted on request after scoping.

  1. Scoping call. We discuss your operation, the methods you perform, the codes and customer specifications you work to, any audit dates and what has gone wrong before.
  2. Document request. If you have an existing written practice, procedures and certification files, you send them for review. If you are starting from nothing, we gather the information needed to build the programme.
  3. Proposal. You receive a written scope: deliverables, what is done remotely, what needs a site visit, and who does it. Quotes are provided on request; there are no published rates.
  4. Delivery. Documents are drafted and reviewed with your quality team. Examinations are scheduled and administered under your written practice. Onsite visits are arranged around your production schedule or outage windows.

Your Level III

Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Buyers in this field want to know who the Level III is, because that person's name sits on the written practice and the procedures. With Atlantis that is stated up front. Anoop also leads Atlantis NDT's SNT-TC-1A-based training, so programme documents and training content stay consistent.

Frequently asked questions about NDT Level III consulting in Massachusetts

Do I need a Level III to run an NDT programme in Massachusetts?

If your company certifies its own personnel to SNT-TC-1A, yes. The recommended practice expects a Level III to be responsible for the written practice, procedures and examinations. That Level III can be an employee or an outside agency, as long as the arrangement is defined in your written practice.

Can an outsourced Level III sign our procedures and written practice?

Yes, when your written practice designates that Level III and they are certified in the relevant methods. The approval must be traceable, and the Level III must actually review the documents, not just sign them.

Who licenses industrial radiography in Massachusetts?

Massachusetts is an NRC Agreement State. Industrial radiography is licensed and inspected by the Massachusetts Department of Public Health Radiation Control Program. That licence covers radiation safety; NDT certification of radiographers is handled under the employer's written practice.

Who inspects boilers and pressure vessels in Massachusetts?

The Boiler and Pressure Vessel Program in the Office of Public Safety and Inspections, part of the Division of Occupational Licensure, registers and inspects non-residential boilers and pressure vessels. NDT for repairs and alterations is done to the ASME and National Board requirements that apply.

Can you help us prepare for an aerospace customer audit?

Yes. We review your written practice, procedures, technique sheets, certification files and process control records against what the customer will check, run a mock audit and help close findings. We do not grant approvals or accreditation.

Is SNT-TC-1A accepted by Massachusetts employers?

SNT-TC-1A is widely used across US industry, including by fabricators, inspection contractors and plant owners in Massachusetts. Some aerospace customers require other schemes, such as NAS 410, so check the customer's specification.

How much does Level III consulting cost in Massachusetts?

Cost depends on scope: the number of methods, whether you need a new written practice or a review, how many people need examining, and how much onsite time is required. Quotes are given on request after a scoping call.

How long does it take to write a written practice?

It depends on the number of methods, how much existing material can be reused and how quickly your team can review drafts. We agree a timetable during scoping rather than quoting a generic figure.

Can you administer Level II examinations at our own plant in Massachusetts?

Yes. General and specific examinations can be administered under controlled conditions, and practical examinations are performed onsite on suitable specimens, all under your written practice.

Do you support gas pipeline and utility contractors?

Yes, with API 1104-based procedures, personnel examinations and owner-audit preparation. Intrastate gas pipeline safety is overseen by the Department of Public Utilities' Pipeline Safety Division with PHMSA.

Do you offer API inspector training or certification?

No. We provide Level III technical support to API 510, 570 and 653 inspection programmes, such as NDT technique selection and procedure review. Our training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based.

Can you also train our technicians?

Yes. Atlantis delivers SNT-TC-1A-based Level I, II and III training online and onsite. See the Massachusetts NDT training page.

Talk to a Level III about your Massachusetts programme

Whether you run a three-person penetrant line in Worcester County, an inspection crew working on gas mains in the Merrimack Valley, or a fabrication shop supplying offshore wind on the South Coast, the Level III questions are the same: is the written practice right, are the procedures right, and can you prove your people are qualified? NDT Level III Consulting Services in Missouri

Short answer: Atlantis NDT gives Missouri employers ASNT NDT Level III support without a full-time hire: outsourced Level III of record, interim cover, SNT-TC-1A written practices, procedures and technique sheets, qualification exams under your written practice, and audit preparation. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, leads the work remotely and onsite at your plant, hangar, shop or site. Atlantis has no office in Missouri. Every engagement is scoped on a call and quoted on request.

Missouri's NDT market is built on aerospace, nuclear power, vehicle assembly, rail and the river, not on refining. St. Louis is home to a major military aircraft production site and a deep aerospace supply chain. Callaway County has the state's nuclear power station. Kansas City and Wentzville assemble trucks and vans, Kansas City is a national rail hub, and two of the country's great rivers carry barge traffic past both cities. Missouri is also one of the few states that is not an NRC Agreement State, which sets it apart from all eight of its neighbours: Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee and Kentucky are all Agreement States, so radiography crews crossing the state line change licensing authority. A Level III serving Missouri needs to know aerospace process control, nuclear quality requirements and federal radiography rules in the same week. This page explains how that works and how to request a Missouri Level III consultation.

Why Missouri NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 make a Level III responsible for the written practice, procedure approval and qualification exams in any NDT programme. Missouri's aerospace, nuclear, automotive, rail and power employers are audited by primes, utilities and customers who examine exactly that work, so every programme needs a capable Level III, on staff or outsourced.

St. Louis and the aerospace supply chain

Boeing's St. Louis site builds military aircraft, including fighter, trainer and unmanned programmes, and it sits at the centre of a supply chain of machine shops, forging and casting houses, heat treaters, metal finishers and composite fabricators across the St. Louis region and into the Metro East. Aerospace NDT here means penetrant and magnetic particle lines with tight process control, eddy current on fastener holes and machined features, ultrasonic testing of composites, bonded structures and thick sections, and radiography of castings and welded assemblies. Suppliers are held to prime-contractor specifications and, very often, Nadcap NDT accreditation. A written practice that will not survive a Nadcap auditor is the single most common reason suppliers call a Level III.

St. Louis also has power stations along the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, chemical and pharmaceutical plants, food and beverage production, barge fleeting and repair, and General Motors' Wentzville assembly plant to the west. Across the river in Illinois, refineries and steel mills at Wood River, Granite City and Sauget draw St. Louis-based contractors, and those crews then work under Illinois rules on that side of the river.

Mid-Missouri: Fulton, Jefferson City and Columbia

Ameren's Callaway Energy Center near Fulton is Missouri's nuclear power station. Refuelling outages bring ASME Section XI in-service inspection, and suppliers of components and services to the plant work under nuclear quality assurance programmes. The University of Missouri in Columbia operates a research reactor. Jefferson City and Columbia add manufacturing and state infrastructure work.

Kansas City

Kansas City combines Ford's Kansas City Assembly Plant at Claycomo, the Kansas City National Security Campus, which manufactures non-nuclear components for the National Nuclear Security Administration, the rail yards and shops of several Class I railroads, Evergy's power stations, a large engineering and construction sector, and pipeline and fuels terminals. Rail work brings UT of axles and wheels, MT of couplers, side frames and bolsters, and weld inspection in car repair shops. Defence manufacturing brings strict process control and customer quality requirements.

Southern and rural Missouri

Springfield and Joplin have trucking, food processing and metal fabrication. Fort Leonard Wood and Whiteman Air Force Base add military construction and maintenance. South-east Missouri's lead belt has mining, smelting and recycling operations, and the Bootheel and Cape Girardeau have river industry and cement production. Crude oil, refined products and natural gas transmission pipelines cross the state, bringing construction, integrity digs and compressor station work.

Missouri regulators that touch NDT

Radiography. Missouri is not an NRC Agreement State. Industrial radiography with radioactive sources in Missouri is licensed and inspected by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, through its Region III office, under 10 CFR Part 34. The state keeps jurisdiction over X-ray equipment and certain other radiation sources. Contractors who also work in Illinois, Kansas or other neighbouring Agreement States deal with a different licensing authority on each side of the line, so reciprocity paperwork matters for St. Louis and Kansas City crews. Radiation safety is a separate obligation from SNT-TC-1A RT certification, and a Level III should check that RT procedures and the radiation safety programme agree.

Boilers and pressure vessels. The Missouri Division of Fire Safety's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Unit oversees inspection and certificates of inspection for non-exempt boilers and pressure vessels, with installation permits and inspections carried out within the National Board framework.

Pipelines. The Missouri Public Service Commission oversees intrastate gas pipeline safety. The federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) regulates interstate gas and hazardous-liquid pipelines crossing Missouri.

Direct answer: Atlantis NDT offers outsourced Level III of record, interim Level III, written practices, procedures and technique sheets, qualification exams, programme audits and inspection-programme technique support, separately or as a retained package. Missouri's mix of aerospace, nuclear, rail, automotive and power clients means the package is built around your sector, not a template.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: A written practice is the employer's own procedure for training, examining, certifying and recertifying NDT personnel. Because SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, auditors hold you to your written practice. Atlantis writes new written practices for Missouri employers, rewrites ones that no longer match the work, and audits programmes against them.

For St. Louis aerospace suppliers, the written practice has to do more than satisfy SNT-TC-1A. Prime contractors and Nadcap auditors expect it to address the personnel qualification standard named on the purchase order, which is frequently NAS 410 rather than SNT-TC-1A, along with the responsible Level 3, examination content, and vision and practical exam details. A supplier that holds an SNT-TC-1A written practice but ships parts under an NAS 410 requirement has a gap an auditor will find. See NAS 410 responsible Level 3 for context; Atlantis's own training is SNT-TC-1A-based, and our consulting addresses how your programme meets what your customer specifies.

For nuclear suppliers and service contractors around Callaway, the written practice often needs to align with CP-189 and with the customer's quality assurance programme. For rail shops, it has to cover the methods and components the railroad's or car owner's requirements call for; see NDT for AAR M-1003 tank car facilities. For fabricators and contractors, a lean SNT-TC-1A written practice for VT, MT, PT and UT is usually right.

Points we always settle:

  • Methods, techniques and levels covered, including PAUT, TOFD and digital radiography.
  • Training and experience requirements, linked to the training requirements matrix and your customers' standards.
  • Exam preparation, administration, grading and the role of an outside Level III.
  • Vision examinations and records.
  • Recertification, interrupted service and revocation.
  • How customer-specific requirements override or add to the base document.

See written practice development, written practice for aerospace, written practice for nuclear power and SNT-TC-1A certification. For a review of an existing programme, ask for a Missouri written practice review.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in Missouri

Direct answer: Missouri NDT procedures must follow the document that governs each job: aerospace prime specifications and ASTM practices in St. Louis, ASME Section XI and nuclear quality requirements around Callaway, ASME Section I and B31.1 at power stations, rail industry requirements in Kansas City shops, AWS for structures and bridges, and API 1104 for pipelines. A Level III approves the procedure and the technique sheets under it.

  • Aerospace and defence (St. Louis, Kansas City): prime-contractor process specifications; ASTM E1417 penetrant and ASTM E1444 magnetic particle practices; ultrasonic, eddy current and radiographic specifications named on drawings; customer source-inspection requirements.
  • Nuclear (Callaway and its suppliers): ASME Section XI for in-service inspection, Section III for new components, Section V methods, and the customer's quality assurance programme. See NQA-1 nuclear supplier NDT programmes.
  • Power stations (Ameren and Evergy fleets): ASME Section I and B31.1, the National Board Inspection Code for repairs, and utility standards.
  • Rail (Kansas City and St. Louis shops): industry and car-owner requirements for wheels, axles, couplers, side frames, tank cars and welded repairs.
  • Bridges and structures: AWS D1.5 for bridges and D1.1 for buildings and general structures, with Missouri Department of Transportation requirements on state work, including the Mississippi and Missouri river crossings.
  • Pipelines and terminals: API 1104 for girth welds; ASME B31.3 and API 510, 570 and 653 at terminals and plants.
  • Barges and river equipment: classification and owner requirements for hull and structural welds and thickness gauging.

Technique sheets are where Missouri programmes most often fall short. An aerospace supplier needs technique sheets tied to part numbers and approved by the customer where required; a rail shop needs sheets for each component family; a power-station crew needs sheets for headers, tubes and small-bore piping. Atlantis writes and approves both procedures and technique sheets and supports procedure demonstration where required. For in-service inspection of vessels, piping and tanks, Atlantis supports the NDT side while the owner's certified inspectors make inspection decisions. See API 510, API 570 and API 653 inspector services.

Outsourced and interim Level III for Missouri crews

An interim Level III does the same for a set period while a permanent Level III is recruited or developed. Document work is remote; practical exams and audits are onsite.

The St. Louis aerospace supply chain is full of shops with a handful of NDT inspectors on one or two methods, usually penetrant and magnetic particle. They need a responsible Level III who knows aerospace process control and can face a prime or Nadcap auditor, but not a full-time one. A retained outsourced Level III gives them that: approvals and exam work done remotely, and visits for practical exams, process audits and audit days.

Interim cover is common in Kansas City and St. Louis manufacturing and rail, where long-serving Level IIIs are retiring. When one leaves, certifications and procedure approvals start to age immediately. An interim engagement keeps exams and approvals moving, closes open audit findings and hands over cleanly. See interim NDT Level III, Level III succession planning, what an outside Level III can and cannot do and Level III method scope limitations.

To train technicians or develop a future Level III, see the Missouri NDT training page, plus city pages for St. Louis and Kansas City. Audit readiness: customer, owner and accreditation audits

Direct answer: Missouri NDT programmes face Nadcap-style and prime-contractor audits in aerospace, utility and quality assurance audits in nuclear and power, railroad and car-owner audits in rail, ISO 9001 surveillance and ISO/IEC 17025 assessments for laboratories. Atlantis runs a gap assessment against the relevant criteria, helps you close findings and supports you during the audit.

What tends to surface in programmes like Missouri's:

  • A written practice to SNT-TC-1A while purchase orders call up a different personnel standard.
  • Penetrant and magnetic particle process-control records, such as system performance checks, light intensity and bath concentration, that are incomplete or inconsistent.
  • Certification files missing experience records or a current vision exam.
  • Procedures and technique sheets without traceable Level III approval or at the wrong revision on the floor.
  • Reference standards and probes without traceable calibration or verification.
  • Radiography paperwork that mixes NRC radiation-safety requirements with SNT-TC-1A certification, or fails to cover work across the river in Illinois.

NDT Level III Consulting Services in Montana

Short answer: Montana employers can engage Atlantis NDT for ASNT NDT Level III services delivered remotely and onsite at their own facility: an outsourced or interim Level III of record, SNT-TC-1A written practices and audits, procedures and technique sheets, qualification exams under the employer's written practice, and audit preparation. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, leads each engagement, and scopes are quoted on request.

Montana's NDT demand comes from a short list of heavy industries spread across a very large state. The Yellowstone Valley around Billings and Laurel holds three refineries and the pipelines and terminals that serve them. Great Falls adds a refinery that has moved into renewable fuels and the Air Force base that maintains the state's missile fields. The mining belt runs from the copper pit at Butte to the platinum and palladium mines along the Beartooth front and the smelter and refinery at Columbus. Eastern Montana shares the Bakken and Williston Basin oil play with North Dakota, Colstrip runs one of the largest coal-fired plants in the West, and hydroelectric dams sit on the Missouri, Clark Fork, Flathead and Kootenai rivers. Each of these sectors needs NDT, and each audits its contractors. What Montana inspection companies and plant quality departments rarely have is a full-time Level III. This hub explains how outsourced Level III support works here, which regulators and codes apply, and how to start. To skip ahead, ask for a Montana Level III quote.

Why Montana NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer's NDT programme needs a Level III to own the written practice, approve procedures and examine Level I and II personnel. Montana's inspection companies are mostly small and serve refineries, mines, pipelines and power plants that audit them, so an outside Level III is often the practical way to meet that requirement.

Look at where the work sits. In Billings, the Phillips 66 refinery and the former ExxonMobil refinery now owned by Par Pacific, together with the CHS refinery in neighbouring Laurel, process crude from Canada, the Bakken and Wyoming. Refinery maintenance and turnarounds generate ultrasonic thickness surveys, weld inspection on piping and vessel repairs, radiography of small-bore piping, and positive material identification, while the pipelines and product terminals around Billings add pipeline and tank inspection. In Great Falls, the refinery has added a renewable-fuels unit, which brought new construction and the fabrication inspection that comes with it.

Mining is the second pillar. The Butte open pit and concentrator, the Stillwater and East Boulder underground mines and the Columbus smelter and base-metal refinery run magnetic particle and ultrasonic inspection on haul trucks, shovels, hoists, mill shells, crushers, pressure vessels and process piping, much of it during planned maintenance shutdowns. Mine operators work under the federal Mine Safety and Health Administration, and their NDT contractors are expected to show qualified personnel and documented procedures.

Power and water infrastructure is the third. Colstrip's coal units, gas-fired plants and the federal and utility hydro dams need boiler tube inspection, weld inspection on penstocks and turbine components, and bolting and structural inspection. Add Malmstrom Air Force Base, rail car and locomotive work along the BNSF lines, structural steel fabrication for bridges and buildings, and the eastern Montana oilfield around Sidney, Glendive and Baker, and the state supports more NDT than its population suggests.

Regulators shape the programme. Montana is not an NRC Agreement State. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, through its Region IV office, licenses byproduct material such as iridium-192 used in gamma radiography, while the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services registers radiation-producing machines, including industrial X-ray units. Boilers are inspected under the Montana Department of Labor and Industry's boiler programme, which issues boiler operating certificates after inspection. Intrastate gas pipeline safety is handled by the Montana Public Service Commission's Pipeline Safety Program in partnership with PHMSA, and PHMSA regulates interstate gas and hazardous-liquid lines directly. The Montana Board of Oil and Gas Conservation regulates wells and production. Confirm the current licensing authority for each activity with the agency before work starts.

Level III services for Montana employers

Direct answer: Montana employers typically need an outsourced or interim Level III, a written practice that matches what they really do, procedures and technique sheets written to the right code, qualification exams under their written practice, and audit preparation. Most of this is delivered remotely, with onsite visits for practical exams and audits.

Atlantis provides Level III expertise rather than field crews. We do not supply inspectors, and we do not hold owner approvals for you; the work sits behind your own people. Background on the national service is on the ASNT Level III consulting services page and the consulting overview.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: The written practice is the employer's document that defines how NDT personnel are trained, examined, certified and recertified under SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis writes new written practices for Montana employers and audits existing ones so the document fits the methods, clients and staffing you actually have.

In small markets the written practice is often the weakest document in the quality system. We regularly see three Montana-type problems. First, the practice was inherited from a previous owner or a larger company and still names a Level III who left years ago, which means nobody currently has authority to approve procedures or certify staff. Second, the practice lists methods the company no longer performs and omits the ones it does; a shop that added phased array for refinery work, or eddy current for heat-exchanger tubing, may have technicians performing a technique the practice does not cover. Third, the practice sets experience and examination requirements that the company cannot document, so every certification file is exposed in an audit.

A written-practice engagement defines scope, training and experience requirements referenced to the current SNT-TC-1A edition, examinations and grading, vision examinations, certification, recertification, interrupted service, transfer of certification and the authority of the Level III. Where a customer requires ANSI/ASNT CP-189 or another standard, we show where it changes your document. Training-hour figures are taken from the training requirements matrix. See written practice development and the SNT-TC-1A guide, or request a written-practice review for your Montana company.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in Montana

Direct answer: Montana NDT procedures follow the code that governs each asset: ASME B31.3, Section VIII, API 510 and 570 at refineries; API 650 and 653 for tanks; API 1104 and 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 for pipelines; ASME Section I and the National Board Inspection Code for boilers; AWS D1.1 and D1.5 for structures and bridges; OEM requirements for mining equipment.

Procedure work in Montana spans more sectors than most states of its size, and each has its own pitfalls:

  • Refining. Thickness monitoring, weld inspection on repairs and alterations, and PAUT or TOFD on thick-wall vessels. The procedure has to deliver data in the form the owner's authorised inspector uses, and technique sheets should match component geometry and material.
  • Mining. Magnetic particle inspection of haul-truck frames, wheel motors, shovel and dragline booms and hoist components; ultrasonic inspection of shafts, pins and mill trunnions. Requirements usually come from the equipment manufacturer and AWS D1.1 for weld repairs, and procedures must cover field conditions such as dirty or coated surfaces.
  • Power generation. Boiler tube thickness and weld inspection during outages, high-energy piping inspection, and turbine and generator component inspection, mostly to ASME Section I, B31.1 and owner specifications.
  • Hydro. Penstock welds, gates and hoist components, and turbine runners, often to owner or federal agency specifications.
  • Pipelines. Girth-weld radiography or automated UT to API 1104 and operator specifications, plus integrity digs that need UT, MT and visual inspection.
  • Cold weather. Winter work in Montana raises the same problems as further north: couplant, penetrant and magnetic particle product temperature limits and calibration at examination temperature.

We write procedures and technique sheets, review procedures provided by others, and sort out conflicts between owner specifications, codes and your written practice. For sector context see our audit-support pages for refining, mining, steel and metals, power generation, pipelines and fabrication.

Outsourced and interim Level III for Montana crews

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III is a named ASNT Level III who serves as your programme's Level III of record under a standing agreement; an interim Level III fills a gap. For Montana employers the work is mostly remote, with onsite visits for practical exams, procedure demonstrations and audits at the client's facility.

Three engagement models cover most Montana requests:

  1. Ongoing outsourced (retained) Level III. Atlantis is named as the Level III in your written practice. We approve procedures, administer exams, answer field questions, review the programme annually and support you in audits. This suits Billings-area contractors and plant quality teams that need Level III authority without a full-time salary.
  2. Project-based work. A defined deliverable such as a new written practice, a procedure set for a new refinery or mine contract, technique sheets for a PAUT scope, or an exam campaign before a turnaround.
  3. Audit-preparation sprint. A focused review before a known audit, producing a corrective-action list and support while you close it.

Distances in Montana are long, so remote work is the default: written practices, procedures, exam preparation and record reviews all happen by video call and document exchange. Practical exams need the candidate, real specimens and the examiner in one place, so those are scheduled onsite at your facility in Billings, Great Falls, Butte, Missoula or wherever you operate. Atlantis has no office or training centre in Montana. Read about interim cover on the interim NDT Level III page, or discuss outsourced Level III coverage for your Montana programme.

Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Montana buyers usually want to know who will sign their procedures and examine their people; here that is a named Level III, not an anonymous pool.

Audit readiness: customer, owner and accreditation audits

Direct answer: Montana NDT contractors are audited by refinery and pipeline owners during prequalification and after incidents, by mine operators and OEMs, by prime contractors on construction projects, and by ISO 9001 or ISO/IEC 17025 assessors. A Level III audit-readiness review checks written practice, procedures, certifications and records before the auditor arrives.

The findings are rarely surprising: certifications issued under an outdated written practice; vision exams that lapsed while a technician was on another job; practical exams with no record of the specimens used or how they were graded; procedures that reference a superseded code edition or were never approved by a Level III; calibration records that do not tie to the instruments listed in reports; and technicians performing techniques outside their certification. The answer is to find them first.

An audit-readiness engagement samples personnel files, procedures and reports, maps them against the written practice and the customer specification, and produces a prioritised corrective-action list. We can then support the fixes, from revised procedures to re-examination under your written practice. For aerospace and defence suppliers, we help with Nadcap-style audit preparation as context, while the audit itself is run by the accreditation body. For testing laboratories pursuing ISO/IEC 17025, we help with the NDT technical content. See also infrastructure audit support and aerospace audit support. Audit already scheduled? Book a Montana audit-readiness call.

Inspection programme support for Montana refineries and terminals

Direct answer: At Montana refineries and terminals, API 510, 570 and 653 inspections are performed and signed by the owner's authorised inspectors. Atlantis supports that work on the NDT side, with method selection, procedures, technique qualification, data quality and personnel qualification. We do not provide authorised inspector certification training.

Refineries in Billings, Laurel and Great Falls generate thickness data, weld inspection records and tank floor scans every year, and the value of that data depends on repeatable measurement locations, techniques that can find the damage mechanism of interest, and reporting the authorised inspector can use. A Level III can help a contractor or owner standardise thickness-monitoring practice, choose between conventional UT, PAUT corrosion mapping and profile radiography, and tighten technique sheets for repair welds. Background is on our API 510, API 570 and API 653 support pages.

Cities we support across Montana

Direct answer: Atlantis supports Montana employers statewide, remotely and onsite at the client's facility. Requests come mostly from Billings and Laurel, Great Falls, Butte and Anaconda, the Columbus and Nye mining district, Colstrip, Missoula, Bozeman, Helena and the eastern oilfield around Sidney and Glendive.

  • Billings and Laurel. Refineries, pipelines, product terminals, rail and the largest concentration of inspection and fabrication contractors in the state. Related pages: NDT training in Billings, oil and gas NDT training in Billings, Practical NDT simulator for Billings, NDT ERP for Billings companies and inspection management software for Laurel.
  • Great Falls. Refinery and renewable-fuels production, Malmstrom Air Force Base and agricultural-equipment and fabrication shops.
  • Butte, Anaconda and Helena. Copper mining, mine services, legacy smelter infrastructure and state agencies.
  • Columbus, Nye and the Beartooth front. Platinum-group-metal mining, the smelter and base-metal refinery, and the contractors that maintain them.
  • Colstrip and eastern Montana. Coal-fired power, coal mining and the Montana side of the Williston Basin around Sidney, Glendive and Baker.
  • Missoula, Bozeman and the Flathead. Wood products, hydro dams, aerospace and photonics manufacturing, and general fabrication. See NDT ERP for Missoula.

Statewide: the Montana NDT training hub. Neighbouring consulting hubs: Idaho and South Dakota. Many Montana contractors also work across the Williston and Powder River basins in North Dakota and Wyoming, and the same Level III support applies there.

Training alongside the Level III service

Direct answer: Montana clients often pair Level III consulting with SNT-TC-1A training for their own staff, delivered live online or onsite at their facility. When the same Level III writes the written practice, the procedures and the exams, the training lines up with what technicians are certified to do.

Training covers Level I, II and III in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET. Live online classes suit technicians spread across a large state; onsite classes suit a crew gathered before a refinery turnaround or a mine shutdown. The Practical NDT simulator lets trainees practise twelve methods across five virtual environments before their practical exams; it is for practice only and does not replace a practical exam on real specimens. See training, online NDT training, corporate NDT training and ASNT Level III training.

How an engagement works

Direct answer: A Montana engagement begins with a call about your methods, customers, codes and staffing, followed by a written scope and quote. Document work is remote; practical exams and site visits take place at your facility. Timelines are agreed in the scope, not assumed.

  1. Discovery call. Methods and techniques performed, customers and codes, staffing and certification status, and the trigger: a new contract, an audit, a departing Level III or growth.
  2. Document review. You share your written practice, procedures and a sample of certification files and reports; we identify gaps.
  3. Scope and quote. Deliverables, remote and onsite elements and responsibilities in writing. Pricing is quote on request.
  4. Delivery. Drafting, approval and issue of documents; exams under your written practice; corrective actions; ongoing Level III duties if retained.
  5. Onsite visits. Practical exams, procedure demonstrations and audit support at your Montana site, planned around turnarounds, shutdowns and weather.
  6. Review. Annual programme review for retained clients and updates when codes, customers or methods change.

Ready to start? Request a scoped Level III proposal for Montana.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I find an NDT Level III consultant in Montana?

Montana has few independent Level IIIs, so many employers engage an outside Level III who works remotely and visits onsite. Atlantis offers that service, led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III.

Is Montana an NRC Agreement State?

No. The NRC licenses byproduct material such as iridium-192 used for gamma radiography in Montana, through its Region IV office. The Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services registers radiation machines, including industrial X-ray units. Confirm current requirements before radiography work starts.

Who inspects boilers in Montana?

Boiler safety inspections fall under the Montana Department of Labor and Industry's boiler programme, which issues boiler operating certificates after inspection. Insurance special inspectors also take part in many jurisdictions; check the current arrangement with the department.

Who regulates gas pipeline safety in Montana?

The Montana Public Service Commission's Pipeline Safety Program covers intrastate gas pipelines in partnership with PHMSA, which regulates interstate gas and hazardous-liquid pipelines directly.

They act as the Level III named in your written practice: approving procedures, administering exams, reviewing certifications, answering technical questions and supporting audits. It gives a small company Level III authority without a full-time hire.

Yes. We write new written practices and audit existing ones against the current SNT-TC-1A edition and your customers' specifications.

Quote on request. Cost depends on the methods involved, retained versus project work, the number of exams and onsite visits. Atlantis keeps its services affordable, accessible and fully customisable.

No. Atlantis has no physical office or training centre in Montana; work is delivered remotely and onsite at the client's facility.

NDT Level III Consulting Services in New Brunswick

Short answer: Atlantis NDT provides ASNT NDT Level III services to New Brunswick employers, remotely and onsite at the employer's own facility: an outsourced or interim Level III for SNT-TC-1A programmes, written practices and audits, procedures and technique sheets, qualification exams under the employer's written practice, and preparation for refinery, utility and customer audits. Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, and every scope is quoted on request.

New Brunswick packs a remarkable concentration of inspection-heavy assets into a small province. Saint John is home to Canada's largest oil refinery, an LNG import and regasification terminal at Canaport, a deep-water port, a pulp and paper and tissue complex and a long list of fabrication and maintenance contractors. On the Bay of Fundy coast west of Saint John, Point Lepreau is the province's nuclear generating station. NB Power also runs thermal stations at Coleson Cove and Belledune and the Mactaquac hydro station on the Saint John River. Pulp and paper mills, sawmills, food processors, a gas pipeline network linked to New England, and manufacturers around Moncton, Fredericton and Edmundston complete the map. Much of this work sits close to the US border and serves US customers or US-code projects, which is where an ASNT Level III fits naturally. If you are ready, ask for a New Brunswick Level III quote.

Why New Brunswick NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: A New Brunswick employer that certifies NDT personnel under ASNT SNT-TC-1A needs a Level III who owns the written practice, approves procedures and examines staff. The refinery, the LNG terminal, the nuclear station, utilities and US customers audit their NDT contractors, and most New Brunswick shops are too small for a full-time Level III, so an outsourced Level III is the practical answer.

The Saint John refinery drives the largest single block of NDT demand. Turnarounds bring in crews for vessel and exchanger inspection, piping thickness surveys, weld inspection on repairs and alterations, PAUT and TOFD on thick sections and tank inspection at the refinery and its marine terminals. The contractors who serve it are audited on their personnel records and procedures as closely as on their field results, and turnaround schedules leave no time to fix a written practice once the job has started.

Canaport LNG adds cryogenic service. Stainless and nickel-steel piping, large storage tanks and marine unloading systems need weld inspection techniques suited to austenitic and high-nickel materials, along with careful documentation for the owner. The Brunswick Pipeline carries gas from the terminal toward the US border, and the Maritimes and Northeast Pipeline crosses the province, adding pipeline construction and integrity work.

Point Lepreau brings nuclear-grade expectations. In-service inspection of a CANDU station follows CSA N285-series requirements and the licensee's own programme under the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, and NDT suppliers to the station face strict qualification, procedure and document-control rules. Advanced reactor developers have also proposed projects at the Lepreau site, which would extend that quality culture to new construction. Even contractors who never enter the station feel the effect, because the same standards spread to the shops that supply it.

Power, paper and manufacturing fill out the rest. Coleson Cove and Belledune need boiler tube, header and high-energy piping inspection during outages; the Mactaquac station needs inspection of turbines, gates and structural steel; pulp and paper mills in Saint John, Edmundston and elsewhere run recovery boilers, digesters, pressure vessels and piping that depend on UT, MT, PT and RT. Fabricators and manufacturers around Moncton, Fredericton and the north shore build structures and equipment for Canadian and US customers.

The regulatory picture: boilers and pressure vessels are regulated under the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Act and its regulations by the province's Technical Inspection Services, part of the Department of Justice and Public Safety (confirm the current department name), which handles device registration, inspection before service, registration of quality assurance or quality control plans and registration of welding procedures. Industrial gamma radiography is licensed by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC), which also regulates Point Lepreau; exposure devices must be operated by CNSC-certified exposure device operators or under their direct supervision. Interprovincial and international pipelines fall under the Canada Energy Regulator. Confirm current provincial requirements for X-ray equipment before mobilising.

Which NDT certification scheme applies in New Brunswick?

Direct answer: Canada's national NDT personnel scheme is CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (ISO 9712), and the nuclear station, utilities and many Canadian owners call for it. ASNT SNT-TC-1A is common for US customers and US-code work, and some refinery and fabrication contracts accept it. Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A Level III services plus procedure, technique and audit support; we are not a CGSB or ISO 9712 certification body.

A note on the national scheme, because it changed this year. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026. The standard remains valid, and both Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body and CWB Group, as an accredited certification body, have said they continue to certify. Confirm the current certification body for your method and sector before you rely on it.

Refinery, LNG and terminal work in Saint John

Direct answer: Saint John's refinery, LNG terminal and marine terminals generate most of New Brunswick's NDT volume. Contractors need procedures matched to refinery damage mechanisms and cryogenic materials, technique sheets their technicians can follow under turnaround pressure, and personnel files that pass the owner's audit. Atlantis supports this from the Level III side.

Refinery work covers pressure vessels, heat exchangers, process piping, heaters and storage tanks. Thickness monitoring locations must be consistent from one turnaround to the next; repair and alteration welds need the right volumetric method; exchanger bundles may need eddy current or IRIS; and corrosion under insulation calls for a screening strategy that the inspector trusts. At the LNG terminal, stainless and high-nickel welds call for techniques and calibration blocks suited to coarse-grained austenitic structures, and procedures must say so explicitly.

API 510, 570 and 653 inspections at these sites are performed and signed by the owner's authorised inspectors. Atlantis supports that work from the NDT side, with method selection, procedure fit, technique qualification and data quality; we do not supply authorised inspectors or offer API certification training. See API 510, API 570 and API 653 consulting, plus refining and LNG audit support. Planning ahead of a turnaround? Ask about turnaround procedures and exams for your New Brunswick crew.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: A written practice is the employer's document that defines how NDT personnel are trained, examined, certified and recertified under SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis writes new written practices for New Brunswick employers and audits existing ones so the document matches the methods you perform and the owners who audit you.

Recurring problems: a written practice that names a Level III who has moved on; national-scheme certificates filed as if they were employer certifications, without the employer's own exams or documented review; methods such as PAUT, TOFD or eddy current performed but not listed; experience claims for technicians hired from Alberta or from US contractors left undocumented; practical exams with no specimen or grading records; and vision exams that lapsed between turnarounds.

A written-practice engagement defines scope, training and experience requirements referenced to the current SNT-TC-1A edition, examination content and grading, vision exams, certification and recertification, interrupted service, transfer of certification and the Level III's authority, and records how certificates under other schemes are filed. Where a customer requires CP-189, we show where your practice must differ. Training-hour figures come from the training requirements matrix. See written practice development and the SNT-TC-1A guide, or request a written-practice review for your New Brunswick company.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in New Brunswick

Direct answer: New Brunswick procedures follow the governing code or specification: CSA B51 with the ASME Code for provincially registered pressure equipment; owner specifications and API practice at the refinery and terminals; CSA N285-series requirements and the licensee's programme at the nuclear station; CSA Z662 for pipelines; and CSA W59 or AWS D1.1 for structures.

  • Refining. Thickness monitoring, weld inspection on repairs, PAUT and TOFD on heavy-wall equipment, exchanger tube inspection and tank floor and shell inspection.
  • LNG and cryogenic service. UT techniques for austenitic and high-nickel welds, PT on stainless components, and procedures that address coarse-grained material and calibration-block selection.
  • Nuclear supply. Procedures and records written to the licensee's requirements, with strict revision control and traceability; suppliers should confirm the qualification scheme the licensee requires.
  • Power generation. Boiler tube, header and high-energy piping inspection at thermal stations; turbine, gate and structural inspection at hydro stations.
  • Pulp and paper. Recovery boiler, digester, pressure-vessel and piping inspection during mill shutdowns.
  • Pipelines. Girth-weld radiography or automated UT on construction and integrity-dig inspection, within the radiography company's CNSC licence conditions.
  • Coastal weather. Fog, salt air and winter cold affect surface condition, penetrant and particle product limits and couplant; the procedure should cover them.

Sector notes: petrochemical, nuclear, power generation, pipeline and fabrication. For nuclear suppliers see written practices for nuclear NDT.

Outsourced and interim Level III for New Brunswick crews

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III is a named ASNT Level III who serves as your SNT-TC-1A programme's Level III under a standing agreement; an interim Level III fills a gap. For New Brunswick employers the work is mostly remote, with onsite visits for practical exams, procedure demonstrations and audits at the employer's facility.

Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, so you know exactly who approves your procedures and examines your people.

Audit readiness: customer, owner and accreditation audits

Direct answer: New Brunswick NDT suppliers are audited by the refinery, the LNG terminal, the nuclear licensee, NB Power, mill owners and US customers, and some by ISO 9001, ISO/IEC 17025 or CSA W178.1 assessors. A Level III review before the audit finds gaps in the written practice, certifications, procedures and reports while there is time to fix them.

Common findings: certifications under a superseded written practice; mixed-scheme personnel files with no clear link between certificate and contract; expired vision exams; practical exams without specimen or grading records; procedures not approved by a Level III or tied to an outdated code edition; calibration blocks unsuitable for austenitic welds; and technicians working outside their certified methods. Nuclear suppliers face additional expectations on document control, traceability and corrective action that general contractors may not be used to.

An audit-readiness engagement samples personnel files, procedures and reports, maps them to the written practice and the owner's specification, and delivers a prioritised corrective-action list with follow-up support. Certification and approval decisions remain with the auditing body or owner. Audit coming? Book a New Brunswick audit-readiness call.

Cities we support across New Brunswick

Direct answer: Atlantis supports New Brunswick employers province-wide, remotely and onsite at the client's facility. Most requests come from Saint John, the Point Lepreau area, Moncton and Dieppe, Fredericton and the Mactaquac area, Bathurst and Belledune, Edmundston and the Miramichi.

Direct answer: New Brunswick clients can combine Level III consulting with ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for their own technicians, live online or onsite at their facility. Atlantis training is SNT-TC-1A only and does not prepare candidates for national CAN/CGSB-48.9712 certification or nuclear-specific qualification.

Training covers Level I, II and III in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET for employers whose customers expect SNT-TC-1A certification. The Practical NDT simulator lets trainees practise twelve methods in five virtual environments, including an oil and gas site and a storage tank, before practical exams; it is a practice tool and does not replace a practical exam on real specimens. How an engagement works

Direct answer: A New Brunswick engagement begins with a call about your methods, owners, codes, certification schemes and staffing, followed by a written scope and quote. Document work runs remotely; practical exams and site visits take place at your facility. Timing is agreed in the scope rather than assumed.

Frequently asked questions

How do I find an NDT Level III consultant in New Brunswick?

Independent Level IIIs are scarce in New Brunswick, so many contractors use an outside Level III who works remotely and visits onsite. Atlantis offers that for SNT-TC-1A programmes, led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III.

Who regulates boilers and pressure vessels in New Brunswick?

Technical Inspection Services, part of the Department of Justice and Public Safety, administers the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Act, including device registration, inspection before service and registration of quality plans and welding procedures. Confirm the current department name.

Is ASNT certification accepted at New Brunswick plants?

It depends on the owner. US customers and some contracts accept SNT-TC-1A; the nuclear station, utilities and many Canadian owners call for CAN/CGSB-48.9712. Read the contract or owner specification before assigning technicians.

Is CAN/CGSB-48.9712 still valid after the CGSB closed?

Yes. The Canadian General Standards Board closed on 1 April 2026, but the standard remains valid and certification bodies have said they continue to certify. Confirm the current certification body.

Can you help us become a supplier to Point Lepreau?

We can review your procedures, document control and personnel records against the requirements a nuclear licensee typically imposes. Supplier approval and the required qualification scheme are decided by the licensee.

Do I need a licence for industrial radiography in New Brunswick?

Gamma radiography requires a CNSC licence for the company and CNSC-certified exposure device operators, or work under their direct supervision. Confirm current provincial requirements for X-ray equipment.

Can you write UT procedures for LNG and stainless welds?

Yes. We write and review UT and PT procedures and technique sheets for austenitic and high-nickel welds, including calibration-block selection and coarse-grain considerations.

What does an outsourced Level III do for a Saint John contractor?

They act as the Level III named in your SNT-TC-1A written practice: approving procedures, administering exams, reviewing certifications, answering field questions and supporting owner audits, without a full-time hire.

Can practical exams be done remotely?

No. Practical exams need the candidate, real specimens and the examiner together, so they are held onsite at your facility.

How much does Level III consulting cost in New Brunswick?

Quote on request. Cost depends on methods, retained versus project work, exam volume and onsite visits. Atlantis keeps its services affordable, accessible and fully customisable.

Does Atlantis have an office in Saint John or Moncton?

No. Atlantis has no physical office or training centre in New Brunswick; work is delivered remotely and onsite at the client's facility.

NDT Level III Consulting Services in New South Wales

Short answer: Atlantis NDT gives New South Wales employers a named ASNT NDT Level III, delivered remotely and onsite at the employer's own facility. Services cover outsourced and interim Level III duties under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, written practice development and audits, procedures and technique sheets, qualification exams under the employer's written practice, and audit preparation. Every engagement is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, and quoted on request.

In NSW, as across Australia, the default credentials are local: AINDT certification under ISO 9712 for NDT technicians, AICIP certification for in-service pressure-equipment inspectors working to AS/NZS 3788, and NATA accreditation for laboratories and inspection bodies. Atlantis holds none of these and does not offer them. We serve a specific need inside that market: NSW companies that work for US aerospace and defence primes, US-owned operators, or projects specified to ASME, API or AWS codes, and that therefore run, or need to run, an SNT-TC-1A programme. If that is you, request an NSW Level III quote.

Why New South Wales NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: Any NSW employer certifying NDT personnel under ASNT SNT-TC-1A needs a Level III to own the written practice, approve procedures and run exams. In New South Wales the demand comes mainly from aerospace and defence suppliers in Sydney and the Hunter, steel and heavy fabrication in the Illawarra, power-station outages, and fabricators building to US codes for export or US-owned clients.

New South Wales has a more diversified inspection market than the resource states. The Hunter region around Newcastle combines the world's largest coal export port, the Tomago aluminium smelter, ammonium nitrate production on Kooragang Island, heavy engineering workshops and the coal-fired power stations of the Hunter and Central Coast. Bayswater and Mount Piper continue to generate, and Origin has announced that all four units at Eraring will keep operating until April 2029. Boiler tubes, headers, high-energy piping, turbine components and coal-handling plant need inspection at every outage, and power companies audit their contractors closely. See power generation audit support.

The Illawarra is steel country. The Port Kembla steelworks, with its blast furnaces, coke ovens, rolling mills and service network, plus the Port Kembla port and gas import terminal, sustain a dense cluster of fabrication, maintenance and inspection contractors around Wollongong. Typical work includes UT and MT of structural and pressure welds, crane and lifting equipment inspection, and thickness surveys of process plant. See steel and metals audit support.

Aerospace and defence give NSW its strongest link to US requirements. RAAF Base Williamtown near Newcastle is home to F-35A operations and a surrounding defence industry precinct, Fleet Base East at Garden Island in Sydney supports naval vessels, and Sydney Airport hosts major airline engineering and maintenance. Suppliers to US primes, MRO providers and component manufacturers often face customer requirements that reference NAS 410, ASNT-based qualification or the prime's own NDT specification. See aerospace audit support.

The rest of the map includes ANSTO's research reactor and nuclear medicine facilities at Lucas Heights, the Snowy 2.0 pumped-hydro project with its steel penstocks and tunnels, gas transmission pipelines such as the Moomba to Sydney pipeline, fuel import terminals at Kurnell and Botany, and mining in the Hunter Valley, the Central West around Orange and Parkes, and Broken Hill.

NSW regulation is administered through several bodies. SafeWork NSW handles plant design and item registration for boilers and pressure vessels under the state's Work Health and Safety Regulation. Radiation users, including industrial radiographers, are licensed by the NSW Environment Protection Authority under the state's radiation protection legislation, the Protection from Harmful Radiation Act 1990, with a specific licence category for industrial radiography. Mine safety sits with the NSW Resources Regulator, pipelines are licensed under the state Pipelines Act 1967 and built to AS 2885, and ANSTO's Commonwealth facilities fall under ARPANSA. Confirm the current requirement with the relevant regulator before mobilising.

Which NDT certification scheme applies in New South Wales?

Direct answer: Most NSW NDT work uses AINDT certification under ISO 9712, with AICIP certification for in-service pressure-equipment inspectors and NATA accreditation for laboratories and inspection bodies. ASNT SNT-TC-1A applies where a customer requires it, most often in aerospace and defence supply chains and on US-code or US-owned projects. Aerospace customers may require NAS 410 instead.

For NSW companies, the scheme question is usually answered by the customer, not by the company. A steelworks maintenance contract will normally expect AINDT-certified technicians and a NATA-accredited laboratory for endorsed testing. A US aerospace prime will flow down its own NDT specification, which may reference NAS 410 and require a Responsible Level III. An export fabricator building ASME pressure vessels for a US client may need technicians certified under the employer's SNT-TC-1A written practice. Each customer asks for something different, so many NSW companies end up holding more than one qualification system at once.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: Atlantis writes new SNT-TC-1A written practices for NSW employers and audits existing ones against SNT-TC-1A and customer requirements. Each written practice is built around the methods you actually perform and the flow-downs your customers actually impose, so it survives an audit rather than just existing on file.

NSW written practices often need to do more than the minimum because of the aerospace and defence customer base. A component supplier may need to show how its SNT-TC-1A programme maps to the customer's NDT specification, how it handles a Responsible Level III requirement, and how it controls technique sheets for specific part numbers. A Hunter fabricator, on the other hand, may only need UT, MT and VT for structural and pressure welds, with a lean written practice that a small team can follow without errors.

Audits test whether the programme works in practice. We pick technicians, trace each certification back through training records, experience logs, exam papers and vision tests, and check every approval and signature. We also check how the company handles technicians who arrive with AINDT certificates or certifications from previous employers, because that is a common gap in mixed-scheme programmes. Our SNT-TC-1A guide and written practice development page explain the background, and the training requirements matrix covers hours.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in New South Wales

Direct answer: NSW procedures must match the governing code: ASME V with Section VIII or B31.3 for US-code pressure work, AWS D1.1 or AS/NZS 1554 for structural steel, AS 2885 or API 1104 for pipelines, AS/NZS 3788 for in-service pressure equipment, and customer specifications for aerospace. Atlantis writes and approves procedures for ASME, API, AWS and customer-specified work.

  • Power generation: UT of boiler tubes and headers, PAUT and TOFD of high-energy piping welds, MT of turbine and fan components, with owner-specified acceptance criteria.

  • Aerospace and MRO: ET, PT, UT and MT procedures and technique sheets to customer specifications; part-specific technique sheets with Level III approval.
  • Pipelines and terminals: AS 2885 or API 1104 weld inspection procedures; API 653 tank floor and shell techniques for terminal operators. See pipeline audit support.
  • Hydro and infrastructure: penstock and structural weld inspection on major projects such as Snowy 2.0. See infrastructure audit support.
  • Nuclear and research facilities: nuclear-grade document control expectations around Lucas Heights. See nuclear audit support.

Radiography procedures must stay consistent with the company's NSW EPA radiation licence conditions; the radiation safety side stays with your licensed staff while we handle technique and acceptance.

Outsourced and interim Level III for New South Wales crews

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III gives an NSW company a named ASNT Level III for its SNT-TC-1A programme without the cost and recruitment difficulty of a full-time hire. It suits fabricators, MRO suppliers and inspection firms whose ASNT-specified work is a part, not the whole, of their business.

The NSW pattern is steady rather than seasonal, with peaks around power-station outages and steelworks shutdowns. Aerospace suppliers need continuous Level III oversight because technique sheets change with new part numbers and customer revisions. An outsourced Level III reviews and approves technique sheets as they arise, answers technical questions from the shop floor, keeps certifications and recertifications current, and is the named Level III when a customer auditor asks.

Interim cover is the short-term version: we step in while you recruit, while your Level III is on leave, or when an audit is coming and there is nobody to sign. Engagement options are an ongoing outsourced arrangement, a single project such as a written practice or procedure set, or an audit-preparation sprint, each scoped on a call and quoted on request. Ask about an outsourced or interim Level III in NSW.

Audit readiness: customer, owner and accreditation audits

Direct answer: Atlantis prepares NSW companies for customer and prime-contractor audits of their NDT special process, owner audits of SNT-TC-1A programmes, and the NDT portion of quality-system audits, including Nadcap-style aerospace audits. We run the audit first, list findings by priority and support the fixes. The auditor makes the decision.

Aerospace audits are the most demanding NSW audits we prepare for. Auditors want to see the written practice, each technician's certification file, current vision tests, approved procedures and technique sheets for the specific parts, equipment calibration and process control records, and evidence that the Level III actually reviews the work. Power and steel owners focus more on certification validity, procedures and report quality. In both cases, a mock audit catches the expensive findings before the real one.

Atlantis is not a NATA assessor or a Nadcap auditor and does not hold NATA accreditation. We prepare documents and people; accreditation and approval decisions belong to the accrediting body or customer. Book a pre-audit review for your NSW NDT programme.

Cities and regions we support across New South Wales

Direct answer: Atlantis supports NSW employers in Sydney, Newcastle and the Hunter, Wollongong and the Illawarra, and regional NSW, remotely and onsite at the client's facility. Atlantis has no office or training centre in New South Wales.

How an engagement works

Direct answer: An engagement runs from a scoping call to a written scope and quote, a document review, delivery of documents, onsite work where it is needed and, for ongoing clients, continuing Level III support. Timing is set on the scoping call because it depends on scope and the state of your records.

  2. Written scope and quote: deliverables, remote and onsite elements and responsibilities.
  3. Document review: written practice, certification files, procedures, technique sheets, calibration and reports.
