  6. Continuing support: approvals, questions, recertifications and updates as codes and customer requirements change.

Technician training is a separate service: ASNT SNT-TC-1A training, online NDT training and corporate programmes. For practice before practical exams, see Practical NDT, which is practice only and does not replace an exam on real specimens.

Your Level III

NSW engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, founder of Atlantis NDT. You work with one named Level III from first call to signed documents. More about Atlantis NDT.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I find an NDT Level III consultant in NSW?

Atlantis NDT provides ASNT Level III services to New South Wales employers, led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, delivered remotely and onsite at your facility.

Is ASNT certification valid in New South Wales?

SNT-TC-1A certification is valid wherever the customer or contract accepts it. Most Australian contracts expect AINDT under ISO 9712, while US aerospace, defence and US-code customers often accept or require SNT-TC-1A or NAS 410.

Can Atlantis certify technicians to AINDT, ISO 9712 or NAS 410?

No. Atlantis does not certify or train to those schemes. We design and support employer-based SNT-TC-1A programmes and help them work alongside your other schemes.

Is Atlantis NATA-accredited?

No. Atlantis does not hold NATA accreditation and does not issue NATA-endorsed reports. If your customer requires an accredited laboratory, you need one.

Do I need a licence for industrial radiography in NSW?

Yes. The NSW EPA licenses radiation users, including industrial radiographers, under the state's radiation protection legislation. Confirm current licence categories and conditions with the EPA before work starts.

Who registers pressure vessels in NSW?

SafeWork NSW handles registration of plant designs and items of plant, including boilers and pressure vessels of the relevant hazard levels under AS 4343. In-service inspection follows AS/NZS 3788.

Can you act as the Level III for an aerospace supplier in Sydney?

We can act as the Level III for an SNT-TC-1A programme and prepare you for customer audits. If your customer requires NAS 410 or a specific Responsible Level III arrangement, confirm those flow-downs first so the programme is designed to meet them.

Can you write procedures for power-station outage inspections?

Yes. We write UT, PAUT, TOFD, MT and VT procedures and technique sheets for boiler tubes, headers and high-energy piping, aligned with the owner's specification and the governing code.

Can practical exams be done remotely?

No. Practical exams need the candidate, real specimens and the examiner together, so they are held onsite at your facility. Most other Level III work is remote.

Does Atlantis have an office in Sydney or Newcastle?

No. Atlantis has no physical office or training centre in NSW; work is delivered remotely and onsite at the client's facility.

How much does Level III consulting cost in NSW?

Quote on request. Cost depends on methods, ongoing versus project work, exam volume and onsite visits. Atlantis keeps its services affordable, accessible and fully customisable.

NDT Level III Consulting Services in Newfoundland and Labrador

Short answer: Atlantis NDT provides ASNT NDT Level III services to employers in Newfoundland and Labrador, remotely and onsite at the employer's own facility: an outsourced or interim Level III for SNT-TC-1A programmes, written practices and audits, procedures and technique sheets, qualification exams under the employer's written practice, and preparation for operator, certifying-authority and customer audits. Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, and every scope is quoted on request.

Newfoundland and Labrador's NDT market is built around the offshore. The Jeanne d'Arc Basin fields on the Grand Banks are produced through the Hibernia and Hebron gravity-based platforms and the Terra Nova and SeaRose floating production vessels, and the West White Rose project's concrete gravity structure was built at Argentia. Onshore fabrication yards at Bull Arm, Marystown and Argentia, supply bases and harbour facilities in St. John's and Bay Bulls, and a large offshore supply chain support them. The province also has the Come By Chance site, converted from crude refining to renewable fuels; nickel processing at Long Harbour fed by the Voisey's Bay mine in Labrador; iron ore mining and pelletising in Labrador West; hydro power at Churchill Falls and Muskrat Falls; a thermal station at Holyrood; and pulp and paper in Corner Brook. Many offshore and fabrication contractors serve international operators and US-code equipment, which is where an ASNT Level III fits. If you are ready, ask for a Newfoundland and Labrador Level III quote.

Why Newfoundland and Labrador NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: An employer in Newfoundland and Labrador that certifies NDT personnel under ASNT SNT-TC-1A needs a Level III who owns the written practice, approves procedures and examines staff. Offshore operators, certifying authorities, mine owners, utilities and US customers audit their NDT suppliers, and most local shops are too small for a full-time Level III, so an outsourced Level III is the practical answer.

Offshore production sets the tone. Platforms and floating production vessels in harsh North Atlantic conditions need continual inspection of topsides piping and pressure equipment, structural welds, mooring and riser components, cranes and lifting equipment, and storage and offloading systems. Inspection campaigns are planned around helicopter seats, bed space and weather windows, so the paperwork has to be right before anyone flies. Operators audit their contractors' personnel files and procedures in detail, and so do the certifying authorities whose certificates of fitness offshore installations depend on.

Fabrication and supply bases come next. Bull Arm, Marystown and Argentia have built and outfitted major offshore structures and modules, and they continue to handle fabrication, repair and decommissioning work. In St. John's and around Conception Bay, machine shops, fabrication shops and service companies support the offshore fleet and the province's industry. Their NDT is audited against operator specifications, class rules and the codes the equipment was built to, often ASME or AWS for equipment with US origins.

Mining and processing are concentrated in Labrador and on the Avalon. Iron ore mines, concentrators and pellet plants around Labrador City and Wabush run crushers, mills, conveyors, kilns and heavy mobile equipment; the Voisey's Bay operation and the Long Harbour processing plant handle nickel, copper and cobalt with pressure leaching and other hydrometallurgical equipment that need careful inspection. Hydro stations at Churchill Falls and Muskrat Falls, the Holyrood thermal station and long transmission lines add utility work. The Come By Chance site, now producing renewable fuels, keeps refinery-type inspection on the island, and the Corner Brook mill runs boilers and pressure equipment.

The regulatory picture: onshore boilers, pressure vessels and pressure piping are regulated under the Public Safety Act and the Boiler, Pressure Vessel and Compressed Gas Regulations, administered by the province's Engineering and Inspection Services (formerly under Digital Government and Service NL; confirm the current department name), which handles design registration, contractor licences and inspections. Offshore petroleum and renewable energy activities are regulated by the Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator (C-NLOER), the former C-NLOPB, renamed on 2 June 2025 when its mandate expanded to offshore renewables. Industrial gamma radiography is licensed by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC), and exposure devices must be operated by CNSC-certified exposure device operators or under their direct supervision. Confirm current provincial and offshore requirements for X-ray equipment and any recent changes before mobilising.

Which NDT certification scheme applies in Newfoundland and Labrador?

Direct answer: Canada's national NDT personnel scheme is CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (ISO 9712), and offshore operators and many Canadian owners call for national or ISO 9712 certification. Class societies and certifying authorities apply their own requirements. ASNT SNT-TC-1A is used for US customers and US-code equipment. Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A Level III services and procedure, technique and audit support; we are not a CGSB or ISO 9712 certification body.

A note on the national scheme, because it changed this year. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026. The standard remains valid, and both Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body and CWB Group, as an accredited certification body, have said they continue to certify. Confirm the current certification body for your method and sector before you rely on it.

The practical rule: the operator's specification, the class or certifying-authority requirement, or the referenced code decides. Where national, ISO 9712 or class certification is mandatory, our role is drafting, technical review and audit readiness that your properly certified Level 3 signs. Where the customer accepts employer-based SNT-TC-1A certification, Atlantis can be your Level III of record. Many St. John's contractors run personnel under two schemes and need records that are consistent across both.

Offshore NDT: operators, certifying authorities and campaign planning

Direct answer: Offshore NDT in Newfoundland and Labrador is planned around the operator's integrity programme, the certifying authority's survey requirements and the C-NLOER's regulatory framework. Contractors need procedures and technique sheets that work on topsides and in confined spaces, and personnel files that pass the operator's audit before mobilisation. Atlantis supports this from the Level III side.

Offshore inspection scopes typically include topsides piping and vessel thickness surveys, corrosion under insulation screening, weld inspection on repairs and modifications, structural inspection of decks, crane pedestals and lifting points, and inspection of flare, riser and mooring-related components within reach of rope-access or platform teams. Floating production vessels add hull, tank and marine-system inspection under class rules. Every scope has to fit limited bed space, so a technique that fails on the first day costs a trip.

A Level III adds value before the helicopter leaves: confirming that procedures cover the actual materials, thicknesses, temperatures and access; that technique sheets match the inspection plan; that calibration blocks and instruments are certified; and that every technician's certification, scheme and vision exam match what the operator requires. After the campaign, we help review data quality and reporting so integrity engineers can rely on it. We do not supply offshore crews or hold operator approvals. See offshore audit support, written practices for upstream and offshore NDT, maritime audit support and marine and offshore NDT services, or ask about offshore procedures and audit readiness.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: A written practice is the employer's document that defines how NDT personnel are trained, examined, certified and recertified under SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis writes new written practices for employers in Newfoundland and Labrador and audits existing ones so the document matches the methods you perform and the operators and customers who audit you.

Recurring problems: a written practice that names a Level III who has left; national or ISO 9712 certificates filed as if they were employer certifications, with no record of the employer's own exams or review; methods such as PAUT, TOFD or eddy current performed but not listed; experience for technicians who rotate between offshore, mainland and international work left undocumented; practical exams with no specimens on file; and vision exams that lapsed during long rotations.

A written-practice engagement defines scope, training and experience requirements referenced to the current SNT-TC-1A edition, examination content and grading, vision exams, certification and recertification, interrupted service, transfer of certification and the Level III's authority, and records how certificates under other schemes are filed. Training-hour figures come from the training requirements matrix. See written practice development and the SNT-TC-1A guide, or request a written-practice review for your company.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in Newfoundland and Labrador

Direct answer: Procedures in the province follow the governing code or specification: operator and certifying-authority requirements offshore; class rules for vessels; CSA B51 with the ASME Code for provincially registered pressure equipment; CSA W59 or AWS D1.1 for structures; and mine-owner, utility and manufacturer requirements for mining and power equipment.

  • Offshore topsides. Thickness surveys, PAUT corrosion mapping, CUI screening and weld inspection on repairs and modifications, with technique sheets written for access, temperature and coatings.
  • Structures and lifting equipment. MT, UT and VT on structural welds, crane pedestals, padeyes and lifting points, to the operator's and certifying authority's requirements.
  • Fabrication yards. Weld inspection on modules, structures and pressure equipment, often to ASME or AWS for equipment with US origins and to the operator's specification.
  • Mining and processing. MT and UT on crushers, mills, kilns and mobile equipment in Labrador West; inspection of pressure leaching vessels and piping at Long Harbour.
  • Power generation. Turbine, penstock and structural inspection at hydro stations; boiler and high-energy piping inspection at Holyrood.
  • Renewable fuels and pulp and paper. Vessel, piping and tank inspection at Come By Chance and boiler and pressure-equipment inspection at Corner Brook.
  • North Atlantic conditions. Cold, wet, salt-laden environments affect surface preparation, penetrant and particle product limits, couplant and safe access, and procedures should address them.

Sector notes: mining, power generation, fabrication, shipbuilding and repair and refining. For mine operators see mining written practices. For plant and terminal pressure equipment and tanks, see API 510, API 570 and API 653 support; Atlantis does not supply authorised inspectors or offer API certification training.

Outsourced and interim Level III for crews in the province

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III is a named ASNT Level III who serves as your SNT-TC-1A programme's Level III under a standing agreement; an interim Level III fills a gap. For employers in Newfoundland and Labrador the work is mainly remote, with onsite visits for practical exams, procedure demonstrations and audits at the employer's facility.

  2. Project-based work. A new written practice, a procedure set for an offshore campaign or new mining contract, PAUT technique sheets, or an exam campaign before a shutdown.
  3. Audit-preparation sprint. A focused review before a known audit, with a prioritised corrective-action list and support while you close it.

Practical exams need the candidate, real specimens and the examiner together, so they are held onsite at your facility in St. John's, Mount Pearl, Marystown, Labrador City or wherever you operate. Offshore installations are not used for exams. Atlantis has no office or training centre in Newfoundland and Labrador. See interim NDT Level III, or discuss outsourced Level III coverage for your programme.

Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, so you know exactly who approves your procedures and examines your people.

Audit readiness: operator, customer and accreditation audits

Direct answer: NDT suppliers in Newfoundland and Labrador are audited by offshore operators, certifying authorities, class societies, mine owners, utilities and US customers, and some by ISO 9001, ISO/IEC 17025 or CSA W178.1 assessors. A Level III review before the audit finds gaps in the written practice, certifications, procedures and reports while there is time to fix them.

Common findings: certifications under a superseded written practice; mixed-scheme personnel files with no clear link between certificate and contract; expired vision exams after long rotations; practical exams without specimen or grading records; procedures not approved by a Level III or tied to an outdated code edition; calibration and reference standards without certificates; and technicians working outside their certified methods. Offshore operators also expect clear management-of-change records when procedures are revised mid-campaign.

An audit-readiness engagement samples personnel files, procedures and reports, maps them to the written practice and the operator's specification, and delivers a prioritised corrective-action list with follow-up support. Approval and certification decisions remain with the operator, the certifying authority or the accreditation body. Audit coming? Book an audit-readiness call.

Cities and regions we support across Newfoundland and Labrador

Direct answer: Atlantis supports employers across the province, remotely and onsite at the client's facility. Most requests come from St. John's and Mount Pearl, Bay Bulls, the Placentia Bay and Isthmus area (Argentia, Long Harbour, Come By Chance, Bull Arm), Marystown, Corner Brook, Labrador West and Happy Valley-Goose Bay.

  • St. John's and Mount Pearl. Offshore operators' and contractors' offices, supply bases, the harbour, fabrication and machine shops and engineering firms. Related page: the Practical NDT simulator for St. John's.
  • Bay Bulls and the Southern Shore. Marine and offshore support activity.
  • Argentia and Placentia Bay. Port and fabrication activity, including the West White Rose gravity structure build.
  • Long Harbour. The nickel processing plant.
  • Come By Chance and Bull Arm. The renewable fuels site and the large fabrication site on Trinity Bay.
  • Marystown. Shipyard and fabrication on the Burin Peninsula.
  • Corner Brook. Pulp and paper and west-coast industry.

  • Happy Valley-Goose Bay and central Labrador. Muskrat Falls, Churchill Falls access and regional services.

Mainland neighbours: NDT training in Halifax and NDT training in Saint John. National view: NDT consulting across Canada.

Training alongside the Level III service

Direct answer: Employers in the province can combine Level III consulting with ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for their own technicians, live online or onsite at their facility. Atlantis training is SNT-TC-1A only and does not prepare candidates for national CAN/CGSB-48.9712, ISO 9712 or class certification.

Training covers Level I, II and III in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET for employers whose customers expect SNT-TC-1A certification. Live online classes suit technicians on rotation. The Practical NDT simulator lets trainees practise twelve methods in five virtual environments, including an oil and gas site and a storage tank, before practical exams; it is a practice tool and does not replace a practical exam on real specimens. Direct answer: An engagement begins with a call about your methods, operators, codes, certification schemes and staffing, followed by a written scope and quote. Document work runs remotely; practical exams and site visits take place at your onshore facility. Timing is agreed in the scope rather than assumed.

  2. Document review. You share your written practice, procedures and a sample of certification files and reports; we identify gaps.

NDT Level III Consulting Services in North Dakota

Short answer: North Dakota employers can engage Atlantis NDT for ASNT NDT Level III services, delivered remotely and onsite at the employer's own facility: an outsourced or interim Level III of record, SNT-TC-1A written practices and audits, procedures and technique sheets, qualification exams under the employer's written practice, and audit preparation. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, leads each engagement, and every scope is quoted on request.

North Dakota's NDT market is shaped by the Bakken. The Williston Basin in the west of the state supports thousands of producing wells, gas processing plants, gathering systems, crude terminals, rail loading facilities and long-haul pipelines, and all of them were built and are maintained by contractors who need qualified NDT personnel. The centre of the state adds lignite coal mines, coal-fired power stations, a coal gasification plant and the Mandan refinery. The Red River Valley in the east adds agricultural and construction equipment manufacturing, and two Air Force bases sit in the north. Inspection companies in Williston, Watford City, Dickinson, Minot, Bismarck and Fargo grew quickly during the oil boom and many still run programmes that were assembled under pressure. This hub explains why those programmes need a Level III, which state and federal regulators apply, and how an outsourced Level III works. If you are ready, ask for a North Dakota Level III quote.

Why North Dakota NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, every employer that certifies its own NDT personnel needs a Level III to own the written practice, approve procedures and examine staff. North Dakota's oilfield, midstream, power and manufacturing customers audit those programmes closely, and many local inspection companies do not have a full-time Level III, so an outside Level III fills the gap.

Start in the Bakken. Production facilities around Williston, Watford City, Tioga, Stanley, Killdeer and Dickinson include well pads with separators, treaters and storage tanks; compressor stations; gas processing plants that recover natural gas liquids; and saltwater disposal systems. Midstream companies run gathering networks, crude and gas transmission lines, and rail terminals that load crude for shipment. Construction and maintenance of this infrastructure generates girth-weld radiography and automated UT on pipelines, weld inspection on station and plant piping, ultrasonic thickness surveys on vessels and tanks, magnetic particle and penetrant inspection on fabricated components, and visual inspection everywhere. Produced water and sour gas bring corrosion and cracking concerns that need the right technique, not just any technique.

Central North Dakota adds energy conversion. The Mandan refinery processes Bakken crude near Bismarck, and the former diesel refinery near Dickinson now produces renewable diesel. Along the Missouri River and in Mercer and Oliver counties, lignite mines feed coal-fired power stations and the Great Plains Synfuels Plant at Beulah, which turns coal into synthetic natural gas and chemicals. Power plants need boiler tube inspection, high-energy piping inspection and turbine work during outages; the synfuels plant adds process piping and pressure vessel inspection similar to a refinery. Ethanol plants across the state add smaller-scale pressure equipment and tank inspection.

Eastern North Dakota is manufacturing country. Fargo builds large agricultural tractors and electronic components, compact equipment is built in Gwinner, Bismarck and Wahpeton, and dozens of fabrication and machine shops supply them. Manufacturing NDT is weld and casting quality control: magnetic particle and penetrant on welded frames and castings, ultrasonic testing on heavy sections, and visual inspection to AWS D1.1 or customer standards. Grand Forks Air Force Base and Minot Air Force Base add military aircraft and infrastructure maintenance.

The regulators matter. North Dakota is an NRC Agreement State: the North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality's Radiation Control Program licenses radioactive materials, including sources used for gamma radiography, and registers X-ray equipment, under state rules compatible with NRC requirements. The DEQ also runs the state's Boiler Inspection Program, which moved there from the Insurance Department in 2019. The North Dakota Public Service Commission runs the state pipeline safety programme for intrastate gas pipelines in partnership with PHMSA, which regulates interstate and hazardous-liquid pipelines directly, and the Industrial Commission's Oil and Gas Division regulates wells and oilfield activities. Confirm current licensing and inspection requirements with each agency before work starts.

Direct answer: North Dakota clients usually need an outsourced or interim Level III, a written practice rebuilt to match current operations, procedures and technique sheets for pipeline, plant and manufacturing work, qualification exams under their written practice, and preparation for operator or customer audits. Most work is remote, with onsite visits for practical exams and audits.

More detail: written practice development and the SNT-TC-1A guide. To start, request a written-practice review for your North Dakota programme.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in North Dakota

Direct answer: North Dakota procedures follow the governing code: API 1104 with 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 for pipelines; ASME B31.3, B31.4 and B31.8 for plant and station piping; ASME Section VIII with API 510 for vessels; API 650 and 653 for tanks; ASME Section I and B31.1 for power plants; AWS D1.1 and customer specifications for manufacturing.

Procedure work in North Dakota tends to fall into five groups:

  • Pipeline construction. Girth-weld radiography or automated UT to API 1104 and the operator's specification. Technique sheets need to match diameter, wall thickness and joint design, and the procedure must say how repairs and cut-outs are re-inspected.
  • Production and midstream facilities. Thickness monitoring on vessels, piping and tanks; weld inspection on fabricated skids and station piping; and inspection for corrosion and cracking where produced water or sour service is involved. Procedures need clear acceptance criteria and reporting formats that integrity engineers can use.
  • Refining and gas processing. Repair and alteration inspection, PAUT or TOFD on thick sections, and thickness monitoring to support the authorised inspector's work.
  • Power generation. Boiler tube thickness and weld inspection during outages, high-energy piping inspection and turbine component inspection.
  • Manufacturing. MT and PT on welded frames, castings and forgings; UT on heavy sections and axles; visual weld inspection to AWS D1.1 or customer standards.

North Dakota winters are long and cold, so procedures for outdoor work must address temperature limits for couplants, penetrants and magnetic particle media, and calibration at the examination temperature. We write procedures and technique sheets, review procedures supplied by others, and resolve conflicts between operator specifications, codes and your written practice. Sector notes: pipeline, petrochemical, refining, power generation, fabrication and tank terminals.

Outsourced and interim Level III for North Dakota crews

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III is a named ASNT Level III who acts as your programme's Level III of record under a standing agreement; an interim Level III covers a gap. For North Dakota crews the service runs mainly remotely, with onsite visits for practical exams, procedure demonstrations and audits at the employer's facility.

Three engagement models cover most requests:

  1. Ongoing outsourced (retained) Level III. Atlantis is named as Level III in your written practice; we approve procedures, administer exams, answer field questions, review the programme annually and support you in audits. It suits oilfield and midstream inspection contractors that need Level III authority but cannot justify a full-time Level III through activity cycles.
  2. Project-based work. A single deliverable: a new written practice, a procedure set for a new pipeline or plant contract, PAUT technique sheets, or an exam campaign before the construction season.
  3. Audit-preparation sprint. A focused review before a scheduled operator or customer audit, with a corrective-action list and support while you close it.

Activity in the Bakken rises and falls with the oil price, and a retained or interim Level III lets a contractor keep a compliant programme through both. Written practices, procedures, exam preparation and record reviews are handled remotely. Practical exams need the candidate, real specimens and the examiner together, so they are scheduled onsite at your facility in Williston, Dickinson, Minot, Bismarck, Fargo or wherever you operate. Atlantis has no office or training centre in North Dakota. See interim NDT Level III, or talk to us about outsourced Level III coverage in North Dakota.

Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, so clients know exactly which Level III approves their procedures and examines their people.

Audit readiness: customer, owner and accreditation audits

Direct answer: North Dakota NDT contractors are audited by producers and midstream operators during prequalification, by pipeline operators whose own programmes face PHMSA or PSC inspection, by manufacturers' supplier-quality teams, and by ISO 9001 or ISO/IEC 17025 assessors. A Level III review finds the gaps in your written practice, procedures and records first.

The findings that recur are familiar: certifications issued under a written practice that has since been revised; expired vision examinations; practical exams with no specimen or grading record; procedures not approved by a Level III or referencing an outdated code edition; equipment calibration records that do not tie to instruments in reports; and technicians using techniques their certifications do not cover. In a market where people move between employers often, transfer-of-certification records are another frequent weak spot.

An audit-readiness engagement samples personnel files, procedures and reports, maps them against the written practice and the customer specification, and produces a prioritised corrective-action list. We then support the fixes: revised procedures, re-examination under your written practice and a short summary your quality manager can present. For aerospace and defence suppliers, we can help with Nadcap-style audit preparation as context, while the audit itself is run by the accreditation body; for laboratories pursuing ISO/IEC 17025, we help with the NDT technical content. See steel and metals, mining and aerospace audit support. Audit coming up? Book a North Dakota audit-readiness call.

Inspection programme support for refineries, gas plants and terminals

Direct answer: At North Dakota refineries, gas plants and crude terminals, API 510, 570 and 653 inspections are carried out and signed by the owner's authorised inspectors. Atlantis supports that work from the NDT side, with method selection, procedures, technique qualification and data quality. We do not provide authorised inspector certification training.

Gas processing plants and crude terminals in the Bakken were largely built in a short period, which means many of them reach their first major inspection intervals together. The quality of thickness data, weld inspection and tank floor scans depends on consistent measurement locations, techniques matched to the damage mechanism and reporting the authorised inspector can use. A Level III can help standardise these practices across a contractor's crews and choose between conventional UT, PAUT corrosion mapping and profile radiography for a given circuit. See our API 510, API 570 and API 653 support pages.

Cities we support across North Dakota

Direct answer: Atlantis supports North Dakota employers statewide, remotely and onsite at the client's facility. Most requests come from the Bakken cities of Williston, Watford City, Tioga and Dickinson, from Minot, from Bismarck and Mandan, from the coal and power country around Beulah, and from Fargo and Grand Forks.

  • Williston. The service hub of the Bakken, home to inspection contractors, pipeline construction companies and oilfield fabricators. Related pages: NDT training in Williston, oil and gas NDT training in Williston, Practical NDT simulator for Williston and NDT ERP for Williston companies.
  • Watford City, Tioga and Stanley. Production, gas processing and gathering in McKenzie, Williams and Mountrail counties.
  • Dickinson. Southwestern oilfield services, renewable diesel production and fabrication. See inspection management software for Dickinson.
  • Bismarck and Mandan. The refinery, equipment manufacturing, state agencies and engineering firms. See Practical NDT for Bismarck.
  • Beulah, Hazen and the coal country. Lignite mines, power stations and the synfuels plant along the Missouri River.
  • Minot. Air Force base, oilfield services and regional fabrication.
  • Fargo, West Fargo and Grand Forks. Agricultural and construction equipment manufacturing, electronics, fabrication, and Grand Forks Air Force Base. See Practical NDT for Fargo.

Statewide resources: the North Dakota NDT training hub, the Practical NDT simulator page for North Dakota, inspection management ERP for North Dakota and digital twins for North Dakota assets. Neighbouring consulting hubs: Minnesota and South Dakota.

Training alongside the Level III service

Direct answer: Many North Dakota clients combine Level III consulting with SNT-TC-1A training for their own technicians, delivered live online or onsite at their facility. When one Level III writes the written practice, procedures and exams, training lines up with certification and audits go more smoothly.

Training covers Level I, II and III in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET. Live online classes suit technicians working long oilfield rotations; onsite classes suit a crew gathered before the construction season. The Practical NDT simulator lets trainees practise twelve methods in five virtual environments, including an oil and gas site, before their practical exams; it is a practice tool and does not replace a practical exam on real specimens. See training, online NDT training, corporate NDT training and ASNT Level III training.

How an engagement works

Direct answer: A North Dakota engagement starts with a call about your methods, customers, codes and staffing, followed by a written scope and quote. Document work runs remotely; practical exams and site visits take place at your facility. Timing is agreed in the scope rather than assumed.

  1. Discovery call. Methods and techniques performed, customers and codes, staffing, certification status, and the trigger: new contract, audit, departing Level III or growth.
  2. Document review. You share your written practice, procedures and a sample of certification files and reports, and we identify gaps.
  3. Scope and quote. Deliverables, remote and onsite elements and responsibilities in writing. Pricing is quote on request.
  4. Delivery. Drafting, approval and issue of documents; exams under your written practice; corrective actions; ongoing Level III duties if retained.
  5. Onsite visits. Practical exams, procedure demonstrations and audit support at your North Dakota site, planned around construction seasons, outages and weather.
  6. Review. Annual programme review for retained clients and updates when codes, customers or methods change.

Frequently asked questions

How do I find an NDT Level III consultant in North Dakota?

Many Level IIIs in North Dakota work for operators or large contractors, so smaller companies often engage an outside Level III who works remotely and visits onsite. Atlantis offers that service, led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III.

Is North Dakota an NRC Agreement State?

Yes. The North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality's Radiation Control Program licenses radioactive materials, including gamma radiography sources, and registers X-ray equipment. Confirm current licensing and reciprocity requirements before bringing a radiography crew into the state.

Who inspects boilers in North Dakota?

The Boiler Inspection Program of the North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality, which took over the programme from the Insurance Department in 2019.

Who regulates pipeline safety in North Dakota?

The North Dakota Public Service Commission's pipeline safety programme covers intrastate gas pipelines in partnership with PHMSA, which regulates interstate and hazardous-liquid pipelines. The Industrial Commission's Oil and Gas Division regulates wells and oilfield activities.

What does an outsourced Level III do for a Bakken inspection company?

They serve as the Level III named in your written practice: approving procedures, administering exams, reviewing certifications, answering field questions and supporting operator audits, without a full-time hire.

Can you write procedures for API 1104 pipeline work?

Yes. We write radiography and UT procedures and technique sheets for pipeline girth welds to API 1104 and the operator's specification, including repair and re-inspection requirements.

Do you write SNT-TC-1A written practices?

Yes. We write new written practices and audit existing ones against the current SNT-TC-1A edition and your customers' requirements.

Can certifications from a previous employer be transferred?

Under SNT-TC-1A, certification belongs to the employer, so a new employer must certify the technician under its own written practice. The practice should define how documented previous training and experience are accepted; we help write and apply those rules.

Do you provide API 510, 570 or 653 inspectors in North Dakota?

No. We support API inspection work from the NDT side, alongside the owner's authorised inspectors, and do not supply inspectors or offer API certification training.

How much does Level III consulting cost in North Dakota?

Quote on request. Cost depends on the methods involved, retained versus project work, exam volume and onsite visits. Atlantis keeps its services affordable, accessible and fully customisable.

Does Atlantis have an office in Williston or Fargo?

No. Atlantis has no physical office or training centre in North Dakota; work is delivered remotely and onsite at the client's facility.

Can you help us get ready for an operator audit?

Yes. An audit-readiness review samples your written practice, procedures, certifications and reports, then gives you a prioritised corrective-action list with support while you close it.

contentHtml:
HomeTrainingConsultingERPPractical NDTContact

NDT Level III Consulting Services in the Northern Territory

Short answer: Atlantis NDT provides ASNT NDT Level III consulting to Northern Territory operators, contractors and fabricators whose work follows US codes or international project specifications: SNT-TC-1A written practices and audits, NDT procedures and technique sheets to ASME, API and AWS, examinations under your written practice, outsourced or interim Level III cover, and audit preparation before shutdowns and owner audits. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, leads every engagement. Work is delivered remotely, with onsite visits to your Darwin or regional facility when the scope needs them. Atlantis has no Northern Territory office and holds no NATA accreditation or AINDT recognition.

The Territory's NDT market is small in headcount and large in consequence. Two LNG export plants sit on Darwin Harbour, long-distance gas pipelines cross the desert, the defence estate is being expanded with Australian and United States funding, and remote mines run on short shutdown windows with fly-in crews. Many of the projects behind that work were engineered by international contractors to ASME, API and owner specifications, and many of the inspection crews are contractors who rotate in from Western Australia, Queensland or overseas. A clear written practice, procedures that every rotation applies the same way, and a responsible Level III who can answer questions quickly matter more here than almost anywhere else in Australia. If that is the gap you are trying to close, request a Northern Territory Level III consultation.

Why Northern Territory NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: NT NDT work is concentrated in LNG, gas pipelines, defence construction and remote mining. Owners in those sectors often specify ASME and API codes and expect contractors to show a qualified personnel system and approved procedures. Under SNT-TC-1A, a Level III approves the written practice and procedures and examines Level I and II staff.

Darwin Harbour is the centre of gravity. At Wickham Point, Darwin LNG has operated since 2006, originally on Bayu-Undan gas from the Timor Sea and, from September 2025, on gas from the Barossa field roughly 285 kilometres north-north-west of Darwin, delivered via the BW Opal floating production vessel. Across the harbour at Bladin Point, the INPEX-operated Ichthys LNG onshore plant receives gas through a long subsea pipeline from the Browse Basin off Western Australia. Both plants are large, cryogenic, high-pressure facilities with process piping, heat exchangers, columns, storage tanks and flare systems that need inspection through their lives, and both run major turnarounds that pull in contractor inspection crews from interstate and abroad. The government's proposed Middle Arm Sustainable Development Precinct would add more processing plant to the same harbour.

Onshore, gas moves on long transmission lines: the Amadeus Gas Pipeline from Central Australia to Darwin, the Bonaparte Gas Pipeline from the Wadeye area, and the Northern Gas Pipeline from Tennant Creek to Mount Isa, which links the Territory to the east-coast market. Exploration and appraisal in the Beetaloo Basin has brought drilling, gathering and processing work into the Barkly region. Pipeline construction, tie-ins and integrity programmes all depend on weld examination under defined procedures.

Defence is the third pillar. RAAF Base Darwin, RAAF Base Tindal near Katherine, Robertson Barracks and the navy facilities in Darwin are being upgraded, and the Marine Rotational Force-Darwin and wider United States force posture initiatives have brought US-funded construction, fuel infrastructure and aircraft support works to the Territory. US-funded contracts frequently arrive with US quality clauses, and those clauses often cite ASNT personnel qualification and AWS or ASME examination requirements.

Mining completes the map: zinc-lead at McArthur River, manganese on Groote Eylandt, gold in the Tanami, bauxite on the Gove Peninsula, and the rehabilitation of the former Ranger uranium mine. These sites run crushers, mills, kilns, tanks, pressure vessels and long conveyor and slurry systems, inspected in shutdown windows by contractors who may be on site for only a few days. Each of these sectors can be served by AINDT-certified technicians under Australian Standards. The ones that come to an SNT-TC-1A Level III are usually working for, or with, an owner or contractor that writes its specifications in American terms. For them, ASNT Level III consulting services fill a gap that is hard to fill locally.

Regulators and standards for NDT in the Northern Territory

Direct answer: In the Territory, radiation sources used for industrial radiography are licensed by NT Health under the Radiation Protection Act 2004; boilers and pressure vessels fall under NT WorkSafe and the work health and safety laws; onshore pipelines are licensed under the Energy Pipelines Act 1981; and offshore facilities in Commonwealth waters are regulated by NOPSEMA.

Radiography rules come first because the risks are highest. Under the Radiation Protection Act 2004 and the Radiation Protection Regulations, a person must not possess, use, store, transport or otherwise deal with a radiation source except under a licence, and radiation sources are registered. Applications for a licence to possess a radiation source include a radiation protection plan describing the practice, the source, storage, monitoring and incident procedures. NT Health's radiation protection team administers this. A Level III does not hold or replace that licence; what we do is make sure your radiographic procedures, technique sheets and personnel records are consistent with the licence conditions and the radiation protection plan, and that nobody in the field is working from a procedure that assumes a different source, set-up or exclusion arrangement.

For plant, the Territory follows the national work health and safety model through the Work Health and Safety (National Uniform Legislation) Act 2011 and its regulations, which require registration of certain plant designs and items, including many pressure vessels and boilers. NT WorkSafe is the regulator. Onshore pipeline licences are granted under the Energy Pipelines Act 1981, administered by the Territory government's mining and energy department; the technical standard for Australian gas and liquid petroleum pipelines is AS 2885. Offshore facilities, including those supplying Darwin's LNG plants, fall under the National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Environmental Management Authority (NOPSEMA). Other standards in daily use are AS 1210, AS 4041, AS 4037, AS/NZS 3788 for in-service inspection and AS/NZS 1554 for structural welding, alongside ASME Section V, VIII and B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 on internationally engineered projects.

Level III services for Northern Territory employers

Direct answer: Atlantis provides Territory companies with SNT-TC-1A written practices and audits, procedures and technique sheets, examinations under the written practice, outsourced and interim Level III cover, set-up of new NDT departments, and pre-turnaround and pre-audit reviews. All of it is scoped around your owner's specification.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: The written practice is the employer's procedure for qualifying and certifying its NDT personnel under SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis writes written practices for Territory employers, and audits existing ones against SNT-TC-1A, the owner's specification and your actual personnel records.

In a fly-in, fly-out market the written practice carries extra weight. Technicians move between employers, and SNT-TC-1A certification does not travel with them; each employer certifies its own people under its own written practice. That means a Darwin contractor taking on technicians from interstate needs a clear rule for how their previous training, experience and certificates are recognised, what employer-specific examination is required, and how the practical examination is run before they mobilise. Get this wrong and you either over-train experienced people or send someone to site with paperwork an owner's auditor will reject.

A Territory written practice we write typically covers: scope and responsibilities; methods and levels; training and experience requirements, referenced to the training requirements matrix; examination content, grading and re-examination; practical specimens; vision examinations; certification, expiry and recertification; interrupted service; outside agency use; and records. Where staff already hold AINDT certification to AS/NZS ISO 9712, the document explains how that certification is used for Australian-code work and when SNT-TC-1A certification is also required. Our written practice development page explains the deliverable in more detail, and our SNT-TC-1A guide covers the standard. Already have a document and a deadline? Ask for a written practice audit in the Northern Territory.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in the Northern Territory

Direct answer: Atlantis writes and approves NDT procedures and component technique sheets to ASME Section V, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and owner specifications for Territory work, and cross-references Australian Standards where projects use both. LNG turnarounds, pipelines and defence structures each have their own code set.

LNG plants are the most document-intensive. Turnaround scopes typically include thickness surveys on piping and vessels, weld examination after repairs, corrosion mapping, and inspection of exchangers and tanks. Owners expect each activity to have an approved procedure and, increasingly, encoded and recordable data from phased array, TOFD or automated corrosion mapping. Technique sheets fix scan plans, probe and wedge selection, calibration references and coverage for each component, so that results from one turnaround can be compared with the next.

The Territory's climate adds its own requirements. Coastal atmospheric corrosion and corrosion under insulation are common concerns in a tropical, humid environment, and the wet season and cyclone risk shape when outdoor work can be done. Procedures need to address surface preparation, temperature ranges and couplant selection for hot or humid conditions, and they need to be written so a rotating crew can follow them without improvising.

Pipeline work is AS 2885 at heart, with API 1104 appearing where international engineering contractors specify it; automated ultrasonic testing on girth welds is common on large-diameter construction. Defence and US-funded construction typically calls up AWS D1.1 for structural steel, owner or US federal specifications for fuel systems, and ASME codes for pressure equipment. Mining plant uses AS/NZS 1554, AS 1210 and owner standards. Each procedure we write states its scope, personnel qualification, equipment and calibration, technique, coverage, evaluation, acceptance criteria by reference to the governing code, and reporting. Where Atlantis is your Level III, Anoop Rayavarapu approves the procedure; where the owner's Level III must approve it, we prepare it for their review.

Outsourced and interim Level III for Northern Territory crews

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III is a named ASNT Level III outside your company who carries the Level III duties defined in your written practice. Atlantis provides ongoing, project-based and interim Level III cover to Territory employers, mostly remotely, with onsite visits when examinations or audits require them.

Experienced Level IIIs are thin on the ground in the Territory, and the ones who are there are usually committed to the large operators. For a Darwin contractor with a handful of technicians, recruiting a full-time Level III rarely makes sense. Outsourcing the role gives you a named person for approvals, examinations, technical questions from the field and audit support, without the overhead.

Three engagement models cover most needs. Ongoing outsourced Level III: we are named in your written practice and handle approvals, new-hire examinations, technical queries and audits as they arise. Project-based: a defined package of documents, for example a written practice and a set of method procedures for a new contract. Audit or turnaround sprint: a focused review before a specific owner audit or mobilisation. Interim cover bridges the gap if your own Level III leaves.

Remote delivery works well for document review, written examinations under invigilated conditions, records checks and technical advice. Practical examinations on real specimens, procedure demonstrations and some audits need someone in the room, and we scope those as onsite visits to your facility. To discuss cover, ask about outsourced Level III for your Territory crew or read about interim NDT Level 3 cover.

Audit readiness: owner, prime contractor and accreditation audits

Direct answer: Atlantis prepares Territory NDT programmes for owner pre-qualification and contractor audits, US-funded project quality audits and the NDT parts of ISO 9001 audits. We can help with procedures and records ahead of a NATA assessment, but Atlantis is not NATA-accredited and NATA assesses you independently.

LNG operators pre-qualify their inspection contractors and audit them before and during turnarounds. Defence primes and US-funded project managers audit quality systems against contract clauses. Mining owners check contractor competence before shutdowns. Inspection bodies holding NATA accreditation to ISO/IEC 17020 or 17025 face periodic technical assessment.

The preparation process is the same in each case. We read the requirement, compare your written practice, procedures, personnel files and equipment calibration records against it, and deliver a ranked list of findings. Then we help you close them: revised documents, re-examination where evidence is missing, and a short briefing for the people who will meet the auditor. We do not promise an audit outcome and we do not claim approvals we do not hold; the aim is that nothing the auditor asks for is missing or contradictory.

Cities and regions we support across the Northern Territory

Direct answer: Atlantis supports NDT programmes throughout the Territory, remotely and through onsite visits to your facility. Most work centres on Darwin and Palmerston, with regional work in Katherine, the Barkly and Tennant Creek, Central Australia and the remote mine and island sites.

Darwin, Palmerston and the harbour. The LNG plants at Wickham Point and Bladin Point, East Arm Wharf, the marine supply base and most of the Territory's fabrication and inspection contractors are here. Related Darwin pages: ASNT NDT training for Darwin, third-party inspection in Darwin, NDT reporting software for Darwin, NDT ERP for Darwin companies and digital twins for Darwin asset owners.

Katherine and Tindal. Air base upgrades and support works bring structural, fuel and pavement-related construction, often with US-funded scopes and US quality clauses.

Tennant Creek and the Barkly. The Northern Gas Pipeline and Beetaloo Basin activity bring pipeline and gas-processing inspection to a remote region.

Alice Springs and Central Australia. Gas fields at Mereenie and Palm Valley, the Amadeus Gas Pipeline and local power generation support a small but specialised inspection market.

Remote mines and islands. McArthur River, Groote Eylandt, the Tanami and Gove run short, intense shutdowns. Consistent written procedures are the best defence against rotation-to-rotation variation.

Background reading: why US-affiliated LNG operators in Australia ask for SNT-TC-1A. National pages: NDT consulting in Australia and ASNT NDT training in Australia.

How an engagement works

Direct answer: A scoping call, a document review, a written scope and quote, then delivery of documents and examinations remotely and onsite as agreed, ending with signed, revision-controlled deliverables. Timelines are set during scoping around your turnaround or contract dates.

  1. Scoping call. What triggered the need, which owner specification and codes apply, which certificates your staff already hold, and when you mobilise.
  2. Document review. Your current written practice, procedures, sample personnel files and the owner's requirement.
  3. Written scope and quote. Deliverables, remote and onsite elements, approval responsibilities. Pricing is quote on request.
  4. Drafting. Written practice, procedures and technique sheets, sent for your review with explanations.
  5. Examinations. Written examinations under the written practice; practical examinations at your facility on real specimens.
  6. Approval and handover. Signed documents, revision history and an audit pack for the owner's auditor.
  7. Ongoing support. Optional outsourced Level III cover for new hires, approvals and future turnarounds.

Book a scoping call before your next Territory turnaround.

Your Level III

Every engagement is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. The person who scopes your work is the person who reviews and approves your documents. Alongside consulting, Atlantis offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A training delivered online or onsite at your facility, and the Practical NDT simulator for technicians to practise methods in 3D environments, including an oil and gas site and a storage tank, before their practical examination. The simulator is practice only and does not replace a practical examination on real specimens.

Frequently asked questions

Can an outside ASNT Level III act as our Level III in Darwin?

Yes, for an SNT-TC-1A programme. SNT-TC-1A permits an outside agency Level III, named in your written practice. That role does not replace AINDT certification or any owner's own approval process.

Do LNG operators in Darwin require SNT-TC-1A certification?

Requirements are set by each owner's contractor specifications. Some accept AINDT or other ISO 9712 certification, some ask for SNT-TC-1A, and some accept either. Check the specification for your contract.

Who licenses industrial radiography in the Northern Territory?

NT Health, under the Radiation Protection Act 2004 and its regulations. You need a licence to possess and use radiation sources, with a radiation protection plan. Confirm current requirements with NT Health.

Who regulates pressure vessels in the Northern Territory?

NT WorkSafe, under the Work Health and Safety (National Uniform Legislation) Act 2011 and regulations, which require registration of certain plant designs and items.

Who regulates gas pipelines in the Territory?

Onshore pipelines are licensed under the Energy Pipelines Act 1981, administered by the Territory government's mining and energy department. Offshore facilities in Commonwealth waters fall under NOPSEMA.

Can you prepare procedures for an LNG turnaround?

Yes. We write and approve UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET procedures and component technique sheets to the owner's specification and ASME Section V.

Can examinations be done remotely for a Darwin crew?

Written examinations can be administered remotely under invigilated conditions defined in your written practice. Practical examinations need an onsite visit to your facility.

Is Atlantis NATA-accredited or AINDT-recognised?

No. Atlantis holds neither. We support SNT-TC-1A programmes and US-code documents; NATA and AINDT are separate systems.

Do you provide AINDT or ISO 9712 training?

No. Atlantis training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only.

How much does Level III consulting cost in the Northern Territory?

Quote on request after a scoping call. The cost depends on methods, documents, examinations and onsite days. We aim to keep it affordable, accessible and fully customisable.

Can you help with US-funded defence projects in the Territory?

We can prepare NDT procedures and personnel records that answer US-style quality clauses citing ASNT, AWS or ASME. We hold no defence approvals, and the contract specification governs.

Does Atlantis have an office in Darwin?

No. Work is delivered remotely, with onsite visits to your facility when needed.

If an owner, prime contractor or code has asked for an SNT-TC-1A written practice, approved procedures or a named Level III, a short call is the quickest way to scope it. NDT Level III Consulting Services in Nova Scotia

Short answer: Atlantis NDT provides ASNT NDT Level III services to Nova Scotia employers, remotely and onsite at the employer's own facility: an outsourced or interim Level III for SNT-TC-1A programmes, written practices and audits, procedures and technique sheets, qualification exams under the employer's written practice, and preparation for customer, owner and class audits. Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, and every scope is quoted on request.

Nova Scotia's NDT work is shaped by the sea. Halifax has one of the country's major naval shipbuilding programmes and the Atlantic fleet's home port, with ship repair, refit and marine fabrication around the harbour. Offshore energy has moved from the Sable and Deep Panuke gas projects, now decommissioned, toward offshore wind and tidal development under an expanded federal-provincial regulator. Inland and along the coasts are coal, gas and biomass power stations, tire manufacturing plants, pulp and paper, a deep-water energy terminal at Point Tupper on the Strait of Canso, the Maritimes and Northeast gas pipeline, aerospace and defence maintenance near Halifax Stanfield, and a large base of structural, marine and pressure-equipment fabricators. Many Nova Scotia shops supply US customers or work to US codes, and that is where an ASNT Level III adds value. If you are ready, ask for a Nova Scotia Level III quote.

Why Nova Scotia NDT programmes need a Level III

Direct answer: A Nova Scotia employer that certifies NDT personnel under ASNT SNT-TC-1A needs a Level III who owns the written practice, approves procedures and examines staff. Shipbuilders, the navy's maintenance organisations, utilities, offshore operators and US customers audit their NDT suppliers, and most Nova Scotia shops are too small to employ a full-time Level III, so an outsourced Level III is the practical route.

Start in Halifax Harbour. The Halifax Shipyard builds large naval vessels for Canada under the National Shipbuilding Strategy, and the dockyard and fleet maintenance organisations keep the Atlantic fleet running. Around them is a supply chain of fabrication shops, machine shops, coating and blasting firms and inspection companies doing weld inspection on hull structures, piping, foundations and machinery. Naval and marine work demands tight documentation: weld maps, procedure traceability and personnel records that hold up to customer and government quality audits.

Offshore energy is changing. The province's two offshore gas developments have been decommissioned, but the offshore regulator now covers renewable energy as well as petroleum, and offshore wind development and tidal energy testing in the Bay of Fundy are drawing in marine fabrication and inspection work. Offshore and coastal structures bring fatigue, corrosion and coating concerns, underwater and splash-zone inspection, and owner and certifying-authority requirements.

Power and industry make up the rest. Nova Scotia Power operates thermal stations including Lingan and Point Aconi on Cape Breton, Trenton, Point Tupper and the gas-fired Tufts Cove station in Dartmouth, along with hydro and a growing fleet of wind farms. Boiler tubes, headers, high-energy piping, turbines and tanks need outage inspection. Michelin's tire plants in Pictou County, Bridgewater and the Annapolis Valley, pulp and paper at Port Hawkesbury, the Point Tupper terminal, fish and food processors, and the Maritimes and Northeast Pipeline, which runs from Goldboro toward New Brunswick and New England, all need pressure-equipment, tank and weld inspection.

The regulatory picture: boilers and pressure equipment are regulated under the Technical Safety Act and the Boiler and Pressure Equipment Regulations, administered by the Technical Safety Division of the Department of Labour, Skills and Immigration, which handles design registration, permits, equipment licences and periodic re-inspection. Offshore petroleum and renewable energy activities are regulated by the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator (CNSOER), the former CNSOPB, renamed when its mandate expanded in January 2025. Industrial gamma radiography is licensed by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC), and exposure devices must be operated by CNSC-certified exposure device operators or under their direct supervision. Interprovincial and international pipelines fall under the Canada Energy Regulator. Ships answer to Transport Canada Marine Safety and, where classed, to their classification society. Confirm current provincial requirements for X-ray equipment and any recent changes before mobilising.

Which NDT certification scheme applies in Nova Scotia?

Direct answer: Canada's national NDT personnel scheme is CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (ISO 9712), and Canadian owners, naval programmes and offshore projects often call for it or for ISO 9712 certification. Class societies apply their own rules. ASNT SNT-TC-1A is used for US customers and US-code work. Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A Level III services and procedure, technique and audit support; we are not a CGSB or ISO 9712 certification body.

A note on the national scheme, because it changed this year. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026. The standard remains valid, and both Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body and CWB Group, as an accredited certification body, have said they continue to certify. Confirm the current certification body for your method and sector before you rely on it.

Where national or class certification is mandatory, our role is drafting, technical review and audit readiness that your properly certified Level 3 signs. Where the customer accepts employer-based SNT-TC-1A certification, Atlantis can be your Level III of record. Many Halifax-area shops do both kinds of work and need their records kept consistent.

Shipbuilding, naval and marine NDT around Halifax

Direct answer: Shipbuilding and ship repair are the largest single source of NDT work in Nova Scotia. Suppliers to the shipyard and the fleet need procedures, technique sheets and personnel records that stand up to shipyard, government and class audits. Atlantis helps with the technical content and audit preparation; the customer and class approvals belong to them.

Marine NDT differs from refinery or pipeline work. Hull and structural welds are inspected visually and with MT, UT and RT to the shipbuilder's and customer's specification; piping systems, machinery foundations and pressure systems carry their own requirements; and coatings, access and ventilation complicate everything. Thin plate, aluminium structures and dissimilar-metal joints need specific techniques and calibration. Weld maps, traceability and NCR handling matter as much as the inspection itself, because a missing record on a naval programme is a finding even if the weld is sound.

For a supplier, the usual gaps are procedures written for a different code, technique sheets that do not match the joint designs on the drawings, personnel certified under one scheme working on a contract that requires another, and calibration blocks or reference standards without current certificates. We review these against your customer's requirements and give you a clear list of fixes. For classed commercial vessels and offshore structures, we review procedures against the class society's rules, while approval stays with the society. See shipbuilding audit support, maritime audit support, maritime NDT consulting and marine and offshore NDT services, or ask about marine NDT procedures for your Nova Scotia shop.

Written practice development and audits

Direct answer: A written practice is the employer's document defining how NDT personnel are trained, examined, certified and recertified under SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis writes new written practices for Nova Scotia employers and audits existing ones so the document matches the methods you perform, the customers who audit you and the other schemes your people hold.

Problems we often find in Atlantic Canada: a written practice inherited from a previous owner that names a Level III no longer involved; national-scheme or class certificates treated as automatic employer certification under SNT-TC-1A; methods such as PAUT or eddy current performed but not listed; experience for technicians hired from offshore or out-of-province employers undocumented; and practical exams with no specimen or grading records. Seasonal and project-driven hiring around refits and outages leaves vision exams and recertification dates lapsed.

A written-practice engagement defines scope, training and experience requirements referenced to the current SNT-TC-1A edition, examinations and grading, vision exams, certification and recertification, interrupted service, transfer of certification and the Level III's authority, and records how other certificates your people hold are filed. Training-hour figures come from the training requirements matrix. More: written practice development and the SNT-TC-1A guide. To start, request a written-practice review for your Nova Scotia company.

Procedures, technique sheets and code compliance in Nova Scotia

Direct answer: Nova Scotia procedures follow the governing code or specification: shipbuilder, naval and class requirements for marine work; CSA B51 with the ASME Code for provincially registered pressure equipment; CSA W59 or AWS D1.1 for structures; CSA Z662 for pipelines; API 650 and 653 practice for tanks and terminals; and utility requirements for power stations.

  • Marine structures and piping. VT, MT, UT and RT on hull, deck and foundation welds; piping system inspection; technique sheets that reflect plate thickness, materials and access.
  • Power generation. Boiler tube, header and high-energy piping inspection during outages at coal, gas and biomass stations; turbine and generator component inspection; tank inspection at fuel facilities.
  • Tanks and terminals. Floor, shell and roof inspection and weld inspection at Point Tupper, Halifax and other fuel terminals, supporting the owner's inspector.
  • Manufacturing plants. Pressure equipment, piping and rotating machinery at tire, pulp and paper and food plants, under the provincial registration and inspection regime.
  • Pipelines. Girth-weld radiography or automated UT on construction and integrity-dig inspection, under the operator's specification and the radiography company's CNSC licence conditions.
  • Offshore wind and tidal. Weld and bolting inspection on foundations, towers and marine structures to the owner's and certifying authority's requirements as projects progress.
  • Salt air and winter. Corrosion, coating condition, wet surfaces and cold affect penetrant and particle product limits, couplant and safe access, and the procedure should address them.

Sector notes: power generation, offshore, fabrication and pipeline. For tank and terminal owners see API 653 tank inspection consulting, and for plant pressure equipment API 510 and API 570 support. These are NDT support pages; Atlantis does not supply authorised inspectors or offer API certification training.

Outsourced and interim Level III for Nova Scotia crews

Direct answer: An outsourced Level III is a named ASNT Level III who serves as your SNT-TC-1A programme's Level III under a standing agreement; an interim Level III fills a gap. For Nova Scotia employers the work is mostly remote, with onsite visits for practical exams, procedure demonstrations and audits at the employer's facility.

  1. Ongoing outsourced (retained) Level III. Atlantis is named in your written practice, approves procedures, administers exams, answers technical questions, reviews the programme each year and supports you in customer audits.
  2. Project-based work. A new written practice, a procedure set for a new marine or power contract, PAUT technique sheets, or an exam campaign before an outage or refit.
  3. Audit-preparation sprint. A focused review before a known audit date, with a prioritised corrective-action list and support while you close it.

Practical exams need the candidate, real specimens and the examiner together, so they are held onsite at your facility in Halifax, Dartmouth, Sydney, Port Hawkesbury, Truro or wherever you operate. Atlantis has no office or training centre in Nova Scotia. See interim NDT Level III, or discuss outsourced Level III coverage for your Nova Scotia programme.

Engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, so you know exactly who approves your procedures and examines your people.

Audit readiness: customer, owner, class and accreditation audits

Direct answer: Nova Scotia NDT suppliers are audited by shipyards, defence quality representatives, utilities, terminal owners, class societies and US customers, and some by ISO 9001, ISO/IEC 17025 or CSA W178.1 assessors. A Level III review before the audit finds gaps in the written practice, certifications, procedures and reports while there is time to fix them.

Common findings: certifications issued under a superseded written practice; mixed-scheme personnel files with no clear record of which certification applies to which contract; expired vision exams; practical exams without specimen or grading records; procedures not approved by a Level III or tied to an old specification revision; reference standards without certificates; and technicians working outside their certified methods or levels.

An audit-readiness engagement samples personnel files, procedures and reports, maps them to the written practice and the customer's specification, and delivers a prioritised corrective-action list with follow-up support. For organisations seeking CSA W178.1 certification as an inspection organisation, we help with the NDT technical content; the certification decision belongs to the certifying body. Audit coming? Book a Nova Scotia audit-readiness call.

Most requests come from Halifax and Dartmouth, Cape Breton (Sydney and the Point Aconi and Lingan area), the Strait of Canso (Port Hawkesbury and Point Tupper), Pictou County, Truro, Bridgewater and the Annapolis Valley.

  • Port Hawkesbury and Point Tupper. The deep-water energy terminal, pulp and paper, and power generation on the Strait of Canso.
  • Pictou County and Trenton. Tire manufacturing, power generation and railcar and structural fabrication history.
  • Goldboro and the Eastern Shore. The start of the Maritimes and Northeast Pipeline.
  • Bridgewater and the Annapolis Valley. Tire plants, food processing and manufacturing.
  • Bay of Fundy. Tidal energy testing and marine construction.

Neighbouring province: see NDT training in Saint John, New Brunswick. National view: NDT consulting across Canada.

Training alongside the Level III service

Direct answer: Nova Scotia clients can combine Level III consulting with ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for their own technicians, live online or onsite at their facility. Atlantis training is SNT-TC-1A only and does not prepare candidates for national CAN/CGSB-48.9712 or class certification.

Training covers Level I, II and III in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET for employers whose customers expect SNT-TC-1A certification. The Practical NDT simulator lets trainees practise twelve methods in five virtual environments, including a welding workshop, an oil and gas site and a storage tank, before practical exams; it is a practice tool and does not replace a practical exam on real specimens. See training, NDT training in Canada, online NDT training, corporate NDT training and ASNT Level III training.

How an engagement works

Direct answer: A Nova Scotia engagement begins with a call about your methods, customers, codes, certification schemes and staffing, followed by a written scope and quote. Document work runs remotely; practical exams and site visits take place at your facility. Timing is agreed in the scope rather than assumed.

  1. Discovery call. Methods, customers, codes and class rules, the schemes your people hold, and the trigger: an audit, a new contract, a departing Level III or a move into US work.
  2. Document review. You share your written practice, procedures and a sample of certification files and reports, and we identify gaps.
  3. Scope and quote. Deliverables, remote and onsite elements and responsibilities in writing. Pricing is quote on request.
  4. Delivery. Drafting, approval and issue of documents; exams under your written practice; corrective actions; ongoing Level III duties if retained.
  5. Onsite visits. Practical exams, procedure demonstrations and audit support at your Nova Scotia site, planned around refits, outages and weather.
  6. Review. Annual programme review for retained clients and updates when codes, customers or schemes change.

Frequently asked questions

How do I find an NDT Level III consultant in Nova Scotia?

Independent Level IIIs are scarce in Atlantic Canada, so many shops use an outside Level III who works remotely and visits onsite. Atlantis offers that for SNT-TC-1A programmes, led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III.

Who regulates boilers and pressure vessels in Nova Scotia?

The Technical Safety Division of the Department of Labour, Skills and Immigration administers the Technical Safety Act and the Boiler and Pressure Equipment Regulations, including design registration, permits, licences and re-inspection.

Who regulates offshore energy work off Nova Scotia?

The Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator (CNSOER), formerly the CNSOPB. Its mandate expanded to offshore renewable energy in January 2025.

Is ASNT certification accepted in Nova Scotia?

It depends on the customer. US customers and US-code work commonly accept SNT-TC-1A. Many Canadian owners, naval programmes and offshore projects call for CAN/CGSB-48.9712 or ISO 9712 certification, and class societies have their own rules. Check the contract.

Is CAN/CGSB-48.9712 still valid after the CGSB closed?

Yes. The Canadian General Standards Board closed on 1 April 2026, but the standard remains valid and certification bodies have said they continue to certify. Confirm the current certification body before relying on it.

Do I need a licence for industrial radiography in Nova Scotia?

Gamma radiography requires a CNSC licence for the company and CNSC-certified exposure device operators, or work under their direct supervision. Confirm current provincial requirements for X-ray equipment.

Can you write NDT procedures for shipbuilding subcontractors?

Yes. We write and review VT, MT, UT, RT and PT procedures and technique sheets to the shipbuilder's and customer's specifications; customer and class approvals remain with them.

What does an outsourced Level III do for a Nova Scotia shop?

They act as the Level III named in your SNT-TC-1A written practice: approving procedures, administering exams, reviewing certifications, answering technical questions and supporting audits, without a full-time hire.

Can practical exams be done remotely?

No. Practical exams need the candidate, real specimens and the examiner together, so they are held onsite at your facility.

How much does Level III consulting cost in Nova Scotia?

Quote on request. Cost depends on methods, retained versus project work, exam volume and onsite visits. Atlantis keeps its services affordable, accessible and fully customisable.

Does Atlantis have an office in Halifax?

No. Atlantis has no physical office or training centre in Nova Scotia; work is delivered remotely and onsite at the client's facility.
