NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in Manitoba

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution is a fully customized ERP for NDT and inspection companies in Manitoba. It tracks technician certifications across CAN/CGSB-48.9712, NAS 410, SNT-TC-1A and other schemes, controls instrument calibration, dispatches crews from Winnipeg to hydro, mining and oilfield sites, captures NDT reports offline and runs quoting, timesheets and invoicing. Setup is remote and typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff, depending on how clean your existing records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Ask for a Manitoba demo.

Manitoba's NDT market is unusual for the Prairies. Oil and gas matters, but it is not the centre of gravity. Winnipeg is one of Canada's main aerospace manufacturing and engine-overhaul cities, Manitoba Hydro runs a large fleet of hydroelectric stations on the Nelson and Winnipeg rivers, the north has nickel, copper and zinc mining, and the city has a manufacturing base in buses, coaches, agricultural equipment and steel. Most inspection companies here work from Winnipeg and send technicians out to sites that can be a long drive or a flight away. That combination of tightly audited aerospace work and remote heavy-industry work is what your business system has to handle.

Where the NDT work is in Manitoba

Direct answer: Manitoba NDT demand comes from Winnipeg aerospace (engine overhaul, composite and metallic parts), Manitoba Hydro's generating stations and transmission, northern mining around Thompson, Snow Lake and Flin Flon, southwest Manitoba oil production around Virden and Waskada, the Enbridge mainline, and Winnipeg and Brandon manufacturing, fertiliser and steel.

Winnipeg aerospace. StandardAero overhauls and repairs gas turbine engines in Winnipeg, Boeing has a large composite parts plant in the city, and Magellan Aerospace manufactures engine and structural components there. Their suppliers and service shops run eddy current, penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic and radiographic inspection, usually under customer specifications that call for NAS 410 or EN 4179 personnel qualification. That work is heavily audited, and the paperwork is as important as the inspection.

Hydro. Manitoba Hydro generates most of the province's electricity from hydroelectric stations, with the largest on the Nelson River in the north, including Kettle, Long Spruce, Limestone and the newer Keeyask station, and older stations on the Winnipeg River east of the city. Turbines, runners, penstocks, gates, cranes and structural steel need periodic inspection, often during planned unit outages with fixed windows.

Northern mining. Vale operates nickel mining in Thompson, and Hudbay operates around Snow Lake and Flin Flon. Hoists, headframes, crushers, mills, tanks and piping need NDT, and the sites are remote, with fly-in or long-drive access and their own safety rules.

Southwest oil and pipelines. Light oil production around Virden and Waskada in southwest Manitoba brings wellsite facilities, batteries and gathering lines. The Enbridge mainline crosses the south of the province on its way to the US, with a major terminal at Cromer.

Manufacturing and processing. New Flyer and Motor Coach Industries build buses and coaches in Winnipeg, MacDon builds agricultural equipment, Gerdau runs a steel mini-mill in Selkirk and Koch Fertilizer operates a nitrogen plant in Brandon. Welded structures, pressure equipment and process plant generate steady fabrication and in-service inspection. The Port of Churchill on Hudson Bay and the Whiteshell Laboratories decommissioning project at Pinawa add occasional specialised work.

For a Winnipeg-based NDT company, this mix means one technician might spend Monday on an engine component in an aerospace shop and Thursday on a penstock in a northern generating station. The two jobs have different clients, procedures, report formats and audit expectations, and the company has to keep both straight.

Manitoba regulators, codes and certification schemes

Direct answer: Boilers and pressure vessels in Manitoba fall under The Steam and Pressure Plants Act, administered by Inspection and Technical Services (ITS) under the Office of the Fire Commissioner, with CSA B51 as the construction code. Industrial radiography is licensed by the CNSC. Interprovincial pipelines such as the Enbridge mainline are regulated by the Canada Energy Regulator. Personnel certification follows CAN/CGSB-48.9712 for industry and NAS 410 or EN 4179 for aerospace.

ITS Manitoba handles boiler and pressure vessel safety through inspections, design registration, quality assurance plans and welding procedure registration. Owners, repair organisations and their NDT contractors produce the records ITS and insurers rely on. See our notes on ITS Manitoba compliance, CSA B51 and CRN registration. Pipeline work follows CSA Z662; provincial oil and gas facilities are overseen by the province, and the Enbridge mainline by the Canada Energy Regulator.

Radiography anywhere in Canada needs a CNSC licence, and exposure device operators must hold CNSC certification. Workplace Safety and Health rules apply on every site, and Manitoba Hydro, the mines and the large manufacturers all run their own contractor safety prequalification.

Personnel certification is the area with most variety. Industrial clients usually expect CAN/CGSB-48.9712 certificates. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026; CAN/CGSB-48.9712 remains valid, but confirm the current certification body for renewals. Aerospace customers usually require employer certification under NAS 410 or EN 4179 with a responsible Level 3, plus annual vision tests. US-owned plants and US-code work may call for an ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practice. Fabricators and inspection organisations may also hold CSA W47.1 or CSA W178.1 certification.

What aerospace and heavy-industry clients audit

Direct answer: Aerospace customers audit personnel qualifications, vision tests, procedures and technique sheets, equipment and reference standard calibration, and report traceability. Hydro, mining and oil clients focus on certification currency, calibration certificates, safety prequalification, outage readiness and daily reporting. Both want to trace any past report back to the person, instrument and procedure revision behind it.

An aerospace auditor at a Winnipeg shop will pick a report from months ago and ask: who signed it, what was their scheme, level and method certification on that date, was their near-vision and colour-perception test current, which procedure revision applied, and when was the eddy current instrument and its reference standard last calibrated. Each missing link is a finding, and repeated findings can cost a supplier its approval.

A hydro or mining client is less interested in the detail of one report and more interested in readiness. Can you put enough certified technicians on site for a unit outage that starts on a set date? Are their site orientations and safety tickets current? Are the instruments calibrated? Will daily progress arrive on time? Their contractor-management staff will also ask for insurance and safety programme documents.

Most small Manitoba NDT companies hold this information in spreadsheets, shared folders and an accounting package. The records exist, but they are not linked, so a lapsed vision test does not stop a technician being booked on an aerospace job. That link is the main reason to run an NDT ERP.

What the Atlantis ERP does for Manitoba NDT companies

NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in New Brunswick

Short answer: New Brunswick inspection work is dominated by short, intense windows: refinery turnarounds in Saint John, planned outages at generating stations, nuclear maintenance at Point Lepreau, and pulp mill shutdowns. The Atlantis ERP solution is a fully customized ERP for NDT and inspection companies that keeps the records those windows depend on in one place: technician certificates and vision tests, instrument calibration, crew dispatch and availability, offline NDT reports, procedures, timesheets and invoicing. It is implemented remotely, typically in 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff, depending on how clean your existing records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Ask for a New Brunswick demo.

If you run an NDT company in New Brunswick, the hard part is rarely the inspection itself. It is the two weeks before a turnaround, when you have to prove that thirty technicians hold current certificates and vision tests, that every flaw detector and gauge is inside its calibration window, that the procedures on the job are the approved revisions, and that nobody is booked on two sites at once. Then it is the weeks after, when timesheets, standby hours and reports have to be reconciled into invoices that the client's accounts team will accept. This page sets out how the New Brunswick market shapes those demands, what the Atlantis ERP does about them, and what to check before you buy any inspection management software.

The New Brunswick inspection market in practice

Direct answer: Most NDT spend in New Brunswick sits in four places: the Saint John energy and industrial cluster (the Irving Oil refinery, the LNG terminal, port and pulp and paper), power generation (including the Point Lepreau nuclear station and thermal plants), the forest products industry spread across the province, and fabrication and logistics around Moncton, Fredericton and the north shore.

Saint John. The Irving Oil refinery in Saint John is the largest refinery in Canada, and its turnarounds are among the biggest single blocks of inspection work in Atlantic Canada. Crude and product tankage, process piping, heat exchangers, columns and pressure vessels all need examination, and the work arrives in compressed, carefully planned campaigns. Nearby, the Saint John LNG terminal (formerly Canaport LNG) operates cryogenic storage tanks, piping and marine loading infrastructure. The Port of Saint John handles bulk liquids, containers and dry bulk, and the city's pulp, paper and tissue operations run digesters, recovery boilers and pressure equipment that are inspected during mill shutdowns. The result is a dense local market where the same technicians may work for three different clients in one month, each with its own document pack.

Power generation. NB Power's Point Lepreau Generating Station on the Bay of Fundy is the only nuclear power station in Atlantic Canada, and its planned outages bring tightly controlled inspection campaigns. NB Power also operates thermal stations such as Coleson Cove near Saint John and Belledune on the north shore, alongside hydro stations on the Saint John River. Boiler tubes, headers, steam lines and turbine components are typical outage targets, and outage dates are fixed long in advance, so mobilisation and paperwork have to be ready on day one.

Forest products. Pulp and paper mills in places such as Nackawic, Atholville and Saint John, along with sawmills and panel plants across the province, keep a steady stream of thickness surveys, weld inspections and pressure equipment examinations. Mill reliability teams often want results in their own spreadsheet layouts so they can file them against equipment numbers.

Moncton, Fredericton and the north shore. Moncton's logistics and manufacturing base, fabrication shops around Fredericton and the Port of Belledune's industrial activity create demand for in-shop MT, PT, UT and VT, plus field work on structural steel and process equipment. Two interprovincial and international gas pipelines also cross the province, adding pipeline construction and integrity work.

Regulators and standards New Brunswick inspection companies work under

Direct answer: Boilers, pressure vessels and pressure piping are regulated by the Department of Public Safety's Technical Inspection Services under the provincial Boiler and Pressure Vessel Act, with CSA B51 and Canadian Registration Numbers for design registration. Industrial radiography and nuclear facilities answer to the CNSC, international and interprovincial pipelines to the Canada Energy Regulator, and national personnel certification is CAN/CGSB-48.9712.

Technical Inspection Services issues certificates of inspection that owners need in order to operate boilers and pressure vessels, inspects newly installed or modified boilers, pressure vessels and pressure piping before they go into service, and carries out periodic in-service inspections. New designs need a Canadian Registration Number; see our notes on CSA B51 and CRN registration. For an NDT contractor, that means repair and alteration examinations sit directly in the path of an owner's return-to-service approval.

The Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission licenses industrial radiography across Canada and certifies exposure device operators (see CNSC compliance for inspection companies). The CNSC is also the regulator of Point Lepreau, and nuclear work brings the licensee's own quality programme and CSA nuclear standards into play; how those requirements are reflected in your records is worked out with you during scoping. Pipelines that cross provincial or national borders, such as the Maritimes and Northeast Pipeline and the Brunswick Pipeline, are regulated by the Canada Energy Regulator, with CSA Z662 as the governing standard.

For personnel, the national scheme is CAN/CGSB-48.9712, the Canadian adoption of ISO 9712. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026; the standard remains valid, but confirm the current certification body before planning renewals. Many New Brunswick employers also hold employer-based certification under an ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practice for US-owned clients and US-code work, and fabricators working to CSA W47.1 often deal with CSA W178.1 inspection organisations and W178.2 welding inspectors.

None of these bodies approves inspection management software, and the Atlantis ERP makes no such claim. What they share is a demand for traceable evidence, and that is where the ERP helps.

Turnaround and outage readiness: the real buying trigger

Direct answer: New Brunswick inspection companies usually look for an ERP after a turnaround or outage exposes the gaps: a lapsed certificate found at the gate, a gauge out of calibration, a technician double-booked, or weeks spent reconciling standby hours for the invoice. The Atlantis ERP is built to catch those issues before mobilisation.

Think through a Saint John turnaround from the contractor's side. The client asks for a crew list weeks in advance with certificates, vision tests and site orientation records. Instruments must be shown to be calibrated with traceable certificates. Procedures must be the current approved revisions, signed by your Level 3. During the job, daily reports and timesheets are expected every shift, often split between inspection, travel, standby and setup. At the end, the report pack and invoice go to different departments of the client, and both have to match.

In the Atlantis ERP, the crew list comes from technician records that already carry computed certificate status, so an expired or expiring certificate is visible before the name goes on the list. Team assignments block double-booking of technicians and of equipment serial numbers, and warn when assigned equipment is out of calibration. The availability calendar shows leave, training and sick days alongside assignments, so you can see who is genuinely free for the outage window. Timesheets record work type, method, site, client, equipment serial and billable status, with a rate multiplier for overtime or standby, and they warn if a technician's certificate is not valid on the day. Those hours feed invoice lines by method, technician, equipment serial and cost centre.

The same logic applies to a Point Lepreau or Coleson Cove outage or a mill shutdown. The client and the paperwork change; the evidence chain does not.

Turnaround season puts every instrument in the company into the field at once. That is when calibration dates slip and probes go missing. The asset management module records equipment type, assigned person, condition, asset tag, firmware, accessories and lifecycle stage (new, active, in calibration, in repair, rented out, retired or disposed), with calibration frequency and status. The maintenance log records preventive and corrective work, repairs, firmware updates and probe replacement. Bilingual operations and client reporting

Direct answer: New Brunswick is Canada's officially bilingual province, and some clients, employees or public bodies may want documents or interfaces in French as well as English. Bilingual needs are discussed during scoping so the setup matches your clients and your team.

In practice, many New Brunswick inspection companies operate mainly in English while serving some clients and employing some technicians who work in French, particularly in the north and east of the province. Report templates are company-specific and versioned, and can be built in Excel, Word, PDF or HTML with your logo, header and footer. Report records themselves capture work order, request, WPS, contract, drawing, procedure and standard references, method-specific data such as UT probe calibration tables, RT source and IQI details, MT technique, PT method and developer, and PAUT focal laws, plus weld or job lines with defect type and orientation. The workflow runs from draft to in progress, review, approved and sent, with inspector, reviewer and approver signatures and a third-party or authorized inspector's name and signature where needed. Reports can also feed a 3D model through Digital Twin Reporting and Atlantis Digital Twins in Saint John.

NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in New South Wales

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution gives New South Wales NDT and inspection companies one system for technicians, certificates, equipment, calibration, procedures, crew dispatch, field reports, timesheets, quotes and invoices. AINDT (ISO 9712) and ASNT SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 certificates are tracked side by side with automatic expiry status, calibration from NATA-accredited labs is checked before kit leaves the store, and crews can be scheduled across the Hunter, the Illawarra, Sydney and the Central West. New South Wales has the most varied inspection market in the country. In one week a NSW NDT company might be doing weld UT at a steelworks in Port Kembla, MT on a dragline in the Hunter Valley, boiler tube thickness surveys at a coal-fired power station, radiography on a new pipeline, eddy current on aircraft components in western Sydney and visual inspection of a bridge or tunnel structure for a government project. Each of those clients has its own codes, its own paperwork and its own idea of what a finished report looks like. The common problem is admin: certificates in one spreadsheet, calibration in another, crew bookings on a whiteboard and invoices in an accounting package that knows nothing about methods or technicians. This page explains the NSW market, what clients and regulators ask for, what the Atlantis ERP does, and how to compare it with the alternatives.

The New South Wales inspection market, region by region

Direct answer: NSW NDT work concentrates in the Hunter (power generation, aluminium, coal mining, the Port of Newcastle and chemical plant at Kooragang Island), the Illawarra (steelmaking and the port at Port Kembla), Sydney (fuel terminals, Botany industry, infrastructure, defence and aviation), and the Central West and far west (mining and processing). The energy transition is changing the mix of work across all of them.

The Hunter. The Hunter Valley has been the state's heavy-industry engine for a century. The Port of Newcastle is one of the world's largest coal export ports, fed by open-cut mines in the Upper Hunter. Bayswater and Eraring power stations carry boilers, turbines, pressure piping and large structures that need regular NDT during outages; Eraring is scheduled to close later this decade, and the work around the region's coal plants is shifting toward life-extension outages, decommissioning and new energy projects. The Tomago aluminium smelter, whose long-term future was secured under an agreement with the Commonwealth and NSW governments in 2026, and the chemical and fertiliser plants on Kooragang Island add steady shutdown work. A dense base of fabrication and engineering shops around Newcastle and Maitland builds pressure equipment and structural steel for projects across the east coast.

The Illawarra. Port Kembla is home to the BlueScope steelworks and a deepwater port. Steelmaking means furnaces, gas holders, cranes, structures, rolling mills and pressure systems, all with ongoing weld and thickness inspection, plus fabrication shops in Wollongong that build to AS/NZS 1554.

Sydney. Sydney no longer refines crude oil, but the Kurnell and Botany areas hold fuel import terminals, chemical plants and storage tanks. Large transport, tunnelling and water projects, the naval base at Garden Island, airports and aviation maintenance, and a broad base of manufacturing in the west of the city keep NDT companies busy, and many NSW inspection businesses keep their head office, store and calibration room in western Sydney.

The Central West and beyond. Gold and copper mines and processing plants around Orange and Parkes, the Cobar mining district, and pumped hydro and renewable energy construction add remote work where long drives and camp-based crews are normal.

What NSW clients and principal contractors expect from NDT vendors

Direct answer: NSW clients expect certified technicians (usually AINDT under ISO 9712, sometimes ASNT-based employer certification), licensed radiographers, NATA-traceable calibration, approved procedures to the relevant Australian standard, site inductions and medicals, and reports in their format. Government infrastructure and defence work add their own quality and document-control requirements.

  • People: AINDT certification by method and level for most industrial work. US-designed equipment, aviation work under OEM requirements and contractors with SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 based quality systems may ask for employer certification under a written practice instead or as well.
  • Radiography: the NSW Environment Protection Authority licenses radiation users and the management of radiation sources and apparatus under the state's radiation legislation, so clients ask to see the radiographer's licence, the company's management licence, dosimetry and source transport arrangements.
  • Calibration: current certificates for every instrument and reference block, typically from NATA-accredited labs.
  • Procedures: Level 3 approved, revision-controlled procedures referencing standards such as AS 3978, AS/NZS 1554, AS 2885 or ASME Section V.
  • Site and project rules: mine site inductions under the NSW mining safety framework, construction inductions, medicals, and the client's contractor management platform.
  • Reports: signed off by the right level and delivered within the outage or construction schedule.

SafeWork NSW administers work health and safety, including registration of plant designs and items of plant such as many pressure vessels. In-service inspection of pressure equipment generally follows AS/NZS 3788, run by the owner and its inspectors; your NDT results feed that programme. The NSW Resources Regulator oversees safety on mines.

Why NSW NDT companies outgrow spreadsheets

Direct answer: The tipping point usually comes when a company runs more than one client type at once, for example power outages, mine maintenance and fabrication. Certificate, calibration and booking checks then multiply, and the cost of one missed expiry or an unbilled standby day becomes bigger than the cost of a proper system.

The symptoms are familiar. A technician is booked on a Hunter outage while already promised to a fabrication shop in Wollongong. A PAUT set goes to site with a calibration certificate that expired the week before. A Level 2's vision test lapses and nobody notices until a client's auditor does. Travel days to the Central West are left off the invoice. Procedure revisions in the Sydney office and the Newcastle office no longer match. None of this is unusual, and none of it is solved by working harder. It is solved by keeping people, equipment, jobs and billing in one place with the checks built in.

The ERP covers UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ECT, IRIS, PAUT, MFL, TOFD, PWHT, PMI, hardness, UT thickness, ferrite, holiday and coating, and computed radiography reports, each with its own numbering. Method fields include the UT probe calibration table, RT source and IQI details, MT technique and particle type, PT method and developer, PAUT focal laws and UT thickness readings by direction, with weld lines recording defect type and orientation. NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in Newfoundland and Labrador

Short answer: Newfoundland and Labrador inspection companies work across some of the hardest logistics in Canada: offshore production platforms and FPSOs on the Grand Banks, fabrication yards in Placentia Bay and Trinity Bay, mines and hydro projects in Labrador reached by air, and industrial sites spread around a large island. The Atlantis ERP solution is a fully customized ERP for NDT and inspection companies that keeps technician certificates, vision tests, instrument calibration, crew rotations, offline field reports, procedures, timesheets and invoicing in one system. It is implemented remotely, typically in 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff, depending on how clean your existing records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Request a Newfoundland and Labrador demo.

An NDT company based in St. John's or Mount Pearl may have one crew on a rotation offshore, another at a plant in Placentia Bay, a technician flying to Labrador West for a mine shutdown and a radiography crew working on a fabrication job, all in the same fortnight. Each of those clients wants proof that the people are qualified, the instruments calibrated and the procedures approved, and each wants its reports and invoices in its own format. When the evidence lives in spreadsheets and email folders, the office spends its time chasing paperwork. This page explains what the Newfoundland and Labrador market expects from inspection contractors, what the Atlantis ERP does about it, and what to check before buying any inspection management software.

The Newfoundland and Labrador inspection market

Direct answer: NDT demand in Newfoundland and Labrador comes from offshore oil production on the Grand Banks (Hibernia, Hebron, Terra Nova and White Rose), the onshore fabrication and supply base that supports it around St. John's, Placentia Bay and Trinity Bay, mining and processing in Labrador and at Long Harbour, hydroelectric and thermal power, and industrial sites such as the Come By Chance renewable fuels refinery and the Corner Brook paper mill.

Offshore production. The province's offshore industry is built around four producing developments on the Grand Banks. Hibernia and Hebron are gravity-based structures, while Terra Nova and White Rose produce through floating production, storage and offloading vessels. Topsides piping, pressure vessels, structural steel, risers, mooring components and storage tanks all require scheduled and campaign inspection, and the offshore environment (cold water, icebergs, fog, helicopter-only crew access and limited bed space) makes every mobilisation expensive. Equinor's Bay du Nord project in the Flemish Pass is in front-end engineering, with a final investment decision targeted for 2027, which could add a new FPSO to the region.

Fabrication and supply base. The Bull Arm fabrication site in Trinity Bay was used to build the Hebron gravity-based structure, and fabrication and marine yards in Marystown, Argentia and around St. John's support offshore and marine work. The Port of St. John's and the offshore supply bases near the city handle supply vessels and equipment. Fabrication work brings weld inspection to customer and code requirements, often with radiography and ultrasonic testing on critical joints.

Placentia Bay industry. The Come By Chance refinery has been converted to produce renewable diesel and is operated by Braya Renewable Fuels, which keeps tankage, piping, reactors and pressure equipment in service. Vale's Long Harbour processing plant handles nickel concentrate from the Voisey's Bay mine. Both generate shutdown and maintenance inspection campaigns.

Labrador. The Iron Ore Company of Canada operates in Labrador City, and iron ore mining continues in the Wabush area. Voisey's Bay on the north coast is a remote fly-in mine. Churchill Falls and Muskrat Falls are major hydroelectric facilities linked to the island by transmission infrastructure. Mining and hydro bring structural, crane, penstock, mill and pressure equipment inspection, usually on rotation.

Power and industry on the island. The Holyrood thermal generating station, Corner Brook Pulp and Paper on the west coast, fish processing plants and municipal infrastructure round out the onshore picture. Distances between these sites are large, and weather can close roads and ferries, so planning matters.

Who regulates inspection work in Newfoundland and Labrador

Direct answer: Offshore energy activity is regulated by the Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator (C-NLOER). Onshore boilers, pressure vessels and compressed gas systems are regulated by the province's Engineering and Inspection Services division under the Public Safety Act and its Boiler, Pressure Vessel and Compressed Gas Regulations. Radiography is licensed by the CNSC, and national personnel certification is CAN/CGSB-48.9712.

The C-NLOER was known as the Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Petroleum Board until amendments to the Atlantic Accord Acts came into force on 2 June 2025, expanding its mandate to include offshore renewable energy and changing its name. It oversees safety, environmental protection and resource management for offshore activity, and offshore occupational health and safety is set under the Accord Acts. Operators hold certificates of fitness for their installations from independent certifying authorities, and contractors are expected to keep controlled documentation, competence records and traceable inspection evidence. The detail of what each operator requires sits in its contracts and management system, so contractors should expect operator-specific forms and audits.

Onshore, the province's Engineering and Inspection Services division (historically part of Service NL; confirm the current department name) oversees the installation, alteration and periodic inspection of boilers, pressure vessels and pressure systems. Installations and alterations need a permit and an inspection on completion, and new designs need a Canadian Registration Number before manufacture or installation; see our notes on CSA B51 and CRN registration.

The Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission licenses industrial radiography across Canada and certifies exposure device operators; see CNSC compliance for inspection companies. National personnel certification is CAN/CGSB-48.9712, the Canadian adoption of ISO 9712. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026; the standard remains valid, but confirm the current certification body before planning renewals. Fabricators working to CSA W47.1 often deal with CSA W178.1 inspection organisations and W178.2 welding inspectors, and offshore and marine clients may also expect classification-society requirements to be met.

None of these bodies approves inspection management software, and the Atlantis ERP makes no such claim. What they demand is evidence, and that is what the ERP organises.

Offshore and remote-site requirements for NDT contractors

Direct answer: Offshore operators and remote mine sites in the province usually want a contractor prequalification file, current certificates and vision tests for every person on the manifest, offshore survival and medical records handled through their own systems, calibration evidence for every instrument, Level 3-approved procedures and reports in their own format. Because every trip offshore or to Labrador is costly, the paperwork must be right before anyone travels.

The cost of a mistake is higher here than almost anywhere in Canada. If a technician arrives offshore with a certificate that expired last week, the operator may send them back on the next flight and your crew is short until a replacement is mobilised. If a flaw detector's calibration lapses mid-rotation, the results may be challenged. If a procedure revision was superseded and nobody updated the job pack, the report may be rejected. Each of those is a records problem rather than an inspection problem.

The Atlantis ERP addresses them at the point of planning. Technician records carry computed certificate and vision-test status, with warning tasks 90 days before expiry, so a rotation plan made a month ahead already shows who will lapse during the trip. Team assignments record mobilisation and demobilisation dates, block double-booking of technicians and equipment serial numbers, and warn when an assigned instrument is out of calibration. The availability calendar shows assigned, leave, training, sick and unavailable days, so time off between rotations is visible alongside work.

Offshore survival training, medicals and site orientations are managed under each operator's system. The ERP holds the NDT-specific evidence (certificates, vision tests, medical fitness expiry on the NDT profile, calibration and procedures) and anything else you choose to configure during implementation.

Certification tracking for CGSB, ASNT and CNSC records

Direct answer: Each technician certificate is a separate record with scheme, level, method, certifying body and dates. CGSB certificates sit under the ISO 9712 scheme with the certifying body named, employer certifications under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 written practices sit alongside, and CNSC exposure device operator certificates can be recorded so they get the same expiry warnings.

Offshore and fabrication work in the province involves a mix of owners and contractors from Canada, the United States and Europe, so it is common for technicians to hold more than one certification. A UT technician might carry a CGSB Level 2 and an employer certification under an SNT-TC-1A written practice used on a US-code fabrication contract. A radiographer needs method certification plus CNSC certification. Some technicians arrive with PCN or other ISO 9712-based certificates from work in the North Sea.

Each record holds the scheme (SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, ISO 9712, PCN, CSWIP or other), the level (trainee, I, II or III), method, certifying body, industry sector, issue, expiry and renewal dates, OJT hours, training hours, exam result and attachments. Certificate templates per scheme set validity in months, whether a vision test or exam is required and minimum OJT and training hours. Vision tests are recorded with near vision (Jaeger J1 or J2), far vision, colour perception, contrast, examiner, clinic, certificate file and expiry. Examination sheets hold general, specific and practical scores. The employee NDT profile shows highest level, methods certified, radiation safety training, radiation badge number and medical fitness expiry.

Daily checks create warning tasks 90 days before expiry, and configurable email alerts go to your chosen recipients for technician certificates, calibration certificates and company certifications. Company certifications such as ISO 9001 or CSA W178.1 can be tracked with their own alert days.

For the programme side, Atlantis offers Level III support and ASNT SNT-TC-1A training separately from the software; see NDT consulting in Canada and SNT-TC-1A training for Canadian employers. Atlantis does not train toward CGSB, PCN or other ISO 9712 certification, though the ERP records those certificates.

Equipment, calibration and radiography logistics

Direct answer: Every instrument and accessory is tracked by serial number with its calibration status, assigned person, condition and lifecycle stage. Issue and return need approval, reservations prevent clashes, and the system warns when out-of-calibration equipment is assigned. Radiography vehicles are recorded with their source-carrying status and transport licence expiry.

When a phased array set goes offshore for three weeks or a thickness gauge flies to Labrador, it is out of the office's sight. The asset management module records equipment type, assigned person, condition, asset tag, firmware, accessories and lifecycle stage (new, active, in calibration, in repair, rented out, retired or disposed), with calibration frequency and status. Issue and return go through supervisor and manager approval with condition recorded both times, and inbound and outbound movements are logged. Reservations stop two crews booking the same unit for overlapping trips.

Calibration records hold provider, certificate number, standard, range, uncertainty, accredited-lab flag, result and next due date, and the calibration certificate register holds the lab accreditation number, status and PDF, with expiry alerts. NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in the Northern Territory

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution is a fully customized ERP for NDT and inspection companies working in the Northern Territory. It holds AINDT and other ISO 9712 certificates alongside ASNT SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 certifications with automatic expiry status, tracks instrument calibration and equipment issue, dispatches crews to LNG plants, defence bases, vessels and remote mines, lets technicians report offline, and runs quoting through invoicing on one system. Implementation is remote and typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff, depending on how clean your existing records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Ask for a Northern Territory demo.

Running an inspection business in the Territory is mostly a logistics problem. The work is concentrated around Darwin Harbour, but a good share of it sits a long flight or a very long drive away, the wet season closes roads and shifts shutdown windows, and a lot of the workforce rotates in from interstate. Clients range from LNG operators with strict vendor systems to defence contractors, vessel owners and remote mine sites. If your certificates, calibration records, rosters and reports live in different places, every one of those jobs costs more office time than it should. This page explains where Territory NDT work comes from, what clients and regulators look for, and how the Atlantis ERP handles it.

Where NDT work comes from in the Northern Territory

Direct answer: Territory NDT demand centres on the two LNG plants on Darwin Harbour, defence bases and the growing marine sustainment precinct at East Arm, power and gas transmission, and remote mining across the Top End, the Gulf country and Central Australia. Most of it runs out of Darwin and Palmerston.

LNG on Darwin Harbour. Darwin has two LNG export plants. Darwin LNG at Wickham Point, operated by Santos, began receiving gas from the offshore Barossa field after first gas in September 2025, which extends the plant's working life by around two decades. INPEX's Ichthys LNG plant at Bladin Point is fed by an 889 km subsea pipeline from the Ichthys field in the Browse Basin. Both plants run cryogenic and high-pressure process equipment, large storage tanks, flare systems and extensive piping. Turnarounds and routine integrity programmes create demand for UT thickness, PAUT and TOFD weld inspection, radiography, MT, PT and visual inspection, plus positive material identification and hardness testing. Operators of this size run detailed vendor qualification and expect every report to trace back to a certified technician, a calibrated instrument and an approved procedure.

Defence and marine sustainment. The Top End has a heavy defence footprint: RAAF Base Darwin, RAAF Base Tindal near Katherine, Robertson Barracks in Palmerston, the naval base HMAS Coonawarra, and the annual Marine Rotational Force rotation. Aircraft, vehicles and patrol vessels all generate inspection work. The Northern Territory Government is building the Darwin Ship Lift Facility at East Arm as part of a Northern Marine Complex, with staged operations planned from 2027. Once running, it is designed to support defence sustainment, offshore energy servicing and commercial vessel maintenance, which means more hull, weld and structural inspection on vessels lifted out of the water in Darwin rather than sent south or overseas.

Power, gas transmission and onshore gas. Power stations around Darwin and in Alice Springs, the Amadeus Gas Pipeline running north to Darwin and the Northern Gas Pipeline from Tennant Creek to Mount Isa all need pipeline and pressure equipment inspection to AS 2885 and AS/NZS 3788. Onshore gas appraisal in the Beetaloo Sub-basin adds wellsite and facility work when activity picks up.

Remote mining. Glencore's McArthur River zinc-lead mine near Borroloola, bauxite mining at Gove on the Gove Peninsula, gold mining in the Tanami, and mine rehabilitation projects such as the former Ranger uranium mine near Jabiru produce shutdown and maintenance inspection on mills, tanks, pressure vessels, conveyors and structural steel. Nearly all of it is fly-in fly-out or long drive-in drive-out work.

The common thread is distance. A technician might be at Bladin Point on Monday and at a mine site in the Gulf country the following week, and the office needs to know, before they leave, that their certificates, eye test and instruments are all current for that client.

What Territory clients ask NDT vendors for

Direct answer: Clients in the Northern Territory usually ask for current personnel certificates (AINDT or other ISO 9712 certificates, and ASNT-based certification for US-code equipment or US-linked clients), approved procedures, calibration certificates, method-specific reports in the client's format, radiation licences for radiography, site inductions and permits, and often NATA accreditation.

LNG operators generally assess vendors before any work starts and audit again before major shutdowns. Expect to show personnel certification by method and level with expiry and vision-test dates, calibration certificates matched to the serial numbers that will be on site, procedure numbers and revisions, and safety records. LNG plant packages were built by international contractors to a mix of Australian, US and international codes, so ASME Section V references and ASNT-based certification come up regularly alongside AINDT and other ISO 9712 certificates. That makes holding both schemes cleanly on one technician profile a practical requirement in the Territory, not an edge case.

Defence work adds security and quality-system expectations. Primes and sustainment contractors tend to ask for documented competence, controlled procedures and evidence of report review on every component. Vessel work brings classification societies into the picture: hull and machinery repairs may be witnessed by a class surveyor, and the report pack has to include the inspector's certificate and the instrument's calibration certificate.

Pressure equipment work references AS/NZS 3788 for in-service inspection, AS 4343 for hazard levels, AS 1210 for vessels and AS 4041 for piping, and many asset owners want in-service inspectors who are AICIP registered. Mines and gas pipelines bring their own operator standards on top. None of these are certifications an ERP grants, but the ERP is where the evidence for them should live.

What the Atlantis ERP does for Northern Territory NDT companies

Direct answer: The Atlantis ERP brings certification tracking, equipment and calibration control, dispatch and rosters, offline reporting, procedure control, marine report packs, quoting, timesheets and invoicing into one system. Wet season, distance and FIFO: running remote crews from the ERP

Direct answer: The ERP helps you plan around the Territory's distances and seasons by blocking double-booking of people and instruments, recording mobilisation and demobilisation dates, tracking leave and training on one availability calendar, and logging travel and standby as separate timesheet work types so they can be billed correctly.

The wet season, roughly November to April, changes how Territory work is planned. Roads to remote sites can be cut, cyclones can stop work at short notice, and many owners prefer to schedule major shutdowns in the dry. When a job slips, the people and instruments booked to it need to be released and rebooked without anyone forgetting a flaw detector that is still sitting at a site. Team assignments move through planned, dispatched, in field, submitted and closed, so the office can see at a glance where every crew is. Double-booking of technicians and of equipment serial numbers is blocked, which matters when your one calibrated PAUT set is wanted by two clients in the same week.

Travel and standby time is a frequent source of disputes on remote jobs. Timesheets in the ERP record work type (inspection, travel, standby, setup), method, site, client, equipment serial and a billable flag with a rate multiplier, and they go through approval. When the invoice is raised, the lines already show what was inspection and what was travel or standby, which makes it easier for the client's accounts team to match it against the purchase order.

Field expenses and per diems on long rosters can be captured in Expenses and re-billed to the job. Consumables such as couplant, penetrant, developer and magnetic ink are tracked with reorder levels and low-stock flags, so a crew does not arrive at a remote mine without enough consumables to finish the job.

AINDT, ISO 9712 and ASNT certificates side by side

Direct answer: AINDT certificates are recorded under the ISO 9712 scheme with AINDT as the certifying body; ASNT-based employer certifications are recorded under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189. Both sit on the same technician profile with their own expiry status and alerts, so you can answer "who is certified for this method under this client's scheme" quickly.

The technician profile also records highest level, methods certified, radiation safety training, radiation badge number and medical fitness expiry. Vision tests are separate records with near vision (Jaeger J1/J2), far vision, colour perception, contrast, examiner, clinic and expiry. Examination sheets hold general, specific and practical scores for in-house employer certification. Certificate templates per scheme hold validity in months, whether a vision test or exam is required, and minimum OJT and training hours.

If your firm works to SNT-TC-1A for US-code clients, the written practice is the foundation; Atlantis can help with written practice development and an employer certification programme. For technicians, ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for Darwin-based technicians is delivered online or onsite at the employer's facility. Atlantis does not train toward AINDT or ISO 9712 certification; the ERP simply records those certificates.

Compliance and reporting context in the Northern Territory

Direct answer: Radiography in the Territory is licensed by the Department of Health's Radiation Protection unit under the Radiation Protection Act 2004 and Radiation Protection Regulations 2007, with sources and places of use registered. NT WorkSafe administers work health and safety, including plant duties. The ERP holds evidence for these; it does not replace them. Data hosting is discussed during scoping.

Radiation. In the Northern Territory, licences are issued for the use of industrial ionising radiation sources, and sources and their place of use generally have to be registered with the Radiation Protection unit. Store each radiographer's licence as a certificate with expiry alerts, the company's licences and registrations as company certifications with alert days, and source vehicles in fleet records with transport licence details. ARPANSA's national codes, including the code for safe transport of radioactive material, sit behind the state and territory rules.

Work health and safety. The Territory uses the national model work health and safety laws, administered by NT WorkSafe. Duties around plant, including pressure equipment, come from that framework, with Australian standards supplying the technical requirements. The ERP's project records carry safety induction and work permit fields alongside the client PO, methods, codes, scope and acceptance criteria.

Accreditation and reporting. NATA accreditation to ISO/IEC 17025 or 17020 is common among inspection providers to major operators. Assessors look for competence records, calibration traceability, procedure control and report review. The reports workflow (draft, in progress, review, approved, sent) records inspector, reviewer and approver signatures, plus a third-party or authorised inspector where one witnesses the work. The ERP supports accreditation; it does not grant it.

Data residency. Defence and some energy clients ask where data is hosted. That is discussed during scoping, so raise any contract requirements early.

Atlantis has no office in the Territory; scoping, configuration, data import and training are all done online, which suits firms whose people are spread across sites anyway.

NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in Nova Scotia

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution is a fully customized ERP built for NDT and inspection companies, and it fits the way Nova Scotia inspection firms actually work: shipyard and naval refit jobs in Halifax Harbour, utility outages at thermal plants, pulp and paper shutdowns, offshore decommissioning and fabrication shop work. Implementation is done remotely and typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff; it depends on how clean your existing records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Book a Nova Scotia ERP demo.

Most NDT companies in Nova Scotia are small to mid-sized. A typical firm has a handful of Level 2 technicians, one or two Level 3s or an outside Level 3, a mixed fleet of flaw detectors, thickness gauges and yokes, maybe a radiography crew, and a client list that swings between marine, power, pulp and paper, and industrial maintenance. The office side is usually a spreadsheet for certifications, another for calibration, a shared drive of report templates and an accounting package. That arrangement holds until a shipyard or utility auditor asks for the evidence behind a single report from eighteen months ago. This page explains what the Nova Scotia market asks of an inspection company, which parts of that the Atlantis ERP handles out of the box, and what gets configured for your business during implementation.

The Nova Scotia inspection market: where NDT work comes from

Direct answer: NDT demand in Nova Scotia is concentrated around Halifax Harbour (naval shipbuilding, ship repair, the port and fuel terminals), the Strait of Canso and Point Tupper (deep-water industrial port, pulp and paper, fuel storage), Cape Breton and Pictou County (power generation and heavy industry), and a spread of manufacturing, aerospace maintenance and fabrication shops along the Highway 102 corridor. Offshore work today leans toward decommissioning and the new offshore renewables mandate.

Halifax Harbour. Halifax Shipyard, operated by Irving Shipbuilding, is the combat-vessel yard under Canada's National Shipbuilding Strategy. It built the Arctic and Offshore Patrol Ships and began construction of the first of the Royal Canadian Navy's River-class destroyers in 2026, with a build programme expected to run for decades. That means steady demand for weld inspection on hull blocks, piping and structural steel, much of it to classification-society and naval quality requirements. Across the harbour, HMC Dockyard and the navy's fleet maintenance facility handle refit and repair, and commercial ship repair adds dry-dock and afloat work. The Port of Halifax handles container, bulk and roll-on cargo, and the fuel terminal in Dartmouth on the site of the former Imperial refinery keeps tankage, piping and loading infrastructure in service. For an inspection company, the harbour means many short jobs with different paperwork for each client.

Strait of Canso and Point Tupper. The Strait of Canso is one of the deepest ice-free harbours on the east coast of North America. Point Tupper hosts the Port Hawkesbury Paper mill and a large marine fuel terminal, and it has been put forward for new energy projects. Tank, piping and pressure vessel inspection, plus mill shutdown work, are the staple jobs here.

Cape Breton and Pictou County. Nova Scotia Power's thermal generating stations, including Lingan and Point Aconi in Cape Breton and Trenton in Pictou County, plus Tufts Cove in Dartmouth, run boilers, steam piping, turbines and pressure parts that are inspected during planned outages. Outage work is compressed into short windows, so mobilisation, crew certification and calibration status have to be right before the first shift.

Manufacturing and aerospace. Michelin operates tire plants in Granton, Bridgewater and Waterville, and the area around Halifax Stanfield International Airport supports aircraft maintenance and aerospace component work. Fabrication shops in Dartmouth's Burnside park, Truro and the Annapolis Valley supply structural steel, pressure vessels and process skids, and many run in-house MT, PT, UT and VT under CSA W47.1 or a customer's code.

Offshore. The Sable Offshore Energy Project and Deep Panuke have ceased production and moved into decommissioning. The regulator, now called the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator, has an expanded mandate that includes offshore renewable energy. Inspection firms that work offshore or at supply bases in Halifax face the strictest documentation expectations in the province.

Who sets the rules for inspection work in Nova Scotia

Direct answer: Boilers and pressure equipment are regulated by the province under the Technical Safety Act and its Boiler and Pressure Equipment Regulations, administered by the Technical Safety Division, with CSA B51 and Canadian Registration Numbers for design registration. Offshore activity falls under the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator, industrial radiography is licensed federally by the CNSC, and personnel certification nationally is CAN/CGSB-48.9712.

The Technical Safety Act and the Boiler and Pressure Equipment Regulations require boilers and pressure vessels to be installed, inspected in service and repaired under the oversight of the Chief Inspector, and repairs and alterations to boilers, pressure vessels and high-pressure piping are themselves inspected. New pressure equipment needs a Canadian Registration Number before it is fabricated or installed; see our notes on CSA B51 and CRN registration. An NDT company is rarely the regulated owner, but its reports go straight into the owner's file and its repair-weld examinations sit on the critical path of every return to service.

Offshore, the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator (formerly the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Petroleum Board; the name changed when the Accord Act amendments came into force on 31 January 2025) oversees safety and environmental protection for offshore petroleum activity and now offshore renewables. Operators and their contractors are expected to keep controlled documentation, competence records and traceable inspection evidence. Interprovincial and international pipelines, such as the Maritimes and Northeast Pipeline that crosses the province, are regulated by the Canada Energy Regulator, with CSA Z662 as the pipeline standard.

Industrial radiography anywhere in Canada is licensed by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, and exposure device operators need CNSC certification; see CNSC compliance for inspection companies. Provincial occupational health and safety law applies on every site you send a crew to. Personnel certification nationally is CAN/CGSB-48.9712, the Canadian adoption of ISO 9712. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026; CAN/CGSB-48.9712 remains valid, but confirm the current certification body before planning renewals. Fabricators working under CSA W47.1 often need inspection organisations certified to CSA W178.1 and welding inspectors certified to W178.2.

None of these bodies certifies software, and the Atlantis ERP does not claim any regulatory approval. What they create is an evidence chain. For any report, an auditor can ask who did the work, what certification they held on that date, which instrument and probe they used, when it was last calibrated and which procedure revision applied. The ERP's job is to answer that in minutes, not days.

What shipyards, utilities and mills ask of NDT vendors

Direct answer: Nova Scotia clients typically want a prequalification file (safety programme, insurance and often a contractor-management platform account), a personnel file with current certificates and vision tests, a calibration file for each instrument, Level 3-approved procedures, and reports in the client's own format. Defence and offshore clients add tighter document control and traceability.

The requests vary by client type. A shipyard wants technicians certified to the scheme its customer and classification society accept, inspection records tied to drawing and weld numbers, and reports that slot into its own quality system. A power utility wants a crew mobilised for a fixed outage date, with every technician's certificate, vision test and site orientation current before arrival, and a daily record of what was examined. A pulp mill wants thickness surveys and weld inspection reports filed against its equipment numbers, often in an Excel layout its reliability team already uses. An offshore operator or decommissioning contractor wants competence evidence, controlled procedures and full traceability.

Each request lands on a different desk in a small company: HR holds the certificates, the equipment room holds the calibration certificates, the Level 3 holds the procedures, the operations lead holds the schedule and the bookkeeper holds the invoices. When these records live in separate tools, the business depends on one or two people remembering to cross-check them. The Atlantis ERP connects them so that an expired certificate shows up at dispatch, on the timesheet and in the report record, and an out-of-calibration gauge is flagged when someone tries to assign it to a job.

Certification tracking for CGSB, ASNT, CNSC and CSA W178.2 records

CNSC exposure device operator and CSA W178.2 inspector certificates can be recorded the same way so they get the same warnings.

Technicians in Nova Scotia often carry several certifications at once. A UT technician on a shipyard contract may hold a CGSB Level 2 for Canadian work and an employer certification under an SNT-TC-1A written practice for a US-owned customer or a US-code project. A radiographer needs a method certification and a CNSC certification to operate an exposure device. A welding inspector may also hold CSA W178.2. When those records live in different spreadsheets, a renewal eventually slips through.

In the Atlantis ERP each certificate record holds the scheme (SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, ISO 9712, PCN, CSWIP or other), the level (trainee, I, II or III), the method, the certifying body, the industry sector, issue, expiry and renewal dates, OJT hours, training hours, whether the exam was passed, and attachments such as a scanned certificate. Status is computed automatically. Vision tests are tracked separately with near vision (Jaeger J1 or J2), far vision, colour perception, contrast, the examiner, the clinic, the certificate file and the expiry date. Examination sheets hold general, specific and practical scores against a passing score.

Certificate templates per scheme set the validity in months, whether a vision test or exam is required, and the minimum OJT and training hours, so a new record starts from the rules of the scheme it belongs to. Equipment, calibration and radiography logistics across the province

Direct answer: Every flaw detector, gauge, probe, yoke and accessory is tracked by serial number with its calibration status, assigned person and condition. Equipment is issued and returned with approvals, reservations prevent clashes, and the system warns when someone assigns out-of-calibration kit to a job. The Fleet app records which vehicles can carry radioactive sources and their transport licence expiry.

Nova Scotia jobs are not far apart by western Canadian standards, but kit still travels: from a Dartmouth base to Point Tupper on Monday, to a Cape Breton outage on Wednesday and back to a harbour job on Friday. Without a record of who has what, probes and calibration blocks go missing and someone eventually takes an instrument out of its calibration window.

The asset management module records each item's equipment type, assigned person, condition, asset tag, firmware, accessories and lifecycle stage (new, active, in calibration, in repair, rented out, retired or disposed). Issue and return go through supervisor and manager approval with the condition recorded both ways. Reservations stop two crews booking the same phased array unit for the same week, and inbound and outbound movements are logged. Consumables such as couplant, magnetic particle inks, penetrant kits and PPE carry reorder levels and low-stock flags.

Calibration records hold the provider, certificate number, standard, range, uncertainty, accredited-lab flag, pass, fail or conditional result and next due date. A separate calibration certificate register holds the lab's accreditation number, valid, expiring or expired status and the PDF, with expiry alerts. The maintenance log covers preventive and corrective work, repairs, cleaning, firmware updates and probe replacement with condition before and after. Purchase records can mark vendors as OEM, dealer or calibration lab, with accreditation number and expiry.

For radiography, the Fleet app records each vehicle's purpose, whether it can carry radioactive sources, the transport licence number and expiry, and which project and driver it is assigned to, with dates and mileage. Source inventories, leak tests and dosimetry are part of your CNSC licence obligations; the ERP holds the records and dates you choose to configure, and it does not replace your radiation safety officer's own programme.

Shipyard, naval and marine reporting in Halifax

Direct answer: The NDT reports module covers 17 report types, including UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, PAUT, TOFD, UT thickness and hardness, each with its own numbering. Marine mode adds a vessel cover page and merges the class certificate, the inspector's Level II certificate and the calibration certificate into one PDF, which suits ship repair and new-build inspection packs.

Marine and naval work is where Nova Scotia inspection companies feel document pressure most. Each report has to identify the vessel, the block or compartment, the weld or drawing number, the procedure and acceptance standard, and the people who did, reviewed and approved the work. In the Atlantis ERP each report captures work order, request, WPS, contract, drawing, procedure and standard references, carries method-specific data (UT probe calibration tables, RT source, technique, IQI type and placement, MT technique and particle type, PT method and developer, PAUT focal laws) and records weld or job lines with defect type and orientation and an overall result.

The report workflow runs from draft to in progress, review, approved and sent, with inspector, reviewer and approver signatures and the name and signature of a third-party or authorized inspector where one is involved. Marine mode adds the vessel cover page and photo, inspection location and dates, and a PDF that merges the classification-society certificate from a library covering DNV, ABS, Lloyd's Register, BV, RINA, IRS and ClassNK, the inspector's Level II certificate and the calibration certificate. Photos print in a 2-up grid.

Defence work carries its own security and quality requirements set by the prime contractor and the Crown. How data for that kind of work is stored, who can see it and where it is hosted are discussed during scoping, not assumed. Reports can also feed a 3D view through Digital Twin Reporting and Atlantis Digital Twins in Halifax when a client wants indications and thickness trends shown on a model.

Direct answer: The Atlantis ERP keeps the records an auditor asks for, but it is not a regulator-approved system and does not file anything with the Technical Safety Division, CNSOER or CNSC on your behalf. Hosting location, data residency, language and record-retention periods are discussed during scoping so they match your clients' contracts.

Questions Nova Scotia buyers raise most often are practical. Where is the data hosted and can it stay in Canada? How long are records kept, and can a report from five years ago be reproduced with the procedure revision that applied? Can a client be given its own reports without seeing anyone else's? Can the system hold records for a CSA W178.1 audit or an ISO 9001 surveillance visit? Each is answered for your company during scoping, because the right answer depends on your contracts.

What is built in: procedure control with locked approved revisions and full history, report records with signatures and references, certificate and vision-test history with attachments, calibration certificates with lab accreditation details, and NCR and corrective-action workflows configured for your quality system. Procedure first drafts can be generated with AI assistance (falling back to a built-in template), and a Level III still reviews and approves every procedure before it is published. Email reminders go to approvers when approvals are pending.

Implementation for a Nova Scotia inspection company

Direct answer: Implementation is remote and typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff; it depends on how clean your existing records are. The work is importing technicians, certificates, equipment and calibration history, setting up report templates and procedures, configuring invoicing and taxes, and training your office and field staff.

A typical sequence starts with a scoping call to agree which apps you need, which report layouts must be reproduced and which client formats matter most. Your certificate spreadsheet, equipment list, calibration certificates and client list are cleaned and imported. Report templates are built for your common methods, with marine mode switched on if you do ship work. Procedure documents are loaded into the register with their current revision. Invoicing is set up with your cost centres, rate types and HST configured for Nova Scotia. Field technicians install the offline app on their phones or tablets and run a test job before go-live.

The biggest variable is data. If certificates are already in one spreadsheet with consistent dates, import is quick. If they are scattered across folders and email attachments, the first week is spent gathering them. What is the best ERP for a small NDT company in Nova Scotia?

NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in Poland

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution is a fully customized ERP for NDT and inspection companies working in Poland. It holds PN-EN ISO 9712 certificates from UDT-CERT, the Łukasiewicz institute or other bodies alongside ASNT SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 records, with automatic expiry status; it controls calibration on every instrument, plans crews for shipyards, offshore wind, refineries, power plants and fabrication shops, captures reports offline and handles quotation through invoicing. Implementation is remote and typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff, depending on how clean your existing records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Request a Poland demo.

Poland has become one of Europe's busiest places for steel fabrication and inspection. Its shipyards build offshore substations and specialist vessels, its fabricators ship pressure equipment and structures across Europe and beyond, its refineries and chemical plants run regular turnarounds, and the first Polish offshore wind farms are going into the Baltic. Polish NDT technicians are also in demand abroad, so a company may have staff on a Norwegian platform, a German power plant and a Gdańsk yard at the same time, each under a different client's rules. That puts pressure on the back office: certificates in several schemes, instruments moving between sites, reports in several formats, and invoices in more than one language. This page explains where the work is, what clients and regulators expect, and how the Atlantis ERP handles it.

Poland's inspection market: the main clusters

Direct answer: NDT work in Poland centres on the Baltic coast (Gdańsk, Gdynia and Szczecin shipyards, ports, the Gdańsk refinery, offshore wind and LNG), Mazovia (the Płock refinery and petrochemical complex), Silesia and Lesser Poland (steel, coal and power, heavy engineering), the chemical cluster around Tarnów, Puławy, Police and Kędzierzyn-Koźle, the copper industry in Lower Silesia, and the aerospace cluster around Rzeszów and Mielec.

Baltic coast. Gdańsk and Gdynia have large shipbuilding and ship repair yards, and Szczecin has its own maritime industry. These yards have built offshore substation topsides for Polish offshore wind and work for European offshore and naval clients. The Gdańsk refinery, now part of Orlen, runs turnarounds and in-service inspection. The LNG terminal at Świnoujście and the Baltic Pipe gas link to Norway are major energy assets on the coast. Offshore wind is moving fast: Baltic Power, built by Orlen with Northland Power, and Baltica 2, built by PGE with Ørsted, are the first large farms in the Polish Baltic, and further projects follow. Foundations, towers, substations and port works all need weld inspection during construction and periodic inspection afterwards.

Mazovia. Orlen's Płock complex is Poland's largest refinery and petrochemical site, and its turnarounds are among the biggest NDT jobs in the country: many crews, many methods and tight windows.

Silesia and Lesser Poland. The south is Poland's heavy-industry heartland. ArcelorMittal Poland operates steelworks in Dąbrowa Górnicza and Kraków, coal-fired and newer gas-fired power plants run boilers and steam piping across the region, and fabricators and engineering firms build pressure equipment, structures and machinery. Large power stations elsewhere, such as Bełchatów, Kozienice and Opole, add boiler, turbine and pipework inspection during outages.

Chemicals, copper and aerospace. Grupa Azoty runs fertiliser and chemical plants in Tarnów, Puławy, Police and Kędzierzyn-Koźle. KGHM operates copper mines and smelters in Lower Silesia. The "Aviation Valley" around Rzeszów and Mielec hosts aircraft and engine component manufacturing for international primes, where NDT is certified under EN 4179 or NAS 410 and audited closely.

Nuclear, in preparation. Poland plans its first nuclear power plant at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site in Pomerania. That programme is at an early stage, but it is already raising questions about nuclear-grade quality systems, procedure control and personnel records among Polish suppliers.

What Polish clients and regulators expect from NDT companies

Direct answer: Clients expect PN-EN ISO 9712 certificates (and ASNT-based certification on US-code work, EN 4179 or NAS 410 in aerospace), approved procedures, calibrated equipment, method-specific reports in the client's format, and often PCA accreditation. Pressure equipment work runs under the Office of Technical Inspection (UDT), and industrial radiography under the National Atomic Energy Agency (PAA).

Personnel certification. In Poland, NDT personnel are usually certified to PN-EN ISO 9712. UDT-CERT, the certification body of the Office of Technical Inspection, certifies a large share of Polish NDT operators, and the Łukasiewicz Research Network's welding centre in Gliwice (the former Instytut Spawalnictwa) also certifies NDT personnel under PCA accreditation. UDT-CERT is also authorised to approve NDT personnel for pressure equipment in categories III and IV under the Pressure Equipment Directive. Technicians who work abroad often add PCN certificates or employer certification under SNT-TC-1A for US-code projects.

Technical inspection. The Office of Technical Inspection (Urząd Dozoru Technicznego, UDT) supervises pressure equipment, lifting equipment and other technical devices in use, and the Transportation Technical Inspection (TDT) covers transport-related equipment. NDT companies often perform testing that supports those inspections and fabricators' acceptance tests, so UDT inspectors and clients will look closely at certificates, procedures and calibration records.

Accreditation and audits. The Polish Centre for Accreditation (PCA) accredits laboratories and inspection bodies to ISO/IEC 17025 and ISO/IEC 17020. Shipyards and offshore clients add classification-society approvals and their own supplier audits. The ERP does not grant any of these, but it holds the evidence they check: competence, calibration, procedure control and report review.

US codes. Polish fabricators building to ASME or AWS for US-owned clients often need ASNT-based certification under a written practice. That is Atlantis's home ground; see employer certification programmes and Level III consulting.

Certificate tracking: PN-EN ISO 9712, PCN and ASNT for one workforce

Direct answer: Each certificate is a separate record with its scheme, level, method, certifying body and dates. Radiography, data protection and KSeF invoicing in Poland

Radiography companies need tight control over sources, equipment, vehicles and people. The availability calendar holds assigned, leave, training, sick and unavailable days with overlaps blocked, and each technician shows status, current assignment, utilisation and next available date. Instruments are tracked by serial number with equipment type, assigned person, condition, asset tag, firmware, accessories, lifecycle stage and calibration status. Issue and return run through supervisor and manager approval with condition recorded both ways, reservations prevent clashes, and movement records show where each item went. Calibration records hold provider, certificate number, standard, range, uncertainty, accredited-lab flag, result and next due date. Consumables such as couplant, penetrant, developer, magnetic ink and PPE carry reorder levels and a low-stock flag. Purchase orders can be tied to a specific equipment serial, and vendors flagged as OEM, dealer or calibration lab with accreditation details.

On site, the installable offline app handles method selection, readings, photos, on-screen signature and PDF preview without a connection, and syncs later. The ERP supports 17 report types, from UT, RT, MT, PT and VT to PAUT, TOFD, ECT, IRIS, MFL, PMI, hardness, ferrite, holiday/coating, PWHT and computed radiography, each with its own numbering.
