NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in Quebec

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution runs the operations of NDT and inspection companies in Quebec on one system: technician certifications under CAN/CGSB-48.9712, SNT-TC-1A, CP-189 and other schemes, instrument calibration, procedures, crew dispatch, offline NDT reports, quotations, timesheets and invoicing. It is customized to each company and set up remotely, typically in 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff depending on how clean your records are. French-language needs are discussed during scoping. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Request a Quebec demo.

Quebec's NDT market does not look like Alberta's. There is no oil sands sector and very little upstream production. What Quebec has instead is one of the largest aerospace clusters in the world around Montreal, a heavy aluminium industry built on cheap hydroelectric power, Hydro-Québec's dams and transmission network, two refineries, a major shipyard at Lévis, iron ore and gold mining in the north, and pulp and paper across most regions. That mix means a Quebec inspection company may be writing penetrant reports for a jet engine component on Monday and doing UT thickness surveys in an aluminium smelter's potline on Thursday. The software has to handle both without forcing either into the other's format.

The Quebec inspection market, region by region

Direct answer: NDT work in Quebec concentrates in greater Montreal (aerospace manufacturing and maintenance, refining, petrochemicals, fabrication), Quebec City and Lévis (refining and shipbuilding), Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean and the Côte-Nord (aluminium smelting, iron ore, hydro), Centre-du-Québec around Bécancour (aluminium and chemicals) and Abitibi-Témiscamingue (gold and base-metal mining).

Greater Montreal. The aerospace cluster includes Bombardier, Pratt & Whitney Canada in Longueuil, the Airbus A220 line in Mirabel, Bell Textron Canada in Mirabel, CAE and Héroux-Devtek, with hundreds of machining, special-process and repair suppliers behind them. Those suppliers run penetrant, magnetic particle, eddy current and ultrasonic inspection under customer specifications that usually call for NAS 410 or EN 4179 personnel qualification. On the east end of the island, Suncor's Montreal refinery and the Montréal-Est petrochemical area generate turnaround and in-service inspection, and the Port of Montreal adds tank and terminal work. Enbridge's Line 9 delivers crude to Montreal and is regulated federally.

Quebec City and Lévis. Valero's Jean-Gaulin refinery in Lévis is the province's largest refinery. Chantier Davie, also in Lévis, is one of Canada's largest shipyards and is now part of the federal National Shipbuilding Strategy, which means steady weld inspection to class-society and government requirements.

Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean and Côte-Nord. Rio Tinto operates several aluminium smelters in the Saguenay region, and the Côte-Nord has the Alouette smelter in Sept-Îles and Alcoa's Baie-Comeau plant. ArcelorMittal Mining Canada mines iron ore at Mont-Wright and ships pellets from Port-Cartier. Hydro-Québec's Manicouagan and Outardes generating stations sit inland. Smelter potlines, gas treatment centres, anode plants, ore-handling structures and penstocks all need periodic NDT.

Centre-du-Québec and Mauricie. The Bécancour industrial park hosts the ABI aluminium smelter and chemical plants, and Gentilly-2, the province's former nuclear station, is in long-term shutdown. Pulp and paper mills in Trois-Rivières and across the Mauricie run boilers and pressure vessels under RBQ oversight.

Abitibi-Témiscamingue and the North. Gold mines around Malartic, Val-d'Or and Rouyn-Noranda, and Hydro-Québec's La Grande complex in the James Bay region, generate fly-in work with long rotations and limited connectivity.

So a Quebec NDT company's clients range from aerospace quality departments that audit every special process, through heavy industry that needs crews on short notice for outages, to remote mines that need a technician on a plane next Tuesday. Each client asks for different records, and the business has to keep all of them straight.

Regulators, codes and certification schemes in Quebec

Direct answer: Pressure equipment in Quebec is regulated by the Régie du bâtiment du Québec (RBQ) under the Building Act and the Regulation respecting pressure installations, which references CSA B51. Industrial radiography is licensed by the CNSC. Workplace health and safety falls to the CNESST. NDT personnel certification in Canada follows CAN/CGSB-48.9712, and aerospace work usually follows NAS 410 or EN 4179.

The RBQ is the jurisdictional authority for pressure installations in Quebec, covering boilers, pressure vessels, pressure piping and related equipment. It issues the permits required for enterprises that manufacture, install, repair or modify pressure equipment, and it updated the Regulation respecting pressure installations in 2026. If you inspect repairs or alterations on pressure equipment for a permit holder, your reports end up in their quality file. See our notes on RBQ compliance for inspection companies, CSA B51 and CRN registration.

Radiography in Quebec, as everywhere in Canada, requires a CNSC licence, and exposure device operators must hold CNSC certification; see CNSC compliance. The CNESST enforces occupational health and safety on every site your technicians visit. For welding work, many Quebec fabricators are certified to CSA W47.1 through the CWB, and inspection organisations may hold CSA W178.1 certification.

Personnel certification is where Quebec companies carry the most paperwork. Industrial clients in Canada usually expect CAN/CGSB-48.9712 certificates. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026; CAN/CGSB-48.9712 remains valid, but confirm the current certification body for renewals. Aerospace primes and their suppliers usually require employer certification under NAS 410 or EN 4179, with a responsible Level 3. US-owned plants and US-code projects may call for an ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practice. A single Quebec technician can hold certificates under two or three of these schemes at once, each with its own expiry, vision test and work-experience rules.

What aerospace and industrial clients in Quebec audit

Direct answer: Aerospace customers audit personnel qualification records, vision tests, procedures and technique sheets, equipment calibration and process control evidence. Industrial clients such as smelters, refineries and mines focus on certification currency, calibration, safety prequalification and report quality. Both want to pick any past job and see the full evidence chain.

The two audiences are worth separating because they stress different parts of a business system. An aerospace customer's source inspector or a special-process auditor wants to see that the penetrant technician who signed a report on a given date held a valid certification under the right scheme for that method and level, had a current near-vision and colour-perception test, and used a procedure revision approved by the Level 3 at the time. They also want instrument and process calibration history: UV lamp intensity checks, eddy current reference standards, ultrasonic reference blocks. A missing record is a finding.

An industrial client, such as an aluminium smelter planning a potline outage or a refinery planning a turnaround, cares about mobilising enough certified people on a fixed date, with valid site orientations, calibrated equipment and a predictable daily report. Its contractor-management team will ask for safety records and insurance through its own prequalification system, and its maintenance planners will want reports they can file against their equipment numbers.

Spreadsheets can hold all of this, but they do not link it. When a vision test lapses, nothing in a spreadsheet stops that technician being booked for an aerospace job next week. That link between the person, the date, the job and the evidence is what an NDT ERP is for.

What the Atlantis ERP does for Quebec NDT companies

Direct answer: The ERP brings certifications, vision tests, calibration, procedures, dispatch, NDT reports, timesheets and invoicing into one connected system configured for NDT. CAN/CGSB-48.9712 certificates are recorded under the ISO 9712 scheme, NAS 410 or EN 4179 employer certifications under "other" with the scheme named, and SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 certifications under their own scheme. Each record carries method, level, dates, hours and attachments, and its status updates automatically.

Take a typical Montreal technician: a CGSB Level 2 in ultrasonic testing for industrial work, an employer Level 2 in penetrant and eddy current under the company's NAS 410 written practice for an aerospace client, and a current vision test. In the Atlantis ERP that is three or four certificate records and one vision test record attached to one employee. Each certificate shows active, expiring soon (within 90 days), expired or revoked, and the Expiring Soon and Expired menus show the whole company at a glance.

Certificate templates per scheme let you set validity in months, whether a vision test or exam is required, and minimum OJT and training hours, so a new certificate is created with the right rules. The employee's NDT profile shows highest level, methods certified, radiation safety training, radiation badge number and medical fitness expiry. Configurable daily email alerts go to the people who need them, with your own look-ahead days and resend interval, for technician certificates, calibration certificates and company certifications.

Where it matters most is at the point of use. Timesheets warn when a technician's certificate is not valid, and the availability calendar shows training and leave so a technician on a recertification course is not booked onto a job. If your Level 3 needs help writing or reviewing a NAS 410 or SNT-TC-1A written practice, Atlantis offers Level III consulting for Canadian employers. Atlantis does not train toward CGSB, NAS 410 or EN 4179 certification; its training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A based (see NDT training in Montreal).

Calibration, equipment and consumables control

Direct answer: Instruments, probes and accessories are tracked by serial number with lifecycle stage, holder and calibration status. Calibration records and certificates carry due dates and alerts, dispatch warns if out-of-calibration equipment is assigned, and consumables such as penetrant, developer and magnetic particles have reorder levels and a movement ledger.

Aerospace and industrial auditors both ask for calibration evidence, but they ask about different things. An aerospace auditor may look at a penetrant line's UV lamp and a UT reference block; a smelter's quality team may only care that the thickness gauge was in date. The asset management app records equipment type, assigned person, condition, asset tag, firmware, accessories and lifecycle (new, active, in calibration, in repair, rented out, retired, disposed), with calibration frequency and status. Each calibration record holds provider, certificate number, standard, range, uncertainty, whether the lab is accredited, pass, fail or conditional result, and the next due date.

Issue and return run through supervisor and manager approval with condition recorded at both ends, and reservations stop two jobs claiming the same eddy current set. The maintenance log covers preventive and corrective work, repairs, cleaning, firmware updates and probe replacement. Consumables carry a movement ledger with reorder levels and low-stock flags, which helps when a penetrant line runs through materials faster than expected. Calibration labs can be set up as vendors with their accreditation number and expiry, and purchase orders can be linked to a specific equipment serial.

For radiography crews, the fleet app records whether a vehicle can carry radioactive sources, its transport licence number and expiry, and its assignment to a project or driver. The ERP supports your CNSC programme by keeping those dates visible; it does not replace the programme.

Running jobs, reports and timesheets from Montreal to the Côte-Nord

Direct answer: Each job is a project with client PO, site, methods, codes, scope and acceptance criteria, dispatched to a crew as a team assignment. Technicians report in an offline app that syncs later, reports go through review and approval with signatures, and approved timesheets feed the invoice.

Consider a smelter outage on the Côte-Nord. The coordinator creates the project with the client's PO and scope, opens a team assignment with mobilisation and demobilisation dates and the site's GPS coordinates, and books technicians from the availability calendar. The system blocks a technician who is already on another job or on leave, and blocks the same instrument serial being sent to two places. If a gauge's calibration is out of date, the coordinator is warned before the truck leaves Montreal.

On site, the technician picks the method in the offline app, fills the report, takes photos and signs on screen. Drafts and photos stay on the device until there is a connection. Back in the office, the report moves from draft through review and approval to sent, with inspector, reviewer and approver signatures and, where required, the name and signature of the client's authorized inspector. Report references include work order, request, WPS, contract and drawing numbers, procedure and standard. The 17 built-in report types cover UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ECT, IRIS, PAUT, MFL, TOFD, PWHT, PMI, hardness, UT thickness, ferrite, holiday/coating and computed radiography, each with its own numbering.

Timesheets record inspection, travel, standby and setup separately, with method, site, client, equipment serial, billable flag and rate multiplier. Approved hours feed invoices whose lines carry method, technician, equipment serial, rate type and cost centre. The financial dashboard shows revenue, cost of sales, gross margin, operating expenses, EBITDA and outstanding invoices over a 12-month view.

Quebec's private-sector privacy law, as amended by Law 25, and any client hosting or data-residency requirements are also covered at scoping. Technician records include personal information such as vision tests, medical fitness dates and radiation badge numbers. Those sit with plant owners. The ERP runs the inspection company. For inspection data presented on a 3D model, see Digital Twin Reporting and digital twins in Montreal.

NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in Queensland

Short answer: For an NDT company in Queensland, the Atlantis ERP solution is one system for the whole operation: AINDT (ISO 9712) and ASNT certificates per technician with automatic expiry status, instruments and probes by serial number with calibration status, crew dispatch to Gladstone, the Surat Basin gas fields, the Bowen Basin and North Queensland, offline field reports, timesheets, quotes and invoices. It is set up remotely by Atlantis NDT, typically 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff depending on how clean your current records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Request a Queensland demo.

Queensland is a big state with several separate inspection economies. An NDT company based in Brisbane may on the same week have a crew on an LNG train on Curtis Island, a pipeline radiography spread west of Roma, an MT and UT team in a coal handling plant near Moranbah, and a technician doing thickness surveys at a refinery on the Brisbane River. The clients differ, the travel differs, the site rules differ, and the certificates each client wants to see differ. When the office runs on spreadsheets, someone spends every Friday checking expiry dates and calibration certificates by hand. This page explains where the Queensland work is, which certificates and records clients and regulators ask for, what the Atlantis ERP does about it, and how to compare it with the alternatives.

Where the NDT work is in Queensland

Direct answer: Queensland NDT demand concentrates in five areas: Gladstone (three LNG plants on Curtis Island, alumina, aluminium and power), the Surat and Bowen Basin gas fields and their pipelines, the Bowen Basin coal mines and the Mackay coal ports, the North West Minerals Province around Mount Isa and the Townsville refineries, and the Brisbane industrial corridor with its refinery, port and fabricators.

Gladstone and Curtis Island. Gladstone has one of the densest concentrations of process plant in Australia. On Curtis Island sit the three coal seam gas to LNG projects: Queensland Curtis LNG, Gladstone LNG and Australia Pacific LNG. On the mainland are the Queensland Alumina and Yarwun alumina refineries, the Boyne aluminium smelter, Gladstone Power Station and a busy export port. Shutdowns at these plants bring in large crews for UT thickness, PAUT and TOFD on welds and vessels, radiography, MT and PT, and visual inspection of tanks and structures. The Gladstone ERP page goes into more local detail.

Gas fields and pipelines. The coal seam gas fields of the Surat and Bowen basins feed the Curtis Island plants through long transmission pipelines, with large gathering networks, compressor stations and water treatment plants in between. Pipeline construction, tie-ins and integrity digs mean weld radiography or automated UT, coating inspection and thickness work, usually against AS 2885. These are remote jobs, often with camp accommodation and limited signal.

Coal country. The Bowen Basin coal mines around Moranbah, Dysart, Emerald and Blackwater, and the coal terminals at Hay Point, Dalrymple Bay and Abbot Point, generate structural, weld and wear inspection on draglines, shovels, conveyors, stackers and ship loaders, plus fixed plant in preparation plants. Mackay is the service hub; see the Mackay ERP page.

The north and north-west. Mount Isa and the North West Minerals Province carry mining and smelting plant, and Townsville hosts a zinc refinery, a copper refinery and a port that handles minerals from the region. Distances are long, so travel and standby days make up a real share of each job.

Brisbane and the south-east. The Lytton refinery on the Brisbane River, the Port of Brisbane, power stations, water infrastructure, and a large base of fabrication and engineering workshops that build vessels, skids and structural steel for projects across the state. Many Queensland NDT companies keep their head office, store and calibration room here; see NDT ERP in Brisbane.

Certificates and records Queensland clients ask NDT vendors for

Direct answer: Queensland clients usually ask for AINDT certification under ISO 9712, current radiation use licences, NATA-traceable calibration, approved procedures to the relevant Australian standard, inductions and medicals, and reports in their own template. US-designed equipment packages and some operators' contractor rules add ASNT-based employer certification to the list.

What turns up in prequalification questionnaires and on gate-check lists:

  • Technician certification by method and level, most often AINDT certification. Where a project works to ASME or API codes, or the contractor's own quality system is built on SNT-TC-1A or CP-189, the client may want to see the employer's written practice and the technician's certification under it.
  • Radiation licences. Radiation Health Queensland, part of Queensland Health, licenses radiation users and possession of radiation sources under the Radiation Safety Act 1999, including industrial radiography use and possession licences.
  • Calibration evidence for every instrument on site, usually from a NATA-accredited laboratory.
  • Procedures and technique sheets referencing AS 3978, AS/NZS 1554, AS 2885 or ASME Section V, approved at Level 3 and revision-controlled.
  • Site requirements such as coal mine or petroleum and gas site inductions, medicals, fitness for work, and the principal's contractor management platform.
  • Reports in the operator's format, reviewed and signed off on time for the shutdown or construction schedule.

Two state regulators matter most for plant. Workplace Health and Safety Queensland handles plant design and item registration under the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011, which covers many pressure vessels. Resources Safety and Health Queensland regulates mines and the petroleum and gas sector, including the pressure equipment rules that apply on gas sites. AS/NZS 3788 is the usual reference for in-service inspection of pressure equipment, and the plant owner and its registered inspectors run that programme; your NDT results feed it.

Certificates, calibration, procedures, dispatch, field reports, timesheets, quotes and invoices share one database, so a coordinator can build a compliant crew for Gladstone or a pipeline spread without opening five files.

Tracking AINDT and ASNT certificates in one register

Direct answer: Every certificate a technician holds is its own record with scheme, level, method, sector, certifying body, dates, hours and attachments. AINDT certificates sit under the ISO 9712 scheme with AINDT as certifying body; employer certifications sit under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189. Status updates automatically and warnings start 90 days out.

Queensland technicians move between employers and projects more than most. A Level 2 radiographer might work a pipeline spread under AINDT certification, then a fabrication job for a US equipment supplier that asks for employer certification under an ASNT-based written practice. Keeping both certificates as separate records, each with its own expiry and attachment, removes the guesswork when a client asks for evidence.

  • Schemes: SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, ISO 9712, PCN, CSWIP or other.
  • Levels: trainee, I, II and III.
  • Detail: method, certifying body, issue, expiry and renewal dates, industry sector, OJT hours, training hours, exam passed and attached certificate copies.
  • Vision tests: near vision (Jaeger J1/J2), far vision, colour perception and contrast, examiner, clinic, file and expiry.
  • Exams: general, specific and practical scores against a passing score that defaults to 70 percent and can be changed, for companies that qualify technicians under their own written practice.

Certificate templates per scheme hold validity in months, whether a vision test or exam is required, and minimum OJT and training hours. Daily checks raise warning tasks 90 days before certificate or vision-test expiry, and configurable email alerts can go to the operations manager, the Level 3 and the technician. Radiation safety training and the radiation badge number are part of each employee's NDT profile, and copies of radiation use licences can be attached. Timesheets warn when a certificate is not valid, so an invalid day cannot slip quietly into a bill.

If your company qualifies technicians under an ASNT-based written practice, Atlantis can also help with written practice development and SNT-TC-1A training. Atlantis does not train toward AINDT certification.

Instruments, calibration and the Brisbane store

Direct answer: Every instrument, probe, gauge, crawler, source container and accessory is tracked by serial number with lifecycle state, assigned person, condition and calibration status. Calibration records hold the provider, certificate number, standard, range, uncertainty, accredited-lab flag, result and next due date, and the certificate register raises expiry alerts.

Most Queensland companies run one main store, usually in Brisbane, Gladstone or Mackay, and send kit out on utes or freight. The ERP's issue and return workflow records who took which serial number, with supervisor and manager approval and the condition at issue and return. Reservations stop two coordinators promising the same PAUT set to two jobs, and inbound and outbound movements give a trail if something goes missing on a long job.

  • Lifecycle states: new, active, in calibration, in repair, rented out, retired and disposed, with rental rates recordable for hired-in or hired-out kit.
  • Maintenance log for preventive and corrective work, cleaning, firmware updates and probe replacement, with condition before and after.
  • Consumables such as couplant, penetrant, developer, magnetic particle ink, film and PPE, with reorder levels and low-stock flags.
  • Purchase records with vendor types (OEM, dealer, calibration lab), accredited-lab flag, accreditation number and expiry.
  • Fleet records that mark which vehicles can carry radioactive sources, with transport licence number and expiry, and assignment to a project or driver.

Company certifications, such as NATA accreditation, ISO 9001 certification and radiation possession licences, can be held as company certification records with their own alert days.

Field reports from gas fields, mines and camps

Direct answer: Technicians write reports in the offline field app, which keeps drafts and photos on the device and syncs when the camp or the ute gets a connection. Reports then go through review and approval with signatures, and the approved PDF goes to the client.

The ERP covers 17 report types, each with its own numbering: UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ECT, IRIS, PAUT, MFL, TOFD, PWHT, PMI, hardness, UT thickness, ferrite, holiday and coating, and computed radiography. Weld and job lines record defect type and orientation, and every report captures the work order, request, WPS, contract, drawing numbers and procedure and standard references, plus an overall result of acceptable, not acceptable or acceptable with remarks. Inspector, reviewer and approver signatures sit on the report, along with the client's third-party or authorised inspector name and signature when they witness.

For coating-heavy pipeline work the holiday and coating report type is useful; for the alumina and power plants, UT thickness readings by direction and IRIS reports for heat exchanger tubes cover most routine scopes. For the reporting product on its own, see Digital Twin Reporting Software.

Quotes, timesheets and invoices for Queensland jobs

Direct answer: Quotes carry job type, site, project dates and applicable codes, with NDT service lines flagged by method. Accepted quotes become orders, timesheets record billable work, travel and standby, and invoices show labour, equipment and consumables subtotals with cost centres and the client's PO.

Queensland work is often priced with mobilisation, daily rates, travel allowances and standby, and these are the lines most often missed. Timesheet work types (inspection, travel, standby, setup), method, site, client, equipment serial, billable flag and rate multiplier all flow to billing. Invoice lines can carry cost centre, method, equipment serial, technician, rate type and days or hours, so a Gladstone client can check the invoice against its own records. The financial dashboard shows revenue, cost of sales, gross margin, operating expenses, EBITDA, outstanding invoices, bills and expenses over twelve months. The CRM tracks leads by service line, industry sector and estimated technicians and days, which helps when bidding shutdown packages.

Ask to see a Queensland quote-to-invoice walkthrough.

Regulators, tax and data questions in Queensland

Direct answer: The ERP keeps the records Queensland regulators and clients ask about, but your company stays responsible for compliance. GST, BAS reporting and Peppol e-invoicing are configured during implementation, and hosting location and data residency are discussed during scoping.

  • Radiation Health Queensland: radiation use and possession licences under the Radiation Safety Act 1999.
  • Workplace Health and Safety Queensland: work health and safety and registration of plant designs and items under the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011.
  • Resources Safety and Health Queensland: safety on mines, quarries and petroleum and gas sites.
  • NATA: accreditation of labs and inspection bodies to ISO/IEC 17025 and ISO/IEC 17020.

For companies holding or seeking NATA accreditation, the controlled procedure register, technician competence records, calibration register with accreditation numbers, and NCR and CAPA workflows set up during implementation make audits easier to prepare for. The ERP does not grant accreditation or replace your quality manual.

Implementation in 2 to 4 weeks, remotely

Direct answer: A typical Queensland implementation takes 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff, depending on how clean your existing records are. It is run remotely during Brisbane business hours, starting with technicians, certificates, equipment and calibration data, then report templates and billing.

  1. Scoping: methods, schemes, clients, report formats, billing model, apps needed, integrations and hosting questions.
  2. Data import: technicians, certificates, vision tests, equipment, calibration records, consumables, clients and price lists.
  3. Templates: client report templates, quotation and invoice layouts with your branding.
  4. Workflows and alerts: report and procedure approvals, equipment issue approvals, alert recipients and look-ahead days.
  5. Training and go-live for office, dispatch and field staff.

Queensland does not use daylight saving, so session times stay steady through the year.

Integrations with client and accounting systems

Direct answer: The Atlantis ERP has an open REST API and integrates with SAP, Maximo, NetSuite, QuickBooks or any system that accepts API connections, scoped per implementation.

LNG operators, miners and utilities in Queensland commonly use SAP or Maximo. For an NDT contractor the useful link is usually work-order and PO numbers in, and report references and status out. The field app's own API covers jobs assigned to the technician, issued equipment, report submission and sync.

NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in Saskatchewan

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution gives Saskatchewan NDT and inspection companies one system for technician certifications (CAN/CGSB-48.9712, SNT-TC-1A, CP-189 and more), equipment calibration, crew dispatch to oilfield, potash, refinery and mine sites, offline NDT reports, timesheets and invoicing. It is customized to each company and set up remotely, typically in 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff depending on how clean your existing records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Book a Saskatchewan demo.

Most Saskatchewan inspection companies are small or mid-sized and based in Regina, Saskatoon, Estevan or Lloydminster, but their crews cover the whole province. Distances are long, sites are rural, winter is hard on equipment and people, and the client list mixes oil producers, potash miners, a refinery, steel and pipe makers, utilities and uranium operators. Each of those clients runs its own contractor prequalification, wants its own report format and audits a different part of your paperwork. This page covers the Saskatchewan market, the regulators and schemes your records have to satisfy, what the Atlantis ERP actually does, and how a remote implementation works.

Three industries drive NDT demand in Saskatchewan

Direct answer: Saskatchewan NDT work comes from oil and gas (heavy oil around Lloydminster, light oil in the southeast Bakken and the southwest, pipelines and gathering systems), mining (potash across the centre and south, uranium in the Athabasca Basin) and processing and manufacturing (the Regina refinery, pipe and steel making, fertiliser, power generation and agricultural equipment).

Oil and gas. The Lloydminster area on the Alberta border is built on heavy oil, with Cenovus's Lloydminster upgrader and asphalt refinery processing local crude. The southeast around Estevan and Weyburn produces light oil from the Bakken and older fields, including the Weyburn CO2 enhanced oil recovery project. The southwest around Kindersley and Swift Current has its own light-oil and gas plays. All of this means batteries, treaters, separators, tanks, compressor stations and thousands of kilometres of flowlines and gathering lines that need weld inspection during construction and thickness and corrosion surveys in service. The Enbridge mainline also crosses the province, with terminals and pump stations along the route.

Potash and uranium. Saskatchewan holds the largest potash reserves in the world. Nutrien operates several mines around Saskatoon, including Allan, Cory and Lanigan, and Rocanville in the southeast; Mosaic operates at Esterhazy and Belle Plaine; K+S runs the Bethune mine; and BHP is building the Jansen mine east of Saskatoon. Potash mills have brine-handling vessels, crystallisers, evaporators, dryers, hoists and headframes where corrosion and fatigue are constant concerns. In the north, Cameco and Orano operate uranium mines and mills in the Athabasca Basin, which are licensed by the CNSC and bring fly-in work with strict site rules.

Processing, power and manufacturing. The Co-op Refinery Complex in Regina is the province's major refinery, with regular turnarounds. Evraz in Regina makes steel and large-diameter pipe. SaskPower runs coal, gas and hydro stations, including Boundary Dam near Estevan with its carbon capture unit, and gas plants that need boiler and piping inspection. Fertiliser and chemical plants, ethanol and canola crushing plants, and agricultural equipment manufacturers add steady fabrication and in-service NDT.

For an inspection company this means crews that might do radiography on a flowline tie-in near Estevan one day and a UT thickness survey in a potash mill near Saskatoon the next. The business has to know at all times who is certified for what, which instruments are calibrated, where each crew is and what each client will be billed.

Regulators and codes your records must satisfy

Direct answer: Boilers and pressure vessels in Saskatchewan are regulated by the Technical Safety Authority of Saskatchewan (TSASK) under The Boiler and Pressure Vessel Act, 1999. Pipelines and flowlines are licensed by the Ministry of Energy and Resources under The Pipelines Act, 1998, with CSA Z662 as the technical standard. Radiography and uranium sites fall under the CNSC, and interprovincial pipelines under the Canada Energy Regulator.

TSASK is an arm's-length agency that administers The Boiler and Pressure Vessel Act, 1999 and its regulations, registers pressure equipment designs, and inspects boilers and pressure vessels. CSA B51 is the construction code. See our notes on TSASK compliance, CSA B51 and CRN registration. Saskatchewan's pipeline regime changed significantly after a 2016 amendment brought flowlines, the lines from wellheads to batteries and facilities, into licensing. For contractors that means more integrity and construction records attached to flowline work. CSA Z662 sets the design, construction and inspection requirements.

Industrial radiography needs a CNSC licence, and exposure device operators need CNSC certification. The CNSC also licenses the uranium mines and mills, so contractors working there face nuclear-site training and access rules on top of normal safety prequalification. Saskatchewan's Occupational Health and Safety rules apply on every site.

On personnel certification, Canadian industrial clients expect CAN/CGSB-48.9712 certificates. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026; CAN/CGSB-48.9712 remains valid, but confirm the current certification body for renewals. US-owned operators and pipe or equipment makers selling into the US often want an ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practice as well. Fabricators certified to CSA W47.1, and inspection organisations certified to CSA W178.1, add their own record requirements.

What Saskatchewan clients check before and during a job

Direct answer: Producers, miners and the refinery expect prequalification (safety programme, insurance, often a contractor-management platform), current personnel certificates, calibration certificates for every instrument, approved procedures, and daily reports and timesheets on the job. Potash and uranium sites add their own site training and access records.

A producer in the southeast wants to see that the radiography crew's CNSC certifications and dosimetry records are current before they arrive at a tie-in. A potash mine wants the UT technician's certificate and the thickness gauge's calibration certificate in its contractor file, and wants readings it can file against its equipment numbers. The refinery wants a turnaround crew with valid site orientations on a fixed date, plus daily progress. A pipe mill's customer may want inspection records tied to specific heats or lots.

Saskatchewan firms often keep this together with spreadsheets, a shared drive and accounting software. The weak point is the connection between them. A certificate that lapsed last week is visible in the spreadsheet only if someone looks, and nothing stops that technician being sent out. The Atlantis ERP connects certificates, equipment, jobs, timesheets and invoices so problems show up at the point of dispatch or approval, not in an auditor's finding.

Certification tracking for CGSB, ASNT and CNSC certificates

Direct answer: Each technician can hold any number of certificate records, each with scheme, level, method, certifying body, dates, hours and attachments. CGSB certificates are recorded under the ISO 9712 scheme; SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 under their own; CNSC exposure device operator certificates as separate records so they get the same expiry status and alerts.

In a typical Saskatchewan crew, a radiographer holds a CGSB RT certificate and a CNSC exposure device operator certificate; a UT technician holds CGSB UT and an employer SNT-TC-1A certificate for a US-owned client; an apprentice is logging OJT hours toward Level 1. The certificate app records the scheme, the level (trainee, I, II or III), method, certifying body, industry sector, issue, expiry and renewal dates, OJT hours, training hours, exam result and scanned attachments for each one.

Vision tests are separate records with near vision (Jaeger J1/J2), far vision, colour perception, contrast, examiner, clinic and expiry. Daily checks create warning tasks 90 days before a certificate or vision test expires, and configurable daily emails go to the people you choose, with your own look-ahead and resend settings. Certificate templates per scheme hold validity periods, exam and vision requirements and minimum OJT and training hours, which helps when you are bringing trainees through to Level 1 and 2 under a written practice. Examination sheets record general, specific and practical scores.

Company certifications, such as ISO 9001 or CSA W178.1, have their own alert days. If your written practice or procedures need review by an outside Level III, see NDT consulting across Canada. Atlantis training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A based (NDT training in Canada); it does not train toward CGSB certification.

Equipment and calibration in a cold, spread-out province

Direct answer: The asset app tracks every instrument and probe by serial number, who has it, its condition and lifecycle stage, its maintenance history and its calibration status. Issue and return need supervisor and manager approval, reservations prevent clashes, and consumables have reorder levels.

Saskatchewan winters are hard on gear. Cables crack, batteries fail, screens fog and probes get dropped on frozen ground. When equipment lives in trucks that come back to base once a week, it is easy to lose track. The asset app records equipment type, asset tag, firmware, accessories and lifecycle (new, active, in calibration, in repair, rented out, retired, disposed). Condition is recorded on issue and return, so damage is traced to a job. The maintenance log covers preventive and corrective work, repairs, cleaning, firmware updates and probe replacement with condition before and after.

Calibration records hold provider, certificate number, standard, range, uncertainty, accredited-lab flag, pass, fail or conditional result and next due date. The calibration certificate register shows valid, expiring and expired status, holds the PDF and sends expiry alerts. Calibration labs can be set up as vendors with accreditation number and expiry, and purchase orders can be tied to a specific equipment serial. Consumables like couplant, film, penetrant, developer and PPE carry reorder levels and a movement ledger.

Out-of-town radiography also involves vehicles. The fleet app records vehicle purpose, whether it can carry radioactive sources, transport licence number and expiry, and assignment to a project or driver with dates and mileage.

Dispatch, reports and billing from Regina, Saskatoon or Estevan

Direct answer: Jobs are projects with client PO, site, methods, codes and scope, dispatched as team assignments to technicians and equipment checked for clashes and calibration. Reports are written offline and go through review and approval with signatures. Approved timesheets feed invoices with labour, equipment and consumables subtotals.

A typical week: the Regina office books a turnaround crew for the refinery, a two-person RT crew for a flowline tie-in near Estevan, and a UT technician for a potash mill near Saskatoon. Each job is a team assignment with GPS coordinates, mobilisation and demobilisation dates and status (planned, dispatched, in field, submitted, closed). Calendar, kanban and list views show who is where. If the UT technician is already booked or on leave, the booking is blocked; if the only calibrated thickness gauge is reserved elsewhere, that clash shows up too.

On site, technicians fill method-specific reports in the offline app, with photos and on-screen signatures. Seventeen report types are built in, including RT with source, technique and IQI details, UT with probe calibration, PAUT focal laws, MFL scan modes for tank floors, UT thickness readings by direction and computed radiography. Reports go from draft to review, approval and sent, with inspector, reviewer and approver signatures and, if needed, a third-party inspector's name and signature.

Timesheets record inspection, travel, standby and setup separately with method, site, client and equipment serial, then go through approval. NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in South Australia

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution is a fully customized ERP for NDT and inspection companies working in South Australia. It records AINDT and other ISO 9712 certificates next to ASNT SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 certifications with automatic expiry status, controls instrument calibration, dispatches crews between Adelaide, the Spencer Gulf towns and remote sites in the Far North, captures reports offline and runs quoting through invoicing on one system. Implementation is done remotely and typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff, depending on how clean your existing records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Ask for a South Australia demo.

South Australian inspection companies run a mixed book of work. In one month the same crew might do weld inspection on naval shipbuilding blocks at Osborne, a shutdown at a mineral processing plant in the Far North, pipeline work on the gas network out of the Cooper Basin and pressure equipment inspections at a food or wine processor in the Barossa. Each client brings its own certification expectations, report formats and site rules. The software you run the business on has to keep all of that straight without a second spreadsheet for every client. This page covers where the work is in South Australia, what clients and regulators expect, what the Atlantis ERP actually does, and what to check before you choose any system.

The South Australia inspection market: where NDT companies find work

Direct answer: NDT demand in South Australia clusters around naval shipbuilding and defence at Osborne and Edinburgh, copper and uranium mining and processing in the Far North, oil and gas in the Cooper Basin, heavy industry around the upper Spencer Gulf (Whyalla, Port Pirie, Port Augusta, Port Bonython), and power, water and general fabrication across greater Adelaide.

Naval shipbuilding at Osborne. The Osborne Naval Shipyard on the Lefevre Peninsula is the centre of Australia's continuous naval shipbuilding programme. BAE Systems Maritime Australia laid the keel of the first Hunter class frigate there in August 2026, ASC sustains the Collins class submarines, and the site is being expanded for SSN-AUKUS submarine construction from the 2030s. For NDT companies this means a long run of weld inspection on hull blocks, structural steel and piping systems, much of it under defence quality systems where traceability of personnel, procedures and equipment is checked closely. Defence work also tends to arrive with security, induction and document-control requirements that small inspection firms find hard to evidence from paper files.

Mining and mineral processing in the Far North. BHP's Olympic Dam at Roxby Downs, together with the Prominent Hill and Carrapateena copper operations, runs smelting, refining, concentrators, tailings and water infrastructure. Shutdowns on mills, crushers, tanks, pressure vessels and slurry pipelines create steady UT thickness, MT, PT and visual work, often on fly-in fly-out rosters. Because Olympic Dam also produces uranium oxide, radiation management is part of normal site life, which makes clean records of radiation safety training and dosimetry for your own radiographers more important, not less.

Oil and gas in the Cooper Basin. Santos operates the Moomba gas processing plant, which also hosts Moomba carbon capture and storage, one of the largest onshore CCS projects in Australia since it started in late 2024. Gathering lines, compression, processing equipment and the transmission pipelines that carry gas south to Adelaide and east to the other states are inspected to AS 2885 and to operator specifications. Liquids flow to the Port Bonython facility near Whyalla, which adds tankage and marine loading work on the Spencer Gulf.

Upper Spencer Gulf heavy industry. The Whyalla steelworks has been in administration since 2025 while a sale process runs, and the Nyrstar smelter at Port Pirie continues under joint government support. Both sites are large, ageing industrial plants with pressure equipment, cranes, structural steel and process piping that need inspection whatever their ownership. Port Augusta and the surrounding solar, wind and transmission projects add structural and fabrication work.

Greater Adelaide. Gas-fired power stations at Torrens Island and Pelican Point, water and desalination infrastructure, aerospace and defence suppliers around Edinburgh and Mawson Lakes, and fabrication shops in Wingfield, Lonsdale and the northern suburbs make up the steady base load. Wine, food and dairy processors in the Barossa, Clare Valley and Riverland run boilers, pressure vessels and stainless pipework that need periodic inspection under AS/NZS 3788.

For an inspection company, that map means long drives or flights between jobs, mixed client codes and very different documentation demands from a defence prime and a winery. The software problem is not writing one report. It is proving, for any job on any date, that a certified person used a calibrated instrument under an approved procedure, and then billing it correctly.

What clients in South Australia ask NDT vendors for

Direct answer: South Australian clients usually ask for current personnel certificates (AINDT or another ISO 9712 certificate, and sometimes ASNT-based employer certification for US-code or US-owned work), approved procedures, calibration certificates for every instrument, method-specific reports in the client's own format, radiation licences for radiography, site induction records, and often NATA accreditation to ISO/IEC 17025 or 17020.

Defence and shipbuilding primes generally want quality systems that can show who did what, with which instrument and under which revision of which procedure, on every weld or component. That is the kind of question an inspection company answers in seconds when the data is in one system and in days when it sits in folders. Mining and oil and gas operators typically run vendor prequalification that checks certificates, calibration, insurance and safety performance, then audit again before a shutdown. Their contracts often specify which certification schemes are acceptable for which methods.

Pressure equipment work brings Australian standards to the front: AS/NZS 3788 for in-service inspection, AS 4343 for hazard levels, AS 1210 for unfired pressure vessels and AS 4041 for pressure piping. Pipelines follow AS 2885. Many clients also expect in-service pressure equipment inspectors to hold AICIP registration. An ERP does not make anyone registered or accredited, but it holds the evidence an auditor or client asks for: competence records, calibration traceability, procedure control and report review.

Some South Australian work is done to US codes. Equipment built by or for US manufacturers, defence programmes with US partners, and suppliers to US-owned operators often reference ASME Section V and ask for ASNT-based certification under the employer's written practice. That is why technicians in the state can hold an AINDT certificate and an employer certification to SNT-TC-1A at the same time, and why your system needs to hold both cleanly.

What the Atlantis ERP does for NDT companies in South Australia

Direct answer: The Atlantis ERP covers technician certification tracking, NDT equipment and calibration control, crew dispatch, offline field reporting, procedure control, quoting, timesheets and invoicing. AINDT, ISO 9712 and ASNT certificate tracking in one register

Direct answer: Each certificate is a record with a scheme, level, method, certifying body and dates. An AINDT certificate is recorded under the ISO 9712 scheme with AINDT as the certifying body, and an ASNT-based employer certification sits in the same technician profile, so you see both at a glance and get alerts for each.

In practice a South Australian technician might hold AINDT Level 2 in UT and MT, an employer certification under your SNT-TC-1A written practice for a US-code client, a radiation use licence from the EPA if they do radiography, and a current vision test. The ERP keeps each of those on the technician's NDT profile. The profile also records highest level, methods certified, radiation safety training, radiation badge number and medical fitness expiry, which matters on mine sites with medical requirements.

Vision tests are tracked separately with near vision (Jaeger J1/J2), far vision, colour perception, examiner, clinic and expiry, because a lapsed eye test invalidates a certificate under most schemes even when the certificate itself is in date. Examination sheets hold general, specific and practical scores with a configurable passing score for in-house employer certification. Certificate templates per scheme set validity in months, whether a vision test or exam is required, and the minimum OJT and training hours.

Alerts are the part people notice first. Daily checks create a warning task 90 days before a certificate or vision test expires, and you can configure daily email alerts with recipients, look-ahead days and a resend interval for technician certificates, calibration certificates and company certifications. When someone books time against a job with an invalid certificate, the timesheet warns. If your company runs to SNT-TC-1A for some clients, Atlantis can also help with written practice development so the ERP's records match a current, signed document.

Atlantis does not train toward AINDT or ISO 9712 certification. The ERP records those certificates; Atlantis training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A based only.

Compliance and reporting context in South Australia

Direct answer: The ERP supports evidence for South Australian regulators and clients but does not replace licences or accreditation. Radiography is licensed by the EPA under the Radiation Protection and Control Act 2021, plant and pressure equipment duties sit under SafeWork SA, and clients often require NATA accreditation. Data hosting and residency questions are discussed during scoping.

Radiation. The Environment Protection Authority (EPA) administers the Radiation Protection and Control Act 2021. It reduced the old licence categories to two: a radiation use licence for people who operate apparatus or handle radioactive material, and a radiation management licence for businesses that possess radiation sources. Your radiographers' use licences can be stored as certificates with expiry alerts, your company's management licence as a company certification with alert days, and source vehicles in the fleet records. The Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA) publishes the national codes that state regulators draw on, including the code for safe transport of radioactive material.

Work health and safety. South Australia's work health and safety law follows the national model, with SafeWork SA as the regulator. Pressure equipment design and item registration and the duties of people who manage plant come from that framework, with the Australian standards above providing the technical detail. Your ERP should make site induction records, work permit fields and safety documentation easy to produce; the Atlantis ERP's project records carry safety induction and work permit fields alongside methods, codes and acceptance criteria.

Accreditation. NATA accreditation to ISO/IEC 17025 or 17020 is the trust signal many South Australian buyers look for first. Assessors ask for competence records, equipment calibration traceability, procedure control and evidence of report review. The ERP's certificate records, calibration register, procedure workflow and report approval workflow (draft, in progress, review, approved, sent, with reviewer and approver signatures) map to those questions. It does not make you accredited.

Data residency. Some defence and government-adjacent clients ask where data is hosted and who can access it. Hosting location and access controls are discussed during scoping, so tell us early if a contract has specific requirements.

Invoices carry the job and PO numbers, site and cost centre that mining and defence clients' accounts payable teams look for.

Australian e-invoicing runs on the Peppol network, with the ATO as the Peppol authority. At the time of writing it is voluntary for business-to-business invoices, while Commonwealth agencies are set up to receive Peppol e-invoices. Large mining and energy companies increasingly prefer electronic invoices through their own supplier portals or Peppol, so it is worth raising during scoping.

The invoice header holds the NDT project, job or PO number, site, invoice type and industry sector, with subtotals for labour, equipment and consumables. Lines carry cost centre, method, equipment serial, technician, rate type and days or hours. The financial dashboard shows revenue, cost of sales, gross margin, operating expenses, EBITDA and outstanding invoices over a 12-month view, which helps when long remote jobs tie up cash.

Direct answer: Implementation is remote and typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff; the main variable is how clean your existing records are. Atlantis configures the system for your methods, certification schemes, report formats, rates and tax settings, imports your data and trains your team online.

NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in Sweden

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution is a fully customized ERP for NDT and inspection companies working in Sweden. It records EN ISO 9712 certificates beside ASNT SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 records with automatic expiry status, keeps calibration evidence for every instrument and probe, controls procedure revisions, plans crews for nuclear outages, steel works, refineries, pulp mills and fabrication shops, captures reports offline and takes each job from quotation to invoice. Sweden is a demanding place to run an NDT company. Its nuclear plants operate under some of the most formal inspection qualification rules in Europe. Its steel, mining and pulp industries run large, hot, heavy equipment that wears out in predictable and unpredictable ways. Its aerospace and automotive manufacturers expect traceability down to the probe serial number. And the distances are real: a crew may finish an outage on the east coast and drive a day north to a steel works or a hydropower station. In each of those settings the question an auditor or client asks is the same: who did this test, were they certified, was the equipment calibrated, which procedure revision applied, and who approved the result? This page explains how the Atlantis ERP answers that question and what else to look for.

Sweden's NDT market by region and industry

Direct answer: Swedish NDT work is concentrated in nuclear power (Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals), steel and specialty metals (Luleå, Borlänge, Oxelösund, Avesta, Sandviken and Hofors), refining on the west coast (Lysekil and Gothenburg), mining in the north, pulp and paper along the Bothnian coast, hydropower in the northern rivers, and aerospace, defence and automotive manufacturing in the south and west.

Nuclear. Sweden's operating reactors are at Forsmark north of Stockholm, Oskarshamn on the Småland coast and Ringhals south of Gothenburg. Annual outages bring concentrated in-service inspection of reactor components, piping and welds, and each of those inspections has to follow qualified procedures and personnel rules. Nuclear work also brings strict demands for documentation, change control and record retention.

Steel and specialty metals. SSAB produces steel at Luleå, Borlänge and Oxelösund; Outokumpu makes stainless steel at Avesta; Alleima at Sandviken and Ovako at Hofors and elsewhere make tube, wire and engineering steels. These plants need inspection of their own process equipment (furnaces, cranes, rolling mills, pressure equipment) and often product testing as well, from ultrasonic testing of plate and bar to eddy current testing of tube.

Refining and chemicals. Preem runs refineries at Lysekil and Gothenburg, and Gothenburg also has St1's refinery and a cluster of energy and chemical terminals around the port. Stenungsund, north of Gothenburg, is Sweden's main petrochemical cluster. Turnarounds at these sites are the classic large NDT jobs: many technicians, many methods, short windows.

Mining, pulp and paper, and hydropower. LKAB's iron ore operations at Kiruna and Malmberget and Boliden's mines and smelters in the north run heavy structural and rotating equipment. Pulp and paper mills along the coast operate recovery boilers and digesters where tube thickness surveys and weld inspection are routine. Hydropower stations on the northern rivers have penstocks, gates and turbines that need periodic inspection.

Aerospace, defence and automotive. Saab builds aircraft at Linköping, GKN Aerospace makes engine components at Trollhättan, Saab Kockums builds submarines and naval vessels at Karlskrona, and Volvo and Scania run large vehicle and engine plants around Gothenburg and Södertälje. Aerospace NDT is typically certified under EN 4179 or NAS 410 and audited closely by primes and Nadcap.

What Swedish clients and regulators expect from NDT companies

Direct answer: Clients expect EN ISO 9712 certification (plus EN 4179 or NAS 410 in aerospace and ASNT-based certification on US-code work), approved and controlled procedures, calibrated equipment, signed and reviewed reports, and often accreditation by Swedac. Nuclear work adds qualification of NDT systems; pressure equipment work adds accredited inspection bodies under Arbetsmiljöverket rules.

Nuclear. The Swedish Radiation Safety Authority (Strålsäkerhetsmyndigheten, SSM) regulates nuclear safety and has long required that non-destructive testing of reactor components and connected piping be performed with qualified inspection systems: the procedure, equipment and personnel together are evaluated by an independent qualification body. The Swedish Qualification Centre (SQC) has carried out this qualification work since the 1990s. An NDT company working in Swedish nuclear plants therefore has to keep very precise records of which technician is qualified on which procedure and technique, alongside their ordinary certificates.

Pressure equipment. The Swedish Work Environment Authority (Arbetsmiljöverket) sets the rules for using and inspecting pressure equipment; since 1 January 2025 they have been in AFS 2023:11. Equipment in the higher control classes must be inspected by an inspection body accredited by Swedac. NDT companies supply much of the testing behind those inspections, so the inspection body will expect certificates, procedures and calibration evidence to be clean and quickly available. New pressure equipment for the European market falls under the Pressure Equipment Directive, which requires third-party approval of NDT personnel for category III and IV equipment.

Accreditation. Swedac accredits laboratories and inspection bodies to ISO/IEC 17025 and ISO/IEC 17020, and many Swedish clients buy only from accredited providers. The ERP does not grant accreditation, but it holds the competence records, calibration traceability, procedure control and report review evidence an assessor looks for.

US codes. US-owned plants, suppliers to US primes and fabricators building to ASME or AWS often ask for ASNT-based certification under the employer's written practice. That is the side of the work Atlantis knows best; see employer certification programmes.

NDT ERP Software for Inspection Companies in Tasmania

Short answer: The Atlantis ERP solution is a fully customized ERP for NDT and inspection companies working in Tasmania. It records AINDT and other ISO 9712 certificates next to ASNT SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 certifications with automatic expiry status, tracks instrument calibration, schedules small crews across Hobart, the Tamar Valley, the North-West coast and the West Coast mines, captures method-specific reports offline and runs quoting through invoicing on one system. Implementation is remote and typically takes 2 to 4 weeks from kickoff, depending on how clean your existing records are. Affordable. Accessible. Fully customizable. Ask for a Tasmania demo.

Tasmanian inspection companies tend to be small, versatile and busy. A team of a few technicians might cover penstock welds for a hydro scheme, aluminium hull welds at a shipbuilder, pressure vessels at a smelter, crane and structural checks at a port, and a salmon feed barge, all in the same month. Some work comes from local asset owners; some comes as subcontracts from mainland firms that fly people across Bass Strait. With that much variety and so few people, the business usually runs on one or two people's memory and a set of spreadsheets. This page explains where Tasmanian NDT work comes from, what clients and regulators expect, and how the Atlantis ERP takes the admin load off a small team.

Where NDT work comes from in Tasmania

Direct answer: NDT demand in Tasmania comes from hydro-electric generation and new transmission, heavy industry in the Tamar Valley and on the Derwent (aluminium, zinc, paper), aluminium shipbuilding and marine work in Hobart, West Coast mining, ports at Burnie, Devonport and Bell Bay, and fabrication for aquaculture, construction and agriculture.

Hydro and transmission. Hydro Tasmania runs one of the largest hydro-electric systems in Australia, with dozens of dams, power stations, penstocks, gates, valves and turbines across the Central Highlands, the West Coast and the Derwent and Mersey-Forth catchments. Ageing penstocks and pressure pipelines need UT thickness surveys and weld inspection; turbine runners, shafts and generator components need MT, PT, UT and visual inspection during outages. The Tarraleah power scheme redevelopment went to tender in 2026, and construction of Marinus Link, the new interconnector to Victoria, is scheduled to start in 2026 with completion targeted for 2030. Large projects like these bring fabrication, structural and weld inspection to the state, often with mainland or international principal contractors who expect full documentation.

Tamar Valley and Bell Bay. Rio Tinto's Bell Bay Aluminium smelter is one of the state's largest industrial sites, and in October 2026 Rio Tinto, the Tasmanian Government and the Commonwealth agreed arrangements to keep it operating until the end of 2031 on Hydro Tasmania power. Smelters have potlines, anode plants, cranes, gas and compressed-air systems, and structural steel that all need periodic inspection. The Bell Bay industrial area also includes the former TEMCO manganese alloy smelter, which has been in limited operations, and the Port of Bell Bay on the Tamar.

The Derwent. Nyrstar's Hobart zinc smelter at Lutana is supported by state and federal funding while modernisation options, including germanium and indium production, are studied. The Boyer paper mill sits upstream. Both run boilers, pressure vessels, tanks and acid or process piping inspected under AS/NZS 3788 and the owner's integrity programme.

Aluminium shipbuilding and marine. Incat in Hobart builds large aluminium high-speed catamarans, including battery-electric ferries, and the Hobart waterfront supports vessel maintenance for the Antarctic programme, fishing, tourism and aquaculture fleets. Aluminium weld inspection relies heavily on PT, RT and UT, and classification societies witness much of it. Salmon farming in Macquarie Harbour, the D'Entrecasteaux Channel and Storm Bay depends on vessels, feed barges, moorings and steel structures that need inspection and repair.

West Coast mining and the North-West coast. Underground and open-cut mines around Rosebery, Renison and Savage River, the iron ore pellet plant at Port Latta, Burnie's port and its mineral and timber exports, and Devonport's ferry and freight terminal create shutdown, structural and pressure equipment inspection. Cement manufacturing at Railton and food processing across the north add steady base work.

With that mix, a small team in Tasmania can deal with hydro, aluminium, zinc, marine and mining clients in a single quarter. Each has a different idea of what a complete report pack looks like.

What Tasmanian clients and contractors expect from NDT vendors

Direct answer: Tasmanian clients usually ask for current AINDT or other ISO 9712 certificates (and sometimes ASNT-based employer certification for US-code equipment or US-linked contractors), approved procedures, calibration certificates, method-specific reports in their format, radiation licences for radiography, site inductions, and often NATA accreditation. Class societies add their own documentation on marine work.

Generators and smelters typically run contractor prequalification that checks certifications, calibration, insurance and safety records, then audit before major outages. Principal contractors on large energy projects tend to apply their own quality plans, with inspection and test plans that call for certified personnel by method, approved procedures and calibrated equipment, and they will reject a report that cannot show those links. Hydro turbines, generators and some process equipment come from overseas manufacturers, so ASME, EN and ISO references all appear on Tasmanian drawings.

Pressure equipment work references AS/NZS 3788 for in-service inspection, AS 4343 for hazard levels, AS 1210 for unfired pressure vessels and AS 4041 for piping, and many owners want in-service inspectors to hold AICIP registration. Marine work brings classification-society rules and surveyor witness points. Structural steel on bridges, ports and energy projects follows Australian structural and welding standards and the project's specification.

For small firms, the hard part is not knowing what each client wants. It is keeping the evidence ready without a full-time administrator. That is where an NDT-specific ERP pays its way.

Running a small Tasmanian NDT firm on one system

Direct answer: In a small firm the owner is often also the Level 3, the estimator and the bookkeeper. The ERP helps by turning certificate, calibration and roster checks into automatic warnings, by reusing job data from quote to report to invoice, and by keeping procedures and report templates under control without a separate document system.

The practical gain is fewer re-keyed numbers. A quote carries the job type, site and applicable codes. When accepted, it becomes a sales order and a project with client PO, methods, codes, scope and acceptance criteria, plus assigned technicians and equipment. Technicians report against that job in the field, and timesheets record work type (inspection, travel, standby, setup), method, site and equipment serial with a billable flag and rate multiplier. The invoice is built from the same data, with lines showing method, technician, equipment serial and rate type, and subtotals for labour, equipment and consumables.

Procedures are another pressure point. Clients ask for the current revision, and small firms often have three slightly different copies. The procedure register records document number, revision, method, scope, material, applicable standard and acceptance criteria; procedures move through draft, submitted, reviewed, approved and published, approved revisions are locked, and every revision keeps a snapshot. An AI-assisted first draft can speed up writing a new procedure, but a Level 3 still reviews and approves it.

Ferry crossings and flights to the mainland also matter. If you send technicians to Victorian jobs, or mainland firms bring people to Tasmania, the availability calendar and blocked double-booking stop anyone being promised to two places in the same week.

AINDT, ISO 9712 and ASNT certificate tracking

Direct answer: AINDT certificates are recorded under the ISO 9712 scheme with AINDT as the certifying body, and ASNT-based employer certifications under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189. Both sit on the same technician profile with separate expiry status, vision-test records and alerts.

The technician's NDT profile records highest level, methods certified, radiation safety training, radiation badge number and medical fitness expiry. Vision tests are separate records with near vision (Jaeger J1/J2), far vision, colour perception, contrast, examiner, clinic and expiry, so an out-of-date eye test does not slip past while the certificate itself still looks current. Examination sheets hold general, specific and practical scores for in-house employer certification, and certificate templates per scheme hold validity in months, vision-test and exam requirements and minimum OJT and training hours. Company certifications such as ISO 9001 or NATA accreditation can be tracked with their own alert days.

If you certify staff under an SNT-TC-1A written practice for US-code work, Atlantis can help with written practice development. Atlantis training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A based only, delivered online or onsite at the employer's facility; Atlantis does not train toward AINDT or ISO 9712 certification.

Compliance and reporting context in Tasmania

Direct answer: Industrial radiography in Tasmania needs a licence under the Radiation Protection Act 2005, administered by the Department of Health's Radiation Protection Unit, with licences renewed each year. WorkSafe Tasmania administers work health and safety, including plant duties. The ERP holds the evidence; it does not issue licences or accreditation. Data hosting is discussed during scoping.

Radiation. In Tasmania, using, possessing, storing or transporting a radiation source requires a licence under the Radiation Protection Act 2005 and the Radiation Protection Regulations 2016, and licences are renewed annually by 31 August. Holding every radiographer's licence as a certificate with an expiry date, and the company's licences as company certifications with alert days, means the August renewal does not catch anyone out. Fleet records note which vehicles can carry radioactive sources and their transport licence details. ARPANSA's national codes, including the transport code, sit behind the state rules.

Work health and safety. Tasmania follows the national model work health and safety laws, with WorkSafe Tasmania as the regulator. Plant duties, including those for pressure equipment, come from that framework, with Australian standards for the technical detail. Project records in the ERP hold safety induction and work permit fields.

Accreditation and review. NATA accreditation to ISO/IEC 17025 or 17020 is valued by larger Tasmanian asset owners and mainland principals. Assessors ask about competence, calibration traceability, procedure control and report review. The ERP's report workflow (draft, in progress, review, approved, sent) records inspector, reviewer and approver signatures, plus a third-party or authorised inspector where one witnesses the work.

Tax and data. GST settings and the records your bookkeeper needs for BAS are configured during implementation. Peppol e-invoicing is scoped and configured during implementation if you need it; it is voluntary for business-to-business invoices in Australia at the time of writing. Victoria's inspection market is shaped by a refinery, an offshore gas province that is moving from production into decommissioning, a power system in transition, a defence manufacturing base that has grown fast, and the largest fabrication and manufacturing workforce in the country around Melbourne. For an NDT company that means a mix of shutdown crews, long-running fabrication inspection, defence quality requirements and a growing share of decommissioning and life-extension work. The certificates, procedures and paperwork differ for each, and they all have to be correct before the first technician walks onto site. This page explains where the Victorian work is, which rules and records apply, what the Atlantis ERP actually does, and how to compare it with other options.

A note on the name: this page is about the state of Victoria in Australia. Our separate page for Victoria, Texas covers a different market.

Where NDT companies find work in Victoria

Direct answer: Victorian NDT work concentrates around Geelong (the Viva Energy refinery, port and defence manufacturing at Avalon), Gippsland (Bass Strait oil and gas processing, offshore decommissioning and Latrobe Valley power stations), Melbourne's west and north (fuel terminals, chemical plants, fabrication, aerospace and defence), and regional centres such as Portland and Bendigo.

Geelong and Corio Bay. The Viva Energy refinery at Corio is one of only two oil refineries still operating in Australia, alongside Lytton in Brisbane. It carries a large inventory of pressure vessels, exchangers, furnaces, piping and tanks, and its turnarounds and ongoing maintenance bring in UT thickness, PAUT, TOFD, radiography, MT, PT, IRIS and visual inspection teams. The port, fuel storage and chemical sites around Corio Bay add work, and defence vehicle manufacturing at Avalon has brought weld inspection to defence and OEM quality requirements into the region. See NDT ERP in Geelong.

Gippsland and Bass Strait. For more than fifty years, oil and gas from the Gippsland Basin has come ashore at the Longford gas plants, with liquids processed at Long Island Point near Hastings. As fields deplete, offshore platforms and pipelines are moving into decommissioning, and onshore plant into life extension or wind-down. That brings a different flavour of inspection: integrity surveys before removal, weld and structural checks on lifting points, and thickness and condition surveys on ageing plant. Offshore work in Commonwealth waters is regulated by NOPSEMA.

The Latrobe Valley. Brown-coal power stations at Loy Yang and Yallourn have boilers, pressure piping, turbines, coal handling plant and very large structures. Outage work has long been a staple for Victorian NDT companies; with closures scheduled over the coming years, the mix is shifting toward life-extension outages and decommissioning, alongside new transmission, storage and renewable generation projects.

Melbourne's west and north. Altona, Laverton, Brooklyn and Dandenong host fuel import terminals, chemical plants, food and beverage processing, and a large base of pressure vessel, structural and pipeline fabricators. Aerospace manufacturing at Fishermans Bend and defence suppliers across the metropolitan area bring work under OEM and defence quality systems, often with eddy current, penetrant and ultrasonic inspection of components. Major transport and tunnelling projects add structural and weld inspection. Many Victorian NDT companies keep their head office, store and calibration room in Melbourne; see NDT ERP in Melbourne.

Regional Victoria. The Portland aluminium smelter in the south-west, defence vehicle manufacturing in Bendigo, gold mining in the central goldfields, and water and irrigation infrastructure across the north add regional work that needs travel planning.

What Victorian clients ask NDT vendors for

Direct answer: Victorian clients ask for certified technicians (usually AINDT under ISO 9712; ASNT-based employer certification for US-code, aerospace and some defence work), licensed radiographers, NATA-traceable calibration, approved procedures, inductions and medicals, and reports in their format. Defence and aerospace clients add tighter document-control and traceability expectations.

  • Technician certification. AINDT certification by method and level is the common baseline. Aerospace and defence suppliers working to US OEM requirements often expect employer certification under an ASNT-based written practice or a NAS 410 style system, and refinery or offshore work on US-designed equipment may ask the same.
  • Radiation licences. In Victoria the Department of Health administers the Radiation Act 2005. Industrial radiographers need a use licence, and the company needs a management licence covering its sources and units. Clients will ask to see both, plus dosimetry and source transport arrangements.
  • Calibration. Current certificates, usually from NATA-accredited labs, for every flaw detector, thickness gauge, yoke, UV lamp, light meter and reference block.
  • Procedures. Level 3 approved, revision-controlled procedures to AS 3978, AS/NZS 1554, AS 2885, ASME Section V or the customer's specification.
  • Site and project rules. Inductions, medicals and the principal's contractor management system.
  • Traceability. Defence and aerospace clients often want each result traceable to the technician, the instrument serial, its calibration certificate and the procedure revision used.

Victoria works under its own Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 rather than the model WHS laws adopted by most other states. WorkSafe Victoria administers it, including registration of certain plant designs and items of plant. Energy Safe Victoria oversees gas and pipeline safety. In-service inspection of pressure equipment generally follows AS/NZS 3788, with the owner and its inspectors running the programme; your NDT results feed it.
