Is there an NDT simulator available in Manitoba?

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app, so it works in Winnipeg and anywhere else in Manitoba with a connection. There is no physical centre to visit; delivery is online.

Is it useful for aerospace NDT in Winnipeg?

Yes for core skills. The Aircraft Hangar environment has 54 airframe and component jobs covering eddy current, penetrant, UT and visual inspection. Your OEM procedures and employer qualification still govern real work.

Does Practical NDT count toward CGSB or NAS 410 certification?

No. It is practice only. Each scheme has its own training, experience and examination requirements, including practical exams on real specimens. Confirm the current CGSB certification body before planning.

Can it help hydro outage crews?

Yes. Thick-section UT, PAUT and TOFD weld sizing, MT and VT jobs in the Welding Workshop and NDT Lab match the weld and structural work found in hydro stations.

Does it include radiography?

Yes, as technique and image interpretation practice with no radiation source. It does not count toward CNSC exposure device operator certification.

Which Manitoba industries is it most useful for?

Aerospace engine overhaul and aerostructures, bus and equipment manufacturing, fabrication, hydroelectric generation, nickel and base-metal mining, pipelines, the southwest oil patch and chemical plants.

What experience level is it for?

All levels: guided fundamentals for trainees, rare-defect refreshers for working technicians, and scenario building and crew benchmarking for Level IIIs.

Can technicians on northern rotation use it?

Yes, during downtime, subject to the site's connectivity and rules.

Does Atlantis offer ASNT training in Manitoba?

Atlantis training follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A and is delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility. See NDT training in Winnipeg or all training.

How do we start?

Request a demo. We will map the environments to your Manitoba work and provide a quote on request.

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in the Netherlands

Few countries pack as much inspectable steel into as little space as the Netherlands. Refineries, tank terminals and chemical plants line the Rotterdam port, chemical complexes stand at Moerdijk, Terneuzen and Geleen, a large integrated steelworks sits at IJmuiden, shipyards and offshore fabricators work along the rivers south of Rotterdam, and the Dutch North Sea is filling with offshore wind farms. Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and Dutch inspection teams are exactly the kind of users it was designed for. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. A technician chooses a job in a virtual NDT lab, welding workshop, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank, sets up the technique, inspects, records the result and is scored as soon as the job is done. It supports every level, from a trainee learning to calibrate a probe to a Level 3 benchmarking a crew before a turnaround, without booking bench time or using a single physical specimen.

This hub covers the whole of the Netherlands: where the work is, which simulator environments and methods fit Dutch industry, how simulator practice relates to EN ISO 9712 certification and Dutch rules, and how to arrange a demo. The Rotterdam page goes deeper on the port.

The Netherlands' NDT workforce and where the work is

Short answer: Dutch NDT work is centred on the Rotterdam-Moerdijk port and industrial complex, with further clusters in Zeeland, Limburg, the Amsterdam and IJmuiden area, the northern ports of Eemshaven and Delfzijl, the shipbuilding river belt and the offshore sector served from Den Helder, IJmuiden and Rotterdam.

Rotterdam and the port. The Port of Rotterdam is Europe's largest port and one of its biggest energy and chemical complexes. The industrial zones run west from the city through Pernis, Botlek, Europoort and out to the Maasvlakte. Several large refineries operate here, including the biggest in Europe at Pernis, alongside crude and product tank terminals with enormous storage capacity, an LNG import terminal on the Maasvlakte, chemical plants, power stations, and new energy transition projects in hydrogen and carbon capture. Inspection demand is constant: corrosion and thickness surveys on piping and vessels, exchanger tube inspection, alloy verification, tank shell and floor inspection, and weld inspection on new construction.

Moerdijk and West Brabant. South of Rotterdam, the Moerdijk industrial area hosts a large petrochemical complex and logistics and tank storage operations. Like the port, its workload is dominated by in-service inspection during turnarounds and by weld inspection on modifications.

Zeeland. Zeeland has the Netherlands' only operating nuclear power station at Borssele, where new reactors are also planned, plus the chemical complex at Terneuzen, industrial sites at Vlissingen-Oost and the cross-border North Sea Port that links Vlissingen and Terneuzen with Ghent in Belgium. Naval and commercial shipbuilding at Vlissingen adds weld inspection on hull structures.

Limburg. Chemelot at Geleen is one of the country's largest chemical sites, with chemical and materials plants, steam and utility systems and extensive piping. Plant inspection skills are the core requirement.

Amsterdam, IJmuiden and Schiphol. The steelworks at IJmuiden is the Netherlands' largest industrial site of its kind, with blast furnaces, gas holders, cranes and heavy structural steel, and it is in the middle of a long transition to lower-carbon steelmaking. Amsterdam's port is a major hub for petrol blending and fuel storage. Schiphol is home to large airline engineering and maintenance operations, and aviation component and services companies sit around the airport.

The river belt and shipbuilding. The Drechtsteden area and the rivers around Gorinchem, Kinderdijk, Alblasserdam and Schiedam host shipyards, dredging-vessel builders, offshore equipment fabricators and heavy-lift specialists. Welding is the heart of this industry, and with it weld inspection with UT, PAUT, TOFD, MT and RT.

The north and the offshore sector. Groningen's gas field has been closed and its wells and facilities are being decommissioned, while Eemshaven and Delfzijl host power generation, chemicals, data centres and offshore wind service bases. Den Helder is the base for much of the Dutch offshore oil and gas service industry and for the Royal Netherlands Navy. Offshore wind farms in zones such as Hollandse Kust and IJmuiden Ver are supplied from ports along the coast, and monopile and foundation fabrication in the Rotterdam area adds heavy weld inspection work.

Aerospace. Aerostructures and aircraft wiring production at Papendrecht and Hoogeveen, military aircraft maintenance at Woensdrecht, and aviation maintenance around Schiphol together make a sizeable aerospace NDT community, working mainly with eddy current, penetrant and ultrasonic methods.

Practical NDT by city and region in the Netherlands

Short answer: Rotterdam has its own Practical NDT page. The table below covers Rotterdam and the other main Dutch clusters, with the simulator environments and methods that fit each.

City or regionMain local sectorsEnvironments & methods to practise
RotterdamRefining, tank storage, LNG, chemicals, offshore wind fabricationOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank, Welding Workshop; UT, PAUT, IRIS, PMI, MFL, TOFD
MoerdijkPetrochemicals, tank storageOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; UT, IRIS, PMI, MFL
Zeeland (Borssele, Terneuzen, Vlissingen)Nuclear power, chemicals, shipbuilding, portOil & Gas Site, Welding Workshop; UT, PAUT, TOFD, ET, RT
Limburg (Geleen)Chemicals and materialsOil & Gas Site; UT, IRIS, PMI, LRUT
IJmuiden and AmsterdamSteelmaking, fuel terminals, aviation at SchipholStorage Tank, Welding Workshop, Aircraft Hangar; UT, MT, MFL, ET, PT
River belt (Gorinchem, Kinderdijk, Schiedam)Shipbuilding, dredging vessels, offshore equipmentWelding Workshop; UT, PAUT, TOFD, MT, RT
North (Eemshaven, Delfzijl, Den Helder)Power, chemicals, gas decommissioning, offshore servicesOil & Gas Site; UT, LRUT, PAUT, PMI

Rotterdam is the largest single concentration of NDT work in the country. Refinery and chemical turnarounds bring large crews for short, intense periods, and tank terminals keep a steady flow of shell and floor inspections. The Oil & Gas Site environment, with 73 jobs, covers corrosion mapping, exchanger tubes with IRIS, alloy verification with PMI and LRUT screening, and the Storage Tank environment covers shell thickness and MFL floor screening. Monopile and foundation fabrication adds PAUT and TOFD on very thick welds, which the Welding Workshop supports. Atlantis also has an ASNT SNT-TC-1A training page for Rotterdam for employers who work to US codes.

Moerdijk shares Rotterdam's plant workload on a smaller footprint. Turnaround preparation with IRIS, PMI and thickness work is the most useful practice, together with tank inspection for the storage operations nearby.

Zeeland combines nuclear, chemical and marine work. Nuclear plant inspection relies on qualified techniques and tightly controlled personnel requirements; the simulator supports general method practice in UT, PAUT, ET and RT interpretation without replacing those qualifications. Terneuzen's chemical complex suits the Oil & Gas Site, and the shipyards at Vlissingen suit the Welding Workshop.

Limburg technicians at Geleen work mainly on chemical plant: piping, vessels, exchangers, furnaces and utilities. Thickness surveys, IRIS on tubes, PMI and LRUT screening of pipe racks are the most relevant jobs.

IJmuiden and Amsterdam combine heavy industry and aviation. Steelworks inspection involves structural welds, cranes, gas holders and vessels, with MT and UT at the centre. Amsterdam's fuel terminals need tank inspection. Schiphol's maintenance organisations rely on ET, PT and UT on airframes and components, which the Aircraft Hangar environment's 54 jobs cover.

The river belt is welding country. Shipyards and offshore equipment builders inspect butt and fillet welds on hulls, cranes, pipe-laying equipment and heavy structures. The Welding Workshop's 52 jobs give repeated practice in UT, PAUT, TOFD, MT and RT interpretation on realistic weld flaws.

The north is changing fast. Decommissioning of Groningen gas facilities, new power and data-centre construction at Eemshaven and offshore services from Den Helder all need plant and pipeline inspection skills: UT, LRUT screening and PAUT corrosion mapping.

Environments and methods that match Dutch work

Short answer: the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments match the port and chemical clusters, the Welding Workshop matches shipbuilding, steel and offshore wind fabrication, the Aircraft Hangar matches Schiphol and the aerospace sites, and the NDT Lab covers fundamentals.

The simulator includes five environments, twelve methods and 33 guided lessons. Surface methods are PT, MT and VT. Volumetric methods are contact UT, PAUT, TOFD and RT. Electromagnetic methods are ET and MFL. The specialist techniques are LRUT guided-wave screening, IRIS internal rotary UT for heat-exchanger and boiler tubes, and PMI for alloy verification.

  • Oil & Gas Site (73 jobs): weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant. The core environment for Pernis, Botlek, Europoort, Moerdijk, Terneuzen and Geleen.
  • Storage Tank: UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank. Highly relevant to the Netherlands, which has some of the largest tank storage capacity in Europe in Rotterdam and Amsterdam.
  • Welding Workshop (52 jobs): weld coupons and fabrication joints. Relevant to shipyards, offshore equipment builders, steelworks maintenance and monopile and jacket fabrication.
  • Aircraft Hangar (54 jobs): airframe and component inspection. Relevant to Schiphol maintenance, aerostructures production and military aircraft maintenance.
  • NDT Lab (52 jobs): bench specimens and reference blocks. Relevant to trainees, students in technical vocational programmes, and anyone working on calibration and set-up fundamentals.

Two Dutch specialities stand out. The first is mechanised weld inspection with PAUT and TOFD, used widely on pipelines, pressure equipment and offshore wind structures, where set-up decisions (focal laws, probe separation, scan plans, encoder settings) make or break the result. The simulator lets technicians make those choices repeatedly and see the consequences. The second is tank inspection: with so much storage capacity in the country, shell and floor inspection skills are in constant demand, and the Storage Tank environment provides a full-size tank to practise on without draining, cleaning and gas-freeing a real one.

Regulators and requirements Dutch technicians meet

Short answer: Dutch NDT personnel are normally certified to EN ISO 9712; radiography is regulated by ANVS under the Dutch basic safety standards for radiation protection; pressure equipment in use falls under the Warenwetbesluit drukapparatuur 2016 and the Netherlands Labour Authority. Practical NDT is practice for any scheme and is not a certification.

Personnel certification. EN ISO 9712 is the standard basis for NDT personnel certification in the Netherlands, issued by accredited certification bodies. KINT, the Dutch society for quality surveillance, inspection and non-destructive testing, supports training, qualification and certification activities and joint industry projects in the sector. Aerospace NDT personnel are qualified to EN 4179 within their organisation's approved procedures. Some contractors working for US-owned operators, US OEMs or EPCs on US-code projects also qualify staff to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis training covers ASNT SNT-TC-1A only; Atlantis does not provide EN ISO 9712 or EN 4179 training or examinations.

Radiation protection. The Authority for Nuclear Safety and Radiation Protection (ANVS) regulates ionising radiation in the Netherlands under the Besluit basisveiligheidsnormen stralingsbescherming, the Dutch implementation of the EU basic safety standards. Industrial radiography with sources or X-ray equipment needs authorisation, and the sector has its own practice guideline on radiation protection for NDT, published through KINT. Simulator practice involves no radiation at all, which is one reason it is a useful way to practise radiographic technique and interpretation.

Pressure equipment. The EU Pressure Equipment Directive is implemented in the Netherlands through the Warenwetbesluit drukapparatuur 2016 and its associated regulation. Unlike the directive itself, which concerns new equipment, the Dutch rules also set requirements for the use phase, including commissioning inspections and periodic re-inspection of certain categories of equipment by authorised inspection bodies. The Netherlands Labour Authority (Nederlandse Arbeidsinspectie) supervises, and Seveso establishments carry an additional duty of care for their pressure equipment. NDT is a routine part of both new-build conformity assessment and in-service inspection.

Mining, offshore and nuclear. Oil and gas production, including the Groningen field and offshore installations, is supervised by the State Supervision of Mines (SodM). Nuclear installations such as Borssele fall under ANVS. Aviation maintenance is overseen under EASA rules by the Dutch Human Environment and Transport Inspectorate. Codes in daily use include EN ISO weld testing standards, EN 13445 for pressure vessels and, on US-specified projects, ASME and API codes.

For written practices, procedures and technique sheets for Dutch projects that work to US codes, see NDT Level III consulting in the Netherlands. To track EN ISO 9712, EN 4179 and ASNT certificates in one system, see the Atlantis ERP for Dutch inspection companies.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in the Netherlands

Short answer: trainees build fundamentals with 33 guided lessons, working technicians keep rare defects and less-used methods fresh, and Level 3s and team leads benchmark crews before turnarounds and offshore campaigns.

Trainees. Many Dutch NDT technicians enter through technical vocational education (MBO) or from welding and mechanical trades, then build experience with an inspection company. The bottleneck is supervised hands-on time: specimens are limited and senior technicians are busy on client sites. The guided lessons start with calibration, reference blocks and simple flaws in the NDT Lab and progress to weld coupons, plant piping, tanks and aircraft components. Trainees can repeat a job as often as they need to, and every attempt is scored.

Working technicians. Dutch technicians often move between very different jobs: a refinery turnaround in Pernis, a tank inspection in Amsterdam, a weld inspection campaign at a shipyard, an offshore wind foundation project. The job library includes rare and hard-to-source flaws such as lack of sidewall fusion, transverse cracking, tube wall loss at supports, pitting under insulation and corrosion at tank floor edges, so technicians can practise the findings that really matter before they meet them on a client's asset.

Level 3s and team leads. Turnarounds in the Rotterdam area bring together technicians from many companies and countries. A responsible Level 3 can assemble a scenario set for the work ahead, assign it before mobilisation and compare results objectively. That supports decisions about who goes where, which refreshers are needed and whether a procedure is being read the same way by everyone on the crew.

Practice vs certification

Short answer: Practical NDT is a practice and readiness tool. It does not grant EN ISO 9712, EN 4179 or ASNT certification, and it does not replace the practical examination on real specimens.

Every certification route used in the Netherlands requires documented training, supervised industrial experience and examinations, including a practical examination on real specimens. Under EN ISO 9712 that happens through the certification body and its examination centres; under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer administers it according to its written practice; under EN 4179 the employer's responsible Level 3 or an outside agency controls it. Simulator hours are not industrial experience under any of these schemes unless an employer's own procedures choose to recognise them, and Atlantis does not claim otherwise.

What the simulator changes is readiness. Candidates arrive at their practical exams having already set up, scanned, interpreted and sized many times. Supervisors have an extra, objective view of a technician's progress. Experienced people can warm up on a method before a job. For formal ASNT SNT-TC-1A training, see Atlantis NDT training.

Turnarounds, tank terminals and offshore wind: why Dutch crews practise virtually

Short answer: Dutch inspection work is intense and campaign-driven, crews are international and mixed, and physical practice specimens are scarce. A browser-based simulator gives every technician the same practice jobs, wherever they are.

The rhythm of inspection work in the Netherlands is set by turnarounds and projects. A large refinery or chemical turnaround in the port can need many inspectors for a few weeks, and the crews are often drawn from several Dutch, Belgian, German, British and other European companies. The people on the crew have different certification histories and different habits. A shared set of practice jobs is a neutral way to bring them to a common standard before work starts.

Offshore wind adds another rhythm. Foundation and transition-piece fabrication involves very thick welds inspected with PAUT and TOFD, and fabrication yards work to tight project schedules. New technicians joining those projects need to become productive quickly, and the Welding Workshop provides repeated practice on mechanised weld inspection set-up and interpretation.

The Netherlands also shares Europe's workforce challenge: experienced technicians retiring while energy transition, decommissioning and new nuclear plans add work. Getting new entrants to a useful level faster, and giving experienced technicians a structured way to stay current, matters to every Dutch inspection manager.

Finally, practising in a simulator involves no radiation, no confined space entry, no work at height and no gas-free certificates. A trainee can make mistakes that would be dangerous on a live plant and learn from the score instead.

Bring Practical NDT to your Dutch team

Short answer: request a demo, tell us what your team inspects, and we will show the right environments and set up a pilot. Pricing is quote on request.

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience. Its scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Practical NDT is affordable, accessible and fully customisable: Dutch inspection companies, plant owners, shipyards, training providers and vocational schools can use the standard library or ask for scenario sets aligned to their own procedures and job mix.

Getting started takes one short call about your work, whether that is turnaround inspection in the port, tank terminals, shipyard weld inspection, offshore wind fabrication or aviation maintenance. We then show the relevant environments live, agree a pilot group and set up access in a browser or app. Team leads see results from day one. Delivery is online; Atlantis has no physical training location in the Netherlands.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an NDT simulator I can use in the Netherlands?

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs online in a browser or app, so it can be used anywhere in the Netherlands. Demos are arranged through the contact form.

Does Practical NDT count towards EN ISO 9712 certification?

No. EN ISO 9712 certification requires training, industrial experience and examinations through an accredited certification body. The simulator is practice only, and Atlantis does not offer EN ISO 9712 training or exams.

Is it useful for refinery and chemical turnarounds in Rotterdam?

Yes. The Oil & Gas Site environment covers corrosion, weld, tube and screening work, including IRIS, PMI and LRUT, and the Storage Tank environment covers shell and floor inspection.

Does it cover PAUT and TOFD for offshore wind fabrication?

Yes. The Welding Workshop includes PAUT and TOFD practice on weld coupons and fabrication joints, which suits mechanised weld inspection on thick sections.

Can aviation technicians at Schiphol use it?

Yes. The Aircraft Hangar environment has 54 jobs covering airframe and component inspection with ET, PT, UT and VT. It does not replace EN 4179 qualification.

Does it include radiography?

Yes, focused on technique and image interpretation. No radiation is used, so ANVS authorisation does not apply to simulator practice; real radiography remains regulated by ANVS.

Can it help with NDT practical exam preparation?

Yes, as preparation. It builds set-up, scanning, interpretation and sizing habits, but the exam itself must be taken on real specimens.

What experience level is it for?

All levels, from trainees on guided lessons to working technicians and Level 3s who build and assign scenario sets.

Can contractors from Belgium, Germany or the UK on a Dutch turnaround use it?

Yes. Access is online, so every member of a mixed international crew can work the same scenario set before mobilisation, wherever they are based.

Does Atlantis offer ASNT training in the Netherlands?

Yes, ASNT SNT-TC-1A only, delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility for employers that need SNT-TC-1A personnel. See training.

How do we start?

Request a demo and we will agree a pilot. Pricing is quote on request.

contentHtml:
HomeTrainingConsultingERPPractical NDTContact

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in New Brunswick

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and New Brunswick's heavy industry gives it plenty to work with. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. Technicians enter a virtual oil and gas site, storage tank, welding workshop, NDT lab or aircraft hangar, pick a job, set up the technique and get a score as soon as they finish. New Brunswick's NDT work is concentrated but intense. Saint John is home to Canada's largest oil refinery, an LNG import terminal, a deep-water port with major crude and product terminals, and pulp, paper and tissue mills. West of the city, on the Bay of Fundy, sits Point Lepreau, the only nuclear generating station in Atlantic Canada. The Saint John River carries hydroelectric stations including Mactaquac, the province's largest. Belledune on the north shore has a port and a generating station, and forestry mills operate across the province. Refinery turnarounds, nuclear outages and mill shutdowns draw large inspection crews in short windows. Practical NDT lets New Brunswick technicians arrive at those windows ready, at any level from first-week trainee to working Level III, without booking lab time or using up specimens.

This is the New Brunswick hub for Practical NDT. It maps where the province's NDT work happens, how the simulator's environments and methods fit it, the regulators that apply, and what a simulator can and cannot do. For a walkthrough tailored to your crew, request a Practical NDT demo for New Brunswick.

New Brunswick's NDT workforce and where the work is

New Brunswick's inspection work clusters in a handful of places: Saint John and the Fundy coast, the Saint John River valley, the north shore, and the Moncton and Fredericton areas. Each has a different equipment mix.

Saint John: refining and energy. The refinery in east Saint John is the largest in Canada by capacity and supplies fuel across Atlantic Canada and to the US Northeast. A refinery of that size has thousands of pressure vessels, heat exchangers, fired heaters and piping circuits, large tank farms, and a marine terminal for crude and products. Turnarounds bring in hundreds of contract workers, including inspection crews running UT thickness surveys, PAUT corrosion mapping, exchanger tube inspection, alloy verification, weld inspection on repairs and tank inspection. Nearby, the Canaport area hosts a deep-water crude receiving terminal and an LNG regasification terminal, adding cryogenic and marine equipment to the inspection load.

Saint John: port and mills. Port Saint John handles bulk liquids, containers, potash and forest products. Pulp, paper and tissue mills in and around the city run boilers, digesters, pressure vessels and chemical recovery equipment, which need regular thickness surveys and weld inspection. Fabrication and industrial service companies support all of these.

Point Lepreau. Point Lepreau Generating Station is a CANDU 6 reactor on the Bay of Fundy. Nuclear inspection in Canada follows CSA N285 series standards, including periodic inspection of pressure-retaining systems and components, with feeder pipes, steam generators, heat exchangers and balance-of-plant piping all subject to detailed inspection programmes during planned outages. Nuclear NDT relies heavily on qualified UT, PAUT, eddy current of tubes and visual examination, delivered under strict procedures.

The Saint John River valley. Mactaquac, upstream of Fredericton, is the province's largest hydroelectric station, with other stations along the river. Hydro inspection involves penstocks, turbines, gates and hoists, large structural welds and concrete-embedded steel. Fredericton itself is the provincial capital and a centre for government, engineering and research.

The north shore and the forest belt. Belledune has a deep-water port and a generating station. Pulp, paper, lumber and panel mills operate around Edmundston, Miramichi, Bathurst and elsewhere, and base-metal mining has historically been important in the Bathurst area. Mills and power stations need boiler-tube inspection, thickness surveys and weld inspection during shutdowns.

Moncton and the southeast. Greater Moncton is a logistics, distribution and manufacturing hub with an international airport and aviation training and maintenance activity. Manufacturing, food processing and transport equipment add fabrication and pressure-equipment inspection. Transmission pipelines that carry natural gas through the province pass through southern New Brunswick.

Practical NDT by city in New Brunswick

Saint John has its own Practical NDT page and an ASNT training page. The table links it and maps New Brunswick's other main work centres to the environments and methods that fit.

City or areaMain local sectorsEnvironments & methods to practise
Saint JohnRefining, LNG and crude terminals, port, pulp and paperOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; IRIS, PMI, UT, PAUT, TOFD, MFL
Point LepreauNuclear generation (CANDU 6)Oil & Gas Site, NDT Lab; UT, PAUT, ET, IRIS, VT
Fredericton and the river valleyHydroelectric generation, government, engineeringWelding Workshop, NDT Lab; UT, PAUT, MT, VT
MonctonManufacturing, logistics, aviation, pipelinesAircraft Hangar, Welding Workshop; ET, PT, RT, UT
Belledune, Bathurst, Miramichi, EdmundstonPort, power, pulp and paper, sawmillsOil & Gas Site, NDT Lab; UT thickness, IRIS, MT, PT

Saint John. For Saint John technicians the Oil & Gas Site, with 73 jobs, is the heart of the library. Refinery turnarounds call for IRIS on exchanger tubes, PMI on alloy circuits, UT and PAUT corrosion mapping on piping and vessels, and TOFD on pressure welds. The Storage Tank environment covers the shell thickness and MFL floor screening work found at refinery tank farms and the crude terminal. Mill technicians also benefit from thickness and weld practice. See Practical NDT Saint John and NDT training in Saint John.

Point Lepreau. Nuclear inspection is procedure-driven and qualification-heavy. The simulator cannot reproduce plant-specific qualified techniques, but it can build and refresh the underlying UT, PAUT and eddy current tube skills that outage technicians rely on, and help a Level III check technique discipline before an outage.

Fredericton and the river valley. Hydro station inspection centres on thick structural and pressure welds and large mechanical components. UT, PAUT and MT in the Welding Workshop and NDT Lab match that work.

Moncton. Manufacturing and fabrication bring weld inspection, while aviation activity around the airport links to the Aircraft Hangar for eddy current and penetrant practice. Pipeline work in the southeast adds RT and UT of girth welds.

Belledune, Bathurst, Miramichi and Edmundston. Mill and power-station shutdowns bring boiler-tube inspection, digester and tank thickness surveys and structural weld checks. IRIS, UT thickness, MT and PT are the core practice.

Environments and methods that match New Brunswick work

Practical NDT has five environments, twelve methods and 33 guided lessons. In New Brunswick the balance tilts strongly toward process-plant and tank work because of Saint John's refinery and terminals, with mills, power and nuclear adding tube and weld inspection.

Oil & Gas Site (73 jobs). Weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant: contact UT and PAUT corrosion mapping, TOFD weld sizing, IRIS internal rotary UT on exchanger and boiler tubes, LRUT guided-wave screening of long pipe runs, and PMI alloy verification. This is the closest match to refinery turnaround work and to mill and power-plant outages.

Storage Tank. UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank. Refinery tank farms, crude and product terminals at Saint John, and fuel storage across the province make this an everyday skill.

Welding Workshop (52 jobs). Weld coupons and fabrication joints for RT interpretation, UT and PAUT sizing, TOFD, MT and VT, matching fabrication shops, repair welding during turnarounds, hydro station welds and pipeline work.

NDT Lab (52 jobs). Bench specimens and reference blocks for calibration, probe handling and fundamentals. New trainees start here and experienced technicians use it to rehearse before a practical examination under any scheme.

Aircraft Hangar (54 jobs). Airframe and component jobs for aviation maintenance around Moncton, Fredericton and Saint John airports: eddy current, penetrant, UT and VT.

Across the twelve methods, New Brunswick technicians lean most on UT, PAUT, IRIS and PMI for refinery and plant work, MFL for tank floors, ET for heat-exchanger and steam-generator tubing and aviation, and MT, PT and VT for structural and mill inspection.

Regulators and requirements New Brunswick technicians meet

Short answer: NDT personnel certification is national, nuclear facilities and radiography sources are regulated federally by the CNSC, and boilers and pressure vessels are regulated by the province. Practical NDT is practice for any scheme and replaces none of them.

National NDT certification. Canada's national NDT personnel certification scheme is based on CAN/CGSB-48.9712, the Canadian adoption of ISO 9712, and New Brunswick employers commonly expect technicians to hold certification under it. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026; Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body has said it continues to operate and the standard remains valid, but confirm the current certification body and arrangements before planning a route. Some employers, especially those working for US-owned operators or to US codes, also use ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practices. This is market context only. Atlantis training aligns with ASNT SNT-TC-1A and Atlantis does not train toward, certify or administer the CGSB/ISO 9712 scheme.

Nuclear. The Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) licenses Point Lepreau, and inspection of its pressure-retaining systems follows the CSA N285 series, including periodic inspection requirements. Nuclear NDT personnel and procedures are qualified to the licensee's programme. Practical NDT is not part of any nuclear qualification.

Radiation safety. The CNSC also licenses radioactive sources used in industrial radiography, and only a CNSC-certified exposure device operator, or a trainee under direct supervision, may operate a gamma exposure device. Practical NDT's RT jobs involve no radiation and do not count toward that certification.

Pressure equipment. Boilers, pressure vessels and pressure piping in New Brunswick are regulated by the province's Technical Inspection Services, which requires inspection of newly installed or modified equipment before it enters service and periodic in-service inspection, with certificates of inspection to operate. CSA B51, ASME Section V and VIII, ASME B31.3 and, for in-service work, API 510, 570 and 653 are commonly referenced.

Pipelines and marine. Interprovincial and international pipelines fall under the Canada Energy Regulator, with CSA Z662 as the core standard. Marine terminals and vessels follow Transport Canada and classification society requirements.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in New Brunswick

New trainees. Trainees in New Brunswick often come from mill, refinery or trades backgrounds, and the gap is hands-on hours before their first turnaround. Guided fundamentals let them repeat calibration, scanning, PAUT setup and indication interpretation with instant feedback. It is useful NDT practical exam preparation, provided everyone understands the real exam is done on real specimens.

Working technicians. New Brunswick's work arrives in bursts: a refinery turnaround, a nuclear outage, a mill shutdown. Between them, technicians may not touch a particular method for months. Rare-defect refreshers between assignments, on things like exchanger tube pitting and wall loss, stress corrosion cracking, hydrogen damage indications, or weld lack of fusion, help them arrive ready rather than relearning on the client's equipment.

Level IIIs and team leads. Level IIIs can build and assign scenario sets, benchmark crews objectively and find coverage gaps before a campaign. Before a turnaround that brings in contract technicians from across Atlantic Canada and beyond, a consistent scenario set gives a fair, like-for-like picture of who is ready for IRIS, PAUT or tank work.

Practice vs certification

Practical NDT is a practice and readiness tool. It is not a certification. It does not grant a level under CAN/CGSB-48.9712, ASNT SNT-TC-1A or an employer's written practice, it is not part of any CSA N285 or nuclear qualification, and it does not replace the practical examination on real specimens these schemes require. It does not satisfy CNSC exposure device operator requirements. It gives technicians more realistic repetition before exams and between jobs, alongside formal NDT training and supervised experience. The formal practical exam remains the step that counts.

Turnarounds, outages and short windows: why New Brunswick crews use virtual NDT training

New Brunswick's biggest inspection jobs happen in short, expensive windows. Every day a refinery unit, a reactor or a mill line is down costs money, so owners want crews that are productive from the first shift. Yet the technicians who staff those windows often spend the months in between on different work, or come in from other provinces with different habits.

A browser-based NDT simulator closes some of that gap. Crews can rehearse IRIS on tube bundles, PAUT corrosion mapping and tank floor MFL screening before mobilisation. Supervisors can see scores rather than rely on self-reported experience. Level IIIs can push the same scenario set to every incoming technician. Because it runs on a laptop or tablet, technicians can practise at home, in a hotel during mobilisation, or in the site trailer. It does not replace time on real equipment or the formal qualifications a refinery or nuclear plant requires, but it makes the first hours on site more productive.

Bring Practical NDT to your New Brunswick team

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience. The scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, who also leads Atlantis training. Whether you run a refinery turnaround inspection team in Saint John, a mill maintenance group on the north shore, a fabrication shop in Moncton, or an outage contractor, rollout starts with a short demo and a conversation about which environments and methods fit your work. Technicians then get access by browser or app.

Pricing is quote on request; the offer is affordable, accessible and fully customizable. Book a New Brunswick Practical NDT demo, read the Practical NDT overview, or write to info@atlantisndt.com.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an NDT simulator available in New Brunswick?

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app, so it works in Saint John, Moncton, Fredericton and anywhere else in the province with a connection. There is no physical centre; delivery is online.

Is it useful for refinery turnaround inspection in Saint John?

Yes for core skills. The Oil & Gas Site has 73 jobs covering UT and PAUT corrosion mapping, TOFD, IRIS, LRUT and PMI, and the Storage Tank environment covers shell thickness and MFL floor screening.

Can it be used for nuclear outage preparation?

It can refresh underlying UT, PAUT and eddy current skills. It is not part of any nuclear qualification, and plant-specific qualified procedures still govern work at Point Lepreau.

Does Practical NDT count toward CGSB (ISO 9712) certification?

No. It is practice only. Certification requires its own training, experience and examinations, including a practical exam on real specimens. Confirm the current certification body before planning.

Does it include radiography?

Yes, as technique and image interpretation practice with no radiation source. It does not count toward CNSC exposure device operator certification.

Which New Brunswick industries is it most useful for?

Refining, crude and LNG terminals, pulp and paper, power generation including hydro and nuclear, fabrication and manufacturing, pipelines and aviation maintenance.

What experience level is it for?

All levels: guided fundamentals for trainees, rare-defect refreshers for working technicians, and scenario building and crew benchmarking for Level IIIs.

Can contractors coming from other provinces use it before mobilisation?

Yes. Access is by browser or app, so a Level III can assign a scenario set to incoming technicians wherever they are.

Does Atlantis offer ASNT training in New Brunswick?

Atlantis training follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A and is delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility. See NDT training in Saint John or all training.

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in New South Wales

New South Wales does not have one dominant inspection industry. It has several: coal export, aluminium smelting, chemicals and power generation in the Hunter; steelmaking and a deep-water port in the Illawarra; airline engineering, naval maintenance, fuel terminals, rail and infrastructure in Sydney; and mining, hydro and processing in the regions. That variety is the reason a practice tool has to cover a wide range of methods. Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and the Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. Technicians work through realistic jobs in a virtual NDT lab, welding workshop, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank. They choose and set up the technique, carry out the inspection, record what they find and receive a score and feedback when the job closes. A trainee in Newcastle, a Level II in Wollongong between steelworks outages and a Level III in Sydney planning a crew's next campaign can all use the same library.

This is the New South Wales hub. It maps the state's NDT work by region, matches the simulator's five environments and twelve methods to that work, sets out the regulators and standards NSW technicians operate under, and explains how to arrange a demo. Atlantis does not yet have Practical NDT city pages in NSW, so the city section links the related Atlantis training, consulting and ERP pages that exist for Sydney, Newcastle, Wollongong and Port Kembla.

New South Wales's NDT workforce and where the work is

Short answer: NSW NDT work clusters in the Hunter (coal export, smelting, power, chemicals, defence aerospace), the Illawarra (steelmaking, port, gas import, coal), greater Sydney (aviation, naval maintenance, fuel terminals, nuclear research, rail and civil infrastructure), and the regions (Snowy hydro, Central West and Far West mining, regional power).

The Hunter. Newcastle is home to one of the world's largest coal export ports, fed by rail lines from the Hunter Valley mines. Around it sit an aluminium smelter at Tomago, an ammonium nitrate and chemicals complex on Kooragang Island, coal-fired power stations at Bayswater, Eraring and Vales Point, newer gas-fired generation at Kurri Kurri, and a heavy engineering and fabrication supply chain that has served mining and power for generations. RAAF Base Williamtown, north of the city, is the home of the F-35A fleet and the centre of a defence aerospace precinct. The Hunter coast has also been declared an offshore wind zone, and the energy transition is bringing new fabrication and inspection work alongside the old. The methods in demand range from MT and UT on mining and port structures to boiler tube inspection at the power stations and ET and PT on aircraft.

The Illawarra. Port Kembla, just south of Wollongong, has an integrated steelworks, a major port, coal export terminals for the Illawarra's metallurgical coal mines, and a gas import terminal. Blast furnaces, steel plant structures, cranes, gas mains, boilers and port loaders all need inspection, much of it concentrated in planned outages. The Illawarra coast has also been declared an offshore wind area. Weld inspection, UT thickness, MT on structures and plant inspection methods are the core skills.

Greater Sydney. Sydney's inspection work is unusually varied. Sydney Airport hosts airline engineering and heavy maintenance, and Western Sydney International Airport is opening. Garden Island in the harbour is Fleet Base East, where naval ships are maintained. The former refineries at Kurnell and Clyde now operate as fuel import terminals and storage, and Port Botany has chemical and fuel terminals. Lucas Heights in the south hosts Australia's research reactor. Underground rail, motorway tunnels and bridges, including the steel of the Harbour Bridge, add structural inspection. Western Sydney has a large manufacturing and fabrication base, and RAAF Base Richmond and HMAS Albatross at Nowra add military aviation.

The regions. The Snowy Mountains Scheme and the Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro project involve penstocks, steel-lined tunnels and turbine components where weld quality is critical. The Central West has large gold and copper mines near Orange and Parkes, Broken Hill in the Far West has a long mining history, and Mount Piper near Lithgow is another coal-fired power station. Regional fabrication shops, mine maintenance contractors and power station outage crews make up much of the inspection workforce outside the cities.

Practical NDT by city in New South Wales

Short answer: there are no city-level Practical NDT pages in NSW yet, but Atlantis has related pages for Sydney, Newcastle, Wollongong and Port Kembla. The table maps the state's main centres to the simulator environments and methods that fit their work.

City or areaMain local sectorsEnvironments & methods to practise
SydneyAirline engineering, naval maintenance, fuel terminals, rail and tunnels, manufacturingAircraft Hangar, Storage Tank, Welding Workshop; ET, PT, UT, PAUT, MFL
Newcastle and the HunterCoal port and rail, aluminium, chemicals, power, defence aerospaceWelding Workshop, Oil & Gas Site, Aircraft Hangar; MT, UT, IRIS, ET, PMI
WollongongSteel, coal mining, engineering servicesWelding Workshop, NDT Lab; MT, UT, PAUT, VT
Port KemblaSteelworks, port, gas import, coal terminalOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank, Welding Workshop; UT, MFL, LRUT, MT
Lake Macquarie and the Upper HunterCoal-fired power stations, coal minesOil & Gas Site, Welding Workshop; IRIS, UT, MT, PT
Snowy MountainsHydro power, penstocks, tunnellingWelding Workshop; PAUT, TOFD, RT, UT
Orange, Parkes and Broken HillGold, copper, lead and zinc mining and processingWelding Workshop, Storage Tank; MT, UT, PT, VT
Nowra and RichmondNaval and air force aviationAircraft Hangar; ET, PT, UT, VT

Sydney is where most of the state's aviation NDT happens, which makes the Aircraft Hangar's 54 jobs especially relevant: eddy current around fastener holes, penetrant inspection of components, UT of structures and detailed visual inspection. The fuel terminals at Kurnell, Clyde and Port Botany need tank and piping work that suits the Storage Tank and Oil & Gas Site environments, and fabrication and infrastructure work suits the Welding Workshop. Atlantis has ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for Sydney employers, Level III consulting in Sydney and an ERP page for Sydney inspection companies.

Newcastle and the Hunter rely on heavy industry. Coal wagons, car dumpers, stackers and ship loaders have fatigue-loaded welds that need MT and UT; the smelter and chemical plants need plant inspection including PMI and corrosion surveys; and the power stations need boiler tube inspection during outages, where IRIS and UT thickness skills matter. Williamtown adds aerospace work. See NDT training in Newcastle for the SNT-TC-1A option.

Wollongong is the population centre of the Illawarra and a base for engineering contractors serving the steelworks, the mines and the port. Weld inspection and structural crack detection are the daily work, and new entrants often learn on steel plant maintenance. Related page: NDT ERP for Wollongong, and the Wollongong digital twin page.

Port Kembla concentrates steelmaking, a busy port and a gas import terminal in a small area. Tanks, gas piping, cranes, conveyors and furnace structures make MFL floor screening, UT thickness, LRUT on pipe runs and MT on structures relevant practice. See NDT ERP for Port Kembla.

Lake Macquarie and the Upper Hunter host large coal-fired power stations whose boilers, headers, steam lines and coal handling plant are inspected during outages, along with the open-cut coal mines of the Upper Hunter. As some stations move towards retirement and others extend their lives, condition assessment remains busy.

The Snowy Mountains are defined by hydro. Snowy 2.0 involves long steel-lined tunnels, penstocks and heavy fabricated components, and the existing scheme has decades-old penstocks and turbines that need inspection. Volumetric weld inspection (PAUT, TOFD, RT) in the Welding Workshop is the closest match.

Orange, Parkes and Broken Hill are mining centres where crushers, mills, flotation tanks and mobile plant need steady MT, UT and PT work. Regional technicians often have limited access to training rooms, so browser-based practice fills a real gap.

Nowra and Richmond host military aviation, and their maintenance supply chains include aircraft NDT technicians who work to defence aviation requirements. The Aircraft Hangar environment supports practice in the methods they use, though military qualification rules still apply.

Environments and methods that match New South Wales work

Short answer: the Aircraft Hangar fits Sydney's airline and defence aviation; the Welding Workshop fits Hunter and Illawarra heavy industry, hydro and fabrication; the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank fit fuel terminals, chemicals, smelting and power stations; and the NDT Lab supports trainees and component inspection.

The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator has five workplace environments, twelve methods and 33 guided lessons. The methods are grouped into surface methods (PT, MT, VT), volumetric methods (UT contact, PAUT, TOFD, RT), electromagnetic methods (ET, MFL), and three specialist techniques: LRUT guided-wave screening, IRIS internal rotary UT for heat-exchanger and boiler tubes, and PMI for alloy verification.

  • Aircraft Hangar (54 jobs). Airframe and component inspection. Sydney Airport's airline engineering, plus military aviation at Williamtown, Richmond and Nowra, make this environment central to the state's practice needs.
  • Welding Workshop (52 jobs). Weld coupons and fabrication joints, relevant to steel plant and port maintenance, coal handling structures, Snowy hydro fabrication, offshore wind supply chain fabrication, bridges and structural steel, and naval ship repair.
  • Oil & Gas Site (73 jobs). Weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant. Relevant to the chemicals complex at Kooragang, Botany industrial sites, the gas import terminal and fuel terminals, and power station boilers and heat exchangers.
  • Storage Tank. UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank, matching the fuel terminals at Kurnell, Clyde, Port Botany and Newcastle, and tank farms at chemical and industrial sites.
  • NDT Lab (52 jobs). Bench specimens and reference blocks for trainees, TAFE students, calibration practice and component inspection, including rail axles, shafts and castings.

For NSW technicians, eddy current deserves particular attention. It is central to aviation maintenance and also used in heat exchanger and surface crack work, and it is a method where interpretation of signals on a display takes many repetitions to master. MT is the daily method of coal, steel and port maintenance, and practising it on realistic fatigue cracks at weld toes builds the eye that finds small indications on big structures. PAUT and TOFD matter for thick welds in hydro penstocks, pressure equipment and new energy fabrication. Radiography can be practised for technique and image interpretation without any radiation, which is useful in a state where real exposures in urban areas need careful control.

Regulators and requirements New South Wales technicians meet

Short answer: AINDT certification, based on ISO 9712, is the local norm for NSW NDT personnel, with ASNT SNT-TC-1A used by some employers and aerospace schemes for aviation. Radiography is licensed by the NSW Environment Protection Authority under the Radiation Control Act 1990. SafeWork NSW covers workplace and plant safety, and the NSW Resources Regulator covers mines and petroleum sites. Practical NDT is practice for any scheme.

Personnel certification. NSW employers commonly require AINDT certification for NDT technicians. Aviation NDT personnel are qualified under aerospace employer schemes within the maintenance organisation's approval from the Civil Aviation Safety Authority, and military aviation follows defence requirements. Some employers on US-code work, or supplying US-owned facilities and OEMs, qualify staff under ASNT SNT-TC-1A through an employer written practice. Atlantis trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A only and does not offer AINDT, ISO 9712 or aerospace scheme training or examinations; the simulator is useful whichever scheme a technician is working towards.

Radiation safety. In NSW, the Radiation Control Act 1990 and its regulation are administered by the Environment Protection Authority. People who use radiation sources or X-ray equipment for industrial radiography need a radiation user licence, and the sources and apparatus must be licensed or registered. ARPANSA, the federal regulator, publishes national codes and also regulates Commonwealth facilities such as the research reactor at Lucas Heights. Confirm current licence conditions with the EPA before any real exposure; simulator practice involves no radiation.

Plant, pressure equipment and mines. SafeWork NSW administers the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW), including registration of certain plant designs and items such as boilers and pressure vessels. The NSW Resources Regulator oversees safety at mines and petroleum sites under the state's mines and petroleum sites legislation. Pressure equipment is commonly designed and inspected to AS 1210, AS 4041, AS 4037 and AS/NZS 3788; pipelines follow AS 2885; and structural steel welding follows AS/NZS 1554, with AS/NZS 5131 for structural steelwork fabrication and erection.

Codes and standards. NSW technicians work to Australian Standards and AS ISO adoptions for UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, to aerospace manufacturer manuals and standard practices for aviation work, and on some projects to ASME, API and AWS codes. The simulator does not certify compliance with any of these; it trains the habits they depend on, such as calibration, coverage, recording and sizing.

For procedures and written practices on NSW sites working to US codes, see NDT Level III consulting in Sydney or the national NDT consulting page for Australia.

Outages, shift work and city distances: why NSW crews practise virtually

Short answer: NSW inspection work is shaped by planned outages at steelworks and power stations, aircraft maintenance shift patterns, and long distances between regional sites. A browser-based simulator lets technicians practise in the gaps, without reference specimens, lab bookings or radiation.

The rhythms of inspection work differ across NSW. Power station and steelworks crews work around planned outages, when a great deal of inspection is packed into a short window and skills that have been idle for months are suddenly in demand. Aviation technicians work rotating shifts in hangars where aircraft availability drives everything, and practice time on real components is hard to find. Mine maintenance contractors in the Hunter, the Central West and Broken Hill travel long distances, and Snowy hydro workers may be on remote sites for long stretches. In all of these patterns, the methods a technician is not using right now are the ones that drift.

Physical refresher practice is difficult to organise. Reference specimens with realistic defects are costly, training rooms are busy with new entrants, and nobody wants to send a crew to a city laboratory just to scan a few coupons. A simulator job on a laptop at home, in a hangar crew room or in a site office is far easier to arrange, and a supervisor can assign exactly the job types a coming outage will demand.

There is a workforce reason too. NSW industry is changing: some coal-fired stations are heading towards retirement, new energy projects are arriving, defence spending on aircraft and ships is rising, and infrastructure construction continues. Inspection companies need to move people between sectors, retrain them in new methods and bring new entrants up to speed quickly. A shared scenario library helps with all three.

Finally, practice in a simulator is safe. Mistakes cost a lower score rather than a missed crack, a damaged component or a radiation incident.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in New South Wales

Short answer: trainees use the 33 guided lessons to learn fundamentals before supervised work, working technicians keep rare defects and less-used methods fresh, and Level IIIs build and assign scenario sets to benchmark crews and find coverage gaps.

Trainees. NSW's NDT trainees come from TAFE engineering courses, aircraft maintenance engineering pathways, boilermaker and fitter apprenticeships, defence careers and other industries. Formal training and supervised practice are essential, but logging the industrial experience required for certification takes time, and on a busy outage or in a busy hangar a trainee often watches more than they inspect. The guided lessons start in the NDT Lab with calibration and simple flaws, then move to weld coupons, process plant, tank and aircraft jobs, so a trainee builds hands-on familiarity before touching real assets.

Working technicians. A Level II at the steelworks who mostly does MT may need to run a UT weld inspection during the next outage; an aviation technician who mostly does eddy current may need a penetrant job on an unfamiliar component. Rare-defect refreshers keep those skills alive: lack of fusion, transverse cracking, laminations, pitting on a single boiler tube, corrosion under a fastener, a misidentified alloy.

Level IIIs and team leads. A Level III can build scenario sets that reflect the site's real job mix, assign them across employees and contractors, and compare results objectively. That supports decisions about who goes on which job and highlights where more training is needed. It adds evidence alongside the employer's own practical assessments rather than replacing them.

Practice vs certification

Short answer: the Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is a practice and readiness tool. It does not grant AINDT, ISO 9712, aerospace or ASNT certification and does not replace any practical examination on real specimens.

Every NDT certification scheme used in NSW requires training, documented industrial experience and a practical examination on real specimens. Under AINDT certification the examination follows the scheme's own rules; under ASNT SNT-TC-1A it is administered by the employer according to its written practice under a Level III; under aerospace schemes it follows the employer's procedures and the responsible Level 3. Simulator time is not counted as industrial experience by these schemes unless an employer's own procedures say so, and Atlantis makes no such claim.

What the simulator does is shorten the distance between theory and confident practice. A candidate who has already performed many set-ups, scans and interpretations goes into the practical exam with fewer surprises, and a supervisor who has watched a technician's results over several weeks can make better decisions about readiness. For formal training, see Atlantis NDT training, which is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only and delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility.

Bring Practical NDT to your New South Wales team

Short answer: request a demo, tell Atlantis which NSW sectors and methods matter to your team, and agree a pilot group. Pricing is quote on request.

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience. Its scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. The product is affordable, accessible and fully customizable: inspection companies in the Hunter and Illawarra, aviation maintenance organisations in Sydney, training providers, TAFE programmes and asset owners' integrity teams can use it as it is or ask for scenario sets aligned to their own procedures and job mix. There is no NSW centre to visit; access is online.

Starting is straightforward. A short call covers your work, whether steelworks outages, coal handling structures, power station boilers, fuel terminal tanks, aviation maintenance or hydro fabrication. Atlantis then demonstrates the matching environments live, agrees a pilot group and sets up accounts so technicians can practise in a browser or app. Supervisors see results and progress. Demos are scheduled to suit Sydney time.

  • Request a Practical NDT demo for your NSW team
  • Ask for an NSW quote for an outage crew, a trainee intake or a whole company
  • Discuss a custom scenario set for steel, coal, power, aviation or hydro work

The Practical NDT overview lists every environment and method.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an NDT simulator I can use in New South Wales?

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app, so it can be used in Sydney, Newcastle, Wollongong, regional NSW or at home. There is no physical centre; demos are booked through the contact form.

Does it count towards AINDT certification?

No. AINDT certification requires training, documented industrial experience and examinations under the scheme's rules, including a practical on real specimens. The simulator helps a candidate prepare but is not part of the scheme, and Atlantis does not offer AINDT or ISO 9712 training or exams.

Can it help with NDT practical exam preparation?

Yes, as preparation. Repeated set-up, scanning, interpretation and sizing build the habits a practical exam tests. The exam itself is taken on real specimens.

Is it useful for aviation NDT in Sydney?

Yes. The Aircraft Hangar environment has 54 jobs covering airframe and component inspection with ET, PT, UT and VT. It does not replace aerospace qualification or the maintenance organisation's own practical examinations.

Does it suit steelworks and coal port maintenance?

Yes for the core methods. MT, UT, PT and VT practice on fabrication joints and components maps well to crack detection on steel plant, cranes, conveyors, ship loaders and rail wagons.

Does it cover power station boiler inspection?

It supports practice in the relevant methods: IRIS and UT thickness on tubes, and surface methods on headers and welds. Site procedures and acceptance criteria still apply.

Is there a phased array and ultrasonic testing simulator?

Yes. UT contact, PAUT and TOFD are included across the NDT Lab, Welding Workshop and Oil & Gas Site, with set-up, scanning and sizing on realistic welds and corrosion.

Does it include radiography?

Yes, RT is one of the twelve methods, focused on technique and image interpretation. No radiation is involved, so simulator use needs no licence under the Radiation Control Act 1990; real exposures still do.

Can a Level III benchmark new starters with it?

Yes. The same scenario set can be assigned to every new starter or contractor and the results compared objectively.

Does Atlantis offer ASNT training in NSW?

Yes, ASNT SNT-TC-1A training only, delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility for employers whose clients or projects require SNT-TC-1A personnel. See NDT training in Sydney and NDT training in Newcastle.

What experience level is it for?

All levels: trainees on guided lessons, working technicians on refreshers and rare defects, and Level IIIs building and assigning scenario sets.

How do we start?

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in New Zealand

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and the Atlantis Practical NDT simulator suits New Zealand better than most places. It is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. A technician opens a job in a virtual NDT lab, welding workshop, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank, sets up the technique, carries out the inspection, records the result and gets a score the moment the job closes. New Zealand's inspection work is spread thinly across a long country: Taranaki gas production and petrochemicals, the fuel import terminal at Marsden Point, geothermal power stations around Taupō and Kawerau, hydro schemes on the Waikato and in the South Island, the steel mill at Glenbrook, the aluminium smelter at Tiwai Point, dairy and food plants in almost every region, and aircraft maintenance in Auckland and Christchurch. Technicians in small crews often go months without using a particular method, and there are few places to practise on real defects between jobs.

This page is the New Zealand hub for Practical NDT. It maps where the country's NDT work is, which simulator environments match each region, how practice relates to the ISO 9712-based certification most New Zealand employers ask for, which regulators set the rules, and how to arrange a demo for your team. The Auckland Practical NDT page has more city detail.

Where New Zealand's NDT work is, region by region

Short answer: New Zealand NDT demand sits in five clusters: Taranaki energy and petrochemicals, the central North Island geothermal and forestry belt, the Auckland and Northland industrial and aviation base, the Waikato power and steel corridor, and the South Island hydro, smelting, aviation and food-processing sites. Crews are small and travel widely, so one technician may cover several of these in a year.

Taranaki. Almost all of New Zealand's oil and gas comes from the Taranaki basin, onshore and offshore. Production stations, gas treatment plants, pipelines that carry gas north and south, and the methanol plants near Waitara and Motunui keep inspection companies in New Plymouth busy with corrosion monitoring, weld inspection on modifications and shutdown work on pressure equipment. Offshore platforms and floating production add structural and piping inspection, and the gradual decline of older fields brings plugging, abandonment and decommissioning work where the condition of steel has to be checked before it is cut. For Taranaki crews the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments are the obvious practice ground.

Northland and Auckland. Marsden Point near Whangārei was New Zealand's only oil refinery until refining stopped in 2022; the site now operates as a fuel import terminal, and its large tank farm and the pipeline to Auckland still need regular inspection. Auckland itself has the country's biggest concentration of fabrication shops, structural steel, marine engineering, the naval base at Devonport, the Ports of Auckland and the main international airport with its airline engineering base. The Glenbrook steel mill south of the city, which is moving to electric arc steelmaking, adds heavy industrial work.

Waikato and the Bay of Plenty. Huntly Power Station is the country's largest thermal station, and the Waikato River carries a chain of hydro dams with penstocks, gates and turbines that need periodic inspection. Further east, the central North Island geothermal fields around Wairakei, Ohaaki and Kawerau supply a large share of national electricity. Geothermal steam is aggressive: scaling, erosion and corrosion in wells, separators and steam pipework make wall-thickness surveys and weld inspection routine. Kawerau's pulp and paper mills and the Port of Tauranga, New Zealand's busiest port, round out the region.

Wellington and the lower North Island. Wellington has engineering consultancies, port and ferry infrastructure, and government agencies including the regulators described below. Inspection work around the capital leans to structural steel, bridges, seismic strengthening projects and marine assets.

The South Island. Christchurch is home to major aircraft and engine maintenance and a large manufacturing and food-processing base, as well as the port at Lyttelton. Further south, the Clutha and Waitaki hydro schemes and the Manapouri station have large penstocks and hydraulic structures, and the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter near Bluff is one of the country's largest single industrial sites. Dairy processing plants with stainless steel vessels and pipework run the length of Canterbury, Otago and Southland.

Practical NDT across New Zealand cities and regions

Short answer: Auckland already has its own Practical NDT page. The table below covers Auckland and the other main New Zealand clusters, with the simulator environments and methods that best match the work in each one. Every environment is available to every user; the table simply shows where to start.

Fabricators building structural steel, pressure equipment and marine structures need weld inspection, so PAUT, TOFD and MT jobs in the Welding Workshop are the core practice. New Plymouth and Taranaki technicians work production stations, gas plants and pipelines where corrosion under insulation, internal corrosion and weld integrity matter most. The Oil & Gas Site environment covers corrosion mapping, weld inspection, LRUT screening of pipe runs, IRIS on exchanger tubes and PMI on alloy lines, which matches a Taranaki shutdown closely. See also the New Plymouth NDT ERP page.

Whangārei and Marsden Point are now mostly about storage and distribution. The Storage Tank environment, with UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank, is the closest match to terminal work, and it lets technicians practise the systematic coverage a tank survey needs.

The geothermal belt around Taupō, Rotorua and Kawerau has steam pipework, separators and wellhead equipment under constant attack from scaling and erosion. Thickness surveys and corrosion mapping with UT and PAUT, and weld inspection on repairs with PAUT and TOFD, are the practice priorities. Pulp and paper mills add digesters, recovery boilers and tanks.

Hamilton and Huntly crews support thermal and hydro power, so boiler tube inspection, weld inspection on headers and penstocks, and IRIS on condenser and exchanger tubes are relevant. Dairy plants across the Waikato add stainless steel welds where PT and VT matter.

Christchurch is New Zealand's other aviation centre, with heavy aircraft and engine maintenance. The Aircraft Hangar environment, with 54 jobs on airframe and component inspection using ET, PT, UT and VT, is the natural match. Manufacturing and food processing across Canterbury add NDT Lab and Welding Workshop practice.

Southland and Otago combine the Tiwai Point smelter, hydro stations with large penstocks and many dairy plants. Weld inspection on structural steel and penstocks, thickness surveys on tanks and vessels, and PMI on alloy components are useful practice areas.

Environments and methods that match New Zealand work

Short answer: the Atlantis Practical NDT simulator has five environments and twelve methods. In New Zealand, the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments serve Taranaki and Marsden Point, the Welding Workshop serves fabrication, power and geothermal, the Aircraft Hangar serves Auckland and Christchurch aviation, and the NDT Lab supports trainees everywhere.

The five workplace environments are the NDT Lab (bench specimens and reference blocks, 52 jobs), the Welding Workshop (weld coupons and fabrication joints, 52 jobs), the Aircraft Hangar (airframe and component inspection, 54 jobs), the Oil & Gas Site (weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant, 73 jobs) and the Storage Tank (UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank). Thirty-three guided lessons take a new user through the fundamentals before they move on to jobs.

The twelve methods fall into four groups. Surface methods are penetrant testing (PT), magnetic particle testing (MT) and visual testing (VT). Volumetric methods are contact ultrasonic testing (UT), phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT), time-of-flight diffraction (TOFD) and radiographic testing (RT). Electromagnetic methods are eddy current testing (ET) and magnetic flux leakage (MFL). The advanced group covers long-range ultrasonic testing (LRUT) guided-wave screening, internal rotary inspection system (IRIS) ultrasonic testing of heat-exchanger and boiler tubes, and positive material identification (PMI) for alloy verification.
