Geothermal is the one area where New Zealand differs most from other markets. Steam lines and separators lose wall through erosion and corrosion that follows flow patterns, so systematic grid thickness readings and corrosion mapping matter more than they would on a clean hydrocarbon line. The simulator does not model a specific geothermal plant, but the corrosion-mapping and thickness-survey jobs in the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments train exactly the habits a geothermal survey needs: consistent coverage, careful couplant and probe handling, correct recording and recognising a reading that does not make sense.

Radiography deserves a separate note. RT practice in the simulator focuses on technique selection and image interpretation. No radiation is involved, so practising in the simulator needs no licence under the Radiation Safety Act 2016. Real exposures do, as described below.

Certification, regulators and standards New Zealand technicians work under

Short answer: most New Zealand employers ask for NDT personnel certified under an ISO 9712-based scheme, such as AINDT certification or the New Zealand CBIP scheme, while some work for US-owned plants and US-code projects uses ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Radiation use is regulated under the Radiation Safety Act 2016, and pressure equipment under WorkSafe's regulations.

Personnel certification. New Zealand NDT certification is normally to ISO 9712 (published locally as AS ISO 9712). Technicians commonly hold certificates issued by the Australian Institute for Non-Destructive Testing (AINDT) or by New Zealand's Certification Board for Inspection Personnel (CBIP), and the New Zealand Non-Destructive Testing Association (NZNDTA) supports the local profession. Check the scheme your employer or client names in its contract, because recognition between schemes is not automatic. Atlantis does not train for or issue AINDT, CBIP or any ISO 9712 certificates. Atlantis training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only, which suits employers whose clients specify SNT-TC-1A, such as US-owned operators or projects built to US codes. Practical NDT, by contrast, is practice in the methods themselves, so it is useful whichever scheme a technician holds.

Radiation safety. The Radiation Safety Act 2016 and the Radiation Safety Regulations 2016 govern the use of radioactive sources and X-ray equipment, including industrial radiography. The Office of Radiation Safety, part of the Ministry of Health, administers the system of source licences and user authorisations. Companies doing site radiography in Taranaki or Auckland need the right licences and authorised operators, plus the employer's own radiation safety procedures. Confirm current requirements with the Office of Radiation Safety before any exposure work.

Workplace health and safety and pressure equipment. WorkSafe New Zealand regulates workplace safety under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015. Pressure equipment such as boilers, pressure vessels and piping falls under the Health and Safety at Work (Pressure Equipment, Cranes, and Passenger Ropeways) Regulations, which require design verification and periodic inspection by accredited inspection bodies. In-service inspection commonly references AS/NZS 3788. Major hazard facilities, including some fuel and chemical sites, have extra safety-case duties under their own regulations.

Codes and standards in daily use. New Zealand fabrication and inspection draws on joint Australian and New Zealand standards: AS 1210 for pressure vessels, AS/NZS 1554 for structural steel welding, AS 2885 for gas and liquid petroleum pipelines, AS/NZS 3788 for in-service inspection, plus ISO standards for NDT techniques. ASME, API and AWS codes appear where owners or licensors specify them, for example on imported process packages or US-designed plant. The simulator teaches method skills rather than any one code's acceptance criteria, so Level IIIs set the acceptance rules their procedures require.

For help writing or reviewing procedures, see NDT consulting in New Zealand. To track ISO 9712 and ASNT certificates side by side, see the New Zealand NDT ERP page.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in New Zealand

Short answer: trainees use guided lessons and NDT Lab jobs to learn the fundamentals, working technicians use the simulator to refresh methods and rare defects between assignments, and Level IIIs and team leads build and assign scenario sets to benchmark crews and find coverage gaps across a small, widely spread workforce.

New trainees. New Zealand is a small market, and many trainees join a company with only a handful of senior technicians who are often away on site. The 33 guided lessons give a trainee a structured path through set-up, calibration, scanning and interpretation for each method, and the NDT Lab gives them bench jobs to repeat without tying up a senior technician or a reference block. That means time on real specimens can be spent on the points that actually need a supervisor.

Working technicians. A Taranaki technician may do mostly UT thickness work for months and then be asked for PAUT weld inspection on a shutdown. An Auckland fabrication inspector might go a year without an IRIS job. The simulator lets technicians rehearse a less-used method or a rare defect type before the job, rather than relearning it on the client's asset. Because it runs in a browser or app, practice can happen at home, at a motel during a remote job, or at a site office between tasks.

Level IIIs and team leads. Level IIIs can build and assign scenario sets that mirror the company's own work, for example a set of geothermal pipework thickness surveys or aerospace eddy current jobs, then compare results across the team. Objective scores make it easier to decide who is ready for which job, to spot a method where the whole crew is weak, and to show a client that its contractor checks competence between certifications.

Practice vs certification

Short answer: the Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is a practice and readiness tool. It is not a certification, it does not issue certificates, it is not part of any AINDT, CBIP or ISO 9712 examination, and it does not replace the practical examination on real specimens that SNT-TC-1A or any other scheme requires.

Certification under ISO 9712 schemes requires training, documented industrial experience and examinations set by the certification body. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the employer's written practice governs training, experience and the general, specific and practical exams, administered under Level III oversight. Neither system accepts simulator scores in place of a practical exam on real specimens, and neither should. A real probe on a real weld, with real noise, coupling and geometry, is what a practical exam checks.

What the simulator does is make that exam, and real work, less of a first attempt. A candidate who has set up, scanned, interpreted and sized dozens of virtual flaws arrives with habits that a few hours on a borrowed specimen cannot build. A technician who has rehearsed a rare defect type is more likely to recognise it on site. Employers should treat simulator results as one piece of evidence about readiness, alongside supervised work and formal examinations, never as a substitute for them. Practical NDT is also not an operator approval, a client prequalification or a WorkSafe authorisation of any kind.

Remote sites, small crews and shutdown seasons: why New Zealand teams practise virtually

Short answer: New Zealand's NDT workforce is small and spread across a long country, specimen sets are expensive and scarce, and shutdowns arrive in bursts. A browser-based simulator lets technicians practise anywhere, keeps skills current between shutdowns, and lets employers check readiness before a crew travels.

Geography is the first reason. A company based in Auckland or New Plymouth may send technicians to Kawerau, Huntly, Bluff and Marsden Point in the same quarter. Bringing everyone back to a single workshop to practise on reference specimens costs travel and lost billable time. A simulator that runs on a laptop or tablet removes that problem.

Specimens are the second reason. Flawed specimens with known, realistic defects are expensive to make or buy, and a small company may own only a few. They also wear out and get familiar: once a trainee has seen the same block several times, it stops testing anything. A simulator offers many jobs across five environments, so practice stays varied.

Timing is the third reason. Planned outages at power stations, geothermal plants and production facilities cluster in particular seasons, and inspection companies often bring in contract technicians to cover the peak. A short refresher in the right environment before mobilising helps a returning or new technician arrive ready. Afterwards, Level IIIs can look at where crews struggled and plan practice before the next outage.

Safety is the fourth. Practising radiography technique and interpretation without a source, or practising tank and plant surveys without working at height or entering confined spaces, removes risk from the learning stage. Real work still needs all the usual controls, but technicians arrive with the method already rehearsed.

ASNT training, consulting and ERP for New Zealand employers

Short answer: beyond the simulator, Atlantis offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A training, Level III consulting and an NDT ERP to New Zealand companies, all delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility. There is no Atlantis office or training centre in New Zealand.

Some New Zealand employers need SNT-TC-1A personnel because a client, licensor or overseas owner specifies it, or because technicians want to work on projects in North America or the Middle East. For them, Atlantis delivers ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for Level I, II and III candidates, led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, with written-practice support through written practice development. Level III procedure, technique and audit support is available through New Zealand consulting, and the Atlantis NDT ERP records ISO 9712 and ASNT certificates together, with expiry reminders, equipment calibration and reports. These services are quoted on request, and none of them replaces the certification scheme your client requires.

Bring Practical NDT to your New Zealand team

Short answer: request a demo through the contact form. Atlantis will show the environments that match your work, agree a pilot group and set up accounts. There is nothing to install beyond a browser or app, and pricing is quote on request. Affordable, accessible and fully customizable.

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and the scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Inspection companies, asset owners, training providers and polytechnics in New Zealand can use it as it stands or ask for scenario sets aligned to their own procedures and job mix.

A typical start is simple. We hold a short call to understand your work, whether that is Taranaki production, geothermal plant, terminal tank surveys, fabrication or aviation maintenance. We demonstrate the matching environments live, agree a pilot group and set up accounts so your technicians can start practising in a browser or app. Team leads get visibility of results to track progress and find gaps. Because sessions are online, time zones are handled by scheduling the demo at a time that suits New Zealand.

  • Request a Practical NDT demo for your New Zealand team
  • Ask for a New Zealand quote for a crew, a training cohort or a whole company

You can also read the Practical NDT overview for the full list of environments and methods.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an NDT simulator I can use in New Zealand?

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app, so it works anywhere in New Zealand with an internet connection, from Auckland to Invercargill. There is no centre to visit; access is online, and demos are arranged through the contact form.

Does Practical NDT count towards AINDT or ISO 9712 certification?

No. ISO 9712 certification, whether through AINDT, CBIP or another body, requires training, documented experience and examinations set by the certification body. Simulator practice can help you prepare, but it is not part of any scheme, and Atlantis does not offer ISO 9712 training or exams.

Can it help with NDT practical exam preparation?

Yes, as preparation. Repeating set-up, scanning, interpretation and sizing builds the habits a practical exam checks. The exam itself must still be taken on real specimens under your scheme's rules.

Is it useful for geothermal plant inspection?

Yes for the methods involved. Thickness surveys, corrosion mapping and weld inspection in the Oil & Gas Site and Welding Workshop environments build the skills geothermal pipework and separator surveys need. The simulator does not model a specific geothermal station.

Does it cover Taranaki oil and gas work?

Yes. The Oil & Gas Site environment has 73 jobs covering weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant, including LRUT, IRIS and PMI, and the Storage Tank environment covers shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening.

Does it include radiography, and do I need a radiation licence to practise?

RT is included, focused on technique and image interpretation. No radiation is used, so simulator practice needs no licence. Real industrial radiography needs licences and authorisations under the Radiation Safety Act 2016, administered by the Office of Radiation Safety.

Can it be used for aviation NDT in Auckland and Christchurch?

Yes. The Aircraft Hangar environment has 54 jobs on airframe and component inspection with ET, PT, UT and VT. It does not replace the aerospace qualification your maintenance organisation requires.

What experience level is it for?

All levels: new trainees on guided lessons, working technicians refreshing rarely used methods and rare defects, and Level IIIs building and assigning scenario sets to benchmark crews.

Can a New Zealand inspection company use it to assess new hires?

Yes. Team leads can give every candidate or new starter the same scenario set and compare scores objectively. Use the results alongside supervised work and certification, not in place of them.

Does Atlantis offer ASNT training in New Zealand?

Yes, ASNT SNT-TC-1A training only, delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility, for employers whose clients or projects need SNT-TC-1A personnel. See Atlantis training.

Is Practical NDT a WorkSafe or client approval?

No. It is a practice tool. It is not a WorkSafe authorisation, an operator approval or a client prequalification, and it does not change any duty your company has under New Zealand law.

How much does it cost and how do we start?

Pricing is quote on request and depends on the number of users and any custom scenarios. Request a demo and we will show the environments that fit your work.

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in Newfoundland and Labrador

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and few places in Canada need remote practice as much as Newfoundland and Labrador. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. Technicians enter a virtual oil and gas site, welding workshop, storage tank, NDT lab or aircraft hangar, choose a job, set up the technique and get a score the moment the job is done. The province's NDT work is split between the sea and the interior. Offshore, production platforms and floating production vessels on the Grand Banks produce oil hundreds of kilometres from St. John's. On land, Placentia Bay hosts a large fabrication site that built offshore gravity-base structures, a refinery that now produces renewable fuels, a crude transshipment terminal and a nickel processing plant. Labrador has some of Canada's largest iron ore mines, a major nickel mine, and two of the country's largest hydroelectric developments. Much of this work is done on rotation, offshore or in remote camps, often for weeks at a time. Practical NDT lets technicians keep their skills sharp wherever they are, at any level from first-week trainee to working Level III, without waiting for lab time or specimens.

This is the Newfoundland and Labrador hub for Practical NDT. It covers where the province's NDT work is, how the simulator's environments and methods fit it, the regulators that apply, and an honest view of practice versus certification. To see it mapped to your own work, request a Practical NDT demo for Newfoundland and Labrador.

Newfoundland and Labrador's NDT workforce and where the work is

The province's inspection work falls into four zones: the offshore, the Avalon Peninsula around St. John's, Placentia Bay and the industrial east, and Labrador. The equipment and conditions in each are very different.

The offshore. The Jeanne d'Arc Basin on the Grand Banks hosts the province's producing oil fields. Hibernia and Hebron are fixed platforms built on concrete gravity-base structures designed for icebergs and harsh North Atlantic weather, while Terra Nova and White Rose produce through floating production, storage and offloading vessels. Further offshore, the Bay du Nord development in the Flemish Pass has been under evaluation. Offshore inspection covers topsides process piping and vessels, structural steel, risers and mooring components, hull structures on the floating units, cranes and lifting gear, and tanks. Corrosion under insulation, erosion, fatigue cracking in structures and weld defects in repairs are constant concerns. Technicians fly out on rotation, and the time available for inspection during a hitch is precious.

St. John's and the Avalon. St. John's is the centre of the province's offshore industry: operators' offices, engineering firms, supply and service companies, inspection firms and the supply bases that support offshore operations. The Port of St. John's and nearby Bay Bulls handle supply vessels and marine services. Ship repair and marine fabrication, power generation, and the provincial government and university add to the city's industrial and technical base.

Placentia Bay and the industrial east. Bull Arm, at the head of Trinity Bay near the Placentia Bay isthmus, is a large fabrication site where the Hibernia and Hebron gravity-base structures and topsides were built and integrated. Come By Chance hosts a refinery that has been converted to produce renewable fuels. Whiffen Head has a crude transshipment terminal serving the offshore fields with large storage tanks. Long Harbour hosts a hydrometallurgical nickel processing plant that treats concentrate from Labrador. Marystown and the Burin Peninsula have fabrication and marine yards. Together these mean refinery-type process inspection, tank work, heavy fabrication weld inspection and corrosive-service plant inspection.

Western and central Newfoundland. Corner Brook has a newsprint mill with boilers and pressure equipment, and the west coast and central regions have hydro stations, ports and smaller industry. Mining has a long history in central Newfoundland, with gold projects active in recent years.

Labrador. Labrador West, around Labrador City and Wabush, is one of North America's main iron ore regions, with open-pit mines, concentrators, pellet plants and a rail line to the coast. Voisey's Bay on the north coast is a major nickel, copper and cobalt mine that has moved to underground production. Churchill Falls is one of the largest hydroelectric stations in the world, and Muskrat Falls on the lower Churchill River sends power to the island through a subsea and overland transmission link. 5 Wing Goose Bay supports military aviation. Mining inspection covers crushers, mills, conveyors, tanks and heavy mobile equipment; hydro covers penstocks, turbines, gates and transmission structures.

St. John's has its own Practical NDT page. The table links it and maps the province's other main work centres to the environments and methods that fit.

St. John's. Most of the province's NDT technicians are based in or around St. John's, working offshore on rotation or onshore for service and inspection firms. The Oil & Gas Site is their core environment: UT and PAUT corrosion mapping on process piping, TOFD on pressure welds, LRUT screening and MT on structural welds. Marine fabrication and repair add weld inspection in the Welding Workshop. See Practical NDT St. John's.

The Grand Banks offshore. Offshore technicians face corrosion under insulation, erosion in production piping, fatigue in structures and repairs that must be inspected quickly. Rehearsing PAUT corrosion mapping and structural weld inspection before a hitch means less time relearning offshore.

Placentia Bay. The refinery at Come By Chance brings exchanger tube inspection (IRIS), PMI and thickness surveys during turnarounds. Whiffen Head's large crude tanks call for shell thickness and MFL floor screening. Long Harbour's corrosive process environment needs regular thickness and weld inspection, and Bull Arm and Marystown fabrication bring RT and TOFD on heavy welds.

Labrador City and Wabush. Iron ore operations inspect crushers, grinding mills, conveyors, pellet plant equipment and mobile fleets. MT and UT are daily tools in harsh winter conditions, and remote rotations make on-demand practice valuable.

Churchill Falls, Muskrat Falls and Goose Bay. Hydro outages need thick-section UT, PAUT and MT on penstocks, turbines and gates, and military aviation at Goose Bay links to the Aircraft Hangar.

Environments and methods that match Newfoundland and Labrador work

Practical NDT has five environments, twelve methods and 33 guided lessons. In this province the weight falls on the Oil & Gas Site and Welding Workshop, with tank and mining work close behind.

Oil & Gas Site (73 jobs). Weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant: contact UT and PAUT corrosion mapping, TOFD weld sizing, IRIS on exchanger and boiler tubes, LRUT guided-wave screening of long pipe runs, and PMI alloy verification. It matches offshore topsides, the Come By Chance refinery and the Long Harbour plant.

Welding Workshop (52 jobs). Weld coupons and fabrication joints for RT interpretation, UT and PAUT sizing, TOFD, MT and VT. It fits Bull Arm and Marystown fabrication, offshore structural repairs, ship repair in St. John's and hydro station welds.

Storage Tank. UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank, matching Whiffen Head, refinery tankage and fuel terminals around the island and in Labrador.

NDT Lab (52 jobs). Bench specimens and reference blocks for calibration and fundamentals, and for rehearsing before a practical examination under any scheme. Mining and mill technicians use these skills daily.

Aircraft Hangar (54 jobs). Airframe and component inspection jobs, relevant to helicopter operations supporting the offshore, military aviation at Goose Bay and civil maintenance at St. John's and Gander.

Across the twelve methods, the province leans on UT, PAUT, TOFD and LRUT for offshore and plant integrity, MFL for tank floors, IRIS and PMI for refining and processing, MT, PT and VT for structures and mining, and ET for aviation.

Regulators and requirements Newfoundland and Labrador technicians meet

Short answer: NDT personnel certification is national, offshore activity has its own joint federal-provincial regulator, radiography sources are federally licensed, and onshore boilers and pressure vessels are regulated by the province. Practical NDT is practice for any scheme and replaces none of them.

National NDT certification. Canada's national NDT personnel certification scheme is based on CAN/CGSB-48.9712, the Canadian adoption of ISO 9712, and employers in the province commonly expect technicians to hold certification under it. The Canadian General Standards Board, which published the standard, closed on 1 April 2026; Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body has said it continues to operate and the standard remains valid, but confirm the current certification body and arrangements before planning a route. Offshore operators and international contractors may also accept or require other schemes, and some employers working to US codes use ASNT SNT-TC-1A. This is market context only. Atlantis training aligns with ASNT SNT-TC-1A and Atlantis does not train toward, certify or administer CGSB/ISO 9712 or other schemes.

Offshore. Offshore oil activity is regulated by the Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator, renamed in 2025 with a mandate that now includes offshore renewable energy. Offshore installations also require certificates of fitness issued by recognised certifying authorities, which shapes inspection programmes on platforms and floating units.

Radiation safety. The Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) licenses radioactive sources used in industrial radiography, and only a CNSC-certified exposure device operator, or a trainee under direct supervision, may operate a gamma exposure device. Practical NDT's RT jobs involve no radiation and do not count toward that certification.

Pressure equipment. Onshore, boilers, pressure vessels and compressed gas systems are regulated under the Public Safety Act and the Boiler, Pressure Vessel and Compressed Gas Regulations, administered by the province's Engineering and Inspection Services within Digital Government and Service NL. Installations and alterations need a permit and inspection, and equipment is inspected periodically. CSA B51 and ASME codes apply, with API 510, 570 and 653 common for in-service inspection.

Pipelines and structures. CSA Z662 governs oil and gas pipeline systems, while structural fabrication commonly references CSA W59 and CSA W47.1. Marine work follows Transport Canada and classification society requirements.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in Newfoundland and Labrador

New trainees. New technicians in the province often come from welding, marine or mining backgrounds, and the gap is enough hands-on time before their first offshore hitch or plant job. Guided fundamentals let them repeat calibration, angle-beam setup, PAUT setup and indication interpretation as often as needed, with instant feedback. It is useful NDT practical exam preparation, provided everyone understands the real exam happens on real specimens.

Working technicians. Rotational schedules offshore and in Labrador mean long stretches away from some methods. A technician who spent a hitch on structural MT may be asked to run PAUT corrosion mapping on the next. Rare-defect refreshers between assignments, on corrosion under insulation, fatigue cracks, erosion patterns, tube pitting or weld defects, help them arrive ready.

Level IIIs and team leads. Level IIIs can build and assign scenario sets, benchmark crews objectively and find coverage gaps before a campaign. When an offshore campaign or a refinery turnaround brings in technicians from different employers, a consistent scenario set gives a fair picture of who is ready for which method.

Practice vs certification

Practical NDT is a practice and readiness tool. It is not a certification. It does not grant a level under CAN/CGSB-48.9712, ASNT SNT-TC-1A or an employer's written practice, and it does not replace the practical examination on real specimens those schemes require. It does not satisfy CNSC exposure device operator requirements or any offshore certifying authority requirement. It gives technicians more realistic repetition before exams and between hitches, alongside formal NDT training and supervised experience. The formal practical exam remains the step that counts.

Offshore hitches and remote camps: why the province suits virtual NDT training

Newfoundland and Labrador's NDT workforce is spread across platforms, floating production vessels, fabrication sites, remote mines and hydro stations, often far from any lab. Getting a crew together to practise a technique on real specimens is hard, and flying specimens offshore is not realistic. Weather can delay travel, and winters in Labrador limit outdoor work for months.

A browser-based NDT simulator fits that reality. Technicians can practise at home during time off, in a camp room or, where connectivity and site rules allow, during downtime on a hitch. Supervisors can see scores rather than rely on self-reported confidence. Level IIIs can push the same scenario set to everyone joining a campaign. An ultrasonic testing simulator and phased array simulator cannot replace real equipment or the formal qualifications offshore operators require, but they make the hours spent offshore more productive and reduce the risk of a technician meeting a rare defect type for the first time on live equipment.

Bring Practical NDT to your Newfoundland and Labrador team

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience. The scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, who also leads Atlantis training. Whether you run an offshore inspection team out of St. John's, a fabrication crew at Bull Arm or Marystown, a refinery or processing plant group in Placentia Bay, or a mining maintenance team in Labrador West, rollout starts with a short demo and a conversation about which environments and methods fit your work. Technicians then get access by browser or app.

Pricing is quote on request; the offer is affordable, accessible and fully customizable. Book a Newfoundland and Labrador Practical NDT demo, read the Practical NDT overview, or write to info@atlantisndt.com.

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app, so it works in St. John's, Labrador and anywhere else with a connection. There is no physical centre; delivery is online.

Is it useful for offshore corrosion and structural inspection?

Yes for core skills. The Oil & Gas Site has 73 jobs including UT and PAUT corrosion mapping, TOFD and LRUT, and the Welding Workshop covers structural weld inspection with MT, UT and PAUT.

Does Practical NDT count toward CGSB (ISO 9712) certification?

No. It is practice only. Certification requires its own training, experience and examinations, including a practical exam on real specimens. Confirm the current certification body before planning.

Does it include radiography?

Yes, as technique and image interpretation practice with no radiation source. It does not count toward CNSC exposure device operator certification.

Is it relevant for mining in Labrador?

Yes for the underlying skills: MT, UT thickness, PT and VT on structures, mills, conveyors and tanks. Site procedures still come from your employer and Level III.

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in the Northern Territory

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and the Northern Territory is a place where that matters more than most. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app: a technician opens a job in a virtual NDT lab, welding workshop, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank, sets up the technique, inspects, records the indications and is scored when the job closes. The Territory's inspection economy is concentrated and demanding. Two LNG plants sit on Darwin Harbour, Ichthys LNG at Bladin Point and Darwin LNG at Wickham Point, which restarted in early 2026 on gas from the offshore Barossa field. Around them are the East Arm port and marine industry precinct, fuel terminals, power stations, defence bases from Darwin to Tindal, gas pipelines running the length of the Territory, and remote mines from the Gulf country to the Tanami. The population is small, the distances are huge, and the climate is hard on steel. Practical NDT lets trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs practise without flying to a southern training room or waiting for a free bench.

This is the Northern Territory hub. It covers where the work is, how the simulator's environments match it, how practice sits alongside AINDT certification and NT radiation licensing, and how to arrange a demo. Practical NDT is practice, not certification, and it never replaces a practical examination on real specimens.

The Northern Territory's NDT workforce and where the work is

Short answer: most Territory NDT work is in and around Darwin Harbour, at the two LNG plants, the East Arm port, power and fuel infrastructure and defence bases. The rest follows the gas pipelines south through Katherine, Tennant Creek and Alice Springs, and out to remote mines and the Beetaloo Basin.

Darwin Harbour LNG. Ichthys LNG at Bladin Point on the Middle Arm peninsula takes gas from the offshore Ichthys field through a subsea pipeline of roughly 890 kilometres and processes it in large liquefaction trains, with cryogenic storage tanks, extensive stainless and alloy piping, heat exchangers, compressors and a product loading jetty. Darwin LNG at Wickham Point, the older of the two plants, was refitted to take gas from the Barossa field and shipped its first cargo of the new phase in January 2026. LNG plants need corrosion monitoring in a marine tropical environment, corrosion under insulation programmes, heat exchanger tube inspection, alloy verification on replacement components, tank inspection and weld inspection during every shutdown and modification.

East Arm and Middle Arm. The Port of Darwin at East Arm handles bulk, container and fuel cargo, and the area hosts fuel storage, offshore supply bases and a marine industry park with ship lift and vessel maintenance facilities. The Territory Government's planned Middle Arm precinct is intended for further gas processing and industrial development. Marine maintenance brings hull, weld and structural inspection on patrol craft, offshore support vessels and commercial ships.

Defence. RAAF Base Darwin, RAAF Base Tindal near Katherine, Robertson Barracks and the naval base at Larrakeyah make Defence a large presence, with major infrastructure upgrades and the annual rotation of US Marines through Darwin. Aircraft maintenance relies on eddy current, penetrant and ultrasonic inspection, and new fuel, runway and building works bring weld and structural inspection.

Power and pipelines. Channel Island Power Station near Darwin and gas-fired stations in Katherine, Tennant Creek and Alice Springs run boilers, turbines and heat recovery equipment. The Amadeus Gas Pipeline carries gas from Central Australian fields to Darwin, and the Northern Gas Pipeline links Tennant Creek to Mount Isa in Queensland. Exploration and pilot production in the Beetaloo Basin may bring further pipeline and processing work. Long pipelines need weld inspection at construction and repair, corrosion monitoring at above-ground stations and integrity work under AS 2885.

Remote mining. Zinc-lead mining at McArthur River near Borroloola, bauxite at Gove on the Gove Peninsula and gold in the Tanami Desert all run on fly-in fly-out rosters. Their inspection needs include structural weld inspection on processing plant, wear and thickness surveys on chutes and pipework, tank inspection and shutdown work on mills and pressure equipment.

Practical NDT by city and region in the Northern Territory

Short answer: the Territory has no city-level Practical NDT page yet, so this hub covers it all. Darwin has an Atlantis ASNT training page. The table maps each part of the Territory to the simulator environments and methods that fit.

City or regionMain local sectorsEnvironments & methods to practise
Darwin and PalmerstonLNG, port, fuel storage, power, defence, marine maintenanceOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank, Welding Workshop, Aircraft Hangar; UT, PAUT, IRIS, PMI, MFL, ET
Bladin Point and Wickham PointIchthys LNG and Darwin LNG plantsOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; UT, PAUT, IRIS, PMI, RT, LRUT
Katherine and TindalRAAF Base Tindal, gas-fired power, regional infrastructureAircraft Hangar, NDT Lab; ET, PT, UT, VT
Tennant Creek and the BarklyGas pipelines, compressor stations, Beetaloo exploration, miningOil & Gas Site, Welding Workshop; UT, LRUT, RT, MT
Alice Springs and Central AustraliaAmadeus Basin gas fields, power, regional servicesOil & Gas Site, NDT Lab; UT, IRIS, PMI, PT
Gulf and Arnhem Land (McArthur River, Gove)Zinc-lead and bauxite mining, port loadingWelding Workshop, Storage Tank; UT, MT, MFL, VT

Darwin and Palmerston. Almost all Territory inspection companies and contractors are based here, serving the LNG plants, East Arm, Defence and the power and water utility. A Darwin technician may move from a heat exchanger campaign at an LNG plant to a fuel tank survey to weld inspection on a Defence construction project in the same quarter. The simulator gives that technician one place to refresh each method. Employers that need ASNT SNT-TC-1A personnel can see ASNT training for Darwin.

Bladin Point and Wickham Point. LNG plant shutdowns compress a great deal of inspection into short windows: IRIS on exchanger tubes, PMI on alloy piping and replacement parts, UT and PAUT corrosion mapping, radiography or phased array on new welds, and tank inspection. Rehearsing those jobs in the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments before mobilisation helps crews start the shutdown at speed.

Katherine and Tindal. RAAF Base Tindal is a fighter base that has been expanded with major infrastructure works. Aircraft and component inspection relies on ET, PT and UT, which the Aircraft Hangar environment covers. Regional power and infrastructure add general weld and plant work.

Tennant Creek and the Barkly. Pipeline compressor stations, gas exploration and mining in the Barkly region bring weld inspection on pipelines and facilities, corrosion monitoring and guided-wave screening of pipe runs. These sites are remote, so browser practice between visits is useful.

Alice Springs and Central Australia. The Amadeus Basin gas fields and processing facilities, and the town's power and water assets, need corrosion surveys, exchanger work and alloy checks. Local technicians often cover a wide area alone, which makes a broad practice library valuable.

The Gulf and Arnhem Land. McArthur River and Gove are among the most remote industrial sites in Australia. Shutdown crews fly in for intense campaigns of structural, tank and pipework inspection. Pre-shutdown simulator jobs help them arrive ready.

Environments and methods that match Territory work

Short answer: the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments match the LNG plants, fuel terminals and gas fields; the Welding Workshop matches construction, pipelines and marine repair; the Aircraft Hangar matches Defence aviation; and the NDT Lab is where trainees start.

The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator has five environments. The NDT Lab provides bench specimens and reference blocks for calibration and fundamentals. The Welding Workshop holds weld coupons and fabrication joints. The Aircraft Hangar covers airframe and component inspection. The Oil & Gas Site puts weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice inside a process plant. The Storage Tank environment covers UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank.

Twelve methods are available: PT, MT and VT on the surface; UT contact, PAUT, TOFD and RT for volumetric inspection; ET and MFL as electromagnetic methods; and LRUT guided-wave screening, IRIS internal rotary UT for heat exchanger and boiler tubes, and PMI alloy verification. The product includes 33 guided lessons and a job library of 52 NDT Lab jobs, 52 Welding Workshop jobs, 54 Aircraft Hangar jobs and 73 Oil & Gas Site jobs.

For Territory work the most valuable combinations are clear. LNG and gas processing lean on IRIS for exchanger tubes, PMI for alloy verification, UT and PAUT corrosion mapping on piping and vessels, LRUT screening of long pipe runs and pipe racks, and tank shell and floor surveys. Fuel storage at East Arm and the Defence fuel installations needs tank inspection, which the Storage Tank environment's UT shell surveys and MFL floor screening reproduce. Construction and pipelines need weld inspection with RT, PAUT and UT, practised in the Welding Workshop. Defence aviation needs ET, PT and UT on aircraft structure and components, practised in the Aircraft Hangar. Mining mixes structural welds, wear surveys and tanks.

Corrosion deserves a special mention. Darwin's tropical climate, with a long wet season, high humidity and salt air, is severe for carbon steel, insulation systems and coatings. Corrosion mapping and thickness surveys are routine, and the ability to recognise and size corrosion reliably is a core skill for every Territory technician. Repeated scored practice on corrosion jobs helps keep that skill consistent across a crew.

Regulators and requirements Territory technicians meet

Short answer: industrial radiography in the Northern Territory is licensed under the Radiation Protection Act 2004, administered by NT Health; workplace and plant safety fall under the Territory's work health and safety laws and NT WorkSafe; pipelines are built to AS 2885; and offshore facilities in Commonwealth waters are regulated by NOPSEMA. AINDT certification, based on ISO 9712, is the usual personnel scheme.

Radiation. Under the Radiation Protection Act 2004, a licence is needed to use, possess, store, transport or otherwise deal with a radiation source, including industrial X-ray equipment and sealed sources used for radiography. NT Health's radiation protection team administers licensing and codes of practice. Confirm current licence conditions and recognised qualifications with NT Health before any radiography work. Simulator RT practice uses no radiation and is outside this regime, but it does not substitute for the licence or for radiation safety training.

Plant and pressure equipment. The Territory applies the national model work health and safety laws, administered by NT WorkSafe. Boilers and pressure vessels are plant, with design and item registration requirements for certain hazard levels. In-service inspection is commonly carried out to AS/NZS 3788, and design and fabrication refer to AS 1210, AS 4037, AS 4041 and AS/NZS 1554. Check specific registration requirements with NT WorkSafe.

Pipelines and offshore. Onshore pipelines are designed and operated to AS 2885 under Territory energy pipeline legislation. The offshore fields that feed the Darwin LNG plants are in Commonwealth waters, where NOPSEMA regulates safety and integrity.

Defence. Defence aviation and infrastructure work is governed by Defence requirements and airworthiness rules, with prime contractors setting qualification requirements for inspectors on their programmes.

Certification. AINDT certification, aligned with ISO 9712, is the common requirement for NDT personnel in Australia. LNG operators and their contractors may also accept or require other schemes depending on their own standards, and some contractors working to US codes use ASNT SNT-TC-1A, under which the employer's written practice governs certification. Atlantis trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A only and does not train toward or administer AINDT or ISO 9712 certification. The simulator is scheme-neutral practice.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in the Territory

Short answer: trainees get guided fundamentals without waiting for scarce bench time; working technicians refresh less-used methods between rosters; Level IIIs build scenario sets and benchmark crews before a shutdown.

Trainees. The Territory has a small local workforce and a long-standing need to grow it, with Charles Darwin University and regional training providers feeding new entrants into trades and engineering. NDT trainees often join a contractor and learn on the job. The 33 guided lessons give a structured start: probe selection, calibration, scanning, recognising indications and recording results. Trainees reach their first plant job knowing the basics.

Working technicians. Many Territory technicians are FIFO or drive-in drive-out, or rotate between the Territory, Western Australia and Queensland. A technician who spends months on corrosion surveys may then be called to a shutdown needing IRIS or PMI. Short scored jobs on a phone, tablet or laptop between swings keep those methods fresh, and rare defect types that are hard to see on real specimens can be practised repeatedly.

Level IIIs and team leads. Before a shutdown at an LNG plant or a mine, a Level III can assemble a scenario set matching the planned scope, assign it to the crew, and see who is consistent and who needs more support. The same approach works for screening new hires objectively. In a small market where every technician counts, that visibility is valuable.

Why simulator practice suits the Territory

Short answer: distance, a small workforce, short shutdown windows and a harsh climate all make practice on real specimens hard to schedule. A browser-based simulator removes the travel and the specimen bottleneck.

Darwin is a long way from the training rooms and reference specimen collections of the southern capitals. Flying technicians south for practice is expensive and takes them away from work, and bringing specimens north for every new starter is impractical. Inside the Territory, sites such as McArthur River, Gove and the Tanami are hours or days from Darwin.

LNG and mining shutdowns are planned to the hour, and inspection is often on the critical path. Crews that arrive ready, with methods fresh and procedures familiar, help the shutdown hold its schedule. The wet season adds its own constraints, limiting outdoor work and travel at times of the year.

Practice in a simulator also carries no safety risk: no radiation, no work at height, no confined spaces, no heat stress on an exposed pipe rack. Mistakes cost a lower score rather than a reinspection or an incident.

Real field experience remains essential. The aim is to make every hour on a real plant more productive by moving the basic and refresher practice to a place where it is cheap and safe to repeat.

Practice vs certification

Short answer: Practical NDT does not grant certification, is not an AINDT or ISO 9712 examination, and does not replace the practical examination on real specimens required by an employer's written practice under ASNT SNT-TC-1A. It is a skills-practice and readiness tool.

Every NDT certification scheme combines training, documented experience and examinations, including a practical examination on real specimens. Under AINDT's scheme those examinations are controlled by the certification body. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the employer's written practice sets the rules and the employer certifies its personnel. Simulator scores are not exam results under either.

What the simulator offers is preparation. Repeated, scored practice builds the habits that exams and real jobs test. A Level III can use simulator results to judge readiness, but the decision to certify rests on the scheme's own examinations. For radiography, the simulator gives technique and interpretation practice; the NT Health licence and radiation safety training remain separate legal requirements.

Atlantis training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only, delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility; see Atlantis NDT training and ASNT training in Australia. Atlantis has no training centre in the Territory.

Bring Practical NDT to your Territory team

Short answer: request a demo, tell us which Territory sites and methods your team works on, and we will show the matching environments and agree a pilot. Pricing is quote on request.

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and its scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. It is affordable, accessible and fully customizable. Inspection contractors, LNG and mining maintenance teams, Defence suppliers and training providers can use it as supplied or ask for scenario sets aligned to their own procedures.

Getting started is straightforward. A short call establishes your work: LNG shutdowns, tank and terminal inspection, pipeline integrity, Defence aviation or mining. We demonstrate the relevant environments, agree a pilot group and set up accounts. Team leads see results to track readiness. Nothing needs to be installed on site.

  • Request a Practical NDT demo for your Northern Territory team
  • Ask for a Northern Territory quote for a crew or a company
  • Discuss pre-shutdown scenario sets for LNG or mining work

See the Practical NDT overview or return to the Australia hub.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an NDT simulator I can use in Darwin?

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app, so it works in Darwin, Katherine, Alice Springs or a remote camp with a connection. There is no Territory centre to visit; demos are arranged through the contact form.

Can it help prepare for LNG plant shutdowns?

Yes. The Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments cover IRIS tube inspection, PMI, corrosion mapping, LRUT screening, weld inspection and tank surveys, the typical scope of an LNG shutdown.

Does Practical NDT count towards AINDT certification?

No. It is practice only. AINDT certification follows its own ISO 9712 based training, experience and examination rules, and Atlantis does not provide AINDT or ISO 9712 training.

Does it cover corrosion inspection for tropical conditions?

It covers the inspection techniques used for corrosion, including UT thickness surveys, PAUT corrosion mapping, MFL tank floor screening and LRUT pipe screening. It does not model climate itself, but it builds the detection and sizing skills Darwin's corrosion work demands.

Does simulator radiography need an NT licence?

No radiation is involved, so no licence is needed for simulator practice. Real radiography in the Territory requires a licence under the Radiation Protection Act 2004.

Is it useful for aircraft inspection at Tindal or Darwin?

The Aircraft Hangar environment offers airframe and component practice in ET, PT, UT and VT. Defence airworthiness and qualification rules still apply to real work.

What experience level is it for?

All levels, from trainees on guided lessons to working technicians refreshing rare defects and Level IIIs building scenario sets for their crews.

Can a Darwin contractor use it to benchmark new hires?

Yes. A Level III can assign the same scenario set to every candidate and compare scores objectively.

Does Atlantis offer ASNT training in the Northern Territory?

Yes, ASNT SNT-TC-1A training only, online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility. See NDT training in Darwin.

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in Norway

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and Norway is a country where that kind of practice fits the way NDT people actually work. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. A technician enters a virtual NDT lab, welding workshop, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank, takes a job, sets up the technique, scans or interprets, and gets a score the moment the job is closed. Norway's inspection work is dominated by the Norwegian continental shelf: offshore platforms, subsea systems and floating production units, the gas processing plants and terminals at Kårstø, Kollsnes, Nyhamna and Melkøya, the Mongstad refinery, and the fabrication yards along the west coast that build modules, jackets and hulls. Around that core sit the maritime cluster of Møre og Romsdal, aluminium smelters and hydropower, and a young offshore wind industry. Many inspectors work rotations of two weeks offshore and longer periods at home, and spend long spells on a single method. Practical NDT gives them a way to keep every method sharp between hitches, at any level from first-week trainee to working Level III, without booking lab time or consuming specimens.

This page is the Norway hub for Practical NDT. It covers where Norwegian NDT work happens, how the simulator's environments and methods map onto it, the certification and regulatory framework technicians work inside, and an honest account of what a simulator can and cannot do. To see it with your team's work in mind, request a Practical NDT demo for Norway.

Norway's NDT workforce and where the work is

Norwegian NDT work follows the oil and gas value chain from offshore fields to onshore terminals and yards, with significant additional demand from maritime, metals, hydropower and offshore wind. The west coast between Stavanger and Kristiansund holds most of it, with a northern outpost at Hammerfest.

Stavanger and Rogaland. Stavanger is the administrative capital of the Norwegian oil industry. Operators, contractors, inspection companies and the offshore regulator Havtil are based there, and the region has supply bases, module and maintenance yards, and the Kårstø gas processing plant north of Haugesund. Inspectors based in Rogaland work offshore on platform topsides, risers and process piping, and onshore at terminals and yards. Corrosion under insulation, erosion in production piping, fatigue cracking in structural nodes and weld integrity on modifications are constant themes.

Bergen and Vestland. The Bergen region holds the Mongstad refinery and crude terminal, the Kollsnes gas processing plant and the Sture terminal, plus supply bases and maintenance yards at Ågotnes and elsewhere, and the fabrication yards of Sunnhordland and Stord. Refinery and gas plant work brings exchanger tube testing, alloy verification, tank surveys and turnaround inspection; yard work brings weld inspection on modules, jackets and floaters.

Møre og Romsdal and Trøndelag. The Nyhamna gas plant near Kristiansund, the maritime cluster around Ålesund with its offshore vessel designers and shipyards, the aluminium and metals plants of Sunndalsøra and other fjord towns, and the yards and research community around Trondheim add shipbuilding weld inspection, process plant work and materials testing.

Northern Norway. Hammerfest LNG on Melkøya processes gas from the Barents Sea, and Barents fields are served from Hammerfest and other northern bases. Arctic conditions, cold-service materials and long travel distances make remote practice especially useful.

Oslo and the east. Oslo hosts engineering head offices, the Norwegian NDT and research community, and much of the country's aviation maintenance and industrial manufacturing in the surrounding counties. Hydropower penstocks, dams and turbines across the country add a steady load of weld and structural inspection.

Offshore wind. Floating offshore wind has been pioneered from Norway, with the Hywind Tampen project supplying power to offshore fields, and government plans for further offshore wind areas. Mooring components, floating hulls and tower welds add new inspection work for yards and service companies.

Practical NDT by city in Norway

Stavanger already has its own Practical NDT page. The table below links it and adds the other main NDT work centres, mapped to the simulator environments and methods that fit.

City or areaMain local sectorsEnvironments & methods to practise
StavangerOffshore operators and contractors, supply bases, Kårstø gas plant, yardsOil & Gas Site, Welding Workshop; PAUT, TOFD, IRIS, LRUT, RT
Bergen and MongstadRefining, crude terminals, gas processing, maintenance yardsOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; IRIS, PMI, MFL, UT
Stord and SunnhordlandModule, jacket and platform fabricationWelding Workshop; PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, VT
Ålesund and KristiansundShipbuilding, offshore vessels, Nyhamna gas plantWelding Workshop, Oil & Gas Site; UT, PAUT, MT
TrondheimResearch, engineering, yards, metalsNDT Lab, Welding Workshop; UT, ET, PT
HammerfestLNG processing, Barents Sea supplyOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; IRIS, PMI, UT, MFL
Oslo regionEngineering offices, aviation maintenance, manufacturingAircraft Hangar, NDT Lab; ET, UT, PT

Stavanger. Most of Norway's offshore inspection planning starts here. Topside piping and vessels need corrosion mapping with UT and PAUT, guided-wave LRUT screening on long pipe runs and inaccessible sections, IRIS on exchangers, and RT or TOFD on modification welds. The Practical NDT Stavanger page has more detail, and Atlantis also has an NDT training page for Stavanger and an offshore asset digital twin page for Stavanger.

Bergen and Mongstad. The Mongstad refinery and terminal and the Kollsnes gas plant give the Bergen region the most process-plant style work in Norway: exchanger bundles, mixed-alloy piping, fired equipment and large crude and product tanks. IRIS, PMI, MFL floor screening and tank thickness surveys are the practice priorities. See the Mongstad digital twin page and the Bergen ERP page.

Stord and Sunnhordland. Large fabrication yards build topside modules, jackets and platform structures. Thick welds, tight schedules and strict project specifications make PAUT and TOFD sizing and RT interpretation the key skills, all covered in the Welding Workshop.

Ålesund and Kristiansund. The maritime cluster builds and maintains advanced offshore and fishing vessels, while Kristiansund supports Norwegian Sea fields and the Nyhamna plant. Weld inspection on hulls and outfitting, and process work at the gas plant, both apply.

Trondheim. A strong research and engineering community, yards in Trøndelag and nearby metals industry make the NDT Lab and Welding Workshop the natural fit. See the Trondheim ERP page.

Hammerfest. LNG processing equipment, cryogenic piping and storage tanks bring IRIS, PMI, UT and tank work in a remote Arctic setting where travel to a training lab is a real cost.

Oslo region. Aviation maintenance, manufacturing and engineering head offices make Oslo a coordination and training hub. See the Oslo NDT training page.

Environments and methods that match Norwegian work

The short answer: offshore and onshore process work maps to the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank, yard fabrication and shipbuilding to the Welding Workshop, aviation to the Aircraft Hangar, and materials and manufacturing work to the NDT Lab. All twelve methods are available in each rollout.

Oil & Gas Site (73 jobs). The largest scenario set, covering weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant. It is the closest virtual match to Norwegian topsides and onshore gas plants: UT and PAUT corrosion mapping, LRUT guided-wave screening, IRIS on exchanger and boiler tubes, PMI alloy verification on duplex, super duplex and other corrosion-resistant alloy piping, and RT on piping welds.

Welding Workshop (52 jobs). Weld coupons and fabrication joints for the yards at Stord, Verdal, Ågotnes and the Møre cluster: PAUT and TOFD on thick structural and pressure welds, RT interpretation, MT on structural steel and VT. It suits jacket nodes, module steel, hull blocks and floating wind structures.

Storage Tank. UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank, matching the crude and product tanks at Mongstad, Sture, Kårstø, Melkøya and coastal depots.

NDT Lab (52 jobs). Bench specimens and reference blocks for calibration habits and fundamentals, used by new entrants and by technicians moving into a new method.

Aircraft Hangar (54 jobs). Airframe and component inspection for the helicopter and fixed-wing maintenance that supports offshore logistics and Norwegian aviation: eddy current, ultrasonic, penetrant and visual practice.

The twelve methods are PT, MT and VT; UT contact, PAUT, TOFD and RT; ET and MFL; and LRUT, IRIS and PMI, supported by 33 guided lessons.

Regulators and requirements Norwegian technicians meet

In Norway, NDT personnel are normally certified to EN ISO 9712 under the Nordtest scheme, run by accredited Nordic certification bodies, and offshore work follows NORSOK standards under oversight from Havtil, the Norwegian Ocean Industry Authority. Practical NDT is practice for any scheme and is not part of Nordtest or other EN ISO 9712 certification.

Personnel certification. The Nordtest scheme for examination and certification of NDT personnel, aligned with EN ISO 9712, is the main scheme in the Nordic countries, and certification is issued by accredited certification bodies. NORSOK fabrication and inspection standards, including NORSOK M-101 for structural steel fabrication and NORSOK M-601 for welding and inspection of piping, set requirements for NDT on offshore projects. US-owned assets, US OEM equipment and projects to ASME, API or AWS codes may also specify ASNT SNT-TC-1A, which is where Atlantis's ASNT experience is relevant.

Offshore regulator. The Petroleum Safety Authority Norway became Havtil (Havindustritilsynet), the Norwegian Ocean Industry Authority, on 1 January 2024. It supervises safety and the working environment for petroleum activities on the shelf and certain onshore plants, and has responsibilities for offshore renewable energy.

Radiography. Industrial radiography is regulated by the Norwegian Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority (DSA), which sets requirements for the use of radiation sources and the competence of radiographers. The simulator's RT scenarios involve no source and do not count toward any radiation protection qualification.

Pressure equipment onshore. Pressure equipment is placed on the market under rules implementing the EU Pressure Equipment Directive, and onshore pressure equipment and hazardous installations fall under the Norwegian Directorate for Civil Protection (DSB). Confirm the current requirements for your installation with the relevant authority.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in Norway

The short answer: trainees and apprentices get guided fundamentals, rotational technicians get rare-defect refreshers during their time onshore, and Level IIIs get objective crew benchmarking and scenario control across offshore and onshore teams.

Trainees and apprentices. Norway's apprenticeship system trains industrial technicians, welders and materials testers, and the offshore industry recruits heavily from it. New entrants need many repetitions before they are trusted on a platform. Guided lessons and NDT Lab and Welding Workshop jobs with instant scored feedback provide them.

Working technicians. Rotation work means long periods away from one method and long periods at home. A rope-access inspector who has been doing UT thickness for a hitch may need PAUT weld sizing or TOFD on the next job. Practising rare defects, such as fatigue cracks in nodes, lack of sidewall fusion, corrosion under insulation and exchanger tube pitting, during time onshore keeps those skills current.

Level IIIs and team leads. Level IIIs and inspection coordinators can assign scenario sets, compare performance across crews and installations, and spot gaps before a campaign. The results support their judgement; they do not replace procedures, NORSOK requirements or certification records.

Practice vs certification

Practical NDT is a practice and readiness tool. It is not a certification, it does not grant or renew Nordtest, EN ISO 9712 or ASNT qualifications, and it does not replace the practical examination on real specimens that every scheme requires.

Under EN ISO 9712 and the Nordtest scheme, certification requires documented training, industrial experience and an examination including a practical part on real specimens, administered by an accredited certification body. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the employer's written practice sets training, experience and examinations, including a practical exam on real specimens, and the employer certifies. A simulator builds familiarity and confidence; the formal steps remain.

Atlantis's training product follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A only and is delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility; Atlantis does not train toward Nordtest or other EN ISO 9712 certification. For Norwegian employers, ASNT-based training mainly matters for work to US codes or for US clients. See NDT training in Norway and SNT-TC-1A training and certification.

Rotations, remote bases and offshore campaigns: why Norwegian teams use virtual NDT training

Norwegian NDT work is highly mobile. Offshore rotations, campaigns on remote installations, yard projects that start and stop, and turnarounds at gas plants and Mongstad all pull technicians away from labs and specimens. A browser-based NDT simulator fits that pattern because practice happens wherever the technician is, including at home between hitches.

Offshore bed space and time on an installation are expensive; nobody wants to discover that an inspector has forgotten a setup step once they are on the platform. Practising scan plans, calibration and interpretation onshore before a campaign helps crews arrive ready. Yard projects ramp up quickly with large numbers of contract inspectors; a common set of scenarios gives the NDT coordinator a fast, objective view of who is ready for which welds.

Representative flawed specimens in duplex, super duplex, clad and thick carbon steel are expensive and quickly memorised. The simulator's job library keeps defects varied and lets Level IIIs assign different sets to different people.

The energy transition adds new work, from floating wind structures to carbon capture and storage infrastructure, and with it a need to train inspectors who come from oil and gas into new asset types. Scenario practice helps that transfer without taking people off billable work.

Bring Practical NDT to your Norwegian team

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience. The scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Access is by browser or app, so offshore and onshore staff use the same platform, and there is no physical centre to visit.

A rollout starts with a demo and a short scoping call on your methods, assets and crew levels. An offshore inspection contractor might focus on PAUT, LRUT, IRIS and corrosion mapping in the Oil & Gas Site; a yard on PAUT, TOFD and RT in the Welding Workshop; a terminal operator on MFL and shell thickness in the Storage Tank. Level IIIs then assign scenario sets and follow results.

The offer is affordable, accessible and fully customizable, with a quote on request. Book a Practical NDT demo for your Norwegian team, read the Practical NDT overview, or write to info@atlantisndt.com. Inspection companies can also look at Atlantis ERP in Norway.

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app and works anywhere in Norway with an internet connection, including at home between offshore rotations. There is no physical Atlantis centre in Norway.

Does Practical NDT count toward Nordtest or EN ISO 9712 certification?

No. It is practice only. Nordtest certification requires training, experience and examinations, including a practical exam on real specimens, through an accredited certification body. The simulator helps you prepare.

Can it help with NDT practical exam preparation?

It can help you build familiarity, speed and confidence with setups, scanning and interpretation before a practical exam. It does not replace the exam or any required hands-on hours.

Can offshore technicians use it during rotations?

Yes during time off, and offshore during downtime if the installation's connectivity and rules allow. Practising between hitches is one of the main reasons Norwegian employers look at it.

Does it cover NORSOK-style weld and piping inspection?

It covers the underlying skills: PAUT, TOFD, RT and MT on welds, corrosion mapping and guided-wave screening on piping. Acceptance criteria and procedures for a given project still come from the project specification and your Level III.

Among other things, yes. It covers UT contact, PAUT and TOFD, plus IRIS for tubes, LRUT guided-wave screening, and surface, electromagnetic and PMI methods.

What experience level is it for?

All levels: guided fundamentals for apprentices and trainees, rare-defect refreshers for working technicians, and scenario building and crew benchmarking for Level IIIs and coordinators.

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in Nova Scotia

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and Nova Scotia's maritime industries are a natural fit for it. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. Technicians step into a virtual welding workshop, NDT lab, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank, choose a job, set up the technique and receive a score the moment the job is complete. Nova Scotia's NDT work is shaped by the sea. Halifax is home to a naval shipyard building Canada's new Arctic and offshore patrol ships and its next generation of warships, to Canada's Atlantic naval fleet and dockyard, and to one of the country's major container ports. Military and civil helicopters and aircraft are maintained around Halifax. Cape Breton and the Strait of Canso have deep-water marine terminals, power stations and heavy industry. Offshore gas production has wound down, but the province is now preparing for offshore wind, and onshore wind, tidal energy trials in the Bay of Fundy, pulp and paper, tire manufacturing and fuel terminals all need inspection. Practical NDT gives Nova Scotia technicians a way to rehearse weld, corrosion and aerospace inspection at any level, from first-week trainee to working Level III, without waiting for lab time or specimens.

This is the Nova Scotia hub for Practical NDT. It covers where the province's NDT work is, how the simulator's environments and methods match it, the regulators that apply, and an honest explanation of practice versus certification. To see it applied to your own work, request a Practical NDT demo for Nova Scotia.

Nova Scotia's NDT workforce and where the work is

Nova Scotia's inspection work clusters around Halifax Harbour, the Strait of Canso and Cape Breton, with smaller centres across the mainland. Shipbuilding and marine work dominate, with aerospace, energy and manufacturing close behind.

Halifax and Dartmouth: shipbuilding and naval work. The Halifax Shipyard is the combat-ship yard under Canada's National Shipbuilding Strategy. It has built the Arctic and Offshore Patrol Ships and is building the River-class destroyers, and it carries out work on existing naval vessels. Shipbuilding at this scale means enormous volumes of structural and pressure welds, inspected by visual, magnetic particle, ultrasonic, phased array and radiographic methods to naval specifications and classification rules. Canadian Forces Base Halifax and HMC Dockyard support the Royal Canadian Navy's Atlantic fleet, adding refit and maintenance inspection. A network of fabrication shops, marine service companies and inspection firms in Dartmouth and the Burnside industrial area supports both.

Halifax: port, terminals and aerospace. The Port of Halifax handles containers, bulk and cruise traffic, and the harbour hosts fuel and product terminals with tank farms and marine loading equipment. Aerospace maintenance is a long-standing Halifax specialty: heavy maintenance and modification of military aircraft and helicopters, maritime helicopter operations at 12 Wing Shearwater, and civil maintenance around Halifax Stanfield International Airport. That work relies on eddy current, penetrant, ultrasonic and visual inspection to OEM and military requirements.

The Strait of Canso and Port Hawkesbury. The Strait of Canso offers one of the deepest ice-free harbours on the east coast of North America. Point Tupper and the surrounding area host marine and petroleum terminals, a paper mill, a power station and bulk-handling facilities, along with proposed energy export projects. Tank, terminal and mill inspection are the main NDT activities.

Cape Breton. Sydney's harbour, power generation at coal-fired stations, and the legacy of steelmaking and coal mining shape Cape Breton's industrial base. Boiler-tube and pressure-part inspection at power plants, structural and marine inspection around the harbour, and fabrication work keep local technicians busy.

Offshore energy, then and next. The Sable Offshore Energy Project and Deep Panuke produced natural gas for years and have since been decommissioned. The offshore regulator was renamed the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator in 2025 with a mandate that now includes offshore renewable energy, and the province has set out plans for large-scale offshore wind. Onshore wind farms across the mainland and tidal energy testing in the Minas Passage add tower, foundation and structural inspection.

The mainland. Tire manufacturing in Pictou and Kings counties, food and seafood processing along the coast, forestry, and the Annapolis Valley's agri-food sector all operate boilers, pressure vessels, refrigeration plants and structural steel that need periodic inspection.

Practical NDT by city in Nova Scotia

Halifax has its own Practical NDT page and an ASNT training page. The table links it and maps Nova Scotia's other main work centres to the simulator environments and methods that fit.
