NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in the UAE

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and the United Arab Emirates is a natural home for it. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. A technician opens a job in a virtual NDT lab, welding workshop, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank, sets up the technique, inspects, records the result and gets a score the moment the job closes. UAE inspection work is unusually broad for its size: Abu Dhabi's onshore and offshore oil and gas, the gas processing and refining complexes at Habshan, Das Island and Ruwais, the Barakah nuclear power plant, one of the world's largest oil storage and bunkering hubs at Fujairah, shipyards and offshore fabrication yards in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Sharjah, two of the busiest aviation hubs anywhere, and a construction sector that never stops. Crews are multinational, mobile and frequently asked to prove competence before they reach site.

This page is the UAE hub for Practical NDT. It maps where the country's NDT work is emirate by emirate, which simulator environments match each cluster, how practice sits alongside the ASNT SNT-TC-1A and ISO 9712 certification UAE employers ask for, which regulators matter, and how to arrange a demo. City pages for Abu Dhabi and Dubai have more detail.

Where the UAE's NDT work is, emirate by emirate

Short answer: UAE NDT demand clusters in five places: Abu Dhabi's upstream, gas and refining assets from offshore fields to Ruwais; the Barakah nuclear plant in Al Dhafra; Dubai's port, dry-dock, aviation and construction base; Sharjah and the northern emirates' fabrication yards; and Fujairah's storage terminals on the east coast. Each relies on a different mix of methods.

Abu Dhabi. Abu Dhabi holds most of the country's oil and gas. Offshore fields in the Arabian Gulf are produced through platforms, artificial islands and processing at Das Island and Zirku, while onshore fields feed large gas processing at Habshan and Bab. The Ruwais industrial complex in Al Dhafra combines one of the region's largest refineries with petrochemical and fertiliser plants. Abu Dhabi city, Mussafah and the Khalifa Industrial Zone near Khalifa Port host most of the emirate's inspection companies, laboratories, fabrication yards and offshore construction bases. Corrosion monitoring, weld inspection on new construction and modifications, and turnaround inspection of exchangers, vessels and piping run all year.

Al Dhafra and Barakah. The Barakah nuclear power plant is the Arab world's first commercial nuclear station. Nuclear plants have their own qualified inspection programmes and strict personnel requirements, but they also widen the local pool of technicians trained in volumetric weld inspection and in-service inspection practice.

Dubai. Jebel Ali is the region's largest port and free zone, with heavy fabrication, fuel terminals and storage, power and desalination at Jebel Ali, and an aluminium smelter. The Dubai dry docks and maritime city handle ship repair, conversion and offshore construction. Dubai International and Al Maktoum airports support a very large airline engineering and MRO operation. Construction across the emirate adds structural steel, pipelines and building services inspection.

Sharjah and the northern emirates. Hamriyah Free Zone and the industrial areas of Sharjah, Ajman and Ras Al Khaimah host many fabrication yards, pipe and vessel manufacturers, offshore and marine contractors and cement and industrial plants. Ras Al Khaimah has further ports and manufacturing.

Fujairah. On the Gulf of Oman, outside the Strait of Hormuz, Fujairah has grown into a major oil storage and bunkering hub, with large tank farms, jetties and a terminal for crude arriving by pipeline from Abu Dhabi's fields. Tank inspection, floor screening, shell thickness surveys and pipeline work dominate there.

Practical NDT across UAE cities and emirates

Short answer: Abu Dhabi and Dubai already have their own Practical NDT pages. The table below covers those and the other main UAE clusters, with the simulator environments and methods that match the work. Every user can open every environment; the table shows where to start.

City or areaMain local sectorsEnvironments & methods to practise
Abu Dhabi and MussafahOffshore and onshore oil and gas, gas processing, fabrication, offshore constructionOil & Gas Site, Welding Workshop; UT, PAUT, TOFD, LRUT, PMI
Ruwais and Al DhafraRefining, petrochemicals, fertilisers, nuclear powerOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; IRIS, PMI, ET, UT, PAUT
Dubai and Jebel AliPort and free zone, dry docks, power and desalination, aviation MRO, constructionWelding Workshop, Aircraft Hangar, Storage Tank; PAUT, ET, PT, MT
Sharjah, Hamriyah and the northern emiratesFabrication yards, pipe and vessel manufacturing, marine contractorsWelding Workshop, NDT Lab; PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT
FujairahOil storage, bunkering, terminals, pipelineStorage Tank, Oil & Gas Site; UT shell thickness, MFL, LRUT
Al AinAerostructures manufacturing, industryAircraft Hangar, NDT Lab; ET, UT, PT, VT

Abu Dhabi technicians move between offshore facilities, onshore plants and the fabrication yards of Mussafah and the Khalifa industrial area. Corrosion mapping and LRUT screening in the Oil & Gas Site environment, and PAUT and TOFD weld inspection in the Welding Workshop, cover most of their work. Abu Dhabi employers can also use ASNT training in Abu Dhabi and Level III consulting in Abu Dhabi.

Ruwais turnarounds are dominated by exchangers, columns, reactors and alloy piping. IRIS on exchanger tubes, ET on non-ferrous tubes and PMI on alloy lines are the methods technicians most often feel unpractised in, and all three are in the Oil & Gas Site environment, which has 73 jobs. See ASNT training in Ruwais.

Dubai crews cover a wider mix than anywhere else in the country: ship repair and offshore conversion welds at the dry docks, tank and terminal surveys at Jebel Ali, boiler and condenser work at power and desalination plants, and airline maintenance. The Welding Workshop, Storage Tank and Aircraft Hangar environments all apply. See ASNT training in Dubai and consulting in Dubai.

Sharjah and Hamriyah fabrication yards build vessels, spools, skids and offshore structures, often to ASME and AWS codes for export. Weld inspection with PAUT, TOFD, RT and MT in the Welding Workshop is the core practice. See ASNT training in Sharjah.

Fujairah is tank country. The Storage Tank environment, with UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank, matches terminal work closely, and LRUT screening suits jetty and transfer lines. See ASNT training in Fujairah.

Al Ain hosts aerostructures manufacturing, where composite and metallic parts are inspected with ultrasonic and other methods under aerospace quality systems. The Aircraft Hangar environment, with 54 airframe and component jobs, is the closest match for practice.

Environments and methods that match UAE work

Short answer: the simulator has five environments and twelve methods. In the UAE, the Oil & Gas Site matches upstream, gas and refining work; the Storage Tank matches Fujairah and Jebel Ali terminals; the Welding Workshop matches yards and construction; the Aircraft Hangar matches airline MRO and aerostructures; and the NDT Lab supports trainees.

The five workplace environments are the NDT Lab (bench specimens and reference blocks, 52 jobs), the Welding Workshop (weld coupons and fabrication joints, 52 jobs), the Aircraft Hangar (airframe and component inspection, 54 jobs), the Oil & Gas Site (weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant, 73 jobs) and the Storage Tank (UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank). Thirty-three guided lessons cover the fundamentals. The twelve methods are PT, MT and VT; contact UT, PAUT, TOFD and RT; ET and MFL; and LRUT guided-wave screening, IRIS for heat-exchanger and boiler tubes, and PMI for alloy verification.

UAE workEnvironmentMethods to practise
Offshore platforms, islands and onshore gas plantsOil & Gas SiteUT, PAUT corrosion mapping, LRUT, PMI
Refinery and petrochemical turnarounds at RuwaisOil & Gas SiteIRIS, ET, PMI, UT
Tank farms and terminals at Fujairah and Jebel AliStorage TankUT shell thickness, MFL floor screening
Offshore structures, vessels and spools in fabrication yardsWelding WorkshopPAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, VT
Ship repair and conversion at dry docksWelding WorkshopUT thickness, MT, PAUT, VT
Airline MRO and aerostructures manufacturingAircraft HangarET, PT, UT, VT
Power and desalination boilers and condensersOil & Gas SiteIRIS, ET, UT

Desalination deserves a mention because it is so central to UAE infrastructure. Thermal desalination and combined power and water plants have large numbers of heat-exchanger and condenser tubes, often in copper-nickel or titanium, where eddy current testing is the main screening method and IRIS is used to size wall loss. Practising ET and IRIS data interpretation in the simulator helps technicians who only see these jobs during planned outages.

Radiography is still widely used on pipeline and yard work, but it is tightly controlled. The simulator lets technicians practise RT technique and image interpretation without any source, so radiation licensing does not apply to simulator practice.

Certification, vendor requirements and regulators in the UAE

Short answer: UAE employers commonly ask for NDT personnel certified to ASNT SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712 schemes, and national operators add their own contractor requirements. Radiation sources, including industrial radiography, are regulated by the Federal Authority for Nuclear Regulation (FANR). Simulator practice supports all of these but replaces none of them.

Personnel certification. Inspection companies in the UAE serve owners, EPCs and licensors from many countries, so ASNT SNT-TC-1A employer-based certification and ISO 9712 schemes such as PCN are both common, often within the same crew. Some work asks for ASNT central certification. Atlantis training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only; Atlantis does not train for or issue ISO 9712, PCN or CSWIP certificates.

Owner and contractor requirements. ADNOC and its group companies, and other national energy and utility owners, set engineering standards, contractor prequalification and quality requirements, including requirements for NDT procedures and personnel. National programmes such as In-Country Value (ICV) also shape how contractors are evaluated. Requirements are set by each owner and change over time, so always work from the documents your contract names. Atlantis makes no claim of approval or registration with ADNOC or any other owner, and Practical NDT is not an owner-approved qualification.

Radiation regulation. The Federal Authority for Nuclear Regulation (FANR) regulates the nuclear sector and the use of radiation sources across the UAE, including industrial radiography. Companies need the appropriate FANR licence, trained personnel and radiation protection arrangements. Confirm current requirements with FANR before exposure work. FANR also regulates Barakah, where nuclear-specific inspection requirements apply.

Workplace safety and codes. Occupational safety is overseen at federal and emirate level; Abu Dhabi, for example, has its own occupational safety and health framework, and free zones have their own rules. UAE plants and yards work mainly to ASME, API, AWS and owner specifications, with ISO and EN standards in some sectors and DNV or other class rules for marine work. ASME Section V, Section VIII, B31.3, API 1104, API 650 and 653 and AWS D1.1 are everyday references. The simulator teaches method skills, not code acceptance criteria; a company's Level III sets those. Atlantis does not offer API 510, 570 or 653 or CWI training.

For procedures and written practices, see NDT consulting in the UAE; to track ASNT and ISO 9712 certificates side by side, see the UAE NDT ERP page.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in the UAE

Short answer: trainees, including Emirati technicians entering the industry, use guided lessons and NDT Lab jobs to learn fundamentals; working technicians refresh methods and rare defects between projects; Level IIIs build and assign scenario sets to benchmark multinational crews before mobilisation.

New trainees. Emiratisation goals and industry training programmes are bringing new UAE nationals into technical roles, alongside new expatriate hires. The 33 guided lessons give each trainee a structured route through set-up, calibration, scanning and interpretation, and NDT Lab jobs can be repeated as often as needed without consuming a reference block or a senior technician's time.

Working technicians. UAE technicians move between very different jobs: yard weld inspection one month, an offshore campaign the next, a Ruwais turnaround after that. The simulator lets them rehearse the next job's method, or a rare defect type, in camp, at the accommodation or at home, in a browser or app.

Level IIIs and team leads. For a crew assembled from several nationalities and certification backgrounds, a common scenario set gives the Level III an objective, comparable picture of readiness. Results help allocate technicians, plan refreshers and show clients that competence is checked between certifications.

Practice vs certification

Short answer: the Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is a practice and readiness tool. It is not a certification, does not issue certificates, is not an owner or operator approval and does not replace the practical examination on real specimens that ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practices or ISO 9712 schemes require.

Under SNT-TC-1A, the employer's written practice governs training, experience and examinations under Level III oversight, and the practical exam uses real specimens. ISO 9712 certification bodies set their own training, experience and exams. Owners' requirements sit on top. None of these accepts simulator results as a substitute. The value of the simulator is preparation: a candidate who has worked through many virtual flaws arrives at a real exam, and a real job, with established habits. Treat scores as one piece of evidence alongside supervised work and formal certification.

Offshore campaigns, outages and summer heat: why UAE crews practise virtually

Short answer: UAE crews rotate between offshore, plant and yard work, outages bring in large teams at short notice, and summer heat limits outdoor practice. A browser-based simulator lets technicians practise anywhere and lets employers check readiness before anyone mobilises.

Offshore and island rotations are the first reason. Technicians on platforms and islands have long shifts and little access to specimens. A simulator on a laptop or tablet fills the gap. Outages are the second: refinery, gas plant and power and water plant shutdowns create sudden demand for IRIS, ET and PMI, methods many technicians only use a few weeks a year. Specimens are the third: realistic flawed specimens are expensive and quickly become familiar, while a job library across five environments stays varied. Safety and climate are the fourth: practising radiography without a source, and tank and plant surveys without heat exposure, height or confined spaces, removes risk from learning. Real work still needs every usual control, but the method is rehearsed before the technician arrives.

ASNT training, consulting and ERP for UAE employers

Short answer: Atlantis also offers UAE companies ASNT SNT-TC-1A training, Level III consulting and an NDT ERP, delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility. There is no Atlantis training centre in the UAE.

Employers whose clients specify SNT-TC-1A can use ASNT SNT-TC-1A training in the UAE for Level I, II and III candidates, led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT, with written practice development. Level III procedure, technique and audit support is available through UAE consulting, and the Atlantis NDT ERP keeps ASNT and ISO 9712 certificates, calibration records, jobs and reports in one system. City training pages cover Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ruwais and Fujairah. All are quoted on request.

Bring Practical NDT to your UAE team

Short answer: request a demo through the contact form. Atlantis will show the environments that match your work, agree a pilot group and set up accounts. Nothing needs installing beyond a browser or app, and pricing is quote on request. Affordable, accessible and fully customizable.

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and the scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Inspection contractors, fabrication yards, EPCs, laboratories and technical institutes in the UAE can use it as it stands or ask for scenario sets aligned to their own procedures. A typical start is a short call about your work, a live demonstration of the matching environments, a pilot group and accounts for your technicians, with results visible to team leads.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an NDT simulator available in the UAE?

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app and works anywhere in the UAE with an internet connection. There is no centre to visit; demos are arranged through the contact form.

Is Practical NDT approved by ADNOC or other UAE owners?

No. It is a practice tool, not an owner-approved qualification. Owners' personnel and procedure requirements must be met through the routes their contracts specify.

Does it replace the SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712 practical exam?

No. Practical exams must be taken on real specimens under the employer's written practice or the certification body's rules. The simulator helps you prepare for them.

Can it help with NDT practical exam preparation in Dubai or Abu Dhabi?

Yes. Repeating set-up, scanning, interpretation and sizing builds the habits an exam checks, wherever you sit it.

Does it cover tank inspection for Fujairah and Jebel Ali terminals?

Yes. The Storage Tank environment covers UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank.

Does it include radiography, and does it need a FANR licence?

RT is included for technique and interpretation practice. No radiation is used, so simulator practice needs no licence. Real industrial radiography requires a FANR licence and the employer's radiation protection arrangements.

Is it useful for aviation NDT technicians in the UAE?

Yes. The Aircraft Hangar environment has 54 airframe and component jobs with ET, PT, UT and VT. It does not replace the aerospace qualification your organisation requires.

Does it cover desalination and power plant tube inspection?

Yes. ET and IRIS tube inspection are part of the Oil & Gas Site environment and transfer directly to condenser and exchanger work.

Can a UAE inspection company use it to assess a new crew?

Yes. A Level III can assign one scenario set to every technician and compare scores objectively, alongside certification and supervised work.

Does Atlantis offer ASNT training in the UAE?

Yes, ASNT SNT-TC-1A training only, delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility. See NDT training in the UAE.

How much does it cost and how do we start?

Pricing is quote on request, depending on users and any custom scenarios. Request a demo to see the environments that fit your work.

contentHtml:
HomeTrainingConsultingERPPractical NDTContact

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in the UK

The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is what Atlantis describes as the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and the United Kingdom is a country where that kind of practice earns its keep. It is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. A technician opens a job in a virtual NDT lab, welding workshop, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank, chooses and sets up the technique, carries out the inspection, records what was found and gets a score as soon as the job is closed. UK inspection work is unusually varied for a country of its size: North Sea production platforms and their decommissioning, a growing offshore wind fleet, refineries and chemical complexes on the Solent, the Mersey, the Humber, the Tees and Milford Haven, a nuclear estate from Sellafield to Sizewell, aerospace manufacturing from Derby to Broughton, naval shipbuilding on the Clyde and at Barrow, and a rail network that is tested by ultrasound every day. Practical NDT gives trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs a place to put hours into the methods they need without booking a lab bench or consuming a specimen.

This page is the UK hub. It maps where the work is, which simulator environments fit each part of the country, how practice sits alongside PCN and other EN ISO 9712 certification, and how to get a demo for your team. City pages with more local detail are linked where they exist.

Where the UK's NDT work is, nation by nation and region by region

Short answer: UK NDT demand clusters in six places: Aberdeen and the North Sea, the Scottish central belt, the North East and Humber energy coast, the North West nuclear and chemical belt, the Midlands and South West aerospace corridor, and the South and Welsh refinery coasts. Each leans on a different mix of methods, which is why a single practice library has to cover all twelve.

Aberdeen and the North Sea. Aberdeen remains the operational centre of UK offshore oil and gas. Platforms, subsea infrastructure and onshore terminals such as Sullom Voe, Flotta, St Fergus and Cruden Bay need corrosion monitoring, weld inspection and structural surveys, and a growing share of the work is decommissioning: checking the condition of steel that is about to be cut, lifted and brought ashore. Rope-access technicians, inspection engineers and integrity teams based in and around the city rotate offshore, and the same supply chain is moving into offshore wind foundations and substations.

The Scottish central belt. Grangemouth on the Forth is Scotland's best-known industrial site. Crude refining there ended in April 2025 and the refinery has moved to fuel import and distribution, while the wider site keeps chemical operations, tanks and pipework that still need inspection. On the Clyde, naval shipbuilding at Govan and Scotstoun produces frigates whose structural welds are inspected at every block, and Rosyth in Fife handles naval vessel assembly and maintenance. Glasgow and Edinburgh host engineering consultancies, inspection companies and university research groups in ultrasonics and NDT.

The North East, Teesside and the Humber. Teesside has a long heavy-industry history: steelmaking, the chemical parks at Wilton, Billingham and Seal Sands, and the Hartlepool nuclear station. Large regeneration and energy transition projects, including carbon capture and hydrogen schemes, are bringing new fabrication. The Tyne has offshore fabrication and subsea manufacturing yards. Further south, the Humber estuary around Immingham and South Killingholme is home to refining, gas-fired power, a major port and the onshore bases for some of the largest offshore wind farms in the world.

The North West and Cumbria. Sellafield, the Heysham power stations and the fuel facilities near Preston make this the most nuclear-heavy region in the country. Barrow-in-Furness builds the Royal Navy's submarines, where weld quality is controlled to some of the strictest standards in UK manufacturing. Stanlow refinery at Ellesmere Port, the chemical works around Runcorn and Widnes, and the Cammell Laird yard at Birkenhead add process-plant and marine work. Lancashire hosts military aircraft manufacturing at Warton and Samlesbury.

The Midlands and the South West. Derby is the centre of UK aero-engine manufacturing and also of rail rolling-stock building and submarine reactor work. Bristol and Filton host aerospace design and aerostructures, and Yeovil builds helicopters. These sites rely heavily on penetrant, eddy current and ultrasonic inspection of high-value components, and they employ NDT staff certified to aerospace schemes. The Midlands also has a dense base of castings, forgings and precision engineering suppliers.

The South, Wales and Northern Ireland. Fawley on Southampton Water is the UK's largest refinery. In Wales, Milford Haven has the Valero Pembroke refinery and two LNG import terminals, Port Talbot is changing from blast furnace to electric arc steelmaking, and Broughton in Flintshire builds wings for Airbus aircraft. Hinkley Point C in Somerset is the largest construction project in the country, with nuclear-grade welding and inspection on a huge scale. In Northern Ireland, Belfast has shipbuilding and offshore fabrication heritage and aerospace manufacturing.

Practical NDT across UK cities and regions

Short answer: two UK cities already have their own Practical NDT pages, Aberdeen and Teesside. The table below covers those and the other main UK clusters, with the simulator environments and methods that suit each one.

City or regionMain local sectorsEnvironments & methods to practise
AberdeenNorth Sea oil and gas, decommissioning, subsea, offshore windOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; UT, PAUT, LRUT, MFL, ET
TeessideChemicals, steel, energy transition projects, nuclear, fabricationOil & Gas Site, Welding Workshop; PAUT, TOFD, IRIS, PMI
Humber (Immingham, Hull)Refining, power, port, offshore wind operationsOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; UT, MFL, IRIS, PMI
Clyde and Forth (Glasgow, Rosyth, Grangemouth)Naval shipbuilding, fuel terminal, chemicalsWelding Workshop, Storage Tank; PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT
Cumbria and LancashireNuclear, submarines, military aircraftWelding Workshop, Aircraft Hangar; UT, PAUT, RT, PT, ET
Derby, Bristol, Yeovil, BroughtonAero-engines, aerostructures, helicopters, railAircraft Hangar, NDT Lab; ET, PT, UT, VT
Solent, Mersey, Milford HavenRefining, LNG, chemicals, marineOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; IRIS, PMI, UT, MFL

Aberdeen technicians spend much of their working lives offshore, where there is no spare bench time and no reference specimens to experiment on. Topsides piping corrosion, caisson and riser inspection, structural nodes and tank and vessel surveys on terminals are routine, and decommissioning adds condition checks before cutting and lifting. The Oil & Gas Site environment covers corrosion mapping with UT and PAUT, LRUT screening of pipe runs and ET on tubes, and the Storage Tank environment covers shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening for terminal work. Between hitches, a browser-based job is a practical way to keep a less-used method fresh. Atlantis also runs ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for Aberdeen employers that work to US codes or for US-owned operators.

Teesside combines old and new industry. The chemical parks need in-service inspection of pressure equipment and piping, with IRIS on exchanger tubes and PMI on alloy lines during shutdowns. New energy transition projects and fabrication yards bring weld inspection of new-build structures and pipework, where PAUT and TOFD in the Welding Workshop are the relevant practice. Trainees joining local inspection companies can start with guided NDT Lab fundamentals before moving on to plant jobs.

The Humber has two refineries in its recent history, gas-fired power, a very large port and offshore wind operations and maintenance bases. Plant inspection skills (thickness surveys, tank floor screening, exchanger tubes and alloy verification) are the core of the local workload, and the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments match them closely.

The Clyde and the Forth are dominated by naval shipbuilding and by the transition at Grangemouth. Shipyard weld inspection relies on UT, PAUT, MT and RT, all of which can be practised in the Welding Workshop on butt and fillet joints with realistic flaw types. Tank and terminal work at Grangemouth suits the Storage Tank environment. Atlantis has ASNT training pages for Glasgow and Edinburgh for employers who need SNT-TC-1A personnel.

Cumbria and Lancashire bring nuclear and defence quality regimes, where inspection techniques are tightly qualified and technicians must be consistent from shift to shift. Simulator practice does not replace those qualifications, but it gives staff extra repetitions on weld volumetric inspection and surface methods. Warton and Samlesbury aircraft work fits the Aircraft Hangar environment.

Derby, Bristol, Yeovil and Broughton are the aerospace heart of the UK. Penetrant inspection of engine components, eddy current around fastener holes, UT of composite and metallic structures and visual inspection of airframes all map to the Aircraft Hangar environment, which has 54 jobs. Rail work around Derby adds UT of axles and wheels, practised in the NDT Lab.

The Solent, Mersey and Milford Haven refinery and terminal coasts share the same core workload as the Humber, plus LNG storage and marine structures. Fawley, Stanlow and Pembroke turnarounds draw contractors from across the country, and a common scenario set helps supervisors check readiness before mobilisation. Atlantis also has an ASNT training page for London, where many engineering and inspection head offices sit.

Environments and methods that match UK work

Short answer: the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments match the North Sea, refinery and terminal work; the Welding Workshop matches shipbuilding, nuclear and energy-transition fabrication; the Aircraft Hangar matches the aerospace corridor; and the NDT Lab supports fundamentals and rail and component work.

The simulator has five workplace environments, twelve methods and 33 guided lessons. The methods are grouped the way most UK technicians already think about them: surface methods (PT, MT, VT), volumetric methods (UT contact, PAUT, TOFD, RT), electromagnetic methods (ET, MFL) and three specialist techniques that appear constantly in UK plant work, namely LRUT guided-wave screening, IRIS internal rotary UT for heat-exchanger and boiler tubes, and PMI for alloy verification.

  • Oil & Gas Site (73 jobs). Weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant. Relevant for offshore topsides, onshore terminals, refineries on the Solent, Mersey, Humber and Milford Haven, and chemical parks on Teesside and in the North West.
  • Storage Tank. UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank. Relevant to fuel terminals such as Grangemouth's post-refining operation, refinery tank farms and LNG and product storage at ports.
  • Welding Workshop (52 jobs). Weld coupons and fabrication joints. Relevant to shipyards on the Clyde, at Barrow, Rosyth and Birkenhead, to nuclear new build at Hinkley Point C, to offshore wind foundation fabrication and to pipeline and pressure-vessel fabrication shops.
  • Aircraft Hangar (54 jobs). Airframe and component inspection. Relevant to aero-engine, wing, helicopter and military aircraft work, and to MRO operations at airports.
  • NDT Lab (52 jobs). Bench specimens and reference blocks. Relevant to trainees, to apprentices in college programmes, to calibration and set-up practice and to component inspection in rail and precision engineering.

Two methods deserve a specific mention for UK users. TOFD and PAUT are now standard for weld inspection on thick-walled pressure equipment and on offshore wind monopile and transition-piece welds, and they take time to learn because set-up choices (probe angle, focal law, probe centre separation, scan plan) drive everything that follows. The simulator lets a technician make those set-up choices repeatedly and see the consequences. Radiography is the other: real exposures carry radiation protection obligations and need controlled areas, so practising film and digital image interpretation in a simulator is a safe way to build the interpretation side of the skill without a source anywhere near the trainee.

PCN, EN ISO 9712 and the UK rules technicians work under

Short answer: most UK NDT personnel are certified to EN ISO 9712, usually through PCN, the scheme administered by BINDT (the British Institute of Non-Destructive Testing). Aerospace work follows EN 4179 and employer approval. Practical NDT is practice for any of these schemes and is not a certification under any of them.

Personnel certification. PCN is the dominant third-party scheme in the UK, and many UK technicians also hold CSWIP or other certificates for weld inspection. Aerospace NDT personnel are qualified under EN 4179, with the employer's written procedures and Level 3 oversight. Some employers, particularly those working for US-owned operators, US OEMs or EPC contractors on US-code projects, also qualify staff to ASNT SNT-TC-1A through an employer written practice. Atlantis's own training covers ASNT SNT-TC-1A only. Atlantis does not offer PCN, EN ISO 9712, CSWIP or EN 4179 training or examinations, and the simulator is useful whichever scheme a technician is working towards.

Radiation protection. Industrial radiography in Great Britain falls under the Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017, enforced by the Health and Safety Executive. IRR17 uses a graded approach of notification, registration and consent, and industrial radiography is among the practices that need HSE consent. Holding radioactive sources also needs a permit from the environment regulator (the Environment Agency in England, Natural Resources Wales or SEPA in Scotland). Northern Ireland has its own equivalent regulations enforced by HSENI. A radiography employer's radiation protection adviser and local rules govern real exposures; the simulator involves no radiation at all.

Pressure equipment and plant. In-service pressure systems in Great Britain are covered by the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000, which require a written scheme of examination drawn up or certified by a competent person, and NDT is often part of those examinations. New pressure equipment placed on the market follows the Pressure Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016, which mirror the EU PED. Offshore installations operate under the Offshore Installations (Safety Case) Regulations 2015, with HSE's energy division as the regulator, and nuclear sites are regulated by the Office for Nuclear Regulation. Aviation maintenance is overseen by the Civil Aviation Authority.

Codes and standards. UK technicians routinely work to BS EN ISO standards for weld testing and acceptance levels (for example the ISO 17640 and ISO 11666 family for UT, ISO 17636 for RT, ISO 23277 for PT and ISO 17638 for MT), to PD 5500 and EN 13445 for pressure vessels, and to ASME and API codes on US-owned assets. The simulator does not certify compliance with any of these documents, but it trains the habits each of them depends on: correct set-up, consistent scanning, honest recording and careful sizing.

For help writing or reviewing procedures and written practices for UK sites that work to US codes, see NDT Level III consulting in the UK. If you need to track PCN, CSWIP, EN 4179 and ASNT certificates in one place, the Atlantis ERP for UK inspection companies records all of them alongside each other.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in the UK

Short answer: trainees use guided lessons to build fundamentals before supervised site work, working technicians use rare-defect jobs to stay sharp between assignments, and Level IIIs and team leads build scenario sets to benchmark crews and find coverage gaps.

Trainees and apprentices. The UK has a mix of routes into NDT: engineering apprenticeships, college courses, armed forces leavers, and people moving across from welding, fabrication or mechanical trades. All of them face the same bottleneck. Formal course hours give theory and a few days of supervised practical work, but the hours of experience required before certification are gained slowly on real jobs, and a trainee often watches more than they scan. The 33 guided lessons start in the NDT Lab with calibration, reference blocks and simple flaws, then move to weld coupons and plant jobs. A trainee arriving on site has already made the common mistakes in a place where they cost nothing.

Working technicians. Many UK technicians hold several methods but use two or three regularly. An offshore technician might do UT thickness and corrosion mapping for months and then be asked to do MT on a structural repair, or a refinery contractor might run IRIS once a year at turnaround. The jobs in the Oil & Gas Site and Welding Workshop include rare and hard-to-source defects (lack of sidewall fusion, transverse cracking, pitting under insulation, tube wall loss at baffles) that a technician might otherwise see only a handful of times in a career.

Level IIIs and team leads. A Level 3 or Level III responsible for a team can assemble scenario sets that reflect the work coming up, assign them before mobilisation and compare results objectively. That makes it easier to decide who goes on a critical job, where refresher training is needed and whether a procedure is clear enough for technicians to follow consistently. For inspection companies that run mixed crews, some PCN-certified and some ASNT-qualified, a common set of practice jobs is a neutral way to compare people.

Practice vs certification

Short answer: Practical NDT is a practice and readiness tool. It does not grant PCN, EN ISO 9712, EN 4179, CSWIP or ASNT certification, and it does not replace any practical examination on real specimens.

Every certification scheme used in the UK requires a practical examination on real specimens under controlled conditions, plus documented training and industrial experience. Under PCN that examination is run at an authorised qualifying body; under ASNT SNT-TC-1A it is run by the employer according to its written practice; under EN 4179 it is controlled by the employer's responsible Level 3 or an external agency. Simulator hours are not counted as industrial experience by any of these schemes unless an employer's own procedures say otherwise, and Atlantis makes no claim that they are.

What the simulator does is make those real examinations and real jobs less of a shock. A candidate who has already set up a PAUT scan plan dozens of times, interpreted a range of radiographic images and sized indications against acceptance criteria goes into the real exam with more confidence. An employer who has watched a technician's simulator scores over a few weeks has an extra piece of evidence when deciding whether that technician is ready. For formal training, see Atlantis NDT training, which is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only.

Offshore hitches, turnarounds and outages: why UK crews practise virtually

Short answer: UK inspection work arrives in concentrated bursts, from offshore campaigns to refinery turnarounds to nuclear and power outages, and technicians often go weeks between uses of a given method. A browser-based simulator fits the gaps.

The UK's inspection calendar is shaped by campaigns. Offshore work follows rotations and weather windows. Refinery and chemical turnarounds on the Solent, the Mersey, the Humber and Teesside pull in large contractor crews for a few intense weeks. Power stations and nuclear sites run planned outages where every day offline is expensive. In between, many technicians are on shorter or less varied jobs, and skills in the methods they are not using start to drift.

Physical practice is hard to arrange in those gaps. Reference specimens with realistic flaws are expensive and scarce, inspection company training rooms are busy, and offshore personnel are by definition away from them. A technician on leave in Inverness, Hull or Swansea is not going to drive to a lab to scan a weld coupon for an hour. Opening a simulator job at home or in a hotel room is a different proposition.

There is also the workforce question. Like the rest of Europe, the UK NDT sector has many experienced technicians approaching retirement and a steady need for new entrants, while offshore wind, nuclear new build and energy transition projects are adding work. Getting new people to a useful standard faster, and giving experienced people a structured way to pass on what good looks like, matters to every UK inspection manager. Scenario sets designed around real job types are one practical way to do that.

Finally, practice in a simulator is safe. There is no radiation, no work at height, no confined space entry and no hot work permit. Trainees can make mistakes that would be dangerous or expensive on a real site and learn from the score and feedback instead.

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and the scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. The product is affordable, accessible and fully customisable: inspection companies, operators, training providers and colleges in the UK can use it as it is or ask for scenario sets aligned to their own procedures and job mix.

A typical start looks like this. We hold a short call to understand your work, whether that is North Sea integrity, shipyard weld inspection, aerospace components or refinery turnarounds. We then show the matching environments live, agree a pilot group, and set up accounts so technicians can begin practising in a browser or app. Team leads get visibility of results so they can see progress and gaps. There is no hardware to install and no lab to book.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an NDT simulator I can use in the UK?

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app, so it can be used anywhere in England, Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, including offshore where connectivity allows. There is no UK centre to visit; access is online, and demos are arranged through the contact form.

Does Practical NDT count towards PCN certification?

No. PCN certification to EN ISO 9712 requires training, documented industrial experience and examinations at an authorised qualifying body. Simulator practice can help a candidate prepare, but it is not part of the PCN scheme and Atlantis does not offer PCN training or exams.

Can it help with NDT practical exam preparation?

Yes, as preparation. Repeated set-up, scanning, interpretation and sizing jobs build the confidence and habits a practical exam tests. The exam itself must still be taken on real specimens under the rules of the relevant scheme.

Is it useful for North Sea and offshore wind inspection?

Yes. The Oil & Gas Site environment covers corrosion mapping, weld inspection, tube inspection and LRUT screening, and the Welding Workshop covers PAUT and TOFD on thick welds of the kind found in monopiles, transition pieces and jackets.

Does it cover aerospace NDT for UK manufacturers and MROs?

Yes. The Aircraft Hangar environment has 54 jobs covering airframe and component inspection with ET, PT, UT and VT. It does not replace EN 4179 qualification or the employer's own practical examinations.

Does it include radiography?

Yes. RT is one of the twelve methods, focused on technique and image interpretation. No radiation is involved, so there are no IRR17 obligations for simulator practice; real exposures remain subject to HSE consent and the employer's local rules.

Can a UK inspection company use it to benchmark new hires?

Yes. Level IIIs and team leads can assign the same scenario set to every candidate or new starter and compare scores objectively, which helps decide who is ready for which job.

What experience level is it for?

All levels: new trainees and apprentices on guided lessons, working technicians refreshing rarely used methods and rare defects, and Level IIIs building and assigning scenario sets.

Does Atlantis offer ASNT training in the UK?

Yes, ASNT SNT-TC-1A training only, delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility for employers who need SNT-TC-1A personnel, for example on US-owned assets or US-code projects. See Atlantis training.

Is it relevant for nuclear work at Sellafield, Hinkley Point C or Barrow?

It can support practice in the methods used there, especially volumetric weld inspection and surface methods. Nuclear and defence sites have their own qualified techniques and personnel requirements, which the simulator does not replace.

Request a demo. We will show the environments that fit your work and agree a pilot. Pricing is quote on request.

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in Victoria, Australia

Victoria's inspection work is a mix of old and new. It includes a refinery on Corio Bay, ageing Bass Strait platforms and the gas plants that serve them, brown coal power stations in the Latrobe Valley, an aluminium smelter at Portland, aerostructure manufacturing and defence work around Melbourne, and offshore wind starting off Gippsland. Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and the Atlantis Practical NDT simulator gives Victorian technicians somewhere to practise all of it. It is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. A technician opens a job in a virtual NDT lab, welding workshop, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank, sets up the technique, carries out the inspection, records the result and gets a score and feedback as soon as the job closes. It works for a first-year trainee, a Level II who has not run a particular method for months, and a Level III building scenario sets for a crew.

This is the hub page for Victoria, Australia (not Victoria in Texas or British Columbia). It covers where Victorian NDT work is, how the simulator's environments and methods fit that work, the regulators and standards Victorian technicians work under, and how to arrange a demo. It links the Melbourne Practical NDT page and the other Atlantis pages for Melbourne and Geelong.

Victoria's NDT workforce and where the work is

Short answer: Victorian NDT work clusters in five places: Geelong and Corio Bay (refining, port, defence storage, Avalon aviation); Melbourne and the western industrial suburbs (port, fuel terminals, chemicals, aerospace, shipbuilding, infrastructure); Gippsland and Bass Strait (offshore oil and gas, gas processing, decommissioning, offshore wind); the Latrobe Valley (brown coal power); and the regions, including Portland, Bendigo and Ballarat.

Geelong and Corio Bay. The refinery at Corio, on the northern edge of Geelong, is one of only two oil refineries still operating in Australia, and it is the largest single source of process plant inspection work in the state. Turnarounds there bring in large crews for corrosion mapping, weld inspection, exchanger tube inspection, alloy verification and tank surveys. The Port of Geelong handles fuel, grain, fertiliser and bulk cargo, and defence explosives are handled at Point Wilson nearby. Avalon Airport, between Geelong and Melbourne, has aircraft maintenance hangars and hosts a major international airshow.

Melbourne and the west. The Port of Melbourne is Australia's busiest container port. Along the western side of the bay, the former refinery at Altona now operates as a fuel import terminal, and the surrounding area has chemical and fuel storage facilities, although Altona's petrochemical industry has contracted in recent years. Fishermans Bend hosts aerostructure manufacturing for commercial aircraft and defence technology work, and Williamstown has a long history of naval shipbuilding, including frigates for the Royal Australian Navy. Melbourne's large infrastructure programme of rail tunnels, motorway tunnels and bridges adds structural steel and welding inspection. Melbourne Airport and the general aviation fields around the city carry out aircraft maintenance, and RAAF Base Point Cook and RAAF Base East Sale add military aviation.

Gippsland and Bass Strait. Since the late 1960s, Bass Strait's Gippsland Basin has supplied a large share of south-eastern Australia's oil and gas through offshore platforms, subsea pipelines, the gas plants at Longford and the liquids processing facility at Long Island Point near Hastings. The fields are mature, and a large decommissioning programme is now under way, while remaining gas production continues. Offshore inspection of ageing structures, pipeline integrity, gas plant turnarounds and pre-removal condition surveys all need NDT. The waters off Gippsland have also been declared Australia's first offshore wind zone, and future wind projects will bring fabrication and foundation weld inspection.

The Latrobe Valley. The brown coal power stations at Yallourn and Loy Yang supply a large share of Victoria's electricity, and their boilers, headers, steam pipework, mills and coal conveyors need inspection during planned outages. These stations are heading towards closure over the coming years, but until then condition assessment and life management keep inspection crews busy, and the transition itself brings new work in grid batteries, transmission and potential renewable projects.

The regions. Portland in the south-west has an aluminium smelter and a deep-water port, and the Otway Basin around Port Campbell has gas production and storage. Bendigo builds protected military vehicles and has engineering manufacturing, and Ballarat has manufacturing, rail workshops and gold mining history. Regional food processing plants, from dairies to breweries, have stainless steel pressure equipment, boilers and refrigeration plant that need periodic inspection.

Practical NDT by city in Victoria

Short answer: Melbourne has its own Practical NDT page, and Geelong has related Atlantis pages. The table maps these and Victoria's other main centres to the environments and methods that fit their industries.

Melbourne has the most varied NDT workload in the state. Aerostructure manufacturing at Fishermans Bend and aircraft maintenance at the airports suit the Aircraft Hangar environment's 54 jobs, with eddy current, penetrant and ultrasonic inspection of airframes and components. Port fuel terminals suit the Storage Tank environment, and shipbuilding, structural steel and tunnelling projects suit the Welding Workshop. Atlantis has ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for Melbourne employers, Level III consulting in Melbourne, a third-party inspection page for Melbourne and an ERP page for Melbourne inspection companies.

Geelong is defined by the Corio refinery. Its turnarounds call for PAUT corrosion mapping, IRIS on exchanger and air-cooler tubes, PMI on alloy piping, LRUT screening of long pipe runs and tank inspection, which is exactly the mix the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments cover. Avalon adds aviation work. Related pages: NDT ERP for Geelong and the Geelong digital twin page.

Altona and the western suburbs have fuel import storage and chemical and fuel tank farms. Tank shell thickness surveys, MFL floor screening and piping corrosion surveys are the core work, and inspection crews here often also work Geelong turnarounds.

Sale, Longford and Hastings serve Bass Strait. Gas plant piping and vessels, exchanger tubes, subsea and onshore pipelines and offshore structures need corrosion and weld inspection, and the decommissioning programme adds condition surveys before cutting and lifting. Technicians rotating offshore have little chance to practise less-used methods between hitches, which is where a browser-based simulator helps.

The Latrobe Valley is about boilers and coal handling. Boiler tubes, headers, steam pipework and mills are inspected during outages using UT thickness, IRIS where tube access allows, MT and PT on welds and attachments, and visual inspection. The coal mines and conveyors add structural crack detection.

Portland and the Otway coast combine the aluminium smelter's heavy plant and port facilities with gas production and storage near Port Campbell. Pressure equipment, tanks, structures and piping all need periodic inspection.

Bendigo and Ballarat are manufacturing centres. Armoured vehicle hulls, fabricated structures, rail components and mining equipment need weld inspection with MT, UT, PT and VT, and regional technicians benefit from practice that does not require a trip to Melbourne.

Environments and methods that match Victorian work

Short answer: the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank fit Corio refinery, the Altona terminal, Bass Strait gas plants and power station boilers; the Welding Workshop fits shipbuilding, defence vehicles, offshore wind and infrastructure; the Aircraft Hangar fits aerostructures and aviation maintenance; and the NDT Lab supports trainees and components.

The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator has five workplace environments, twelve methods and 33 guided lessons. The methods are surface (PT, MT, VT), volumetric (UT contact, PAUT, TOFD, RT), electromagnetic (ET, MFL), and three specialist techniques: LRUT guided-wave screening, IRIS internal rotary UT for heat-exchanger and boiler tubes, and PMI for alloy verification.

  • Oil & Gas Site (73 jobs). Weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant, matching the Corio refinery, the Longford gas plants and Long Island Point, the Otway gas facilities and chemical plants.
  • Storage Tank. UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank, matching the refinery tank farm, the Altona and port fuel terminals and gas liquids storage.
  • Welding Workshop (52 jobs). Weld coupons and fabrication joints, relevant to naval shipbuilding and repair, defence vehicle manufacturing in Bendigo, structural steel for Melbourne's tunnels and bridges, future offshore wind foundations and general fabrication.
  • Aircraft Hangar (54 jobs). Airframe and component inspection for aerostructure manufacturing at Fishermans Bend, maintenance at Melbourne and Avalon airports, and military aviation at Point Cook and East Sale.
  • NDT Lab (52 jobs). Bench specimens and reference blocks for trainees, TAFE students, calibration practice and component inspection.

Three methods stand out for Victoria. IRIS matters at the refinery and gas plants, where exchanger bundles are a large part of every turnaround scope, and in power station work. Eddy current matters for aerostructures and aircraft maintenance, where signal interpretation takes many repetitions to master. PAUT and TOFD matter for thick welds in pressure equipment, shipbuilding and future offshore wind foundations. Each can be practised repeatedly with realistic defects and instant scoring. Radiography can also be practised for technique and image interpretation with no radiation involved.

Regulators and requirements Victorian technicians meet

Short answer: AINDT certification, based on ISO 9712, is the local norm for Victorian NDT personnel, with ASNT SNT-TC-1A used by some employers and aerospace schemes in aviation. Radiography is licensed by the Department of Health under the Radiation Act 2005. WorkSafe Victoria covers workplace and plant safety, Energy Safe Victoria covers gas and pipeline safety, and NOPSEMA regulates offshore facilities in Commonwealth waters. Practical NDT is practice for any scheme.

Personnel certification. Victorian employers and asset owners usually specify AINDT certification for NDT technicians. Aviation NDT follows aerospace employer schemes under the maintenance organisation's approval from the Civil Aviation Safety Authority, and military aviation follows defence requirements. Some employers on US-code work, or supplying US-owned facilities and OEMs, qualify staff under ASNT SNT-TC-1A through a written practice. Atlantis trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A only and does not offer AINDT, ISO 9712 or aerospace scheme training or exams; the simulator is useful whichever scheme a technician is working towards. See ASNT training in Australia.

Radiation safety. Industrial radiography in Victoria is regulated under the Radiation Act 2005 (Vic), administered by the Department of Health. Businesses need a management licence for the radiation practice, and individuals who use sources or X-ray equipment for radiography need a use licence. ARPANSA publishes national codes that inform state requirements. Confirm current licence conditions with the Department of Health before any real exposure. Simulator practice involves no radiation.

Plant, pressure equipment, gas and offshore. WorkSafe Victoria administers the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 and its regulations, including registration of certain plant designs and items such as boilers and pressure vessels, and the licensing of major hazard facilities such as refineries and large fuel storage. Energy Safe Victoria regulates gas and pipeline safety. Offshore facilities in Commonwealth waters, including most of Bass Strait, are regulated by NOPSEMA, while state waters and onshore resources have their own state regime. Pressure equipment is commonly designed and inspected to AS 1210, AS 4041, AS 4037 and AS/NZS 3788, and pipelines to AS 2885.

Codes and standards. Victorian technicians work to Australian Standards and AS ISO adoptions for the individual methods, to AS/NZS 1554 for structural welding, to aerospace manufacturer manuals for aviation work, and on some refinery and gas work to API and ASME codes. The simulator does not certify compliance with any of them; it trains the habits they depend on: calibration, coverage, recording and sizing.

For written practices and procedures on Victorian sites working to US codes, see NDT Level III consulting in Melbourne or the national NDT consulting page for Australia.

Turnarounds, decommissioning and the energy transition: why Victorian crews practise virtually

Short answer: Victorian inspection demand comes in peaks around refinery turnarounds, gas plant shutdowns, power station outages and offshore campaigns, while the state's energy mix is shifting fast. A browser-based simulator keeps less-used skills fresh between peaks and helps crews move between sectors.

A Victorian inspection technician's year often looks like a series of campaigns: a turnaround at Corio, a Longford shutdown, an outage at a Latrobe Valley station, an offshore decommissioning survey, a stretch of fabrication work in Melbourne. Each campaign leans on different methods, and the methods a technician has not used for months are the ones that drift. The first shift of a turnaround is a poor time to rediscover how a particular IRIS or PAUT set-up behaves.

Victoria's energy transition makes this sharper. Brown coal stations are heading towards closure, Bass Strait is moving from production to decommissioning, and offshore wind, transmission and storage projects are arriving. Inspection companies need to move technicians between sectors and teach them methods they have not used before. Physical practice is costly: reference specimens with realistic defects are expensive and training rooms are busy. A simulator job on a laptop is easy to assign, and a supervisor can match it to the exact scope of the next campaign.

The workforce question is familiar too. Experienced technicians who learned on Bass Strait and in the Latrobe Valley are approaching retirement, and new entrants arrive from TAFE courses, trades, defence and overseas. A shared scenario library helps new people become useful faster and gives experienced people a structured way to show what good inspection looks like.

Finally, practice in a simulator is safe. There is no confined space entry, no work at height, no offshore transfer and no radiation. Mistakes cost a lower score and a chance to try again.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in Victoria

Short answer: trainees follow the 33 guided lessons from bench fundamentals to plant and aircraft jobs, working technicians keep rare defects and less-used methods fresh between campaigns, and Level IIIs build and assign scenario sets to benchmark crews objectively.

Trainees. Victorian NDT trainees come from TAFE engineering courses, aircraft maintenance pathways, boilermaker and fitter apprenticeships, defence careers and other industries. The logged experience required for certification takes time, and on a busy turnaround a trainee often watches more than they inspect. The guided lessons start in the NDT Lab with calibration and simple flaws and progress to weld coupons, process plant, tank and aircraft jobs, so a trainee arrives on site with real familiarity with the steps.

Working technicians. A Level II who spends most of the year on thickness surveys may be asked to run PAUT on a weld or IRIS on a bundle at the next turnaround; an aviation technician who mostly does eddy current may meet an unfamiliar penetrant job. Rare-defect refreshers help: lack of fusion, hydrogen-related cracking, isolated tube pitting, corrosion under a fastener, a wrong alloy in a spool.

Level IIIs and team leads. A Level III can build scenario sets that reflect a campaign's scope, assign them to employees and contractors, compare results objectively and identify coverage gaps before mobilisation. The results add evidence alongside the employer's own practical assessments rather than replacing them.

Practice vs certification

Short answer: the Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is a practice and readiness tool. It does not grant AINDT, ISO 9712, aerospace or ASNT certification and does not replace any practical examination on real specimens.

Every NDT certification scheme used in Victoria requires training, documented industrial experience and a practical examination on real specimens. Under AINDT certification the examination follows the scheme's rules; under ASNT SNT-TC-1A it is administered by the employer according to its written practice under a Level III. Simulator time is not counted as industrial experience by these schemes unless an employer's own procedures say so, and Atlantis makes no such claim.

What the simulator does is reduce the distance between knowing and doing. A candidate who has carried out many set-ups, scans and interpretations goes into the practical exam with fewer surprises, and a supervisor who has watched a technician's results over several weeks can judge readiness better. For formal training, see Atlantis NDT training, which is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only and delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility.

The product is affordable, accessible and fully customizable: inspection companies in Geelong, Gippsland and Melbourne, aviation maintenance organisations, training providers, TAFE programmes and asset owners' integrity teams can use it as it is or ask for scenario sets aligned to their procedures and job mix.
