h1: NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in Western Australia
contentHtml:
HomeTrainingConsultingERPPractical NDTContact

NDT Simulator & Practical NDT Training in Western Australia

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and Western Australia is one of the places where that idea makes the most sense. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator is an immersive, 3D, game-like platform that runs in a browser or app. A technician opens a job in a virtual NDT lab, welding workshop, aircraft hangar, oil and gas site or full-size storage tank, sets up the technique, scans or exposes or applies the method, records the indications, and gets a score the moment the job is closed. In Western Australia the inspection workforce is spread across a state the size of Western Europe: LNG trains and offshore platforms on the North West Shelf, iron ore railways, car dumpers and ship loaders in the Pilbara, alumina and lithium refineries south of Perth, the Kwinana industrial strip, shipyards at Henderson, and gold and nickel operations in the Goldfields. Many of the people doing that work fly in and fly out on rosters, and they cannot carry a reference block home. A browser-based practice environment travels with them.

This is the Western Australia hub for Practical NDT. It maps where the state's NDT work actually happens, which simulator environments and methods suit each region, how simulator practice sits alongside AINDT certification and the other schemes used in the state, and how to arrange a demo for a WA crew. It links the city pages Atlantis already has for Perth and the surrounding region.

Western Australia's NDT workforce and where the work is

Short answer: WA inspection demand sits in five clusters: the Pilbara LNG and iron ore coast (Karratha, Dampier, Port Hedland, Onslow), the offshore Carnarvon and Browse basins, the Perth metropolitan area with the Kwinana and Henderson industrial strips, the South West alumina, lithium and power belt, and the Goldfields mining district. Each leans on a different mix of methods.

The Pilbara coast and the North West Shelf. Karratha and the Burrup Peninsula are the centre of Australia's oldest LNG province. The North West Shelf project's Karratha Gas Plant, Pluto LNG next door, and the domestic gas plants that feed the Dampier to Bunbury Natural Gas Pipeline together carry an enormous amount of pressure equipment, cryogenic piping, heat exchangers and storage. Further west, Wheatstone sits near Onslow and Gorgon on Barrow Island. Shutdown and turnaround campaigns at these plants bring in large inspection crews for intense, short windows, and the methods that dominate are ultrasonic thickness and corrosion mapping, phased array and TOFD on welds, radiography of piping, IRIS on exchanger tubes, and PMI on alloy lines.

Iron ore from mine to ship. The Pilbara iron ore system is the other half of the north-west economy. Heavy haul railways, car dumpers, stackers, reclaimers, ship loaders, crushers and conveyors run from inland mines to the export ports at Port Hedland, Dampier and Cape Lambert. Port Hedland handles more bulk tonnage than any other port in Australia. The NDT work here is dominated by structural steel and rotating equipment: magnetic particle and penetrant testing of welds and cracks on fatigue-loaded structures, ultrasonic testing of shafts, pins and wheelsets, and visual inspection of large welded fabrications. Fatigue cracking in mobile plant and fixed structures is a constant concern.

Offshore basins. Offshore facilities in Commonwealth waters off WA, including fixed platforms, subsea infrastructure and floating LNG and production units, need corrosion monitoring, weld inspection and structural surveys. Inspection technicians rotate offshore from Perth and the north-west towns, often by helicopter from Karratha or Broome, and the work is planned around production and weather windows.

Perth, Kwinana and Henderson. The Perth metropolitan area is where most WA inspection companies have their head offices, laboratories and fabrication customers. The Kwinana industrial area on Cockburn Sound has a former refinery that now operates as a fuel import terminal, alumina refining history, chemical and fertiliser plants, a power station, and newer lithium hydroxide refining. Just north, the Australian Marine Complex at Henderson is the state's shipbuilding and offshore fabrication hub, building and maintaining patrol boats, ferries, naval vessels and modules for resources projects. Garden Island off Rockingham hosts Fleet Base West at HMAS Stirling, the home of the Collins class submarines, and the base is being expanded for future submarine work.

The South West and the Goldfields. South of Perth, the alumina refineries around Pinjarra and Wagerup, lithium processing at Kemerton, mineral sands, the Bunbury port and the coal-fired power stations at Collie all keep shutdown and maintenance inspectors busy. East of Perth, Kalgoorlie-Boulder and the wider Goldfields host gold mining and processing, nickel operations, and the long pipelines that supply them with gas and water. Mining fixed plant, mills, tanks, pressure vessels in processing plants, and heavy mobile equipment generate steady MT, PT, UT and VT work.

Practical NDT by city in Western Australia

Short answer: Perth already has its own Practical NDT page. The table below covers Perth and the other WA centres where NDT work concentrates, with the simulator environments and methods that suit each one. Links go to Atlantis pages that exist for each place.

City or areaMain local sectorsEnvironments & methods to practise
PerthInspection company head offices, fabrication, resources engineering, aviationNDT Lab, Welding Workshop, Aircraft Hangar; UT, PAUT, TOFD, MT, PT, ET
Karratha and DampierLNG, domestic gas, offshore support, iron ore portOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; UT, PAUT, IRIS, PMI, RT, MFL
Port HedlandIron ore export, rail, ship loaders, powerWelding Workshop, NDT Lab; MT, PT, UT, VT
Kwinana and RockinghamFuel terminal, alumina, lithium, chemicals, powerOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; UT, IRIS, PMI, MFL, LRUT
Henderson and Garden IslandShipbuilding, offshore fabrication, naval maintenanceWelding Workshop; PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, VT
Onslow and Barrow IslandLNG and domestic gas plantsOil & Gas Site; PAUT, IRIS, PMI, LRUT
Kalgoorlie and the GoldfieldsGold and nickel processing, mobile plant, pipelinesNDT Lab, Welding Workshop, Storage Tank; MT, PT, UT
Bunbury, Collie and the South WestAlumina, lithium, port, power stationsOil & Gas Site, Storage Tank; UT, IRIS, PMI, MFL

Perth is where most WA technicians are recruited, trained and based between rosters. It is also where inspection companies run their laboratories, so trainees often learn bench fundamentals there before their first site mobilisation. The NDT Lab's 52 jobs cover calibration, reference blocks and simple flaw detection, and the Welding Workshop builds the weld inspection skills that fabrication shops in Welshpool, Kewdale and Bibra Lake rely on. Perth Airport's maintenance hangars add aviation work that fits the Aircraft Hangar environment. Atlantis also has ASNT SNT-TC-1A training for Perth employers and Level III consulting in Perth.

Karratha and Dampier run on LNG and gas processing. Corrosion under insulation, thickness loss on piping and vessels, cryogenic weld inspection, exchanger tube inspection and alloy verification during turnarounds are the core work, which is exactly what the Oil & Gas Site environment's 73 jobs are built around. Tank farms and condensate storage suit the Storage Tank environment. See also ASNT training in Karratha and third-party inspection in Karratha for local context.

Port Hedland is iron ore country. The structures are huge and fatigue-loaded, and a large share of inspection is crack detection on welds, pins and lugs, conveyor and stacker structures, car dumpers and rail wagons. MT and PT practice on fabrication joints in the Welding Workshop, plus UT of shafts and pins in the NDT Lab, map well to this work. Atlantis has a Level III consulting page for Port Hedland.

Kwinana and Rockingham combine an older refining and alumina base with newer lithium processing. Plant inspection skills dominate: thickness surveys, tank shell and floor surveys, exchanger tubes, PMI on alloy piping, and guided-wave screening of long pipe runs and road crossings. The Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments cover this mix. Related Atlantis pages: NDT ERP for Kwinana inspection companies.

Henderson and Garden Island are about welding quality. Shipyards and offshore fabrication yards inspect butt and fillet welds on hull blocks, modules and structures, using UT, PAUT, MT and RT. The Welding Workshop lets a technician practise scan plans, probe angles and indication sizing on realistic weld coupons before going to a block or a module.

Onslow and Barrow Island are remote LNG and domestic gas sites where crews are accommodated in camps and every day of a shutdown counts. Arriving with recently practised PAUT corrosion mapping, IRIS and PMI skills matters more there than almost anywhere else in the state.

Kalgoorlie and the Goldfields generate mining maintenance work: crack detection on mobile plant, mill and crusher components, processing tanks and pressure vessels, and long-distance pipelines. MT, PT and UT fundamentals and weld inspection are the core skills, and a browser-based simulator is easy to use from a regional town where formal NDT practical facilities are scarce.

Bunbury, Collie and the South West have alumina digesters and calciners, lithium hydroxide plants, port facilities and coal-fired power. Boiler tubes, heat exchangers, tanks and piping drive the local workload, so IRIS, UT thickness, MFL tank floor screening and PMI are the methods to keep fresh.

Environments and methods that match Western Australia work

Short answer: the Oil & Gas Site and Storage Tank environments match LNG, gas processing, refining terminals and alumina and lithium plants; the Welding Workshop matches iron ore structures, shipyards and fabrication; the NDT Lab supports fundamentals and component work; and the Aircraft Hangar covers aviation and defence aircraft maintenance.

The simulator has five workplace environments, twelve methods and 33 guided lessons. The methods fall into four groups: surface (PT, MT, VT), volumetric (UT contact, PAUT, TOFD, RT), electromagnetic (ET, MFL), and three specialist techniques that WA plant crews use constantly, namely LRUT guided-wave screening, IRIS internal rotary UT for heat-exchanger and boiler tubes, and PMI for alloy verification.

  • Oil & Gas Site (73 jobs). Weld, corrosion, tube and screening practice in a process plant. Relevant to the Karratha, Pluto, Gorgon and Wheatstone plants, to domestic gas plants, to the Kwinana terminal and chemical plants, and to alumina and lithium refineries in the South West.
  • Storage Tank. UT shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening on a full-size tank. Relevant to condensate and product storage on the Burrup, fuel import storage at Kwinana, process tanks at alumina refineries, and water and process tanks on mine sites.
  • Welding Workshop (52 jobs). Weld coupons and fabrication joints. Relevant to the Henderson shipyards, Perth and Pilbara fabrication shops, iron ore structures and mobile plant repairs, and pipeline construction.
  • NDT Lab (52 jobs). Bench specimens and reference blocks. Relevant to trainees, to TAFE and inspection company trainee programmes, to calibration and set-up practice, and to component inspection of shafts, pins and castings.
  • Aircraft Hangar (54 jobs). Airframe and component inspection. Relevant to aviation maintenance at Perth Airport and Jandakot, to the fly-in fly-out charter fleet that serves the mines, and to defence aircraft work at RAAF Base Pearce.

Three methods deserve a closer look for WA users. PAUT and TOFD have become standard on thick-wall pressure equipment and on new-build piping in LNG and gas projects, and they are hard to learn because set-up drives everything: focal laws, probe centre separation, scan plans and coverage. The simulator lets a technician make those decisions again and again and see the result. IRIS is the method of choice for exchanger and air-cooler tube inspection during shutdowns, and good IRIS data interpretation depends on having seen many wall-loss and pitting patterns. MT is everywhere in iron ore and mining, and practising it on realistic fatigue cracks at weld toes and in heat-affected zones builds the eye that finds small indications on big structures.

Radiography deserves a mention too. Real exposures in WA need a licensed radiographer, controlled areas and careful planning, especially in an operating plant. Practising image interpretation and technique selection in the simulator involves no radiation at all.

Regulators and requirements Western Australia technicians meet

Short answer: most WA NDT personnel hold AINDT certification, the Australian Institute for Non-Destructive Testing scheme based on ISO 9712, and work to Australian Standards. Some employers on US-code projects also use ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Radiography is licensed under the state Radiation Safety Act, and plant safety sits with WorkSafe WA, with offshore safety under NOPSEMA. Practical NDT is practice for any of these schemes and certifies nobody.

Personnel certification. AINDT certification is the local norm for NDT technicians in Australia, and many WA employers specify it in contracts. Some operators and EPC contractors working to US codes or for US-owned facilities also qualify staff under ASNT SNT-TC-1A through an employer written practice, and aerospace NDT follows aerospace-specific employer schemes. Atlantis's own training covers ASNT SNT-TC-1A only. Atlantis does not offer AINDT or ISO 9712 training or examinations, and the simulator is useful whichever scheme a technician is working towards. For the US-code side, see ASNT training in Australia and the blog on ASNT certification for FIFO NDT technicians in Western Australia.

Radiation safety. Industrial radiography in Western Australia is regulated under the Radiation Safety Act 1975 (WA), administered by the Radiological Council with support from the Department of Health. People who use radioactive sources or X-ray equipment need a licence, and the equipment and premises need registration. National guidance published by ARPANSA, the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency, informs the state requirements. Confirm current licence conditions with the Radiological Council before any real exposure work. The simulator involves no radiation and needs no licence.

Plant, pressure equipment and petroleum. Onshore workplace safety in WA falls under the Work Health and Safety Act 2020 (WA), which commenced in 2022, regulated by WorkSafe WA within the Department of Energy, Mines, Industry Regulation and Safety (DEMIRS). Mines operate under the mines WHS regulations, also administered by DEMIRS, and onshore petroleum and major hazard facilities have their own regimes. Offshore facilities in Commonwealth waters are regulated by NOPSEMA. Pressure equipment is commonly designed and inspected to AS 1210 for vessels, AS 4041 for piping, AS 4037 for examination and testing, and AS/NZS 3788 for in-service inspection, while pipelines follow AS 2885.

Codes and standards. WA technicians routinely work to Australian Standards and AS ISO adoptions for UT, RT, MT, PT and VT of welds and components, to AS/NZS 1554 for structural steel welding, and on many LNG and gas projects to ASME and API codes as well. The simulator does not certify compliance with any of these documents, but it trains the habits each depends on: correct calibration and set-up, consistent coverage, honest recording and careful sizing against acceptance criteria.

For procedures and written practices on WA sites working to US codes, see NDT Level III consulting in Perth. If you need to track AINDT and ASNT certificates side by side, see the Atlantis ERP for Western Australian inspection companies and the pages for Karratha and Port Hedland.

FIFO rosters, remote camps and shutdowns: why WA crews practise virtually

Short answer: WA inspection work comes in bursts on remote sites, and technicians can go weeks without using a given method. A simulator that runs in a browser or app fits around fly-in fly-out rosters, camp downtime and the gaps between shutdowns, with no reference specimens, lab bookings or radiation involved.

Much of the state's inspection work is done by people who live in Perth, Bunbury or interstate and fly to the Pilbara, Barrow Island, the Goldfields or offshore on a roster. A typical pattern is two or more weeks on site followed by time at home. On site, a technician may spend a whole swing on one or two methods; at home, there is no practical NDT equipment at all. Skills in the methods not being used start to drift, and the first day of the next shutdown is a bad time to rediscover how a particular PAUT set-up works.

Physical practice is hard to arrange in WA's gaps. Reference specimens with realistic flaws are expensive, inspection company training rooms in Perth are often busy, and nothing practical exists in a mining camp. Opening a simulator job on a laptop in a donga or at home on a rest day is a different proposition. A team lead can assign the job mix the crew will meet on the next mobilisation, for example exchanger tube inspection before a gas plant turnaround or weld crack detection before a port shutdown, and see who has completed it before the flight.

There is also the workforce question. WA competes with every other resources state, and with overseas projects, for experienced NDT technicians. New entrants arrive from trades, the defence force and interstate, and they need to become useful quickly. Experienced technicians approaching retirement carry knowledge that is hard to pass on during a busy shutdown. Scenario sets designed around real WA job types are one practical way to speed up the first and capture some of the second.

Finally, practice in a simulator is safe. There is no work at height, no confined space, no hot work, no heat stress on a Pilbara summer afternoon, and no radiation. Trainees can make the mistakes that would be dangerous or expensive on a real site and learn from the score and feedback instead.

For trainees, working technicians and Level IIIs in Western Australia

Short answer: trainees use the 33 guided lessons to build fundamentals before supervised site work, working technicians use rare-defect jobs to stay sharp between rosters, and Level IIIs and team leads build scenario sets to benchmark crews before a mobilisation and find gaps in coverage.

Trainees. People come into WA NDT from many directions: TAFE engineering and trade courses, apprenticeships in fabrication and maintenance, defence force careers, and career changers moving across from welding, rigging or plant operation. The bottleneck is always the same. Course hours give theory and a few days of supervised practical work, but the logged experience required for certification is gained slowly, and on a busy site a trainee often watches more than they scan. The guided lessons start in the NDT Lab with calibration, reference blocks and simple flaws, then move on to weld coupons and plant jobs, so a trainee reaches site having already made the common mistakes somewhere they cost nothing.

Working technicians. An experienced Level II may be excellent at the methods used on every job and rusty at the ones that come up twice a year. Rare-defect refreshers between rosters help: lack of fusion in a root, a lamination near a nozzle, cracking at a weld toe on a stacker boom, isolated pitting on an exchanger tube, a wrong alloy in a piping spool. Running through those scenarios on a rest day keeps them in memory for when they appear for real.

Level IIIs and team leads. A Level III responsible for a WA crew can build and assign scenario sets, compare results objectively across technicians, and see where a team's coverage is thin before a campaign starts. That is useful when mixing contractors from different employers on a shutdown, when bringing interstate or overseas technicians into a WA team, and when deciding who is ready for a particular job. It gives an extra piece of evidence alongside the employer's own practical assessments, not a replacement for them.

Practice vs certification

Short answer: Practical NDT is a practice and readiness tool. It does not grant AINDT, ISO 9712 or ASNT certification and does not replace any practical examination on real specimens.

Every certification scheme used in Western Australia requires a practical examination on real specimens under controlled conditions, together with documented training and industrial experience. Under AINDT certification that examination is run under the scheme's own rules; under ASNT SNT-TC-1A it is run by the employer according to its written practice, supervised by a Level III. Simulator hours are not counted as industrial experience by any of these schemes unless an employer's own procedures say otherwise, and Atlantis makes no claim that they are.

What the simulator does is make the real exam, and the real first job, less of a shock. A candidate who has already set up a PAUT scan plan dozens of times, interpreted a range of radiographic images, worked through IRIS data and sized indications against acceptance criteria goes into a practical with more confidence. An employer who has watched a technician's simulator results over several weeks has more to go on when deciding who is ready. For formal training, see Atlantis NDT training, which is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only and delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility.

Bring Practical NDT to your Western Australia team

Short answer: request a demo, tell us which WA sectors and methods matter to your crew, and Atlantis will walk through the matching environments and set up a trial scenario set. Pricing is quote on request.

Atlantis built the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal for practice and hands-on experience, and its scenario library was designed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. The product is affordable, accessible and fully customizable: inspection companies, operators, labour hire firms, training providers and TAFE programmes in Western Australia can use it as it is or ask for scenario sets aligned to their own procedures and job mix. There is no WA centre to visit; everything runs online.

A typical start is simple. A short call establishes what your crews do, whether that is LNG turnarounds on the Burrup, port and rail structures in the Pilbara, shipyard welds at Henderson or mining maintenance in the Goldfields. Atlantis then shows the matching environments live, you choose a pilot group, and accounts are set up so technicians can practise in a browser or app wherever they are on their roster. Team leads see results and progress. There is no hardware to install and no lab to book, and time zone differences are handled by scheduling the demo to suit Perth hours.

  • Request a Practical NDT demo for your Western Australia team
  • Ask for a WA quote for a shutdown crew, a trainee cohort or a whole company
  • Discuss a custom scenario set for LNG, iron ore, mining or shipyard work

Read the Practical NDT overview for the full list of environments and methods.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an NDT simulator I can use in Western Australia?

Yes. The Atlantis Practical NDT simulator runs in a browser or app, so it works in Perth, in a Pilbara camp, in Kalgoorlie or at home between rosters, wherever there is a connection. There is no physical centre to visit. Demos are arranged through the contact form.

Does Practical NDT count towards AINDT certification?

No. AINDT certification requires training, documented industrial experience and examinations under the scheme's rules, including a practical on real specimens. Simulator practice can help a candidate prepare, but it is not part of the AINDT scheme, and Atlantis does not offer AINDT or ISO 9712 training or exams.

Can it help with NDT practical exam preparation?

Yes, as preparation. Repeated set-up, scanning, interpretation and sizing jobs build the habits a practical exam tests. The exam itself must still be taken on real specimens under the rules of the relevant scheme or the employer's written practice.

Is it useful for FIFO technicians?

That is one of the main reasons it exists. A FIFO technician can practise methods not used on the current swing, run rare-defect jobs on rest days, and arrive at the next mobilisation with recent practice instead of a long gap.

Does it cover LNG and gas plant inspection?

Yes. The Oil & Gas Site environment has 73 jobs covering weld inspection, corrosion mapping, exchanger tube inspection with IRIS, alloy verification with PMI and LRUT screening of pipe runs. The Storage Tank environment covers shell thickness surveys and MFL floor screening.

Is there a phased array or ultrasonic testing simulator in it?

Yes. UT contact, PAUT and TOFD are all included, in the NDT Lab, the Welding Workshop and the Oil & Gas Site, so technicians can practise set-up, scanning and sizing on welds and corrosion.

Does it suit iron ore and mining maintenance work?

Yes for the core methods. MT, PT, UT and VT practice on fabrication joints and components in the Welding Workshop and NDT Lab maps well to crack detection on structures, mobile plant and rotating equipment, though site-specific procedures still apply.

Does it include radiography?

Yes. RT is one of the twelve methods, focused on technique and image interpretation. No radiation is involved, so simulator practice needs no licence under the Radiation Safety Act; real exposures remain subject to the Radiological Council's licensing.

Can an inspection company use it to benchmark new hires or contractors?

Yes. A Level III or team lead can assign the same scenario set to every new starter or contractor and compare results objectively, which helps decide who is ready for which job on a shutdown.

Does Atlantis offer ASNT training in Western Australia?

Yes, ASNT SNT-TC-1A training only, delivered online, live-virtual or onsite at the client's facility, mainly for employers whose clients or projects require SNT-TC-1A personnel. See NDT training in Perth and Atlantis training.

What experience level is it for?

All levels: new trainees on guided lessons, working technicians refreshing less-used methods and rare defects, and Level IIIs building and assigning scenario sets for their crews.

How do we start?

h1: NDT Training and Certification in Alabama
contentHtml:
HomeTrainingConsultingERPPractical NDTContact

NDT Training and Certification in Alabama

Alabama technicians and employers get ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based Level I, II and III training from Atlantis NDT through live online classes, live-virtual cohorts, or onsite delivery at their own shop, shipyard, mill or plant. Every programme is led by an ASNT NDT Level III and maps to the employer's written practice, so the classroom hours count toward certification. Methods covered: UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET, plus Level III exam preparation.

Alabama is not one NDT market but several. The Tennessee Valley around Huntsville and Decatur runs on rocket, missile and defence work. Mobile Bay builds ships and aircraft. Birmingham still pours and rolls steel and casts pipe. Paper mills, chemical plants and two nuclear stations sit between them. Each of those employers asks for slightly different methods, codes and documentation, and this page is built around that map rather than around a generic course list. If you already know what you need, request an Alabama training quote and we will reply within one business day.

Where NDT technicians work in Alabama

Most Alabama NDT work clusters in four zones: aerospace and defence in the Tennessee Valley (Huntsville, Decatur, Athens), shipbuilding and aircraft assembly on Mobile Bay, steel, pipe and foundry work around Birmingham and Tuscaloosa, and power, pulp-and-paper and chemical plants spread across the Black Belt and river corridors. Each zone favours different methods and codes.

Tennessee Valley: Huntsville, Decatur and Athens

Huntsville is home to Redstone Arsenal and NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, and the surrounding area hosts rocket and engine manufacturing, including United Launch Alliance's Decatur rocket factory and Blue Origin's engine production facility in Huntsville. That work means large aluminium and composite structures, propulsion hardware and weldments that are inspected with UT, PAUT, RT, ET and PT, frequently under aerospace or defence procedures in addition to an SNT-TC-1A-style written practice. A short drive west, TVA's Browns Ferry nuclear plant near Athens draws outage crews for ASME Section XI in-service inspection, and Nucor's Decatur steel operations and the river-port chemical plants around Decatur add industrial UT thickness and weld work.

Mobile Bay and the Gulf Coast

Mobile combines shipbuilding (Austal USA builds vessels and modules for the US Navy), aircraft final assembly (Airbus builds A320-family and A220 aircraft at the Brookley Aeroplex), aircraft maintenance, the Alabama State Port Authority's terminals, and the terminals, tank farms and chemical plants that ring Mobile Bay. North of the city, the AM/NS Calvert steel complex and the chemical corridor up the Mobile River add plant inspection work. Methods in demand here are VT and MT on structural and hull welds, UT and PAUT on thick sections, RT on piping and pressure parts, and PT and ET on aircraft structure.

Birmingham, Tuscaloosa and the steel belt

Birmingham's industrial base grew out of iron and steel, and pipe and castings are still made there: ductile-iron and steel pipe makers, structural fabricators, steel service centres and foundries all need MT, UT and VT on product and welds. Tuscaloosa adds a Nucor plate mill and the Mercedes-Benz plant at Vance, whose supplier network brings automotive weld and casting inspection into the mix. Alabama Power, headquartered in Birmingham, runs coal, gas and hydro generation across the state, with boiler tube, header and penstock inspection during planned outages.

Montgomery, the Wiregrass and the river mills

Montgomery has Maxwell Air Force Base and the Hyundai assembly plant with its tiered suppliers. In the southeast corner, Southern Nuclear's Joseph M. Farley plant near Dothan needs outage NDT, and Army aviation in the Wiregrass supports helicopter maintenance. Along the Alabama, Tombigbee and Tennessee rivers, pulp and paper mills run recovery boilers, digesters and pressure vessels that are inspected with UT thickness, MT, PT and VT on every shutdown. Anniston Army Depot in Calhoun County repairs combat vehicles and adds weld and casting inspection demand.

Pipelines and infrastructure

Major refined-product and natural gas transmission lines cross Alabama, including the Colonial and Plantation product systems and interstate gas pipelines, with compressor and pump stations that need API 1104 weld inspection and in-service integrity digs. ALDOT bridges, the Port of Mobile's structures and the Tennessee Valley's dams and locks add civil-structure UT, MT and VT.

SNT-TC-1A certification path in Alabama, step by step

Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, certification is issued by your employer, not by the state of Alabama or by a training school. You complete method training, gain documented on-the-job experience, pass general, specific and practical exams administered under a Level III, pass a vision test, and your employer certifies you to its written practice.

  1. Employer written practice. Your Alabama employer must have a written practice that defines levels, training hours, experience, exams and recertification. Without one there is nothing to certify you against. We can write or update it (see below).
  2. Formal classroom training. You complete the method-specific classroom hours the written practice requires, online, live-virtual or onsite. The training requirements matrix shows the SNT-TC-1A recommended minimums by method and level.
  3. On-the-job experience. You log supervised experience in the method, in your employer's work: hull welds in Mobile, pipe in Birmingham, aerospace parts in Huntsville. The log must be signed and kept.
  4. General exam. A written test on the principles of the method.
  5. Specific exam. A written test on the codes, procedures and equipment your employer actually uses, such as AWS D1.1 for structural steel or ASME Section V for pressure work.
  6. Practical exam. Hands-on inspection of real specimens with known flaws, graded by a Level III against a checklist.
  7. Vision test. Near-vision acuity and colour-contrast checks, repeated annually.
  8. Certification. Your employer issues the certification. It stays with that employer; if you move from a Mobile shipyard to a Birmingham fabricator, the new employer re-certifies you under its own written practice, though your documented training and experience carry forward.
  9. Recertification. At the interval the written practice sets, you show continued satisfactory work or re-examine.

A deeper explanation of how employer-based certification works is on our SNT-TC-1A training and certification page.

Radiography licensing and other Alabama requirements

Alabama is an NRC Agreement State. Industrial radiography with radioactive sources is licensed and inspected by the Alabama Department of Public Health's Office of Radiation Control, under state rules that follow the federal industrial radiography model in 10 CFR Part 34. Radiographers and assistants must meet state training, testing and supervision rules in addition to their SNT-TC-1A method certification.

In practice, that means an RT technician in Alabama needs two separate things. The first is method qualification under the employer's written practice, which is what our RT Level I and II courses support. The second is radiation safety qualification: radiation safety training, a state-recognised radiographer certification for those working with sealed sources, and on-the-job supervision as a radiographer's assistant, all under the employing company's state radioactive materials licence. X-ray machines used for industrial radiography are registered with the same state programme. Confirm the current licensing and personnel requirements directly with the Office of Radiation Control before a crew starts work, especially if your company holds a licence from another state and is working in Alabama under reciprocity.

Boilers and pressure vessels. Alabama enacted its Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act in 2000 and began state inspections in 2004. The programme sits with the state's labour agency, which became the Alabama Department of Workforce in 2025. Installation permits and operating certificates are required for regulated equipment, and inspectors hold National Board commissions. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, which pulls NDT requirements from ASME Section V and the construction code, so mill, plant and utility employers often need technicians who can work to those documents.

Pipelines. Intrastate gas pipeline safety is overseen by the Alabama Public Service Commission's gas pipeline safety programme, working with the federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), which regulates interstate gas and hazardous-liquid lines. Pipeline weld inspection commonly follows API 1104, and operator qualification rules apply to covered tasks.

Codes you will meet in Alabama. As local context only: AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.2 for aluminium, ASME Section V and VIII for pressure vessels, ASME B31.1 and B31.3 for power and process piping, API 1104 for pipelines, ASME Section XI for in-service inspection at Browns Ferry and Farley, Navy and shipbuilding NDT standards on Mobile Bay, and NAS 410 or customer-specific aerospace requirements in Huntsville and Mobile. Some local employers also ask for API inspector or AWS CWI credentials; those are separate schemes that Atlantis does not train for. Our training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based.

Alabama crews can take theory live online from anywhere in the state, join a scheduled live-virtual cohort, or have an Atlantis Level III-led programme delivered onsite at their facility. Practical training and practical exams are done on real specimens, at the employer's site or a partner arrangement agreed in advance.

Online theory works well for Alabama because the state's NDT employers are spread out: a crew in Dothan and a crew in Decatur are five hours apart by road, and neither wants to lose a week to travel. Live online sessions are interactive, with the instructor, not recorded videos alone, and they cover the general and specific knowledge the written exams test. See NDT training online for how the virtual classroom runs.

Onsite delivery suits shipyards, mills and plants that want a group trained on their own parts, procedures and equipment. We schedule around the work that matters to you: vessel delivery dates on Mobile Bay, spring and fall outage seasons at Browns Ferry, Farley and the coal and gas units, annual paper-mill shutdowns, and automotive model-year changeovers. If a turnaround is coming, train the crew before it, not during it.

Hands-on skill still has to be built on hardware. We plan practical sessions with real specimens, your own production parts where appropriate, and the equipment your technicians will actually use. For multi-site employers, our corporate NDT training programme keeps training records consistent across Alabama and out-of-state locations. Ask about onsite training for your Alabama crew.

For Alabama employers: written practice and Level III services

Every Alabama company that certifies NDT personnel under SNT-TC-1A needs a written practice and access to a Level III. Atlantis NDT writes and updates written practices, administers and grades exams, reviews procedures and acts as an outside Level III for companies that do not have one in-house.

This is often the real bottleneck. A new Mobile fabrication shop winning its first Navy subcontract, an automotive supplier in Montgomery adding PT to its quality plan, or a Birmingham pipe maker whose long-serving Level III has retired all face the same problem: they cannot certify anyone until the written practice and Level III oversight are in place. Our written practice development service builds a document that fits your methods, your codes and your customers' audits, and our SNT-TC-1A guidance explains what auditors look for.

Level III support for Alabama employers includes procedure writing and review, technique sheets, exam administration and grading, review of training and experience records, and preparation for customer, prime-contractor or registrar audits. For broader programme work, see NDT consulting in Alabama. Training and Level III services can be combined, so your written practice, your course content and your exams all line up. Book a Level III consultation for your Alabama company.

Practise before your practical exam

Practical NDT is Atlantis NDT's 3D simulator. Trainees practise 12 inspection methods in 5 environments: an NDT lab, a welding workshop, an aircraft hangar, an oil and gas site and a storage tank. It builds familiarity and confidence, but it is practice only and does not replace the practical exam on real specimens.

For Alabama trainees the environments map closely to real work. The welding workshop mirrors the fabrication shops of Birmingham and Mobile. The aircraft hangar matches aircraft assembly and maintenance on Mobile Bay and in the Wiregrass. The oil and gas site and storage tank scenes reflect terminals, tank farms and chemical plants along the Mobile River and Tennessee River. Trainees can rehearse scan patterns, set-ups and inspection sequences between classroom sessions, then go into the practical exam already familiar with what they are expected to do.

Simulator time does not count as on-the-job experience and is not graded as a practical exam. See the Practical NDT simulator overview or the state page, Practical NDT for Alabama, with city pages for Huntsville and Mobile.

Your instructor

Courses are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. As a Level III he oversees course content, written practices, exams and the practical assessment criteria, so the training an Alabama technician receives is tied directly to how that technician will be examined and certified. Questions about method choice, written practices or a particular Alabama code requirement can go straight to him through the contact form.

NDT training in Alabama: frequently asked questions

How do I become NDT certified in Alabama?

Most Alabama NDT technicians are certified by their employer under ASNT SNT-TC-1A. You complete classroom training in a method, log on-the-job experience, pass general, specific and practical exams administered under a Level III, and pass a vision test. Your employer then certifies you to its written practice. Atlantis NDT provides the training, exam support and, if needed, the written practice itself.

Is there NDT training online in Alabama?

Yes. Atlantis NDT runs live online NDT theory classes that Alabama technicians can join from Mobile, Huntsville, Birmingham, Montgomery or anywhere else in the state. Practical training and the practical exam still require real specimens, which we arrange onsite at your employer or through an agreed partner arrangement.

Do I need a license to do radiography in Alabama?

The company needs a radioactive materials licence or machine registration from the Alabama Department of Public Health's Office of Radiation Control, and individual radiographers must meet state radiation safety training, testing and supervision requirements. That is separate from, and in addition to, your SNT-TC-1A RT method certification. Confirm current personnel rules with the state programme before starting field work.

How much does NDT training cost in Alabama?

Pricing is quote on request. It depends on the method, the level, the number of trainees, whether the course is online or onsite, and whether you also need a written practice or exam administration. Send us your crew size and methods and we will return a cohort or onsite quote within one business day.

Which NDT method is most in demand in Alabama?

UT, MT and VT are the everyday methods across Alabama's shipyards, steel mills and fabrication shops. RT and PAUT are in demand for piping, pressure parts and thick welds, and PT and ET are important for aircraft assembly and maintenance in Mobile and aerospace work in Huntsville.

Can you train our crew onsite in Mobile or Huntsville?

Yes. Onsite delivery at your shipyard, plant or shop in Mobile, Huntsville or any other Alabama city is available, scheduled around production and outage dates. Atlantis NDT has no physical training centre in Alabama; onsite means at your facility.

Is SNT-TC-1A recognised by Alabama employers?

Yes. SNT-TC-1A is the most widely used employer-based certification framework in the United States and is referenced by the codes Alabama industries use, including ASME and AWS. Some aerospace and nuclear customers add their own requirements on top, which your written practice should address.

How long does UT Level II training take?

It depends on your employer's written practice, which sets classroom hours and experience for each level. SNT-TC-1A gives recommended minimums, shown on our training requirements matrix. Experience usually takes longer than classroom time, because it has to be logged on real work.

Do I need a college degree for NDT training in Alabama?

No degree is required for Level I or Level II under SNT-TC-1A. Education can reduce the experience a written practice requires, and a technical degree shortens the path to Level III, but high-school graduates start in NDT across Alabama every year.

Does my Alabama certification transfer to another employer?

Not automatically. SNT-TC-1A certification belongs to the employer that issued it. A new employer reviews your documented training and experience and re-certifies you under its own written practice, which may require new specific and practical exams.

Can I prepare for the ASNT Level III exams from Alabama?

Yes. Our ASNT Level III training runs live online and covers the Basic and method exams. Practice material such as the UT Level 2 practice questions also helps Level II candidates.

What do NDT technicians earn in Alabama?

Earnings vary by method, level, sector and travel. For published ranges, see our NDT Level 2 salary and NDT Level 3 salary guides rather than relying on a single figure.

NDT Training and Certification in Alaska

Short answer: an Alaska technician or employer gets ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based NDT training from Atlantis NDT through live online classes, live-virtual sessions, or onsite delivery at the employer's shop in Anchorage, Fairbanks or Kenai, or at a field site where logistics allow. Courses cover Level I, II and III in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET, every programme is led by an ASNT NDT Level III, and certification is issued by your employer under its written practice.

Alaska is unlike any other NDT market in the United States. Most inspection work is tied to the North Slope oil fields, the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System and its marine terminal in Valdez, the Cook Inlet oil and gas basin, a handful of refineries, large hard-rock mines, military air bases and one of the world's busiest air-cargo airports. Technicians often work two-week rotations at remote camps, travel by air between job sites, and inspect equipment in extreme cold where corrosion under insulation and brittle-fracture concerns dominate. Sending a crew to the Lower 48 for a week of classroom training is expensive and disrupts rotations, which is exactly why live online theory plus onsite practicals suits Alaska so well. This page explains how training and certification work for Alaska employers and technicians, what regulators apply in Alaska, and how to get a quote. Request an Alaska NDT training quote and we reply with options within one business day.

Where NDT technicians work in Alaska

Direct answer: Alaska NDT work clusters in six areas: the North Slope oil fields around Prudhoe Bay, the Trans-Alaska Pipeline corridor and the Valdez Marine Terminal, the Kenai Peninsula and Cook Inlet, Anchorage (air cargo, military, port and rail), Fairbanks and the Interior (refining, mining, air bases, power), and Southeast and western Alaska (shipyards, ferries, fisheries and mines).

The North Slope

Prudhoe Bay, Kuparuk, Alpine and the newer fields to the west form the largest oil-producing region in the United States outside Texas and the Gulf. Production pads, flowlines, gathering centres, flow stations, gas handling and compression facilities, seawater treatment and pipelines are all operated in Arctic conditions. Corrosion and erosion programmes on decades-old infrastructure drive a huge amount of UT thickness and corrosion mapping, profile radiography of insulated piping to look for corrosion under insulation, PAUT on welds, and VT, MT and PT on repairs and modules. New developments add fabrication and construction inspection, much of it on modules built elsewhere and installed on the Slope. Work is rotational, typically flown in from Anchorage or Fairbanks to Deadhorse or field airstrips, and employers prefer technicians who hold several methods so a small camp crew can cover many tasks.

The Trans-Alaska Pipeline and Valdez

The Trans-Alaska Pipeline System runs roughly 800 miles from Prudhoe Bay over the Brooks Range and Alaska Range to the Valdez Marine Terminal on Prince William Sound. Pump stations, valves, above-ground and buried sections, and the marine terminal's tanks, piping and berths require ongoing integrity inspection, weld inspection on repairs and modifications, and tank inspection. Valdez also has a refinery. Work here uses UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, along with specialised pipeline integrity techniques run by service providers.

The Kenai Peninsula and Cook Inlet

Cook Inlet has produced oil and gas for decades from offshore platforms and onshore fields, and the Nikiski industrial area on the Kenai Peninsula hosts a refinery, a former LNG export plant, tank farms, docks and pipelines. Platform maintenance, subsea and onshore pipelines, and refinery turnarounds generate UT, PAUT, RT, MT, PT and VT work, often under tidal, weather and marine constraints. Gas supply for Southcentral Alaska depends on this basin, so integrity work runs year-round.

Anchorage: air cargo, military, port and rail

Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport is one of the busiest cargo airports in the world, serving as a refuelling and transfer hub for wide-body freighters between Asia and North America. Line maintenance and MRO for those aircraft, along with regional airlines and bush operators, need ET, PT, UT and VT on airframes, wheels, engines and landing gear. Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson hosts fighter and airlift aircraft and Army units. The Port of Alaska, the Alaska Railroad, power plants, utility gas lines and steel and building construction add structural and weld inspection. Most Alaska inspection companies and contractors are headquartered in Anchorage and dispatch crews statewide.

Fairbanks and the Interior

Fairbanks and North Pole host a refinery, Eielson Air Force Base with its fighter squadrons, Fort Wainwright, coal-fired and combined heat and power plants, and the supply base for the northern end of the pipeline and the Slope. Large gold mines operate north and east of Fairbanks, and a coal mine and power plant operate near Healy. Mine maintenance needs MT, UT and PT on shafts, gears, welds and mill components; power plants need boiler-tube UT, RT and VT; Air Force maintenance needs ET and PT.

Southeast and western Alaska

Ketchikan has a shipyard that builds and repairs vessels, including ferries, and Southeast communities support fishing fleets, seafood processing plants, docks and hydroelectric projects. Underground silver and gold mines near Juneau and a large zinc and lead mine in northwest Alaska, with its own port, add heavy equipment and structural inspection. Ship and barge work uses UT thickness gauging, VT, MT and RT to classification society and owner requirements.

Direct answer: Atlantis NDT offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based Level I and Level II courses in eight methods, plus Level III exam preparation. Alaska employers value multi-method technicians more than almost anywhere else, because remote camps and rotations limit how many people can be on site. A North Slope inspection contractor may want new hires certified in UT and VT Level I first, then RT and PAUT as they gain rotations. An Anchorage MRO shop may need ET and PT Level II. A mine may want its own maintenance staff in MT and UT. We plan those pathways around your written practice so classroom hours, exams and on-the-job experience line up across rotations. Level III candidates can see the ASNT Level III training and exam preparation page.

Direct answer: Atlantis NDT serves all of Alaska through online and onsite delivery. Anchorage has a dedicated training page, and Practical NDT simulator pages cover Anchorage, the Kenai refining area and the North Slope. Anchorage. Nearly every Alaska inspection contractor, engineering firm and oilfield service company runs its operations from Anchorage, so it is the natural place for onsite classroom and practical sessions before crews rotate north. Air-cargo MRO and the military base add steady aviation inspection. See the Anchorage NDT training page.

Kenai and Nikiski. Refinery turnarounds, platform maintenance and Cook Inlet pipeline integrity create demand for UT, PAUT, RT and VT technicians who can work in marine conditions. See the Kenai refining practice page.

Prudhoe Bay and Deadhorse. The Slope is the heart of Alaska NDT. Corrosion programmes, CUI radiography and construction of new facilities keep multi-method technicians in constant demand. Training is usually delivered online during off-rotation weeks, with practicals at the employer's Anchorage or Fairbanks shop. See the North Slope practice page.

Fairbanks and North Pole. The Interior combines refinery, power plant, mining and Air Force work. Employers often need technicians who can switch between boiler-tube inspection, mine equipment and aircraft components.

Juneau and Ketchikan. Shipyard, ferry, dock, hydro and mining work make UT thickness gauging, MT and VT the core methods in Southeast Alaska.

SNT-TC-1A certification path in Alaska, step by step

Direct answer: under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, certification in Alaska is employer-based. Your employer's written practice sets the rules; you complete classroom training and on-the-job experience, pass general, specific and practical exams administered under a Level III, pass a vision test, and your employer certifies you. Alaska has no separate state NDT licence; radiography with sources is regulated by the NRC.

  1. Your employer adopts a written practice. Based on SNT-TC-1A, it sets training hours, experience hours, exam content and pass marks, vision requirements and recertification intervals for each method and level. If your company has none, we write it with you; see written practice development.
  2. Complete formal classroom training. Take Level I and then Level II training in your method, live online or onsite. Hours follow your written practice; the training requirements matrix shows SNT-TC-1A recommended hours per method and level.
  3. Build documented on-the-job experience in the method, logged and verified by your employer. On rotational work, keep a log for each hitch so hours are not lost.
  4. Pass the general exam on the principles of the method.
  5. Pass the specific exam on the procedures, codes and equipment you actually use, for example ASME Section V, API 1104 or your operator's corrosion-monitoring procedures.
  6. Pass the practical exam on real specimens with real flaws, graded by a Level III against a checklist.
  7. Pass the vision exam for near-vision acuity and colour contrast, repeated at the interval in your written practice.
  8. Get certified by your employer. Certification is tied to that employer and based on documented training, experience and exams.
  9. Maintain and recertify at the interval in your written practice, and add methods or levels as your career develops.

For more detail on the employer-based system, read SNT-TC-1A training and certification.

Radiography licensing and other Alaska requirements

Direct answer: Alaska is not an NRC Agreement State. Industrial radiography with radioactive sources in Alaska is licensed and inspected directly by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission through its Region IV office, under 10 CFR Part 34. The state's Radiological Health Program registers and inspects X-ray equipment. PHMSA directly regulates both interstate and intrastate pipelines in Alaska, and boilers and pressure vessels fall under the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development.

Industrial radiography

Because Alaska has not signed an Agreement with the NRC, a company using iridium-192, selenium-75 or other sealed sources for gamma radiography in Alaska needs an NRC licence or, if licensed by an Agreement State, must file for reciprocity with the NRC before working in Alaska. Radiographers must meet the NRC's training, examination and certification requirements in 10 CFR Part 34, and radiographer's assistants must work under the supervision rules set there. X-ray machines used for industrial radiography are a state matter: Alaska's Radiological Health Program, within the state public health laboratories, registers X-ray producing devices and the vendors that service them. RT method training under SNT-TC-1A, which is what Atlantis provides, covers technique, exposure, film and digital imaging and interpretation, including profile radiography; it sits alongside, not instead of, the radiation safety training and radiographer certification that NRC rules require. Always confirm current requirements with the NRC and the state program before you deploy a crew.

Pipelines

Alaska is one of only two states that have not taken on jurisdiction over intrastate pipeline safety, so PHMSA's Office of Pipeline Safety inspects and enforces federal rules for interstate and intrastate gas and hazardous liquid pipelines in the state, with staff based in Anchorage. Right-of-way leases on state land, well integrity and oil spill prevention involve other state agencies, including the Department of Natural Resources, the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission and the Department of Environmental Conservation. Pipeline welding inspection usually follows API 1104, with ASME B31.4 for liquids and B31.8 for gas.

Boilers and pressure vessels

The Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development's Mechanical Inspection section inspects boilers and pressure vessels. Alaska follows the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and National Board inspection practice, so repairs and alterations need NDT performed to ASME Section V by personnel certified under the repair organisation's quality programme.

Codes Alaska employers commonly use

  • ASME Section V, Section VIII and B31.3 on North Slope facilities, refineries and the marine terminal
  • API 1104, ASME B31.4 and B31.8 on flowlines, TAPS and Cook Inlet pipelines
  • API 650 and API 653 as context for tank construction and inspection at terminals and tank farms (Atlantis does not train API 653 inspectors; we train the NDT methods those inspections use)
  • AWS D1.1 for structural steel and modules, AWS D1.5 for bridges
  • Classification society and owner rules for ships, ferries and barges

Some Alaska employers also ask for API inspector or CWI credentials for specific roles. Those are separate schemes that Atlantis does not train; our programmes cover ASNT SNT-TC-1A method certification.

Online, live-virtual and onsite training across Alaska

Direct answer: Atlantis NDT has no training centre in Alaska. Theory is delivered through live online or live-virtual classes, and practical training and exams are delivered onsite at your facility, usually your Anchorage, Fairbanks or Kenai shop, using your equipment and specimens under ASNT Level III oversight. Technicians can study during off-rotation weeks without flying south.

Rotations shape everything about Alaska training. A North Slope technician on a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off schedule cannot attend a fixed five-day class in another state without losing a hitch. Online NDT training lets that technician complete the classroom portion of Level I and Level II from home during off weeks, in live sessions with a Level III instructor, asking questions in real time. Practical hours and the practical exam then happen with the employer.

For employers training a group, onsite delivery at the company shop or yard is usually most efficient. We schedule classroom and practical sessions to match your crew change, use your instruments, reference standards and specimens, and build the course around the procedures your crews actually follow, whether that is corrosion monitoring, profile radiography of insulated piping, tank inspection or aircraft ET. Field-site delivery on the Slope or at remote mines depends on the operator's access, safety orientation and camp capacity, and we plan it with you case by case.

Alaska's calendar is driven by the seasons. Summer is short and packed with construction, maintenance and turnaround work; winter brings ice-road and exploration seasons on the Slope and fewer outdoor projects elsewhere. Many employers prefer to run training in the shoulder seasons or in winter for crews whose summer is fully booked. Larger programmes run through corporate NDT training. Ask about onsite training for your Alaska crew.

For Alaska employers: written practice and Level III services

Direct answer: SNT-TC-1A makes the employer responsible for certification, so every Alaska NDT employer needs a written practice and access to a Level III. Atlantis NDT writes and updates written practices, reviews procedures, administers exams, and provides Level III services for companies without a Level III on staff, delivered remotely and onsite.

Many Alaska NDT employers are small or rely on a single Level III who is often in the field. A local inspection company in Anchorage, a mine maintenance department in the Interior, an MRO shop at the cargo airport or a shipyard in Southeast Alaska needs certified technicians but may not have a Level III available when exams or procedure approvals are due. That gap is where audit findings appear: missing hour logs from rotations, practical exams without graded checklists, out-of-date vision tests, or a written practice that does not match how work is actually done on the Slope.

  • Written practice development and revision aligned with the current edition of SNT-TC-1A and your operators' requirements. See written practice development.
  • Exam administration: general, specific and practical exams prepared and graded under Level III oversight, with records your auditors can follow.
  • Procedure review for UT, PAUT, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET procedures against ASME, API, AWS and operator requirements.
  • Audit preparation for operator contractor audits, National Board or ASME reviews and ISO 9001 surveillance.
  • Corporate programmes for multi-site companies through corporate NDT training.

For broader Level III consulting, see our NDT consulting services and our guide to SNT-TC-1A certification. Book a Level III consultation for your Alaska company.

Practise before your practical exam

Direct answer: Atlantis NDT's Practical NDT simulator lets Alaska trainees practise 12 NDT methods in five 3D environments before their practical exam, including from camp or home during off-rotation weeks. It builds familiarity with technique, scan patterns and indications, but it is practice only and does not replace the practical exam on real specimens.

The Practical NDT simulator includes an NDT lab, a welding workshop, an aircraft hangar, an oil and gas site and a storage tank. Those environments match Alaska closely: the oil and gas site for North Slope and Cook Inlet facilities, the storage tank for the Valdez terminal and tank farms, the aircraft hangar for Anchorage air cargo and the air bases, and the welding workshop for modules, shipyards and mine maintenance. Trainees can repeat scans and explore indication types before handling real equipment in front of an examiner.

There is a statewide Practical NDT in Alaska page, plus the Anchorage, Kenai and North Slope pages linked above. For written-exam practice, try the UT Level 2 practice questions.

Your instructor

Direct answer: Alaska programmes are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT.

Anoop leads course design, delivers Level III-led instruction, and oversees the exams and records that make certification defensible under SNT-TC-1A. His focus is practical: connecting method theory to the procedures, codes and equipment your Alaska crew actually inspects, and helping employers build written practices that hold up in operator audits. Ask about his availability when you contact us about Alaska training.

NDT training in Alaska: frequently asked questions

How do I become NDT certified in Alaska?

Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, your employer certifies you. Complete Level I and Level II classroom training in a method, log on-the-job experience, pass general, specific and practical exams administered under a Level III, and pass a vision test. Your employer then issues certification under its written practice. If you are not yet employed, online classroom training prepares you, and certification follows once an employer documents your experience.

Is there NDT training online in Alaska?

Yes. Atlantis NDT runs live online and live-virtual Level I and Level II classes that Alaska technicians can join from Anchorage, Fairbanks, Kenai, Juneau or a remote community, including during off-rotation weeks. Practical training and practical exams are completed with your employer because they need real equipment and specimens.

Do I need a license to do radiography in Alaska?

Alaska is not an Agreement State, so industrial radiography with radioactive sources is licensed by the NRC, not the state. The company holds the NRC licence or files reciprocity, and individual radiographers must meet the training, exam and certification requirements in 10 CFR Part 34. X-ray machines are registered with Alaska's Radiological Health Program. Confirm current requirements before starting work.

How much does NDT training cost in Alaska?

Cost is quoted on request. It depends on the method and level, the number of trainees, whether sessions are live online or onsite, travel logistics for onsite delivery, and whether you need exam administration or written practice support. Send your requirements and we return a cohort or onsite quote within one business day.

Which NDT method is most in demand in Alaska?

UT is the backbone of North Slope and pipeline corrosion programmes, and RT, especially profile radiography for corrosion under insulation, is in steady demand. PAUT is growing for corrosion mapping and welds. ET and PT matter for air-cargo and military aviation, and MT and UT for mines and shipyards.

Can you train our crew onsite in Anchorage, Fairbanks or Kenai?

Yes. We deliver classroom and practical sessions at your shop or facility, using your equipment and specimens, and schedule around crew changes and the summer work season. Delivery at remote field sites is planned case by case with the operator.

Can I study for NDT certification while working North Slope rotations?

Yes. Live online classes can be scheduled during your off weeks, the simulator can be used from home, and your employer logs your experience hours during each hitch. Your practical exam is then arranged at your employer's shop.

Is SNT-TC-1A recognised by Alaska employers?

Yes. SNT-TC-1A is the most widely used basis for employer certification in US industry, including oil and gas operators, pipeline companies, refineries, fabrication and many aerospace maintenance organisations. Operator-specific requirements can be added to your written practice.

How long does UT Level II training take?

It depends on your employer's written practice, which sets classroom and experience hours. SNT-TC-1A gives recommended minimums; see the training requirements matrix. Experience hours usually take much longer than the classroom portion.

Can I prepare for ASNT Level III in Alaska?

Yes. Level III candidates normally have substantial Level II experience and prepare for the ASNT Level III basic and method exams. See ASNT Level III training for exam preparation options.

Does Atlantis have a training centre in Alaska?

No. We deliver training live online and onsite at your facility. There is no Atlantis classroom building in Anchorage or elsewhere in Alaska.

What do NDT technicians earn in Alaska?

Pay varies with method, level, rotation and remoteness. For published ranges by level, read our NDT salary guide.

Start NDT training in Alaska

Whether you are one technician between hitches, an Anchorage inspection contractor, a Kenai refinery maintenance team or a mine in the Interior, Atlantis NDT can build an ASNT SNT-TC-1A programme that fits your work, your rotations and your written practice. Training is quoted on request, and programmes are affordable, accessible and fully customizable. Request your Alaska training quote, explore all NDT training courses, or talk to us about certifying your Alaska crew.

NDT Training and Certification in Alberta

Short answer: Alberta technicians and employers can take ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based NDT training from Atlantis NDT in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET at Level I and II, plus Level III exam preparation. You can join live online classes or a live-virtual cohort, or we can teach onsite at your shop, plant or camp. Every course is led by an ASNT NDT Level III. Your employer certifies you under its written practice.

Before you book anything in Alberta, you need to know one thing. Canada's national NDT personnel certification scheme is CAN/CGSB-48.9712, the Canadian adoption of ISO 9712. It is a third-party scheme: an accredited certification body, not your employer, issues the certificate. Atlantis NDT does not train toward CAN/CGSB-48.9712, and we do not claim any CGSB recognition. What we teach is the American employer-based system, SNT-TC-1A. In Alberta that suits a particular group of people: contractors and fabricators building to US codes for US clients, US-owned operators running their own programmes, pipeline and pressure-equipment suppliers that ship south, inspection companies whose crews rotate between Alberta and US sites, and technicians who plan to work in the US. This page explains when SNT-TC-1A is the right fit in Alberta and when it is not. It then maps where the work is, from Wood Buffalo to Lethbridge, and shows how to get a quote for one seat or a whole crew. Request an Alberta NDT training quote and we will come back with options within one business day.

SNT-TC-1A or CAN/CGSB-48.9712: which one do Alberta employers ask for?

Direct answer: most Alberta code work and most Alberta owners ask for CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (ISO 9712) certification. ABSA, the provincial pressure equipment safety authority, also accepts SNT-TC-1A in some in-service situations. SNT-TC-1A training makes sense for US-code and US-client work, for owner-user programmes that accept it, and for technicians heading south. It does not replace CGSB certification where CGSB is required.

Alberta is one of the few places in Canada where both schemes appear in the same regulatory document, so it is worth being precise. ABSA's AB-506 Inspection & Servicing Requirements for In-Service Pressure Equipment (Edition 4, Revision 0, issued 2025-10-21) says that examiners doing ultrasonic shear-wave examinations must hold Level II CGSB certification for the method. It also permits SNT-TC-1A Level II certification, to the edition listed in the current ASME Section VIII Division 1, provided the owner accepts it. For ultrasonic thickness, magnetic particle and penetrant examinations of in-service pressure equipment, examiners employed by NDE contractors must hold Level I or II CGSB or SNT certification. Examiners employed directly by an owner-user or a certified Integrity Assessment Organization can work under that employer's integrity programme without CGSB or SNT certification, as long as their training, experience and competence are documented. Always read the current edition of AB-506 and your owner's specification yourself. The summary here is context, not legal advice. Our ABSA compliance guide covers more of the inspection-company side.

Your situation in AlbertaScheme usually asked forDoes Atlantis SNT-TC-1A training fit?
Construction NDE on Alberta-registered pressure equipment and CSA-code structural steelCAN/CGSB-48.9712, usually through CSA W178.1-certified inspection organisationsNo. You need CGSB certification. Our training can add background knowledge but does not lead to a CGSB certificate
In-service UT thickness, MT or PT for an owner that accepts SNT certification under AB-506CGSB or SNT Level I/IIYes, if the owner's specification accepts SNT-TC-1A
Fabricating ASME-stamped equipment or API 1104 pipe spools for US clientsSNT-TC-1A per ASME Section V / the client specificationYes. This is the core use case
US-owned operator or contractor running one written practice across Canadian and US sitesSNT-TC-1A (employer written practice), sometimes alongside CGSBYes. Training, written practice and Level III support
Technician planning to work on US turnarounds, pipelines or aerospaceSNT-TC-1A or CP-189 via the US employerYes. The training record travels with you
Nuclear, federal or CSA-only work in CanadaCAN/CGSB-48.9712No

A note on the certification side of CGSB. The Canadian General Standards Board, which publishes the CAN/CGSB-48.9712 standard, ceased operations on 1 April 2026. Published guidance says the standard stays valid for its current cycle and that existing certifications are not affected. Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body has said its certification services continue without interruption, and the CWB Group remains accredited to certify NDT personnel to the same standard. Arrangements are changing, so confirm the current certification body before you plan a CGSB route. Many Alberta technicians hold both a CGSB certificate and an SNT-TC-1A certification from an employer. If that is your plan, the two programmes can run side by side.

Where NDT technicians work in Alberta

Direct answer: Alberta NDT work centres on the Athabasca oil sands around Fort McMurray, the Industrial Heartland refineries and petrochemical plants north-east of Edmonton, Calgary's pipeline and head-office market, the Joffre petrochemical complex near Red Deer, the Montney and Peace gas fields around Grande Prairie, and the fertiliser, agri-processing and manufacturing base of Medicine Hat and Lethbridge.

Wood Buffalo and the Athabasca oil sands

The Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo, with Fort McMurray at its centre, is the densest concentration of pressure equipment, piping and rotating equipment in the province. Mining operations such as Suncor's Base Plant and Fort Hills, Syncrude's Mildred Lake and Aurora sites, Canadian Natural's Horizon and Albian operations and Imperial's Kearl mine run upgraders, extraction plants, hydrotransport lines and tailings systems that wear quickly. In-situ SAGD projects to the south, such as the Christina Lake and Foster Creek areas, add steam generators, well pads and long runs of hot piping. Turnarounds bring in large crews for UT thickness surveys, PAUT corrosion mapping, TOFD on heavy-wall vessels, RT of repair welds, and MT and PT on rotating equipment and structural repairs. Crews usually fly in on rotation and live in camp, which suits short, intensive onsite training blocks. See the Fort McMurray NDT training page for more local detail.

Edmonton and Alberta's Industrial Heartland

The Industrial Heartland spans Strathcona County, Fort Saskatchewan, Sturgeon County and Lamont County. It holds the Scotford upgrader and refinery complex, the Sturgeon Refinery, the Dow Fort Saskatchewan site and a long list of chemical, fertiliser and gas-processing plants. Inside Edmonton's own boundary and next door in Strathcona County sit two large refineries, Suncor's Edmonton refinery and Imperial's Strathcona refinery. The Trans Mountain pipeline starts at its Edmonton terminal. This is where Alberta's fabrication shops, module yards, inspection companies and maintenance contractors cluster. Their work runs from ASME and CSA B51 pressure vessels to process piping, storage tanks and modules shipped across North America. Many Edmonton shops build to US codes for US projects, and that is where SNT-TC-1A training matters most. More detail: NDT training in Edmonton.

Calgary and the pipeline corridor

Calgary is the business and engineering centre of Canada's energy sector. Major pipeline operators, producers and engineering firms have their head offices here, and integrity engineering, NDT procedure work and Level III oversight are often run from the city. In the field, the work is pipeline construction and integrity digs across southern Alberta: API 1104 and CSA Z662 girth-weld radiography and AUT, UT wall-thickness and crack sizing at dig sites, and MT on fittings and repairs. Gas plants, compressor stations, fabrication shops and the CPKC rail network add steady MT, PT and UT work. Calgary's international airport supports airline and helicopter maintenance, where ET and PT are routine. See NDT training in Calgary.

Central Alberta: Red Deer and Joffre

Red Deer sits halfway between the two big cities on the Highway 2 corridor and serves both. The NOVA Chemicals Joffre complex to the east is one of the largest petrochemical sites in Canada, with cracking furnaces, high-temperature piping and pressure vessels that need regular UT, PAUT, RT and ET. Oilfield service companies, fabrication shops and equipment manufacturers in Red Deer, Blackfalds and Sylvan Lake add a steady base of MT, PT and UT on welded structures, trailers and pressure equipment.

Grande Prairie and the Peace Region

North-western Alberta sits on the Montney and Duvernay plays. Gas processing plants, liquids-rich gathering systems, compressor stations and the shops that build and maintain them create pipeline radiography, UT and VT work. Pulp and forestry operations add boiler and pressure-vessel inspection during their maintenance shutdowns. Work here is seasonal: winter access drives pipeline construction, and summer drives plant turnarounds.

Southern Alberta: Medicine Hat, Lethbridge and the farm economy

Medicine Hat has a long history in gas and holds large nitrogen fertiliser and methanol plants. That means heat exchangers, reformers and pressure piping on regular inspection cycles. Lethbridge and the surrounding counties have agri-food processing, irrigation infrastructure, grain handling and equipment manufacturing, where MT, PT and UT are applied to welded structures, shafts and pressure equipment. Smaller shops here often need only one or two certified Level II technicians, so live online training and short onsite practical blocks make more sense than sending people away for weeks.

Rail, bridges and public infrastructure

Two Class I railways cross the province, with major yards in Edmonton and Calgary. Wheel, axle, coupler and weld inspection relies on UT and MT. Alberta's provincial and municipal bridge inventory, including steel river crossings in both big cities, is fabricated and repaired to CSA S6 and CSA W59 welding requirements. Those jobs typically call for CGSB-certified UT and RT personnel through CWB-certified companies, so check the contract before you assume SNT-TC-1A is enough.

ASNT Level I, II and III courses for Alberta employers

Direct answer: Atlantis NDT offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based Level I and Level II courses in eight methods, plus Level III exam preparation. The table shows each method, the levels available, how Alberta employers use it and what a trainee needs first. Your employer's written practice sets the exact classroom and experience hours.

MethodLevelsWhat Alberta employers use it forPrerequisite
Ultrasonic Testing (UT)I, II, III prepOil sands and refinery thickness surveys, pipeline dig-site wall loss, weld inspection on US-code spools and vesselsLevel I: employer requirements only. Level II: Level I training plus documented experience
Phased Array UT (PAUT)II, III prepCorrosion mapping in upgraders and refineries, encoded weld scans on modules and piping for US projectsUT Level II recommended first
Time of Flight Diffraction (TOFD)II, III prepHeavy-wall reactors, separators and drums in the Heartland and at JoffreUT Level II recommended
Radiographic Testing (RT)I, II, III prepPipeline girth welds, piping repair welds, fabrication shop RT for ASME workGamma work requires CNSC exposure device operator certification or direct supervision by a certified EDO; see the licensing section
